en: The *Hṛdayaṅgamā*, a commentary on the *Kāvyādarśa*; First Chapter.

Having prostrated before the Lord of Kamalā (Viṣṇu), who bestows the fruits desired by his devotees, I shall expand this exposition of the *Kāvyādarśa* for the delight of the virtuous. There is a tradition that the illustrious poet Mahāmahopādhyāya Daṇḍin himself composed this work and taught it to a certain prince.

At the beginning of the work, desiring the completion of the undertaking he has commenced without obstacles, he performs an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) in the form of recollecting the Goddess of Speech (*Vāgdevatā*) as the presiding deity of poetry and the book; thus he says: "O four-faced one... and so forth.

The faces of the four-faced Brahmā are themselves groves of lotuses (*ambhojavana*), clusters of *padma* flowers; in them, she is a female swan (*haṃsabadhū*), having the very form of a swan. (By this qualifying term, it is implied: "Just as Sarasvatī, who dwells in the mouths of the four-faced one and consists of the Vedas, is perfectly pure, may such a Sarasvatī enter my mind, and not one who dwells in the mouths of the low-born. For this very reason, he states another qualification: "all-white" (*sarvaśuklā*).

"Entirely white" (*sarvaśuklā*) means in every respect and in every way; that is to say, she is white by her very nature and by her essence. She is "white" because she is stainless due to being free from defects—that is, devoid of the defects that detract from poetry—and because she is white in color in all her limbs. Sarasvatī is the goddess presiding over speech; that is to say, she is a form of the Blessed Viṣṇu. (By this, her nature as poetry is indicated; and the fact that poetry is a form of Viṣṇu is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* as follows: "And those conversations which are poetic...")

"Some [are] songs and all the [Vedic] branches; these are portions of the high-souled Viṣṇu, who bears sound as his form. Thus, may she—who eternally and constantly sports and plays in my mind (the *mānasa*), and in the lake named after it—dwell. The essential meaning is: "May that goddess of speech, who is entirely pure and who, like a female swan in the lotus groves of the Mānasa lake, constantly sports in the lotus-like faces of Brahmā in the form of the Vedas (*śruti*), dwell forever in my heart."

Regarding the word "nityam," in the reading "dīrgham," the meaning is "for a long time. (Here, the superimposition of a lotus-forest upon the face is the cause for the superimposition of a female swan upon Sarasvatī; therefore, this is the figure of speech known as *paramparita-rūpaka*). Now, recollecting the traditional rule: "A listener proceeds to hear that which has a known subject matter and a known relationship [between the subject and the purpose]; therefore, at the beginning of a work, the relationship must be stated along with its purpose," he declares his promise while indicating the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of this treatise, beginning with the words "pūrvaśāstrāṇi."

Having condensed the treatises—the poetic works—of the ancient poets such as Bharata and others, having extracted their essence from them, and having examined and scrutinized the topics employed in great poems (*mahākāvya*) and other genres (by this it is indicated: "Even setting aside ancient treatises that contradict the usage of great poets, we compose this work in accordance with the usage and the preceding treatises that follow such usage").

By us, according to our capacity, according to our strength—that is, according to our knowledge—the *lakṣaṇa* (definition) of poetry, its essential nature, is being composed. By the etymological derivation that "that by which something is characterized (*lakṣyate*) or known is a *lakṣaṇa*," it refers to a specific property that distinguishes [poetry] from others; this is determined by the sentence to be stated later: "A series of words distinguished by a desired meaning. (By this, it is shown that poetry itself is the subject matter of the treatise; the purpose will be stated hereafter. The relationship [between the subject and the purpose] should be understood accordingly through one's own intellect. || 2 ||

Now, in order to state the purpose of the treatise, he explains the utility of speech in worldly conduct through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), beginning with the words "In this world" (*iha*) and so forth. "In this world" means in *saṃsāra*; "by the learned" (*śiṣṭaiḥ*) refers to the steadfast ones such as Maheśvara and others. As it is said in the *Mahābhārata*: "A sage is not fickle with his hands or feet, nor fickle with his eyes; nor is he fickle with his speech or limbs—such is the characteristic of the learned."

Thus, through the grace—that is to say, by the compassion and assistance—of these very words which have been instructed, established, and perfected through the analysis of roots, suffixes, and so forth; which are current, vernacular, and regional; the conduct—that is, the worldly transaction—of the three kinds of people distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior, proceeds and functions in every way and in all manners. Among them, the superior speak using only the refined (saṃskṛta) language, while the middling use a correct speech that is slightly inferior to it.
"Inferior" means by means of a low dialect; the implied meaning is that linguistic usage is likewise determined by distinctions of region and caste.

Regarding the word "this": if sound (*śabda*) is its name—that is, it is called "sound"—it means it consists of speech (*vāṅmaya*). It is "light" (*jyotis*), meaning brilliance; this attribution of such a nature to speech is made by virtue of its inherent quality of being illuminating. (By this, the identity of sound with Brahman is also indicated.)

Furthermore, there are four divisions of the Śabdabrahman: the subtle (sūkṣmā), the visionary (paśyantī), the intermediate (madhyamā), and the articulated (vaikharī). Among these, the state of non-modification is the subtle; for that indeed abides within the interval between the prāṇa and apāna of all beings, and is perfectly attained through the yoga of action—which consists of the thorough cultivation of correct application—and through the yoga of knowledge, such as reflection and so forth, wherein appearance and disappearance have ceased.

The first transformation of that Brahman, due to the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), is *paśyantī*. For she is without sequence (*akrama*) and self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*) because of the non-differentiation of phonemes (*varṇa*). She is called *paśyantī* because she perceives her own prior and subsequent states. Following that, the third transformation—arising from the material cause (*upādāna*) of further ignorance—is *madhyamā*. She possesses sequence in the form of internal volition (*saṅkalpa*) and is devoid of the manifestation of phonemes perceivable by the ear. She is called *madhyamā* because she stands between the two transformations.

Subsequently, when ignorance has extended far, the fourth transformation is *vaikharī*, which consists of a collection of articulated phonemes (*varṇa*)—such as indistinct forms and faltering sounds—manifested through the effort of the articulatory places and organs and perceived by the ear, like the sounds of a lute or a drum. The first three [levels of speech] are eternal and beyond the senses; the last is of the nature of worldly transaction. As it has been said: "When the air is expanded in the articulatory places and assumes the form of phonemes, that is *vaikharī* speech, dependent upon the activity of the breath of speakers."

"Having transcended the function of the vital breath (prāṇa), speech proceeds as the Madhyamā; but Paśyantī is undivided, with its sequence entirely withdrawn, consisting solely of the light of its own nature within, subtle and imperishable. Thus it is said. The Śruti also declares: "Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech, humans speak."

Consequently, when that light in the form of Śabdabrahman does not shine—that is, does not manifest—pervading the world throughout the cycle of saṃsāra, then this entire universe, the triad of worlds consisting of heaven, earth, and the netherworld (rasātala), would become "andhatamas"—meaning pervaded by dense darkness (as Amara states: "in dense darkness, it is called andhatamas"). Alternatively, it would become "tamas," consisting of the darkness of delusion, and thus "blind," as if devoid of sight, being empty of knowledge.

The sense is that in the absence of speech, the world would be as if shrouded in darkness, just as it would be in the absence of the rising sun, because through speech alone all beings attain knowledge. (By this, its purpose is stated to be precisely the form of linguistic communication. Furthermore, the relationship between the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*)—such as that of the signified and the signifier—should be understood accordingly. And thus, the necessity of stating these at the beginning of the work has been established. || 4 ||

Having previously demonstrated the worthiness of words as a means of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), he now shows the worthiness of those very same words when they have attained the nature of poetry (*kāvyasvarūpa*) through the presence of qualities (*guṇa*), ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), and so forth, beginning with the words "The first king."

The reflection of the glory—the form of fame—of the ancient kings, such as Manu, Ikṣvāku, and others, having reached a mirror consisting of speech, composed by groups of poets in the form of poetic works, does not perish nor vanish even in the absence—that is, the non-existence—of those ancient kings; "see this for yourself," he thus addresses the prince.

(In a mirror, the reflection of an object falls only for those things that are present nearby; here, however, in the mirror of the literary form, even those not present nearby [are reflected]. This is the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction), characterized by the excellence of the subject of comparison. Furthermore, one should understand that there are other purposes, such as the glorification of the fame of those whose past deeds are described, as well as the attainment of fame for the composer of the poem. As it was stated by the author of the *Prakāśa*: "Poetry leads to fame, to wealth, to knowledge of worldly conduct, to the destruction of inauspiciousness, to immediate supreme bliss, and, by being like a beloved woman, to instruction. || 5 ||

Having stated the worthiness of poetry in general, he says "Gauḥ" (the Cow), praising it by declaring that one should strive for its possession of qualities (*guṇas*), ornaments (*alaṅkāras*), and so forth, as well as its freedom from defects (*doṣas*). "Gauḥ" refers to speech (*vāk*), properly employed—that is, well-composed through the presence of qualities, ornaments, and the like, and the absence of defects. [The word *go* has these meanings: heaven, water, cattle, speech, thunderbolt, direction, eye, sun, earth, and water.

According to the perspective of the *lakṣya* (the indicated meaning), the word *go* refers to both female and male; thus says Amarasimha. By the wise—that is, by the learned and sensitive-minded—it is remembered (or considered) that *go* is a cow, a "milk-cow of desire," meaning one that fulfills whatever is wished for. This is because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "A single word, well-employed and correctly understood, becomes a cow of plenty in this world and in heaven. And it has also been stated by Vāmana: "Good poetry has both visible and invisible purposes, as it is the cause of pleasure and fame."

And in the commentary on the aforementioned Sūtra: "Poetry has a visible purpose because it is a cause of delight; it has an invisible purpose because it is a cause of fame. Regarding this, there are these verses: The wise know that the foundation of a poetic composition is its style (*saraṇam*), whereas the path of infamy is the mockery of bad poetry. The learned say that fame yields the fruit of heaven as long as the world endures, while infamy is the messenger to the depths of the hell of darkness. Therefore, in order to acquire fame and to ward off infamy..."

"The meaning of the treatises on the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) and meters (*vṛtta*) of poetry should be mastered by the best of poets. Furthermore: "The cultivation of excellent poetry produces proficiency in virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*), as well as in the arts; it brings forth fame and joy."

Thus, however, that very same cow, when "badly employed"—meaning employed or composed with defects and devoid of poetic qualities (*guṇas*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāras*)—proclaims, or indicates, the "bull-ness," that is, the ox-like nature, which implies the ignorance of the *prayoktṛ*, the poet (by this it is understood that a sentence containing a defect, even if it possesses aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), does not lose its status as poetry, but rather its censurability is perceived). 6.

Regarding the word "tat" (that): for that reason, because the motivator [the author] has manifested the nature of poetry, even a slight defect—residing in a single word or merely a portion of a word—is a fault (*doṣaḥ*; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the action itself). It must not be overlooked or tolerated by any means whatsoever. The meaning is that since a fault invariably detracts from poetry, it must be abandoned. If one objects: "But when there is the presence of excellences (*guṇas*), ornaments (*alaṅkāras*), and so forth, what harm is done by a general fault?"—to this he replies with the word "syāt" (it might be).

The body (*vapuḥ*), though naturally beautiful or even handsome (*sudarśana*) due to its possession of [auspicious] qualities and so forth, may become unfortunate (*durbhaga*) or loathsome (*ghṛṇita*) because of a single (*ekena*) small (*kṣudreṇa*) white leprosy (*śvitra*) located on one limb. (By this it follows that a defect (*doṣa*) detracts from poetry, but does not destroy its status as poetry. And it has been said elsewhere: "The status of poetry is considered to exist even in defective works where there is a clear presence of rasa and the like, just as the nature of a gem persists even when pierced by an insect.")

Just as even a beautiful body becomes censurable due to a single instance of vitiligo (śvitraroga), so too does even a minor collection of defects occurring in a word or its part corrupt a poem; because this conveys the relationship between the original object and its reflection, there is the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration) here. As it is stated in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*: "The *dṛṣṭānta*, however, is the reflection of an object possessing common properties."

By this it is shown that the lack of excellence in poetry arises not only from defects such as those of words or their components, but also from the poet’s weakness of genius and deficiency of lineage. As stated in the *Kavigajāṅkuśa*: "The wise should reject a verse composed by a Śūdra like the milk of a dog; however, a poem should be accepted just as one accepts the milk of cows. And as Bhāmaha has said: "Because of its greatness, you are praised here; [for] the riches of poetry are radiant."

Bhaṭṭodbhava has also stated: "Even a poem endowed with the beauty of qualities (guṇa) and ornaments (alaṅkāra), when it is exceedingly brilliant, [shines] through the excellence of its subject matter, like the celestial tree upon Mount Meru. (7) By defining a defect as that which causes the deterioration of poetry, it is implied by the sense that a quality is that which produces excellence; and since the thorough knowledge of excellence and deterioration is not possible without the instruction of a treatise, he demonstrates the utility of the science [of poetics] with the words "qualities and defects."

How can an unlearned person—one who does not know the treatises—discriminate, that is, specifically understand, the merits (*guṇas*) of poetry, which are the qualities that manifest its worthiness of adoption, and the defects (*doṣas*), which are the qualities that manifest its worthiness of rejection? The meaning is: "He cannot at all. The point is that although one may have a general understanding of merits such as clarity (*prasāda*) and defects such as harshness to the ear (*śrutikaṭu*) merely by reading or hearing poetry, specific knowledge is impossible without the mastery of the scientific treatises (*śāstra*).

For instance, in the perception of distinctions among forms—such as beauty and the like—is there any capacity or authority for a blind person? The meaning is: "Certainly not. People become capable of discerning merits and defects through the study of the scriptures; it is for this very reason that I have undertaken this effort. This is the intended sense. (Here too, the figure of speech is *dṛṣṭānta* [illustration]. 8.

"From this": for this reason, because the distinction between merits and defects and so forth is to be understood through the treatise (*śāstra*), the learned ones—the ancient scholars such as Bharata and others—having intended, that is, aiming for, the "instruction" (*vyutpatti*) of people—that is, the knowledge of the variety of speech—[composed] the "rule for composition" (*kriyāvidhi*) of those "speeches" (*vācām*) which possess "varied paths"—that is, whose paths or ways (*mārgāḥ*), such as the Gauḍī and Vaidarbhī styles (*rītayaḥ*), are diverse and manifold. This is the meaning.

They "composed" (nibabandhuḥ), meaning they "wrote" (cakruḥ) or "composed poetic works" (kāvyagranthān racayāmāsuḥ). (By this it is indicated that just as Bharata and others composed their treatises for the sake of worldly instruction, my own effort in composing this work is likewise for that purpose, and not for the sake of proclaiming my own fame. || 9 ||

Now, preceded by a presentation of the ancient discourse, he defines the body of poetry which constitutes Dharma, using the words "by them" (*tair*). By "them," [he means] the former scholars. The "body of poems" (*kāvyānāṃ śarīram*) is that which, as the substratum for qualities (*guṇas*), defects (*doṣas*), and ornaments (*alaṅkāras*), serves as the soul's physical form and its support; and likewise, "ornaments" (*alaṅkāras*)—according to the etymology "those by which the body of poetry is adorned and elevated"—refer to the qualities such as *śleṣa* (conciseness) and so forth, as well as ornaments such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and simile (*upamā*). This is the meaning.

The sense is that this is because of such statements as: "Qualities, ornaments, and styles are declared to be the causes of excellence. They have been "shown," meaning they have been defined by the presentation of their characteristics. Here, the two instances of the word "and" (*ca*) indicate the equal importance of both [qualities and ornaments]. Alternatively, the "and" in "the body and" (*śarīrañca*) is connected with the word "by them" (*taiḥ*), meaning "and by those"; and the "and" in "ornaments and" (*alaṅkārāśca*) serves to include what has not been mentioned, meaning "ornaments, qualities, defects, and so forth."

The plural number in the word *kāvyānām* ("of poems") should be understood as being stated with the intention of expressing the variety of its types. [Now, to the question] "What, then, is poetry (*kāvya*)?"—the author of the *Locana* says: "That which is to be praised (*kavanīya*) is poetry. Bhaṭṭa Gopāla says: "A poet (*kavi*) is one who 'calls out' (*kau*), i.e., sounds forth, or reflects upon aesthetic moods (*rasa*) and emotions (*bhāva*); poetry is his work (*karman*). The author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* says: "Poetry is the work of a poet skilled in extraordinary description. [And: "Imagination (*pratibhā*) is considered to be an intellect characterized by ever-new flashes of inspiration."

"By being animated by that [poetic spirit], the poet skilled in the armor [of style] lives; his work is traditionally known as *kāvya*," says Bhāmaha. The conventional meaning is that *kāvya* is a pair consisting of word and sense endowed with beauty (*cārutā*). In response to the inquiry, "What is its body? he reveals his own view, stating: "The body. The particle *tāvat* is for the purpose of embellishing the sentence. And it has been stated by Vāmana: "The purpose of a sentence-ornament is not to be meaningless."

The meaning is that "desired" (*iṣṭāḥ*) means pleasing to the heart, captivating through the presence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth. The "series of words" (*padāvalī*), which is a collection of words, is "distinguished" (*vyāvacchinnā*)—that is, adorned—by those various meanings (*arthāḥ*) categorized as expressed (*vācya*), indicated (*lakṣya*), and suggested (*vyaṅgya*). This is the summarized sense: such a series of words constitutes the body of poetry (*kāvyasya śarīram*). Here, "desirability" consists in being the cause of extraordinary delight (*āhlāda*). In cases such as "your enemy is dead" or "a son is born to you," there is no status as poetry because the resulting delight lacks this extraordinary quality.

Such a meaning should be understood as arising from the absence of defects, the presence of excellences (*guṇas*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāras*), and through the charmingness produced by the distinction of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). Consequently, the threefold division of poetry—into *dhvani*, *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*, and *citra*—stated by others should be followed here. For instance, where the charm of the suggested meaning is submerged within the charm of the expressed meaning, that is *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*.

And where there is an absence of the aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), and the charm of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) alone has reached its highest excellence, that is called *citra* (pictorial poetry). Here, one should understand that the meaning (*artha*) is threefold according to the distinction between the expressed, the indicated, and the suggested. That meaning which is conveyed by denotation (*abhidhā*) is the *vācya*; that which is understood through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the *lakṣya*; and that which is apprehended through suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is the *vyaṅgya*. In this regard, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is also divided into three types based on the distinctions of fact (*vastu*), ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and emotion (*rasa*) and so forth; however, as that has been explained in detail elsewhere, it is not discussed here.

Here, the term *padāvalī* signifies a mere sentence (*vākya*), for a collection of words that lacks expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*) is not conventionally designated as poetry (*kāvyatva*). Therefore, the qualification "possessing expectancy" (*sākāṅkṣā*) must be applied to it. Consequently, it follows that the body of poetry is a sentence endowed with meaning, rather than being the word and its meaning themselves; by this, common usages such as "poetry is recited" (*kāvyaṃ paṭhyate*) and "the meaning is understood from the poetry" (*kāvyād artho 'vagamyate*) are also rendered consistent.

The moderns, however, say: "Word and meaning are the body, rasa is the soul, the defects (doṣas) are like blindness and other physical infirmities, the qualities (guṇas) are like bravery and other virtues, and the ornaments (alaṅkāras) are like bracelets, earrings, and so forth. In this view, even the status of rasa as the primary element (aṅgin) is not emphasized; for all theorists of poetics have accepted that even works devoid of rasa can still be considered poetry because they possess qualities and ornaments, because they manifest objects and figures of speech, and because they produce aesthetic charm (vaicitrya).

And here, the "body" (*śarīra*) should be understood as the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*)—adorned with poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*)—and the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), which consists of a matter (*vastu*), a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), a rasa, and so forth; this is according to the definition stated: "The 'meaning' established here as the soul of poetry, which is praised by connoisseurs, is traditionally held to have two divisions: the expressed and the suggested.

(10) Now, he demonstrates the divisions of poetry, beginning with the word "prose" (*gadya*): that poetry is established—that is, determined—as being of exactly three kinds, namely prose, verse (*padya*), and mixed (*miśra*); the phrase "by the ancients" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

The term *gadya* is established by adding the suffix *yat* in the sense of the object (*karman*) to the verbal root *gad*, according to the rule "the suffix *yat* is added after the roots *gad*, *mad*, *car*, and *yam* when no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes them," as stated in the rule "when speech is clearly manifest. The term *padya* means "that which exists in verses (*pada*)," [established by adding the suffix *yat* in the sense of "existing in" (*bhava-artha*), with the designation *bha* applied and the substitution of *pad* for *pāda*]. Because verse composition is more difficult to accomplish and master than prose, prose (*gadya*) is mentioned first. Regarding that, he states the definition of verse: "verse" (*padyam*).

The aggregate of four quarters (*pada*) is "four-quartered" (*catuṣpada*); this refers to verse (*padya*) composed in four lines. Although verses consisting of two lines and so forth are seen in the Vedas and elsewhere, and because in common worldly usage only that which consists of four quarters is well-known—and because such [four-line verses] are generally employed in great epics (*mahākāvya*) and the like—it is called "four-quartered. In reality, however, a sentence bound by meter is what constitutes verse.

(As they say: "Verse consists of words bound by meter," and likewise, "A sentence possessing metrical restriction is called verse. That [verse] is also of two kinds: *vṛtta* and *jāti*. *Vṛtta* is that which is not bound by a fixed number of syllables (*akṣara*), while *jāti* is that which is bound by morae (*mātrā*). The definitions of prose (*gadya*) and mixed composition (*miśra*) are of little utility and have therefore not been presented here; it should be understood that prose is devoid of meter, while mixed composition consists of both prose and verse. || 11 ||

Regarding the word *chanda*: in that *Chandoviciti*—whether it be the treatise on prosody composed by Piṅgala and others, or one's own work titled *Chandoviciti*—the entire expansion (*prapañca*) of those [meters], such as *vṛtta*, *jāti*, and so forth, has been demonstrated and defined. That science is the knowledge of prosody; it is "profound" (*gambhīram*), meaning unfathomable or difficult to traverse, and it is the "ocean of poetry" (*kāvyasāgaraṃ*), meaning the sea in the form of poetic composition.

The meaning is that for those desiring to cross—those wishing to traverse—it is like a boat, the very form of a vessel. For just as a boat filled with many provisions is useful to those wishing to cross the exceedingly deep great ocean, so too is knowledge of prosody (chandaḥ) for those who have exerted effort to compose or study poetry—which consists of sentences bound by numerous meters and is profoundly deep due to its aesthetic sentiments (rasa), emotions (bhāva), and so forth. This is the intended sense. 12.

Now, intending to define the *mahākāvya* (great epic poem), [the author] demonstrates the lack of utility in enumerating its sub-varieties by showing that they are already included within it, beginning with the term *muktaka*. A *muktaka* is a single verse (*śloka*) alone that is capable of producing aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) for the wise. A *kulaka* is a poetic composition consisting of five verses. As it has been said: "A pair of verses is to be known as a *yugmaka*; a *viśeṣaka* consists of three verses; a *kalāpa* would consist of four, and a *kulaka* is considered to consist of five."

A *kośa* is a collection of verses that are independent of one another. As it has been said: "A *kośa* is a collection of *ślokas* that are mutually independent. A *saṅghāta* is the completion of a narrative through verses whose meanings are individually complete. As it has been stated: "Where a poet describes a single subject matter through various meters, that is declared to be a *saṅghāta*, such as the *Vṛndāvana*, the *Meghadūta*, and so forth. Thus, in this context, the word "iti" carries the sense of "in this manner."

Such [a work], being of that same kind, including the *yugmaka* and other forms, is an "extension of verses" (*padyavistara*), meaning an expansion of verses; because it serves as a "limb" (*aṅga*)—that is, a constituent part—of the *mahākāvya*, meaning it possesses the nature of a portion of the *mahākāvya* which will be defined hereafter; the sense is that it has not been mentioned—that is, not demonstrated—here, because it has been explained in detail in other texts, for fear of making this work too voluminous. || 13 ||

Since it was previously stated that *muktaka* (isolated verses) and other forms were not mentioned because they lack the nature of being composed of *sargas* (cantos), and since there is a desire for that information, he now defines the *mahākāvya* (great poem) with the words beginning "a composition of *sargas*," and so forth.

A *bandha*—a collection of verses characterized by descriptions of intermediate subjects—is a *mahākāvya*. The *lakṣaṇa*, or essential nature, of that *mahākāvya* is stated and will be defined immediately hereafter. [The components are: *āśīḥ*, which is the pronouncement of auspiciousness; *namaskriyā*, which is salutation—that is, a statement indicating one's own inferiority; for the sense is that salutation is threefold, consisting of physical, vocal, and mental acts.

Alternatively, *vastu* (the subject matter) refers to that which dwells within it; that is, the protagonist of the narrative at hand, or someone else related to him. *Nirdeśa* (indication) is the description of that [protagonist]. The conclusion is that the *mukha* (opening) of that *mahākāvya*, consisting of one of the [three types] beginning with the benediction (*āśis*), must be described first. In this regard, there is a benediction in works such as the *Kīcakavadha*, a salutation (*namaskāra*) in works such as the *Raghuvaṃśa*, and a statement of the subject matter (*vastunirdeśa*) in works such as the *Śiśupālavadha*. || 14 ||

Regarding the term *itihāsa*: it refers to the *itihāsas* such as the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Mahābhārata*, and so forth. [A work] is "produced" (*udbhūta*) or "composed" (*nibaddha*) by means of a "narrative" (*kathā*), that is, the life-story of any one of the characters such as Rāma or Yudhiṣṭhira; or else, it is that in which the "subject matter" (*vṛttānta*) is "existent" (*san*), meaning true, and serves as the "basis" (*āśraya*) for description. The remainder of the sentence implies that even a "narrative" (*vṛtta*) other than those such as the *Rāmāyaṇa* and *Mahābhārata* may be employed in a *mahākāvya*. Thus, a life-story (*carita*) based on a real subject—whether famous from the *Mahābhārata* and similar sources or well-known among the people—is what should be described in a *mahākāvya*.

This [indicates] the essential nature [of the work]. (By this it is demonstrated that events contrary to truth should not be described in a Mahākāvya. Of the four—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—the group is the "fourfold aim" (caturvarga); that itself is the fruit, and by that it is "endowed," meaning possessed. Since all four fruits beginning with dharma cannot coexist in a single instance, all [aims] may indeed be described; however, it should be understood that the fruit is one or another of them. (As it has been said: "Therein there may be four aims, and from among them, one should obtain a single fruit.")

It is that which possesses a hero (*nāyaka*) who is clever (*catura*), skillful in action, noble (*udātta*), great, and a leader (*pradhānapuruṣa*). (The definition of a hero is stated in the *Daśarūpaka* as follows: "A leader is one who is generous, accomplished, of noble birth, possessed of great fortune, endowed with beauty, youth, and energy, skillful, beloved by the people, and characterized by majesty, wit, and good conduct. Here, the word "clever" (*catura*) signifies "steadfast" (*dhīra*); therefore, it should be understood that in a great epic (*mahākāvya*), it is specifically the "steadfast-noble" (*dhīrodātta*) hero who is intended.

The characteristics of the *dhīrodātta* (the noble and self-controlled hero) have been stated as follows: "One who is not boastful, patient, exceedingly profound, possessed of great courage (*mahāsattva*), steadfast, concealing his pride, and firm in his vows is declared to be the *dhīrodātta*. (15) Merely describing the hero does not fulfill the purpose for poets, since such knowledge is already established through sources like history (*itihāsa*). Therefore, while relying on the description of the hero, one should also describe incidental matters such as the city and so forth; for by doing so, the beauty of the poem is enhanced, which will cause the audience to become attentive. With this intention, he says "in the city," and so on.

A city is a region crowded with many prosperous people; an ocean is the sea; a mountain is a peak; a season is spring and so forth; the rising of the moon and sun (this is an elliptical expression, by which their setting is also implied)—by descriptions of these, as well as by sporting in gardens and waters, drinking wine, festivals of love, and the erotic sentiment of union (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*), along with the four types of states of separation (*vipralambha*)—namely, those preceding the erotic sentiment of union such as initial passion (*pūrvarāga*) and the rest.
"But where there is intense passion, yet the desired object is not attained, that is *vipralambha* (love-in-separation).

(Verse 16)—this is the definition of *vipralambha*. Furthermore, the fact that it precedes *sambhoga* (enjoyment of union) is established by this very definition, as in: "Without *vipralambha*, *sambhoga* does not attain fullness. It should be understood that its fourfold nature consists of *pūrvarāga* (first love), *māna* (jealous anger), *pravāsa* (separation due to travel), and *karuṇa* (love in grief).

It is adorned with descriptions of marriages—the activities of wedding ceremonies—and the birth of princes—the accounts of the procreation of sons; likewise, with counsel (*mantra*), meaning secret deliberations conducted with ministers for the purpose of defeating enemies; with envoys (*dūta*), those persons dispatched by a king on business, who are of three types: those with full discretionary powers (*nisṛṣṭārtha*), those with limited authority (*mitārtha*), and messengers carrying specific messages (*sandeśahāraka*); with expeditions (*prayāṇa*), military marches for the sake of conquering foes; with battles (*āji*), which is combat; and with the protagonist’s success, that is, the attainment of victory.

The word "adorned" (*śobhitam*) is to be construed with the verse that follows; the meaning is that cities and other such subjects must be described in a *mahākāvya*. As it has been said: "Twilight, the sun, the moon, night, the evening, darkness, and day; morning, midday, afternoon, hunting, mountains, seasons, forests, and oceans; union and separation; sages, heaven, cities, and sacrifices; battle, military expeditions, marriage, counsel, and the birth of a son—these, along with their various sub-divisions, should be described here as appropriate. || 17 ||

"Adorned" means not condensed—that is, it should not be described in an abbreviated manner, but rather in detail; the sense is that only by being so does it become captivating to the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*). It is "interwoven"—meaning filled—continuously with *rasas* such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, with *bhāvas* (predominant emotions) that are not fully manifested, with *vyabhicārin* (transitory) states, with *sthāyin* (permanent) emotions such as love (*rati*) that are merely awakened, and likewise with passions directed toward deities and other objects.

In this Mahākāvya, it must be accepted—even though others have stated that one among the sentiments of Śṛṅgāra, Vīra, or Śānta should be described as the primary (aṅgin), while the other Rasas and Bhāvas serve as subordinate (aṅga)—that one of these is intended as the principal sentiment, as it has been said: "One Rasa among Śṛṅgāra, Vīra, or Śānta is desired as the primary. It is "endowed with cantos (sargas) that are not overly extensive, regulated by the rules of the Śāstras, complete with [the required] letters beginning with 'ṭa', and named after the conclusion of intermediate narratives"—this is the connection with the verse to be cited later.

The authority for the fact that there should be neither fewer than eight nor more than thirty cantos is stated in the Īśānasaṃhitā: "A great poem, endowed with the glory of a Great Being, should be composed with no fewer than eight cantos and no more than thirty. This rule is, however, general, as instances to the contrary are also observed.

In reality, however, the fact that the creation (*sarga*) is not overly extensive should be understood as consisting of no fewer than thirty and no more than two hundred verses. As it is stated in that very *Īśānasaṃhitā*: "The creation should not be excessively prolix, nor should it be less than three hundred, nor should it exceed two hundred; this is the defining characteristic of the verse. By "verses" (*padyaiḥ*), the meaning is those verses which bring pleasure to the ear through the avoidance of defects, the employment of *guṇas*, and the application of *alaṃkāras*.

(As it has been said: "Those verses in which the mind feels distaste upon hearing them and lacks delight, those should be avoided, as they have fallen away from established excellence. The meaning of "with well-knit joints" is that they are mutually dependent; the intention is based on such statements as, "At the end of one creation, there should be an indication of the story of the future creation."

As for the explanation given by some—namely, that "the five junctures (*saṃdhi*) mentioned in the definition of drama, called *mukha*, *pratimukha*, *garbha*, *vimarśa*, and *nirvahaṇa*, are to be joined"—that is not correct, because such a definition does not apply everywhere. Viśvanātha, however, stated in his definition of the great epic (*mahākāvya*) that "all the junctures of a drama [are present]," and it was only those following his opinion who explained it in that way; this is the general direction [of the argument]. || 18 ||

"Everywhere" means: by those [sargas] in which the narratives (*vṛttānta*) are everywhere distinct—the sense being that this is due to the differentiation of the subject matter to be described in each creation—or else, by those "endowed with" (*upeta*) distinct (*bhinna*) verses (*vṛtta*), meaning poetry (*padya*) composed in separate meters at their ends, since such is generally observed at the conclusion of each individual sarga, and because of the statement: "By verses consisting of a single meter, with other meters at the end. (Since a sarga consisting of a single meter is not seen everywhere, it should be understood that this is the general rule.)

Just as the fourth canto of the *Śiśupālavadha* is composed in various meters—as it has been said: "Nowhere is a single canto seen to consist of various meters"—so too, poetry that possesses ornaments (*sadalaṅkṛti*), meaning one in which figures of speech such as alliteration and simile are present or beautiful, being a delighter of the world and captivating to the hearts of the connoisseurs, shall endure until the end of the aeon; the sense is that it produces long-lasting fame. || 19 ||

If the definition of a *mahākāvya* were merely the inclusion of some of its stated characteristics, then a *khaṇḍakāvya* (minor poem) possessing those same characteristics would also have to be considered a *mahākāvya*. To establish the correct conclusion regarding this, he says: "deficient" (*nyūnam*).

In this epic poem (*mahākāvya*), with respect to the aforementioned constituent parts (*aṅga*)—the sense being that even if it is deficient or lacking some of these parts—it does not become flawed; that is, it does not become censurable by way of failing to meet the formal requirements (*lakṣaṇa*). However, if there is excellence—that is, sweetness of composition—with respect to the subjects taken up and described, it pleases those who know [poetry], meaning it delights connoisseurs of poetry through the presence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth. As it has been said: "The absence of ornaments, figures of speech, and the like is not a fault in the minds of the learned."

"If he is satisfied by the mere description of mountains, rivers, nights, and so forth"—this is the meaning. In the reading "if there is the accomplishment of the intended subject matter," the sense remains the same. By this, it is established that the status of a *mahākāvya* (great poem) consists precisely in its capacity to produce a specific variety of aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya-viśeṣa*); and this specific charm in a *mahākāvya* is indeed distinct from that found in a *khaṇḍakāvya* (minor poem). The inclusion of descriptions of gardens and the like is for the sake of easy comprehension by those of simple intellect; such is the direction of the argument. 20.

Now, he describes two methods for the portrayal of the hero and the antagonist in poetry through the two verses beginning with "guṇataḥ" and "vaṃśataḥ. First, having introduced the hero by way of his qualities and described the hero's virtues, the defeat—meaning the overcoming—of his enemies, that is, the antagonists, by that hero; this path, this mode of description, is naturally beautiful, being inherently charming. (In this context, the hero's qualities and the antagonist's faults [are to be depicted]).

They are to be described; for, having demonstrated the general qualities such as generosity (*tyāga*) of the hero, the specific qualities of human excellence (*pauruṣaguṇa*) have been mentioned, and the defects of the antagonist (*pratināyaka*) have been stated. As it has been said: "Splendor (*śobhā*), grace (*vilāsa*), sweetness (*mādhurya*), profundity (*gāmbhīrya*), fortitude (*dhairya*), valor (*tejas*), charm (*lalita*), and magnanimity (*audārya*)—these eight are the human qualities born of the quality of goodness (*sattva*). And: "The antagonist is one who is haughty, evil-doing, and addicted to vices."

And likewise, in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, there is the description of the slaying of Rāvaṇa—who was arrogant in his own strength and devoted to sinful deeds such as the abduction of Sītā—by Rāma, who, by the command of his father, undertook the difficult vow of enduring the hardships of a long forest exile. [Verse 21: "In the lineage..."—the lineage (*vaṃśa*) refers to the family (*kula*); "valor" (*vīrya*) means prowess (*parākrama*); "learning" (*śruta*) means knowledge of the scriptures; and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), qualities such as compassion and courtesy are to be understood accordingly.

Having described these [qualities] and having "donned" them—that is, by means of his victory over that enemy—the description of the hero's excellence gladdens us; it satisfies us. (By this it follows that, after describing the lineage and other attributes of one who possesses the characteristics of a rival hero, the subsequent description of a hero who is superior in merit produces only the excellence of the hero. For example, in the *Kirātārjunīya*, after describing Duryodhana’s winning over of the subjects, his victory over them was described in order to demonstrate the superiority of Yudhiṣṭhira and others, who were even more virtuous than he. || 22 ||

Since poetry is of three kinds—consisting of prose, verse, and a mixture of both—it is difficult to master them all; therefore, having first stated the definition of verse (*padya*), he now defines prose poetry (*gadyakāvya*) by means of two verses beginning with *apādaḥ* and *nāyakenaiva*. *Apādaḥ* means that which is not composed in metrical feet (*chandas*), where a "foot" (*pāda*) is one-fourth of a *śloka*; that which is devoid of such feet is prose (*gadya*), being a continuous succession or collection of words (*padasantāna*, *padasamūha*). [The types of prose are: *cūrṇaka* (with few compounds), *dīrghasamāsa* (with long compounds), and *utkalikāprāya* (mostly consisting of rhythmic waves).

Having stated that there are varieties of prose (*gadya*) such as "devoid of compounds," "intertwined" (*āviddha*), and "possessing the scent of verse" (*vṛttagandhi*), and not treating them separately because they are included within *ākhyāyikā* and *kathā*, the author—relying on the ancient view of two primary divisions—says: "*Ākhyāyikā*. There are two subdivisions of that prose: *ākhyāyikā* and *kathā*. As it has been said: "In a *kathā*, a charming subject matter is composed entirely in prose; here, occasionally there may be an *āryā* verse, and occasionally a *vaktra* or *apavaktra* verse.
At the beginning, there is a salutation in verse, and the description of the conduct of villains and the like [is provided]. (23)

Thus; for example, the *Kādambarī* and others. "The *ākhyāyikā* shall be like the *kathā*, with a description of the poet’s lineage and so forth; in it, there may also be the account of other poets, and prose here and there. The division of sections of the narrative is designated as an *āśvāsa*. It is composed in any meter, such as *āryā*, *vaktra*, or *apavaktra*; at the beginning of each *āśvāsa*, there is an indication of future events through an *anyāpadeśa* (an indirect reference). Thus; for example, the *Harṣacarita* and others.

Having observed that the mutually exclusive characteristics defined by the two [previous] descriptions have been altered in earlier treatises, he states the following in order to refute even the alternative definition, beginning with the words "tayoḥ" (of those two). Between those two, the *ākhyāyikā* is to be spoken by the hero alone; the meaning is that the hero himself is its narrator. By the use of the particle "eva" (alone), there is an exclusion of others. As it has been said: "That in which the events performed by the hero himself are narrated is the *ākhyāyikā*."

Another type of speech (anyā kathā) is that which is spoken by the hero or someone other than him, such as the dialogue between the hero Candrāpīḍa and Mahāśvetā in the *Kādambarī*. Anticipating the objection that "if the hero is the speaker, the manifestation of his own virtues would be a fault," he says: "svaguṇa... (regarding one's own virtues).

For a hero who proclaims what is real—that is, one who speaks according to the facts—there is no fault in the manifestation of his own virtues (nijaguṇakhyāpana) when he is the speaker here; the ellipsis is "it does not become a fault. The sense is that only the telling of untruth constitutes a fault. || 24 ||

Refuting the previously mentioned ancient view, he says "api tu" (but rather). That is to say: even there—in the *ākhyāyikā*—there is an "aniyama" (lack of restriction), meaning a contradiction to the rule that the narrator must be the hero alone, because of the "udīraṇāt" (utterance) by others, i.e., by characters other than the hero, since others besides the hero also speak. Consequently, there would be the very fault of being too narrow (*avyāpti*); the intention is that such a distinction should not be made at all.

Furthermore, the defining characteristic of the distinction [between the two] is that in a *kathā*, the narrator is either someone other than the protagonist or the protagonist himself; what kind of distinction, then, could this possibly be? The meaning is that it does not hold at all. In an *ākhyāyikā*, the protagonist is the narrator; if in a *kathā* as well the protagonist were the narrator, then because there would be no difference in their essential nature, the attempt to establish a distinction would be useless. This is the intended sense. || 25 ||

Furthermore, he refutes the argument regarding the creation of a division by means of two verses beginning with "vaktram. "Vaktra" and "aparavaktra" are two meters. As it has been said: "In the *anuṣṭubh* meter, that which does not have 'na', 'a', 'dha', 'ya' [in its quarters] is known as *vaktra*; when there are 'na', 'na', 'ra', 'la', and a heavy syllable (*guru*) in the odd quarters, and 'na', 'ja', 'ra', 'ja' in the even, that is *aparavaktra*; and they desire that *vaitālīya* be called *aparavaktra* when it has the *puṣpitāgrā* cadence."

*Ucchvāsa* is the designation for the division of a section of a narrative, a synonym for *āśvāsa*; as it has been said: "The division of the sections of a narrative is called an *āśvāsa*. Being accompanied by that [division] is the differentiator; the word "of the narrative" (*kathāyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 26 ||

These three constitute the defining characteristic of an *ākhyāyikā*. If, even in *kathās*, there is an inclusion of the *āryā* and other meters—such as *vaktra* and *aparavaktra*—by way of incidental occurrence or through the sequence of the narrative, as in the case of the *āryā* and so forth, why would this not be the case? The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "it would indeed be so"; rather, it certainly would be so. (And it has been stated in the definition of *kathā*: "by whatever meter, such as *āryā*, *vaktra*, or *apavaktra*"). Therefore, the intention is that the attempt to establish a distinction between them as previously stated is merely the manifestation of delusion.

Having demonstrated the fault of the distinction between *vaktra* and *aparavaktra*, he refutes the distinction made by means of *ucchvāsa*. "Distinction" (*bheda*) refers to the division of the narrative sections (*kathāpariccheda*), specifically a difference in nomenclature; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), terms such as *ullāsa* are included. The word "or" (*vā*) here has the sense of "and. Thus, *lambha* and so forth, as well as *ucchvāsa*, are the distinct divisions (*bhinnaḥ*) of the *kathā* and *ākhyāyikā*; that is to say, they are sections bearing separate names. In some *kathās*, a section is made using the term *lambha*.

The meaning is that [the division] has been made by means of the term *ucchvāsa* or the term *ullāsa* within a narrative (*ākhyāyikā*). [Objection: "It is observed; let it be so; but what of it? [Response: The meaning is that a difference in mere nomenclature (*saṃjñāmātra*) is of no consequence, because distinction is proclaimed only on the basis of a difference in essential nature (*svarūpavailakṣaṇya*). Just as there is a cognition of distinction between a jar (*ghaṭa*) and a cloth (*paṭa*) due to a difference in their essential natures—such that "a jar is other than a cloth"—it is not so in the case of a jar (*ghaṭa*) and a pot (*kalasa*), which differ only in name, since they are non-different as jars. This is the intended sense. || 27 ||

Now he reveals his own view with the word "tad" (that). The sense is: "tad" means "therefore"; [the two] are marked by the two designations or names, "kathā" and "ākhyāyikā," but not by their essential nature; the sense is that there is one undifferentiated *jāti* (genus), because both consist of prose.

Having established the non-difference between the two primary varieties, *kathā* and *ākhyāyikā*, among the five varieties of prose-kāvya mentioned by others according to the method previously stated, and having analyzed how the differentiating characteristics of the others are inconsistent, he includes them as common [to all] within this very category.

The meaning here is "in these two alone," namely in *kathā* and *ākhyāyikā*. The "remaining" (*śeṣāḥ*) or residual types of narrative (*ākhyānajātayaḥ*), such as *khaṇḍakathā* and others—characterized by the property of being narratives in general—will be included within these two; for the sense is that they are merely varieties of these two.

(The phrase "they will be included" is indicated by the use of the future tense; however, the author of the text has not accepted any divisions of prose poetry (*gadyakāvya*). In reality, this opinion does not currently prevail everywhere as authoritative, since other even more authoritative scholars have established those various divisions. As it is said in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*: "The *ākhyāyikā*, the *kathā*, the *khaṇḍakathā*, the *parikathā*, and the *kathālekha*—thus they consider prose poetry (*gadyakāvya*) to be fivefold.

He also refutes another distinction between *kathā* and *ākhyāyikā* with the words "the maiden" (*kanyā*). The meaning is: the forcible abduction (*haraṇam*)—that is, seizing by force through battle and so forth—of a maiden who has not yet undergone the marriage sacrament and who has made a resolve to bestow herself upon a worthy recipient; this refers to the *rākṣasa* form of marriage. As it is said: "Having killed, cut, and broken [the way], the forcible abduction of a maiden from her home while she is crying out and weeping is called the *rākṣasa* rite."

"Battle" (*saṅgrāma*) means war; "separation" (*vipralambha*) is a division of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and according to the author of the *Darpaṇa*, it is fourfold, consisting of: love at first sight, jealousy, separation due to travel, and sorrow. "Rising" (*udaya*) refers to the rising of the sun or moon, or the exaltation of the hero; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), gardens, cities, and so forth are included. These are the "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*), the remainder being that they belong to the *ākhyāyikā*. The conclusion is that, according to the opinion of others, it is precisely these characteristics—such as the description of the abduction of a maiden—that distinguish the *ākhyāyikā* from the *kathā*.

As stated by Bhāmaha after introducing the *ākhyāyikā*: “It is endowed with the abduction of a maiden, battle, separation, and success,” and so forth—the meaning is that these are simply general characteristics of the *mahākāvya*, being equivalent to those found in the *sargabandha*; what then need be said regarding the *kathā*? Therefore, these are not specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*) that serve as differentiators, nor are they the defining properties that exclude [the *kathā*] from being a *mahākāvya*. Furthermore, one should not say that these are mandatory in the *ākhyāyikā* but not in the *kathā*, or that they are merely incidental in the *mahākāvya*; for they are indeed uncommon [to both].

Because [otherwise] there would be the acceptance of a distinction between the two, whereas it is inappropriate for common properties to possess such [a nature]; and as it has been said: "This alone is indeed the distinction, or the cause of distinction, namely, the superimposition of contradictory properties. (29)

He refutes the view that some arbitrary convention (*ciḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍana*) employed at the poet’s will is the differentiator between *kathā* and *ākhyāyikā*, by stating "the poet's" (*kavīti*). The meaning is that the convention (*ciḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍana*), which is created by the poet’s disposition—that is, composed according to the poet’s intention—should be applied to the *kathā*. (And it has been said by Bhāmaha: "The *kathā* is marked by conventions created according to the poet’s intention.")

Just as the word "śrī" is employed in the concluding verses of the *Śiśupālavadha*, and the word "lakṣmī" is used in the *Kirātārjunīya*, so too its use elsewhere—even in a narrative (*ākhyāyikā*)—is not to be censured. For indeed, for the wise who have disciplined themselves and exerted effort in order to achieve their desired goals and accomplish what they intend, why should the "mouth"—that is, the beginning—not be [at their disposal]? Rather, the meaning is that everything should be placed at their disposal according to their will; thus, they are "unrestrained."

The meaning is "the poets. Regarding the phrases "in the accomplishment of the desired object" (*iṣṭārthasaṃsiddhau*) and "the face" (*mukham*), there are alternative readings: *saṃsiddhau* and *sukham*, respectively. || 30 ||

Now he describes mixed poetry (*miśrakāvya*), beginning with the word *miśrāṇi*. Dramas (*nāṭaka*) and the like are dramatic compositions (*dṛśyakāvya*); they are "mixed" (*miśrāṇi*) because they consist of a mixture of both prose and verse. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), works such as the *prakaraṇa* are included. As it has been said: "The drama (*nāṭaka*), the *prakaraṇa*, the *bhāṇa*, the *vyāyoga*, the *samavakāra*, the *ḍima*, the *īhāmṛga*, the *aṅka*, the *vīthī*, and the farce (*prahasana*)—these are the ten types of dramatic forms (*rūpaka*). Likewise: the *nāṭikā*, the *troṭaka*, the *goṣṭhī*, the *saṭṭaka*, the *nāṭyarāsaka*, the *prasthāna*, the *ullāpyakāvya*, the *preṅkhaṇa*, and the *rāsaka*."

"Saṃlāpaka, Śrīgadita, Śilpaka, Vilāsikā, Durmallikā, Prakaraṇa, Hallīśa, and Bhāṇikā—these eighteen are called minor plays (uparūpaka) by the wise. Thus [it is said]. Regarding these, such as the Nāṭaka and others, their detailed exposition is found extensively elsewhere in the works of Bharata and others; those desiring to know them should strive for that very source. My intention here is that, for fear of excessive bulk, I have not made an effort in this regard.

He states that not only is there a mixture in *dṛśyakāvya* (dramatic poetry), but there is also sometimes a mixture in *śravyakāvya* (poetry for recitation); thus he says "gadyati. A certain [composition] consisting of both prose (*gadya*) and verse (*padya*)—the word "speech" (*vāṇī*) being understood—is called, that is, designated as, *campū*. It does not have the status of *campū* in works such as the *ākhyāyikā*, which are prose compositions, because verses are extremely few therein; for here, there is an abundance of both prose and verse, and this is the distinction between them. (By the word "certain" [*kācit*], its non-universality is indicated).

Therefore, it should be understood that the term *viruda* has been applied to this [type of composition] by others because it is a subject of royal praise; as it has been said: "A *viruda* is defined as a royal eulogy consisting of prose, verse, or both.

(31) Having previously demonstrated the threefold nature of poetry through the statement "prose, verse, and mixed," he now states its fourfold nature according to the distinction of language and so forth, beginning with the word "that" (*tad*).

Therefore, for this reason, the learned (āryāḥ), meaning the wise, declare that this science of poetry consisting of speech—namely, that which is composed in *saṃskṛta* (the divine language), that which is composed in *prākṛta* (the language so named), that which is composed in *apabhraṃśa* (the specific linguistic variety defined by the characteristics of apabhraṃśa to be described hereafter), and likewise that which is *miśra* (mixed, meaning composed of various languages)—is of four kinds.

By the term *miśram* ("mixed"), this is understood: because of the diversity of languages and because poets are subject to their own creative will, they may compose poetry even using many difficult and harsh languages; consequently, poets may produce poetry in one, two, three, or even more than that number of languages. And as Bhoja has said: "A certain meaning can be expressed in Sanskrit alone, another in Prākṛt alone, and yet another can be conveyed through Apabhraṃśa."
"One is composed in Paiśācī, Śaurasenī, and Māgadhī; another in two or three languages; and yet another in all of them. (32)

He explains *saṃskṛta* and so forth with the words "the refined (*saṃskṛtam*)": "Divine" (*daivī*) means pertaining to the gods or used in divine discourse; "speech" (*vāk*) means a sentence; "by the great seers" (*maharṣibhiḥ*) means by the ancient scholars and sages; "named" (*nāma*) means well-known; "refined" (*saṃskṛtam*) means it is designated as such by virtue of its being a refined form; "subsequently explained" (*anvākhyātā*) means it was subsequently employed under the name "refined. (Although the word *saṃskṛta* is neuter, it takes the feminine gender here because it depends on the gender of the referent.)

The primacy of the object to be taught (uddesya) is to be understood from the fact that the great sages, such as Pāṇini and others, demonstrated the means of refinement for the sake of their disciples regarding the eternally existing Sanskrit language; and the use of the prefix *anu-* is likewise appropriate for that very reason, since grammatical exposition (*anvākhyāna*) is possible only for that which already exists.

This *prākṛta* belongs to the common people (*prākṛtānām*) and the low-born (*nīcānām*). Its *krama*—its rule—is manifold (*aneka*), meaning of many kinds. Furthermore, *tadbhava* means that which has arisen (*bhava*) from that *saṃskṛta*; *tatsama* means similar to *saṃskṛta*. Likewise, *deśī* means prevalent in various respective regions. Among these, it should be understood that the Mahārāṣṭrī language arises directly from *saṃskṛta*, while Śaurasenī and others are equal to *saṃskṛta*, and the others are distinguished by their respective regions.

Some maintain that because even the regional dialects (*deśī*) resemble Sanskrit, there are only two varieties [of Prakrit]; as it has been said: "The wise know Prakrit to be of two kinds: that which arises from the *Ārṣa* [language] and that which is equal to the *Ārṣa*. (33) Having stated the definition of Prakrit, he describes its superior and inferior forms with the words "based on Mahārāṣṭra. "Based on Mahārāṣṭra" means having its locus in Mahārāṣṭra—the name of a specific region situated in the Deccan (*dakṣiṇāpatha*). "Based on that" means connected to it, i.e., the language used therein. They know this language to be "superior," meaning excellent; the word "the wise" is to be understood as the subject.

"Sūktiratnānām" means "of the jewels of well-spoken verses," where "sūktayaḥ" refers to eloquent sayings that are themselves like jewels because they produce joy for those with refined taste (*sahṛdaya*). "Sāgaraḥ" means an ocean, in the sense of being a vast receptacle; thus, it is a "jewel-mine. "Setubandhādi" means beginning with the *Setubandha*—a specific Prakrit poetic work of that name—and by the word "ādi" (etcetera), works such as the *Daśamukhabadha* are included. "Yanmayam" means "consisting of which," that is to say, composed in the Mahārāṣṭrī dialect.
From this it follows that ancient poets composed many poems in this language. 34.

By the word "deśa" (region), since there are many regions, it is shown that many varieties of Prākṛta are possible; thus he indicates other Prākṛtas as well, such as Śaurasenī. Śūrasena is the name of a district adjacent to Mathurā; Gauḍa is a specific region; Lāṭa is a certain division of a region. That which is current in those respective regions—being of such a nature or similar to that—is another regional language (*deśīyā bhāṣā*) which is called Prākṛta. In this way, it enters into and attains usage in common practice. (And by the phrase "another such [language]...")

It is also indicated that all languages designated by the names of regions—such as Prācya, Āvantī, Māgadha, Drāviḍa, Ebaḍhi, Dhaṭṭha, Ḍala, Kī, and so forth—are composed by poets under the name "Prākṛta. (35)

He defines Apabhraṃśa as it follows in the sequence, beginning with "Ābhīra, etc. In poetry (*kāvyas*), the *ābhīras*—a specific class of cowherds—and by the word "etc.," the inclusion of fishermen, outcastes (*caṇḍālas*), and so forth; their speech is known as *apabhraṃśa*, that is, it is designated by the name *apabhraṃśa*. However, in the treatises other than poetry, such as the Vedas and others, everything other than *saṃskṛta*—meaning all speech including that of the *ābhīras* and others—is described as *prākṛta*; yet, it is also declared to be *apabhraṃśa*.

(Thus, the definitions of the three types of languages—Sanskrit and the others—among the fourfold classification have been established; as for the definition of the "mixed" type, it was not treated separately because its meaning is obtained through the very force of the term *yoga*, and therefore it should be understood that the definition of the mixed type consists in being a mixture of various languages. || 36 ||

Having defined Sanskrit, Prākṛta, and Apabhraṃśa, he now defines their respective examples as well as mixed examples, beginning with "Sanskrit. A *sargabandha* is a specific type of composition previously mentioned, meaning a *mahākāvya* (great poem); by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), compositions such as *khaṇḍakāvya* (minor poems) are included. "Sanskrit" means composed in the Sanskrit language; (here, since words such as "Sanskrit" denote the respective languages through primary denotation (*abhidhā*), they are used metaphorically [*lakṣaṇā*] to mean "consisting of Sanskrit").

And likewise, the *Agnipurāṇa* states: "That which is begun as a *mahākāvya*—a composition on the theme of creation—in Sanskrit, nothing other than that of the Bhava lineage (Sanskrit) may enter it, nor anything equal to it. By this, it is indicated that in a *mahākāvya*, unlike in a mixed composition (*miśrakāvya*), there is no restriction regarding the specific speaker; thus, even for those of low status, the use of the Sanskrit language alone is prescribed. *Skandhaka* and so forth: *skandhaka* is a specific type of meter, and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), *galitaka* and others are included.

As it has been said: "By means of *chandas* [metres], *skandhaka*s, and likewise *galitaka*s. This means that poetry composed in *skandhaka* and other metres, being in the Prākṛta language, is called *Prākṛta*. Poetry composed in *āsāra* and other such metres is called *Apabhraṃśa*. (In Apabhraṃśa-language poems, the designation *sarga* for a section is mentioned by others, but it was not accepted by the author of this work.)

As it has been stated: "In this work composed in Apabhraṃśa, the cantos are called *kaḍavakas*; likewise, there are various meters suitable for Apabhraṃśa. Regarding the term "nāṭakādi" ("drama and so forth"): "nāṭaka" is the first member of the compound; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of the major dramatic forms (*rūpaka*) such as the *prakaraṇa*, as well as the minor dramatic forms (*uparūpaka*) such as the *nāṭikā*. (It should be known that there are ten major dramatic forms and eighteen minor dramatic forms; their definitions are to be found in other texts).

*Mishraka* means consisting of various languages. (In dramas and similar works, the employment of diverse languages must be understood as being restricted to specific speakers through distinct, fixed languages. Thus it is stated in the introduction to dramas and the like: "Sanskrit should be used for men who are not low-born and are self-cultivated; Śaurasenī should be employed for women of that same status. For the *gāthās* of these very women, one should employ Mahārāṣṭrī. The Māgadhī language spoken here is for those who move within the king's inner apartments.")

The *Ārdhamāgadhī* dialect should be used for servants, princes, and merchants; the *Prācyā* for Vidūṣakas and the like, as well as for rogues; the *Avantīkā* for warriors, citizens, and others; the *Dākṣiṇātyā* for gamblers; and one should employ the *Śākārī* for Śakāras, Śakas, and similar figures. (Thus, verse 37.)

Establishing that the *kathā* is a mixed form of poetry (*miśrakāvya*), he defines its language: for the *kathā*—which is a previously mentioned variety of poetry—is composed in all languages as well as in Sanskrit; therefore, it is designated as "mixed" (the ellipsis being "it is so called"). The *kathā* is of two kinds: consisting of mixed languages and consisting solely of Sanskrit. The sense is that while the former possesses the quality of being "mixed," the latter, such as the *Kādambarī*, does not.

They say that the *Vṛhatkathā*—which is a poetic work (*kāvya*) of that name, composed in the *paiśācī* language (the language of spirits), consisting of that [language], and containing wonderful subjects filled with the sentiment of wonder—is [the work] referred to; the word "scholars" (*vidvāṃsaḥ*) is to be supplied as the subject. It should be understood that the *Vṛhatkathā*, known by that name, is an Apabhraṃśa poem composed in the *paiśācī* language. || 38 ||

Now he states the twofold division of poetry according to the distinction between the visible (*dṛśya*) and the audible (*śravya*), beginning with the word *lāsya*. *Lāsya* is the dance of women permeated by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). As it has been said: "Lāsa is the state of being of a woman and a man; that which is worthy of it, or that which is well-suited for it, is *lāsya*. It causes the mind-born god [Kāma] to flourish, possesses soft limbs and graceful gestures (*hāva*), and because it was instructed by the God [Śiva], it is generally performed by women for the Goddess. And another [source] says: "Lāsya is delicate and sweet, endowed with the erotic sentiment."

That which causes satisfaction to Gaurī and involves the dancing of women is called *strīnṛtya* ("women's dance"). (*Thus it is said*) *chalita* is the dancing of men; as it has been stated: "They know *chalita* to be the male dance. *Śalyā* is a dance performed with the placement of hands upon the forehead; as he says: "Having placed the hand on the forehead, the dance is celebrated as *śalyā*. Regarding the reading "sāmyādi" in place of "śalyādi," in that case, *sāmya* refers to a dance accompanied by song, instrumental music, and so forth, which is designated by the synonym *rāsa*.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *tāṇḍava* and other forms is intended. As it has been said: "The wise know that dance to be of six types: *lāsya*, *tāṇḍava*, *chalita*, *śalya*, *hallīśaka*, and *rāsa*. And: "That which was proclaimed by Tāṇḍu and subsequently made known in the world to Bharata under the name *tāṇḍava*... and also: "The dance initiated by Puruṣa, which is the support of the heroic and furious sentiments (*vīra* and *raudra-rasa*), which is vigorous (*uddhata*) and dear to Śaṅkara, is called *tāṇḍava*."

*Hallīsa* is the dance of women in a circular formation; as it is said: "The dance of women performed in a circle is known as *hallīśaka*; therein there should be one leader, just as Hari is for the cowherd women."

Thus, poetry composed of *lāsya* and other elements is "dṛśyartha" (visible in its subject matter); that is, it is one in which the *artha*—the object to be communicated—is visible (*prekṣya*), because it is the object of observation through the actors' imitation of the states of Rāma and others. Consequently, being an object of observation is the defining characteristic of the "visible" (*dṛśya*), and it should be understood that this refers to works such as the *nāṭaka*. "The other" (*itarat*) means something different from visible poetry, namely, independent verses (*muktaka*) and so forth.

It is "meant to be heard" (*śravya*) precisely because it is the object of hearing alone; thus, it follows that being the object of hearing alone is the defining characteristic of the *śravya*. (And as stated by King Bhoja: "They say that poetry which is neither seen nor enacted is *śravya*; it gives pleasure to the ears alone, and it is of six kinds.")

Thus, in this manner, "this" well-known [classification], even though it is of the form already described—not only those previously mentioned—is further divided into two kinds by way of the distinction between the visible and the audible; such is the meaning of the word "also" (api). This twofold path—that is, the two-fold method for establishing the divisions of poetry—has been illustrated by the ancients; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 39 ||

Having thus defined the varieties of poetry (*kāvya*), he defines its *rīti* (style), stating "it exists. It is manifold—that is, diverse—and this diversity is pointed out by other treatises as consisting of subtle differences, meaning differences of only a slight degree. The "path" (*mārga*) of words—that is, the mode of composition—is what is meant by *rīti*. And that *rīti* consists of the arrangement of words characterized by qualities such as *śleṣa* (conjunction) and the like.

It has been stated by Vāmana: "Rīti is a distinguished arrangement of words," based on the etymology that "the qualities (guṇas) move (rimanti) or proceed within it. As it is said: "The path created by the Vaidarbha and others is known as the 'mārga' (path) in poetry; it is called *rīti* by virtue of its derivation from the verbal root *rīṅ* (meaning 'to go'). This term is also used in other treatises. Regarding this, Vāmana states: "It is threefold: Vaidarbhī, Gauḍīyā, and Pāñcālī. The author of the *Darpaṇa* adds the Lāṭī as a fourth.

"The Vaidarbha, the Pāñcālī, the Gauḍī, the Āvantikā, as well as the Lāṭīyā and the Māgadhī—thus the *rīti* (style) is said to be sixfold," so say King Bhoja and others. Their definitions are stated therein as follows: "In that regard, the Vaidarbha style is held to be free from compounds (*asamāsā*), enriched with all the qualities such as *śleṣa* (punning condensation), and possessing the beauty of the notes of the lute (*vipañcī*). Poets know the Pāñcālī style to consist of five or six words [in a compound], devoid of *ojas* (vigour) and *kānti* (splendor), yet sweet and delicate."

Those who are experts in the *rītis* recognize the Gauḍī as being endowed with the qualities of *ojas* (vigour) and *kānti* (splendor), characterized by entirely exalted words. That which stands between the Pāñcālī and Vaidarbhī styles is the Āvantikā; it consists of all [the qualities] but with two, three, or four compound words. The Lāṭīyā style is held to be a mixture of all the aforementioned styles. Because it fails to carry through the previous styles, the Māgadhī is considered a *khaṇḍarīti* (fragmentary style). Among these, the Vaidarbhī is as follows: "Divinities are present in the homes of those who desire them; where, then, is the need for penance?"* *Note: This verse is cited as an example of the Vaidarbhī style, characterized by its clarity and lack of excessive compounds.*

"And where is your body? A *śirīṣa* flower, though delicate, might endure the touch of a bee, but not that of a bird. Thus [he says]. Furthermore, because defining it through such subtle distinctions would result in an excessive bulk of text, he speaks in order to clarify the views of the two clearly distinct schools, Vaidarbha and Gauḍīya: therein, by the terms "Vaidarbha" and so forth, poets from the Vidarbha region and elsewhere are indicated figuratively; for from the word "Vidarbha," the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "śeṣe" (Pāṇini 4.2.92).

From the word *gauḍa*, the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule "vṛddhācchaḥ," resulting in *gauḍīya*. Thus, *vaidarbha* refers to that which is dear to the poets of the Vidarbha country, and *gauḍīya* refers to the collection of poets residing in the Gauḍa country; these two paths (*mārgau*) are described because they possess a manifest distinction between them—the sense being that there is an extreme dissimilarity due to one being characterized by delicacy (*sukumāratva*) and the other by intensity (*utkaṭatva*).

It appears to me that although the author has mentioned many styles (*rīti*s), he has primarily highlighted the Vaidarbha and Gauḍīya paths; by doing so, he has indicated the superiority of the Vaidarbha style over other styles, and for the purpose of demonstrating its excellence, he has also presented the Gauḍīya style as characterized by its specific distinctions.

For indeed, a distinction between styles (*rīti*) arises from a distinction between qualities (*guṇa*). And the Vaidarbha style possesses excellence because it is endowed with all the qualities. That the Vaidarbha style is endowed with all the qualities has been stated by Vāmana thus: "The Vaidarbha is endowed with all the qualities. And by others [it is said]: "Untouched by even a trace of defects and graced by all the qualities, the Vaidarbha style is desired as possessing the beauty of the sound of a lute."

Thus, praise for it is seen as follows: "When there is a speaker, when there is a true subject matter, and when there is the science of grammar, that [Vaidarbha style] exists—without which the honey of speech flows away. And he will say later: "Thus, the ten qualities are considered the very life-breath of the Vaidarbha style. For this very reason, even Kālidāsa, the crest-jewel of the assembly of poets, composed his poems almost entirely by relying upon that same style; and it has been said: "Kālidāsa excels in compositions in the Vaidarbha style."

And Vāmana has cited the verse composed by Kālidāsa beginning with "gāhantāṃ mahiṣāḥ," which appears in the *Abhijñānaśākuntala* as a statement by Duṣmanta, whose heart was overcome by the longing to behold Śakuntalā and who desired to desist from his hunting excursion. Thus, it should be understood that the Vaidarbha style is demonstrated by him both through its manifest distinction and its preeminence. (40)

He points out by name the ten qualities, such as *śleṣa* (conciseness) and so forth, which constitute the very essence of the Vaidarbha style, using two verses beginning with "śleṣaḥ. The ten qualities, beginning with *śleṣa*, are designated by the term "quality" (*guṇa*) because they bring about the excellence of word and meaning. They are the "life-breaths"—that is, the vital principles—of the Vaidarbha path, or the Vaidarbha manner; the sense is that without them, the people of Vidarbha would not accept [certain compositions] as poetry. By this, it is stated that the nature of the Vaidarbha style consists in being composed of words possessing *śleṣa* and the other qualities.

"They are remembered," with "by the wise" being the ellipsis. (By the word "remembered," it is indicated that according to the ancient traditions, only these ten—namely *śleṣa* and the rest—are accepted as qualities (*guṇas*), whereas others accept only three. And it is said in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "Those [qualities] known as *mādhurya*, *ojas*, and *prasāda* are three, not ten. || 41 ||

Some, however, also say that there are twenty-four qualities (*guṇas*), as follows: "Those among them which reside in words are numbered at twenty-four; they are first set forth according to their connection with the definitions of names. Beginning with *śleṣa* (cohesion) and *prasāda* (clarity), [the others are: *ojas* (vigour), then *aucitya* (propriety), *prauḍhi* (boldness), and *suśabdatā* (euphony); likewise *samādhi* (evenness), *saukṣmya* (subtlety), *gāmbhīrya* (depth), and *vistara* (expansiveness); *saṅkṣepa* (conciseness), *sammitatva* (measuredness), *bhāvikatva* (vividness), *gati* (movement), and *tāta* (extension)."

"Style (rīti), expression (ukti), and maturity (prauḍhi)—these are their definitions and illustrations.
