Furthermore, they state that verbal qualities (śabda-guṇas) are external, while semantic qualities (artha-guṇas) are internal; and those which, despite being essentially defects, attain the status of qualities, they call "distinctive" (vaiśeṣika). As it is said: "Qualities in poetry, as recognized by poets, are of three kinds: external, internal, and distinctive. Among them, the external are verbal qualities, while the internal are based on meaning."

"But those very things which are considered defects are indeed virtues for the Vaiśeṣikas. Thus say the authors of the *Darpaṇa* and others: that the qualities of the *rasa*—which is the soul of poetry—are precisely *mādhurya* (sweetness), *ojas* (vigour), and *prasāda* (clarity), just as bravery and other traits belong to the self. In the Gauḍa path—that is, in the Gauḍa style—there is generally (meaning for the most part) a reversal, or the opposite, of these ten qualities beginning with *śleṣa*. It should be understood that this reversal occurs sometimes entirely and sometimes only in certain respects.

In this context, by the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*), it is implied that in some instances there may even be equality between these two. However, the distinction between them should be understood as follows: the Vaidarbha style is characterized by having very few aspirated consonants (*prāṇākṣara*), whereas the Gauḍīya style possesses qualities contrary to those of the Vaidarbha. As it has been said: "The Vaidarbha style consists of uncompounded words or only single compounds, is endowed with the ten poetic excellences (*guṇa*), abounds in second-class consonants (the dentals), and employs syllables with few aspirants; it is easy to compose. The Gauḍīya style, on the other hand, is characterized by numerous compounds and contains many syllables with great breath-force (*mahāprāṇa*)."

"The style (rīti) is dependent upon the greatness of alliteration and consists of unimpeded speech. Thus [he says]. Vāmana, however, states the distinction as follows: "The Vaidarbhī is possessed of all the guṇas, while the Gauḍīyā possesses the guṇas of ojas and kānti," as in: "Those expert in the styles (rīti) sing of the Gauḍīyā style as being endowed with the guṇas of ojas and kānti, consisting of verses composed of entirely intense words. (42)

Now he defines the characteristics of *śleṣa* (cohesion) and the other qualities, beginning with "śliṣṭam" and so forth. "Alpa-prāṇa" means having little vital force, that is to say, little effort required for pronunciation; those syllables in which such [vowels] are predominant—that is, abundant—constitute such [a quality]. Furthermore, these are syllables consisting of short vowels, consonants belonging to the [first four] classes, and dissimilar letters.

That which is "untouched by looseness" (aspṛṣṭa-śaithilya) refers to a sentence that, due to its arrangement, does not appear loose despite being so; the meaning is that it is "cohesive" (śliṣṭa), endowed with the quality of *śleṣa*. Thus, the result is this: even in a composition constructed from syllables of weak breath-force (*alpaprāṇa*), the occasional placement of syllables with great breath-force (*mahāprāṇa*) serves as the cause for the appearance of a single word even where words are distinct, thereby producing the impression of non-looseness in the composition; this is *śleṣa*.

(Kramadīśvara has also said: "Even among vowels of little breath-force (*alpaprāṇa*), there should be an occasional insertion [of consonants], and there should be a conjunction (*śleṣa*) with those of great breath-force (*mahāprāṇa*), as in this sound 'bhramaradvani'"). Having stated the definition of *śleṣa*, he introduces the Gauḍa school's doctrine by presenting an example of its opposite, *śithila* (loose), stating: "Loose" means that which is of the nature of the reverse of the definition of *śleṣa*, being exceedingly delicate.

The word "yathā" (as for example) is intended to demonstrate an illustration: [the phrase] "mālatīmālā" (garland of jasmine) is "kalilā" (filled/covered) by "lolaiḥ" (fickle) "alibhiḥ" (bees). Here, because of the predominance of dental consonants and its extreme softness, the Vaidarbhas do not accept it as possessing *śleṣa* (punning/sonorous quality); however, the Gauḍas, due to the density of the composition and its possession of *anuprāsa* (alliteration), do accept it as such—this is the sense.

Bhoja, however, considers such an example to be marred by the defect known as *arītimat* (lack of style), as he says: "Where there is a reversal of qualities such as *śleṣa* (conjunction) and the rest, they call it *arītimat*. Having established the definition therein that "by the reversal of *śleṣa*, the composition becomes loose (*śithila*)," he cites a loose example as follows: "This friend is a garland of *mālatī* flowers, dense with restless bees, [captivating] the mind."

In this regard, the interpretation offered by someone—namely, that in the phrase "therefore [the style] is relaxed (*śithilam*)," the word *api* must be supplied so that it means "even though relaxed (*śithilam api*), even though not haughty (*anuddhatam api*), it is untouched (*aspṛṣṭam*) or unmanifested (*aprakāśitam*) as to its relaxation"—and the subsequent demonstration of examples such as *mālatīmālā* as illustrations of this, appears inconsistent. For if that were the case, the two styles, Vaidarbha and Gauḍīya, would be presented as having a single illustration, which would result in the contradiction of the statement: "The two are described as having clearly distinct differences."

Likewise, regarding what will be stated later in the passage beginning with "by the Gauḍas, through the perception of alliteration," the author interprets the word "iti" as "even so. He thereby demonstrates that in cases such as "mālatīmālā," where alliteration is present, the Vaidarbha and Gauḍa styles share the same domain; whereas in cases such as the forthcoming "mālatīdāma," where alliteration is absent, they have different domains. However, this too is not correct, because there is no evidence for postulating such a distinction and because it involves unnecessary complexity (gaurava).

For instance, Bhoja, following the view of Daṇḍin, has clearly stated: "The *śliṣṭa* (compact) style is that which is not touched by looseness, while the *śithila* (loose) style is its opposite; however, this [distinction] is accepted by the Gauḍas because of their regard for the excellence of the composition. For example: 'The winds, dark as the rainy season, blew, carrying away the playful, swaying, and lovely curls of women, and sweeping away the garlands of *mālatī* flowers. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, by defining the characteristic of *śleṣa* (conjunction) as "the quality of being well-knit in its words" (*guṇaḥ suśliṣṭapadatā śleṣa ity abhidhīyate*) and providing the example beginning with "If two separate streams in the sky... (*ubhau yadi vyomni pṛthak pravāhau*), that author has indeed established as authoritative the quality of *śliṣṭatva* (closeness/knitness) in the compositions of the Vaidarbhas, just like *śrutyanuprāsa*. However, according to the Gauḍa school, because the composition appears firm due to the power of *anuprāsa*, the quality called *śleṣa* should be understood here; thus, everything is clear.

Others also from Gauḍa and Iḷā cite *śleṣa* (punning) as follows: "Highly intensified by the continuous forceful impact of the lordly elephants plunging into the water, and making all the regions within the mountain caves resound with echoes—just as this sound rises up piercingly to the ears, so now, for the most part, does this tide emerge, white as countless, swaying conch shells. Thus [they say].

Here, because of the presence of alliteration (*anuprāsa*), the composition being formed of aspirated consonants (*mahāprāṇākṣara*), and the ruggedness (*vikaṭatva*) of the structure, there is the *śleṣa* characteristic of the Gauḍīya style. It should be understood that if alliteration alone were taken as the defining characteristic, it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as the sweetness (*mādhurya*) to be described later, which is composed of those very [aspirated] sounds. || 43 ||

It is considered by the Gauḍas—by poets residing in the Gauḍa country—with the notion of *anuprāsa*. *Anuprāsa* is a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) consisting of the repetition of phonemes; it is "with the notion" of that, meaning through the awareness of it. Due to the density of the composition—that is, because of the firmness of the structure resulting from the presence of *anuprāsa*—that example of *śleṣa*, such as "mālatīmālā," is desired. The sense is that they generally prefer a composition that abounds in *anuprāsa* and possesses the quality of *ojas* (vigorous energy).

(By this, it is implied that for the Gauḍas, even in the absence of the composition of syllables with very great breath (*sumahāprāṇa*), that [style] is also desired where there is an abundance of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and firmness of construction. Consequently, he states what the difference is between Vaidarbhī and Gauḍī: "By the Vaidarbhas," etc.

By the Vaidarbhas—the poets from the Vidarbha country—a sentence such as "The jasmine garland has been trampled by bees" is "desired," meaning it is accepted as being *śliṣṭa* (coalescent/ornamental), even though it is devoid of alliteration; the sense is that for them, it is celebrated as possessing *śleṣa* (coalescence) even in the absence of alliteration.

Although an equality between the Vaidarbha and Gauḍa styles is observed in examples of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and *śleṣa*, nevertheless, because an example devoid of alliteration does not enter the definition of the Gauḍa style, it is shown that the two have distinct domains; such is the direction of the argument. Furthermore, this *śleṣa* is a quality of word alone. As for its being a quality of meaning, as stated by others: "Their *śleṣa* is said to be the skillful arrangement [of words], like the excellence of a well-woven thread"; and as Vāmana also said: "*Śleṣa* is the structural coherence (*ghaṭanā*)."

And *ghaṭanā* (structural coherence) is the conjunction of sequence (*krama*), curvature (*kauṭilya*), lack of excessiveness (*anulvaṇatva*), and logical justification (*upapatti*). Among these: *krama* is the order such that "having done this, this must be done"; *kauṭilya* is a deviation from the ordinary course of worldly affairs; *anulvaṇatva* is the absence of an appearance of being excessive; and *upapatti* is the introduction of specific details that serve to resolve an apparent inconsistency, answering the question, "How is this meaning consistent? Thus, the definition is: *arthaleṣa* (semantic cohesion) is the joining together of meaning through sequence, curvature, lack of excessiveness, and logical justification.

For this very reason, the author of the *Darpaṇa* stated as follows: "Śleṣa (paronomasia) consists of the combination of sequence, artfulness, lack of vulgarity, and logical justification. Among these, 'sequence' is a succession of actions; 'artfulness' is the conduct of a clever person; 'lack of vulgarity' is the absence of description of what is not well-known; 'logical justification' is the arrangement of supporting arguments; the 'combination' is their synthesis, and that which constitutes the nature of the composition is of that form. For example: 'Having seen her beloved seated upon a single seat,' and so forth."

In this [verse], the actions are "seeing" and so forth; the crookedness consists in the form of supporting both [parties]; the lack of vulgarity consists in the form of worldly social conduct; and the supporting factors are "standing on the same seat," "approaching from behind," "closing her eyes," and "with his neck slightly bent"—the combination of these [constitutes the figure]. || 44 ||

He defines clarity (*prasāda*): "possessing clarity. This means that which has a well-known meaning regarding the object to be expressed; it is free from the defect known as *nihitārthatā* (the use of words with multiple meanings in a sense other than the well-known one). Regarding "comprehension" (*pratītau*), it means in the full understanding of the meaning; "elegant" (*subhagam*) means simple, that is, conveying the meaning instantly. "Speech" (*vacas*) refers to the utterance. "Possessing clarity" means endowed with the quality of clarity. An example of this is: "Of Indra... (*indor iti*).

The *induvaram* is the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*); that which possesses a luster like that is of a dark complexion (*śyāmavarṇa*). The *lakṣma* is a mark or blemish. It extends—that is, it spreads—the *lakṣmī*, the splendor, of the *indu*, the moon. Here, it should be understood that words such as *indu* and others, when employed in their well-known senses of the moon and so forth, convey the meaning instantaneously. Thus it is said in the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa*: "That which consists of words with well-known meanings is called *prasāda* (clarity)."

For instance, in the verse beginning with “The buffaloes plunge into the water of the watering-place,” the quality of the word known as *prasāda* (transparency) arises from the employment of words whose meanings are well-known. However, the *prasāda* residing in the meaning has been stated in that very same [work] thus: “That which is the manifestation (*prākaṭya*) of the meaning is called *prasāda*. The manifestation of the meaning is its clarity (*vaimalya*). For this very reason, Vāmana states the definition: “*Prasāda* is the clarity of the meaning.”

For example: "Here rises the breaker of the seal of the lotuses, the teacher of the day-lotus groves, the friend of the pairs of *koka* birds distressed by separation, piercing the darkness with a hue as copper-red as the cheek of an angry monkey, [bearing] a young *mandāra* flower upon its stalk-like rays.

Here, although not explicitly stated, the meaning characterized as the Sun is clearly perceived in his causing the lotuses to bloom, removing the grief of the *koka* birds, and dispelling the darkness; thus, this is *arthaprasāda*. And so, the sense is that *prasāda* consists in the quality of having words whose meanings are perfectly clear, provided there is freedom from defects. (45)

He presents the opinion of the Gauḍas with the words "vyutpannam" (cultivated). By the Gauḍas—that is, by the scholars residing in that region—even that which is not overly conventional (*anatirūḍham*), meaning even that which is beset by the defect of having a hidden meaning (*nihatārthatva*), is accepted as "cultivated"—meaning it is endowed with etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) and composed of its constituent parts (*yogārtha*). Such a sentence is accepted because it imparts a sense of structural firmness (*bandhagāḍhatā*) and produces aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*). However, the Gauḍas consider defects such as *nihatārthatva* to be faults only in poetry characterized by loose composition (*śithilabandha*).

However, it should be noted that when the connection is firm, those faults are not considered defects because they produce a sense of variety; thus they are accepted. He provides an example, beginning with "yathā" (as follows): "anatyarjunājanmasadṛkṣāṅkaḥ"—that which has a mark (aṅka) resembling an unborn (ajanma) lotus that is not excessively white (anatyarjunam); such is the description. [The moon is] "balakṣaḥ," meaning white, and "gauḥ," meaning one whose rays are like a cow (or light). Thus, he refers to the moon.

In this verse, the word *arjuna* is well-known to denote both Kārtavīryārjuna and the Pāṇḍava Arjuna, yet it is not commonly used in the sense of "white-colored"; thus, it is marred by the defect of *nihatārtha* (meaning obscured). Furthermore, the word *abjanman* has never been employed by anyone to mean a blue lotus (*utpala*), and is therefore tainted by the defect of *aprayukta* (unconventional usage). The word *sadṛkṣa* is redundant, as its meaning is already conveyed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound containing the term *upama*; thus, it is possessed of the defect of *adhikapada* (superfluous word). Likewise, the word *balakṣa* is also tainted by the defect of *aprayukta*, and the phrase is *śrutikaṭu* (harsh to the ear).

The words *balakṣa* and *sadṛkṣa* are [instances of this]; likewise, because the word *go*, which is well-known in the sense of a bull (*vṛṣa*) and so forth, is used here in its less common sense of a camel (*kira*), there is also the fault of obscurity (*nihatārthatva*) therein. Furthermore, in the phrase "anatyujjanābjanma," there is harshness (*kaṣṭatva*) in the sandhi. Thus, even though a poem may possess many such faults, the Gauḍas regard it as poetry because of the density of its alliterative compositions (*sānuprāsa-prabandha*). And thus, the Vaidarbhas define clarity (*prasāda*) as the capacity to present the meaning instantly, by virtue of the absence of faults such as harshness.

The Gauḍīya poets do not accept such clarity (*prasāda*); thus, there is a distinction [between this view and theirs]. Furthermore, in the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*, this verse is composed as an illustration of the fault called *arītimat* (lack of style) due to the reversal of the quality [of clarity]: "A sentence would be 'unlucid' (*aprasanna*) because of the reversal of clarity. For example: 'The female swan, being tormented, made the lotus of her body [her] bed; she whose limbs were like a slightly pale lotus was [the one] whose body was white.'"

Thus, the intention is that this verse of the Vaidarbhas should be cited as an example of a defect. Furthermore, this quality called *prasāda* (transparency) resides only in the sense (*artha*); however, that which resides in the word (*śabda*) should be understood as "consisting of looseness mixed with vigor (*ojaḥ*)," as stated by the author of the *Darpaṇa*. And he himself has illustrated it, for example: "Whosoever among the armies of the Pāṇḍavas bears a weapon out of pride in the strength of his own arms; whosoever in the lineage of the Pañcālas is a child, or of advanced age, or even lying in the womb..."

"Whosoever acts as a witness to that deed against me in battle, and whosoever stands in opposition—blinded by wrath—I myself shall be the end-maker of each and every one of them, even though I am already the end-maker of the worlds. Thus [it is said]. Now, one might wonder how there can be a union of the two contradictory qualities of *ojas* (vigour) and *prasāda* (clarity); however, this is not to be doubted, for all authorities have accepted that laxity mixed with vigour constitutes the quality of *prasāda*, whereas pure laxity is considered a defect.

For instance, by defining that "intensity (*ojas*) consists in firmness of bond" and "clarity (*prasāda*) consists in looseness," Vāmana raised the objection that looseness—which is the opposite of intensity—would necessarily be a defect as the opposite of a quality. To refute this, he stated that looseness mixed with intensity is a quality, according to the sūtra: "It is a quality because of its commingling. Then, by the subsequent sūtra, "Not when pure," he again rejected the status of a quality for looseness unmixed with [intensity] and established it as a defect.

To the question, "How can there be a coexistence (*saṃplava*) of the two opposites, *ojas* and *prasāda*? it is said: "It is established through the experience of the *sattva*. On this point, there is a verse: "Just as the coexistence of pleasure and pain is established through experience in [dramatic situations] such as the pathetic (*karuṇa*) and the picturesque (*prekṣaṇīya*), so too is that of *ojas* and *prasāda*. (46)

He defines *samatā* (evenness) as "even" (*samam*). Among compositions (*bandheṣu*), it means not uneven (*aviṣamam*) or non-distinctive; that is to say, it is similar between the beginning and the conclusion. It is "even," meaning endowed with the quality called evenness. Thus, the definition is: that expression which, through any one of the soft, clear, or harsh phonemes, maintains a lack of disparity between the beginning and the conclusion—that is *samatā*. These compositions are of three kinds. Soft phonemes (*mṛdu-varṇāḥ*) are those among vowels that are short and nasalized, and among consonants, those at the end of the classes (*vargāntyāḥ*) and the dentals (*dantyāḥ*).

The meaning is that [the sound] is clear and intense; among vowels, the long vowels, and among consonants, the letters excluding *na*, the *ṭa*-group, *ra*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *ha*, and those consonants joined with dentals—this is the meaning. The "middling" consists of both types. Thus, one should understand here that there is a threefold nature of evenness (*samatā*) based on the threefold nature of the compositions (*bandha*). He states the reason for the softness and so forth of these compositions in the verse beginning with "mṛdu."

Those whose *yoni*—the source or cause—is the arrangement (*vinyāsa*) of syllables that are soft (*mṛdu*), characterized by short vowels and so forth; clear (*sphuṭa*), characterized by long vowels and so forth; and likewise mixed (*unmiśra*), possessing both qualities. (In this context, just as being composed of soft and other syllables is the cause for the threefold division [of *saṅghaṭanā*], so too are the absence of compounds, long compounds, and medium compounds; as it has been said: "That which is adorned with the absence of compounds, with medium compounds, and likewise with long compounds—the threefold *saṅghaṭanā* is thus declared.")

And this *gum* (compactness) pertains exclusively to words; however, the *guṇa* of meaning is *samatā* (evenness), which should be understood as occurring only where the conclusion follows by the very same application of roots and suffixes with which the beginning was made. For this very reason, it has been stated by the author of the *Darpaṇa*: "The non-interruption of the consistency of the meaning through the non-inversion of the roots and suffixes employed at the outset; and that is simply the absence of the defect known as *prakramabhanga* (break of uniformity). And an example has been cited, such as: "The sun rises copper-red, and copper-red indeed it sets," and so forth.

The opposite case is as follows: "Be gracious, O fierce one; abandon your anger quickly; this person stands before you with palms joined in reverence. Why do you sit with your playful grace lost, while your two full breasts are drenched by tears? Here, because the verb *āsya-te* ("is sat") abandons the subjectivity established in the preceding verbs *prasīda* ("be gracious") and *tyaja* ("abandon"), there is a lack of uniformity (*asamatā*). || 47 ||

He demonstrates the threefold nature of the aforementioned evenness (*samatā*) through two verses beginning with "kokila": "The Malaya breeze, talkative with the warbling of cuckoos, approaches me"—the ellipsis being that it approaches either to afflict or to delight. (In this case, there is evenness belonging to soft composition, because that which was begun softly is concluded by that very same means.)

"The Malaya breeze—sprinkled (*ukṣita*), meaning drenched, by the drops and droplets of that exceedingly clear (*acchāccha*) waterfall water which has *ucchalant* (splashing upward) spray (*śīkara*)—comes to me; it is most cool. (In this instance, there is "evenness" (*samatā*) within the *sphuṭabandha*, as the composition begun with a specific structure is concluded with that very same structure. || 48 ||

"Sandalwood" (*candana*); "consisting of sandalwood" (*candanapramaya*) refers to contact with sandalwood; "fragrant" (*udgandhi*) means having an exhaled scent; "gentle" (*manda*) means soft; "Malaya breeze" (*malayamāruta*) means the wind from the Malaya mountains. (Here, because the composition is formed by a mixture of clear, soft, and harsh phonemes, it is a medium composition; since both the opening and the conclusion follow that very same [medium] composition, this is the "evenness" (*samatā*) pertaining to medium composition. Thus, the threefold nature of evenness is seen elsewhere as well, as it has been said: "Regarding the method of composition involving soft, clear, and mixed phonemes...")

"Speaking without unevenness is called *samatā* (evenness). This is the quality of evenness pertaining to words (*śabdagata*). However, the quality of evenness pertaining to meaning (*arthagata*) is defined as: "Evenness is the lack of disparity among successive elements. An example of this is as follows: "In front stands the *kuravaka* flower, pale-red like a woman’s fingernail, dark in its two parts; the young *aśoka* bud, beautiful with its emerging hue, remains on the verge of opening."

"The fresh cluster on the mango tree is slightly reddish-brown at its tips with particles of pollen; O friend, the beauty of spring stands between childhood and youth. Here, because the qualifiers produced by the onset of youth are applied without partiality to the abandonment of childhood by the beauty of spring, there is *samatā* (evenness).

Bhoja, however, considering the three examples of *samatā* (evenness) found in the first half-verse to be unpleasing, provides the definition: "That very same [fault] would be *viṣama* (unevenness), which is the opposite of *samatā*. Having stated this, he identifies the first verse as an example of the fault of *viṣama* consisting in the reversal of evenness, and explains: "In this case, because the first half-verse has a soft composition while the second half-verse has a tight composition, it is uneven among compositions that ought to be even; thus, it is the figure named *viṣama*, which is primarily concerned with sound (*śabda*)."

"He says that 'the fault is the deviation from evenness' (*samatā-viparyaya*). That is not pleasing, because one observes the sequence of showing a counter-example immediately after showing an example in all cases; this should be noted. Having thus shown the three types of evenness (*samatā*) in a single verse-half, he demonstrates the lack of evenness (*vaiṣamya*) in order to define its opposite according to the Gauḍīya school, beginning with the words "it vies" (*spardhate*).

"Then," meaning having obstructed and cast aside, "destroying my fortitude"—this is the sense. It "vies with," that is to say, attains similarity to, the breaths from the mouths of excellent women (*vararāmāṇām*), namely the fragrant breezes exhaled from their mouths; the intention is that this is due to the equality of their fragrance. (In this case, since the composition begins with a clear [firm] structure and concludes with a soft one, there is no occasion for the aforementioned *samatā* [evenness] due to this disparity.
The point is that the Gauḍīyas, however, accept evenness here as well. || 49 ||

He shows the disregard of the Gauḍīyas regarding the equality of etymological characteristics with the words "iti" (thus). "Thus" means in the manner described—that is, the inequality mentioned in the verse beginning with "spardhate" (it vies), which is a defect arising from the opposite of equality. Without considering or reflecting upon this, the Easterners—the Gauḍīyas—meaning those from the eastern region—expect and pursue the "ḍambaram," meaning the ostentation or excellence, of both meanings (the poetic senses) and ornaments such as alliteration, simile, and so forth.

The method of poetic compositions flourished; for they, according to the requirements of the subject matter and the ornaments, sometimes favored softness of structure, sometimes grandiosity, and sometimes a mixture of both, rather than the evenness (samatā) favored by the Vaidarbhas through their partiality for *guṇas* as previously described.

The meaning is this: where there is softness of meaning, there the composition is soft; where, however, there is ruggedness of meaning, there the composition is rugged; and where there is a mixture of meanings, there the composition is middling; it is not the case that one must conclude with the very same manner in which one began.

And this is indeed appropriate; for it is said: "O jackals, what is the use of these harsh, stubborn, and barking cries, or these fruitless displays? O elephants and buffaloes, why do you indulge in pride? Are there no heroes in this empty world? When the ocean resounds with the roar of the enemy's elephant, its trunk raised high and its fierce mane bristling with the intensity of rage, that which vibrates is truly called a 'roar'—only then."

In this case, because the meaning of the second half-verse—describing the enraged lion—is singular, the abandonment of the soft *bandha* (phonetic texture) commenced [in the first half] is indeed a merit (*guṇa*). For this very reason, the author of the *Darpaṇa* has shown that even the defect of *patat-prakarṣatā* (falling excellence) can sometimes be a merit, as in: "The falling excellence is likewise; thus, in some cases, it is a merit," for example, in the verse beginning with "cañcudvaja. Here, in the fourth quarter, the abandonment of verbal ostentation due to the delicacy of the meaning is a merit.

The Vaidarbhas, however, consider it a defect when a composition is not concluded with the same stylistic arrangement (bandha) with which it began, even if there is a disparity in meaning; this is the distinction between these two [schools]. Similarly, regarding the use of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), the view of the Vaidarbhas is that even those ornaments possessing *guṇas* serve to enhance the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and are not independent of it, whereas for the Gauḍas, they may be independent of rasa; this is the distinction between these two. (50)

He defines *mādhurya* (sweetness) as "that which is sweet. *Rasa* refers to sentiments (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth; by virtue of possessing their qualities, even emotions (*bhāva*), semblances of emotion (*tadābhāsa*), and the like are denoted by the word *rasa*. A sentence in which these exist is "sweet," meaning it is endowed with the quality of *mādhurya*.

Some, however, say that *mādhurya* (sweetness) is the capacity of word and meaning to cause the melting of the heart (*cittadruti*) through an immersion in an operation conducive to the manifestation of either the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) or the pathetic (*karuṇa*) sentiments. As it is said: "The erotic sentiment alone is the supreme sweet flavor that intensely captivates the mind; by relying on poetry permeated by it, sweetness is established. In the erotic sentiment known as 'love-in-separation' (*vipralambha*) and in the pathetic, sweetness reaches its highest degree, because the mind is most intensely absorbed therein."

Thus, it follows by implication that sweetness (*mādhurya*) is indeed rasa itself; however, anticipating the objection that the qualities (*guṇas*)—whether directly or indirectly—are essentially *rasa*, he says: "In speech" (*vāci*). This means: in speech, that is, in the phonemes (*varṇa*) which constitute the expressive medium of such speech; and also "in the object" (*vastuni*), that is, in the meaning (*artha*) which is the content expressed by the sentence. "The abiding of rasa" (*rasasthitiḥ*) refers to the presence of rasas such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, existing through the relationship of being manifested (*vyañjakatva*).

Regarding the phonemes that manifest the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*), and the tranquil (*śānta*) sentiments, it is said: "Excluding the letters *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, and *ḍha*, the phonemes joined with the final letter of their respective classes (*varga*), as well as *ra* and *ṇa* when short, serve as the causes for manifesting those [sentiments]. Furthermore, the composition should be without alliteration (*avṛtti*) or possess only slight alliteration (*alpavṛtti*), and be sweet (*madhura*). And regarding the heroic (*vīra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) sentiments: "The first and third letters of a class joined with their respective final letters, or joined above or below by two *s* sounds, or by *ra*, *ṣ*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, and *ḍha* [manifest these sentiments]."

The letters *śa* and *ṣa* have become its manifestors (*vyañjaka*). Likewise, those [styles] characterized by an abundance of compounds are described by these definitions. Furthermore, in the sentiments (*rasa*) of the comic (*hāsya*), the marvelous (*adbhuta*), and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*), the remaining middle letters and middle compounds should be understood [to predominate]; likewise, the meanings that manifest the sentiments are precisely the permanent emotional states (*sthāyibhāva*) such as love (*rati*) and so forth. Consequently, the definition of *mādhurya* (sweetness) is: a sentence possessing letters, meanings, and so forth that manifest the sentiments.

Since it is impossible to fully understand the letters and other elements that manifest *rasa* without knowing the definition of *rasa* itself—which is what is implied by the term "possessing flavor" (*rasavat*)—the author states the definition of *rasa* with the words "by which" (*yena*). The meaning is: "by which" the wise spectators (*sāmājika*), and not those of dull intellect, become intoxicated like honey-bees (*madhuvrata*) are by honey; the sense is that this occurs because [the experience] consists of a supermundane and intense delight. The word "that is *rasa*" (*sa rasaḥ*) is to be supplied as the conclusion.

And thus, for the wise, *rasa* is indeed a particular state of being (*bhāvaviśeṣa*) born from the repeated cultivation of the meaning of such poetry; and this [state] takes the form of a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) whose characteristics are stated as follows: "Love, laughter, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, as well as disgust and wonder—these eight are declared, and tranquility (*śama*) as well."

The stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) such as love (*rati*), when produced by objective excitants (*ālambanavibhāva*) such as a woman, inflamed by determinants (*uddīpanavibhāva*) such as a garden, rendered cognizable through ensuants (*anubhāva*) such as sidelong glances, nourished by transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as longing, inferred as residing in the hero, and directly experienced by the audience through the proximity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), receives the designation "rasa."

And it has been said: "That stable emotion (sthāyibhāva), manifested by those [factors] such as the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth, is known as rasa. And also: "The stable emotion, such as love (rati) and the rest, when manifested through the excitant (vibhāva), the ensuant (anubhāva), and likewise the transitory emotion (sañcārī), attains the state of rasa for those possessed of sensitivity. The stable emotions corresponding to the eight rasas to be described—namely, the erotic (śṛṅgāra), the comic (hāsya), the pathetic (karuṇa), the furious (raudra), the heroic (vīra), the terrible (bhayānaka), the odious (bībhatsa), and the marvelous (adbhuta)—should be understood respectively as love, laughter, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, disgust, and wonder. And for the peaceful rasa (śāntarasa), the stable emotion is tranquility (śama).

And here, it will be established that there are exactly eight *rasas*. However, that statement—“eight *rasas* are traditionally taught for drama”—is made with reference to dramatic performance (*nāṭya*), because in poetry intended to be heard (*śravya-kāvya*), the *śānta-rasa* (the peaceful) is also possible. As it has been said: “Therein is neither pain nor pleasure, neither anxiety, nor hatred or passion, nor any desire whatsoever; that *rasa* is called ‘peaceful’ by the lords of sages, in which tranquility (*śama*) predominates over all mental states (*bhāvas*). Thus should it be considered by the wise.

However, some maintain that *mādhurya* (sweetness) is a verbal quality (*śabda-guṇa*) characterized by the distinctness of words (*pṛthak-padatva*), as stated: "The wise have declared that *mādhurya* is the distinctness of words in a composition. For example: "The drops, struck [by the lashes], rested for a moment on the eyelashes; then crushed by the heavy fall upon the breasts... and so forth. Here, because there is no *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) between the words, there is *mādhurya* through their distinctness. And this has also been stated by Vāmana: "Distinctness of words is *mādhurya*."

The quality of meaning (*arthaguṇa*) and *mādhurya* (sweetness) should be understood according to the definition stated by the teachers: "Sweetness is the absence of intensity even in [states such as] anger. For example: "Though her brow was suddenly knit, her face was brought to a state of extreme humility; she smiled slightly at me, yet uttered no harsh word. Her gaze, dulled by internal tears, did not expand in its lordliness, and while her anger was made manifest, her courtesy was not abandoned by the beloved."

In this instance, even though the object [of the emotion] is Vāsavadattā, the fact that her anger is restrained by modesty—rather than being intensified or unrestrained—is its *mādhurya* (sweetness). Vāmana, however, states that *mādhurya* is the "beauty of expression" (*uktivaicitrya*), defining it as the "sweetness of meaning" (*arthaguṇa*). Observing the difference between these two views, [the author] demonstrates how a collection of phonemes composed with alliteration (*śrutyanuprāsa*) serves to manifest aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), beginning with the words "yayā."

By whatever [articulation]—meaning by that which consists of the throat, palate, and so forth; by *śruti*, meaning by the utterance that serves as the means of hearing; "similar" (*samānam*) means identical, meaning equal to the consonants previously uttered; "is experienced" (*anubhūyate*) means it is perceived; "of that form" (*tadrūpā*) means possessing the consonants that have become the object of such an experience; "proximity of words" (*padāsattiḥ*) means the proximity of words, their existence without interruption; "that is alliteration" (*sānuprāsā*) means it possesses phonetic alliteration (*śrutyanuprāsa*); for this very reason, "it brings forth aesthetic flavor" (*rasāvahā*), meaning it conveys rasa; the particle *hi* is used for the purpose of emphasis.

It is certain that this [alliteration] nourishes aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Furthermore, the fact that alliteration (*anuprāsa*) brings excellence to poetry has been stated: "Just as moonlight [enhances] the autumnal moon, and just as beauty [enhances] full-bodied women, so too is alliteration capable of adorning poetry here. By this, it follows by implication that the similarity between consonant phonemes (*vyañjana-varṇa*) produced in a single location—such as the palate or the teeth—is *śrutyanuprāsa*.

And as stated by the author of the *Darpaṇa*: "When there is a similarity of a consonant (*vyañjana*) in one place, such as the palate or the teeth, due to its high articulation (*uccāryatva*), it is called 'alliteration of sound' (*śrutyanuprāsa*). Although this belongs to the section on figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), its definition is stated here because of the context of the [phonetic] groups (*gaṇa*); and it will be said later: "Certain figures of speech were mentioned previously for the purpose of distinguishing the poetic paths (*mārga*). (52)

He shows an example with the word "eṣa" (this). One whose dear ones are Brāhmaṇas, or who is dear to the Brāhmaṇas—this king, from the moment he attained *lakṣmī*, that is, royal glory, thereupon became a festival of Dharma in the world, in the sense that he protected his subjects through righteousness.

(Here, because the sounds *ṣa* and *va* are uttered from the same root palate (*mūrdhan*), and *ja* and *ya* from the palate (*tālu*), as well as *da* and *ta* from the teeth (*danta*), there is a similarity between them; thus, these are instances of *śrutyanuprāsa*. Furthermore, since they manifest the aesthetic emotion (*rasa*) of love (*rati*) directed toward the king, they possess the quality (*guṇa*) of sweetness (*mādhurya*). Moreover, because there is no euphonic combination (*saṃhitā*) within the words, their status as belonging to the word (*śabda-gata*) is established by virtue of their being separate words—this is how it should be understood. || 53 ||

In this context, showing the difference of opinion between Vaidarbha and Gauḍa, he says "iti" (thus). The word "iti" indicates what has been stated previously. Thus, what was stated before—this verse—is not accepted by the Gauḍas, that is, by the poets residing in Gauḍa, because they do not acknowledge its possession of the quality of sweetness (*mādhurya*) or its nature as a source of aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*); the sense is that even though the letters are distinct, they do not experience a harmony with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) when uttered from a single location.

Alliteration (*anuprāsa*), however, consists in the repetition of sounds; it is dear to those Gauḍas, being favored for its conformity with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). But by the Vaidarbhas, this verse beginning with "eṣa rājā" is generally—more frequently—preferred over the aforementioned alliteration, even over *śrutyanuprāsa* (alliteration of sounds). (Thus, while both types of alliteration—the repetition of sounds and the repetition of phonemes—are dear to the Vaidarbhas, for the Gauḍas only the latter is so; such is the direction of their difference of opinion.

He states [the definition of] *anuprāsa*: "the repetition of phonemes" (*varṇāvṛtti*). The intention is that "phonemes" (*varṇa*) refers to syllables, specifically consonants; "repetition" (*āvṛtti*) means occurring again, which is to say, the perception of similarity residing in that repetition. This is *anuprāsa*, because similarity itself is accepted as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) due to its capacity to produce aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*).

In this context, the word *āvṛtti* (repetition) signifies similarity residing therein. One might object: "How can there be similarity between two instances of the same phoneme, since they are non-different? This objection is not valid; for even a single phoneme is considered distinct due to the difference in the time of its utterance, and thus the two are understood to be different. By this, the definition of *anuprāsa* is established as the perception of similarity through the repetition of a single phoneme, two phonemes, or multiple phonemes. For this very reason, the author of the *Prakāśa* stated: "Anuprāsa is the similarity of phonemes."

Regarding the phrase "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*), it should be understood that by virtue of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) and *dvandva* (copulative) compounds, this applies to a single phoneme as well as to two phonemes. Furthermore, it is of two kinds: occurring in feet (*pāda*) and in words (*pada*). "Feet" refers to the fourth parts of a verse; "in those feet" means in the words—both nominal and verbal—situated within those respective feet. Thus, the meaning is "occurring in feet and words. By using the plural in the expression "and in feet" (*pādeṣu ca*), it is indicated that the presence of alliteration throughout every foot is particularly pleasing. Its definition was stated by Vāmana: "Alliteration in feet is like the *yamaka* (rhyme) of feet."

For example, as it is said: "Without knowing the King of Poets (Kālidāsa), how can there be a regard for the composition of poetry? Furthermore, repetition brings about aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*) even when there is a difference in accent; thus it has been stated by the author of the *Darpaṇa*: "Alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is the similarity of sounds, which occurs even when there is a difference in accent. Repetition is primarily that which is immediate (*avyavahita*); however, even when separated, it should be understood as being grasped as long as the impressions from the previous experience persist due to the proximity of the letters first uttered. To establish this, he says: "pūrva... (referring to the preceding verse).

The connection is as follows: if there exists the experience (*anubhava*) of a previously uttered *varṇa*—which is auditory cognition (*śrāvaṇajñāna*)—the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that, which is a specific state of cultivation (*bhāvanāviśeṣa*), its awakener (*bodinī*) or protector (*pālanī*), and the proximity (*adūratā*) of a second or subsequent *varṇa*, then and only then is there alliteration (*anuprāsa*). This is the syntactical construction.

The meaning is as follows: the formation (*saṃskāra*) arises in the first moment, its persistence (*sthiti*) in the second moment, and its cessation (*nivṛtti*) in the third moment. Thus, by this rule—whether without interruption or with some slight interval—the utterance of phonemes generates the cognition of similarity. Since it is precisely this similarity that produces aesthetic variety (*vaicitrya*), it constitutes a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*); therefore, alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is defined as the similarity produced by the recurrence of such phonetic properties.

And this [style] is of two kinds: *ulvaṇa* (exuberant) and *anulvaṇa* (non-exuberant). *Ulvaṇa* consists of the arrangement of forceful words, while *anulvaṇa* consists of soft words. Among these, an example of the *ulvaṇa* is: "He wanders about, formidable with his mass of matted hair bound by creepers and his staff-like bow twanging."

The moderns, however, state that this [alliteration] is of five kinds: *chekānuprāsa*, *vṛttyanuprāsa*, *śrutyanuprāsa*, *antyānuprāsa*, and *lāṭānuprāsa*. This has been stated by the author of the *Darpaṇa*: "The *cheka* [alliteration] consists of the single occurrence of similarity among a group of consonants in multiple ways; or the multiple occurrence of similarity among many [consonants] in a single way, or even in multiple ways. Even the single occurrence of similarity in one [consonant] is called *vṛttyanuprāsa*. Because it is produced in a single location, such as the palate or the teeth..."

The repetition of consonants alone is called *śrutyanuprāsa* (alliteration of sound). If the consonant, remaining in its original state, is repeated together with the preceding vowel because it is to be joined with the following one, that is indeed *antyānuprāsa* (alliteration of the final). The repetition of word and meaning when there is a difference only in the intended sense (*tātparya*) is called *lāṭānuprāsa*. Thus, alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is fivefold. Regarding this, an example of *lāṭānuprāsa* is found in the same work: "O you whose eyes are like smiling lotuses! Why are your eyes closed?
Behold your beloved, who has conquered Kandarpa [Cupid] yet remains under the sway of Kandarpa. (55)

He provides an illustration with the word "candre" (on the moon). On the crest-ornament (*uttaṃsa*)—meaning the head-adornment—of the autumnal night (*śaranniśā*), which resembles a cluster of *kanda* flowers, that is, like a bunch of *māghya* blossoms; on the moon, the mark (*lakṣma*), meaning the dark spot (*kalaṅka*) resembling a bee (*alī*), imparts (*sandadhāti*), that is, possesses, beauty (*śriyam*), meaning splendor.

Here, in the first, second, and third quarters, there is *vṛttyanuprāsa* because of the repetition of the phonemes śa, ka, ra, na, and la at no great distance, which brings about a perception of similarity; and in the fourth quarter, because the phonemes da, dha, ta, and na are articulated from the same place of articulation—the teeth—there is *śrutyanuprāsa*, which is favored by the Vaidarbha style. Thus, the quality of sweetness (*mādhurya*), manifested by these two types of *anuprāsa* figures of speech, nourishes the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) residing in the verse.

Here, the poetic figure named *nidarśanā* (illustration), enlivened by *rūpaka* (metaphor) and *upamā* (simile), is present; therefore, the wise should discern that sweetness (*mādhurya*) resides in both word and meaning. || 56 ||

Alliteration (*anuprāsa*) was previously shown through dissimilarity of vowels; now it is shown through similarity. Regarding the word *cāru*: "O timid one (*bhīru*), O you who are prone to fear! Behold in the sky (*ambare*) this lunar orb (*cāndramasaṃ bimbaṃ*), the circle of the moon—this very thing being perceived—which is beautiful (*cāru*, meaning pleasing) and makes an effort to strike my mind (*manmanaḥ*) as it were, violently (*nardayan*), being overwhelmed by Love (*manmathākrāntaṃ*), that is, tormented by passion. (This is the speech of a certain hero directed toward an indignant beloved.)

In this first quarter, there is *vṛttyanuprāsa* due to the similarity between the vowels *a* and *u* when accompanied by their respective consonants; furthermore, in the second and third quarters, there is also *chekānuprāsa* because of the similarity between *mba* and *man*, as well as *man* and *manmaya*, respectively. Likewise, in the fourth quarter, there is another kind of *vṛttyanuprāsa* due to the similarity between the two *da*s and the two *ta*s despite the difference in their accompanying vowels.

Moreover, the quality of *mādhurya* (sweetness), by generating aesthetic charm through its presence in both word and meaning, nourishes the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) known as *vipralambha* (love-in-separation). || 57 ||

He states that non-remoteness (*adūratā*) alone is the determining factor for alliteration (*anuprāsa*), using the word "iti" [to introduce the explanation]. That which has an interval (*antara*)—meaning a separation—that is excessively distant (*atidūra*) is "excessively distant-intervened" (*atidūrāntarā*); that which is not so is "not excessively distant-intervened" (*nātidūrāntarā*). Such is the "audition" (*śruti*) or hearing of which; such is the form of the two examples previously demonstrated. The Gauḍas desire this kind of alliteration, as in the phrase "the moon is like the lotus-face of Rāmā. Even though there is a similarity between the *m*-sounds in the third and fourth quarters [of the verse], [this is considered acceptable].

The meaning is "an alliteration (*anuprāsa*) with an excessively great interval"; the word "alliteration" is to be supplied as the object, and the words "they desire" are also to be supplied. The sense is that because the two *m*-sounds situated in the words "rāmā" and "candramā" are too far apart, there is no awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding letter. (58) Since alliteration is proclaimed to bring forth aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), he states [the following] to show that where a sentence is defective such that the flavor is not fully developed, there is no presence of sweetness (*mādhurya*): "O Smara... and so on.

Smara (the god of love) is sharp; Khara (the demon) is exceedingly fierce; Kānta (the beloved) is dear; Khala (the rogue) is cruel. Our body and our anger toward the beloved have become emaciated and vanished. Our pride has fallen away and perished; our passion for attaining the beloved has increased; and delusion has arisen moment by moment. Our vital breaths have departed, as it were.

(This is the speech of regret by a certain passionate woman whose pride has dissolved after she has rejected her lover. Here, because of the similarity between the *repha*s and the two *kha* sounds in the first quarter, and the similarity between the *ka* sounds in the second, there is *vṛttyanuprāsa*; likewise, in the latter half, because of the similarity between the dental consonants beginning with *ta*, there is *śrutyanuprāsa*. Due to being overwhelmed by these defects, such *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation) does not reach full maturity; thus, there is no *mādhurya* (sweetness), but rather—)

This is cited in the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa* as an instance of the defect known as *ojoviparyaya* (the opposite of vigor). Regarding this verse, it is stated: "In this case, although there is an absence of compound words and although there is delicacy (*saukumārya*) of meaning, the Vaidarbha style is not present due to the absence of the full collection of qualities such as *śleṣa* (consonance); nor are the Gauḍīya and other styles present because they lack the aforementioned characteristics. Thus, due to its 'mutilated style' (*khaṇḍitarītitva*), this is said to be the definition of *ojoviparyaya*, as it is stated: 'That which, by breaking the style within a sentence, becomes the opposite of vigor—those who know the subject call that here the defect known as *asamasta* (non-compounded). " (59)

In the verse mentioned previously, the phrase “and so forth” (*ityādi*) refers to such compositions as these, which, even when possessing alliteration (*anuprāsa*), indicate *bandhapāruṣya*—that is, harshness in composition (*bandha-racanā*) due to being difficult to hear—as well as laxity (*śaithilya*) such as the falling away of excellence (*patatprakarṣatā*) and the like. (In this case, there is harshness in the first half-verse due to the presence of many visargas; as it has been said: “Consonants joined with anusvāra and visarga, when occurring without interruption, lead to harshness.”)

Because the arrangement in the first half-verse is not the same as that in the second half-verse, there is what is called *patatprakarṣatā* (falling excellence). For this reason—that is, because it is thus defective—the scholars of the South, those from the Vidarbha country, do not employ or use alliteration (*anuprāsa*), the sense being that sweetness (*mādhurya*) is absent. (The term "southerners" is illustrative; by extension, even the Gauḍas do not accept such examples as being full of defects or containing alliteration.)

However, where harshness and the like possess sweetness (*mādhurya*) by virtue of being conducive to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), there harshness and so forth are not defects; on the contrary, they are indeed virtues. Thus it has been said: "When the speaker is possessed of anger and the subject matter is intense, then in flavors such as the Furious (*raudra*), extreme harshness becomes a virtue. (60)

Now, one might object: "Since a flavorful verse possesses the quality of sweetness (*mādhuryaguṇa*) and since the repetition of syllables (*varṇāvṛtti*) brings forth aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), why is *yamaka*—which consists of the repetition of syllables—not also defined here, following the same logic as the definition of *anuprāsa*? To this he replies with the word "āvṛttim" (repetition). They [the poets] know—that is, they understand—that *yamaka* is that repetition whose scope (*gocara*) is a collection of syllables (*varṇasaṅghāta*), meaning a group of syllables consisting of both vowels and consonants, which occurs again according to the previous sequence. (The word "poets" is to be supplied as the subject.)

In this context, it should be understood that the compound *varṇasahaddhaṭhṭhaḍaghātapada* refers to a collection of vowels and consonants (*svaravyañjanasamudāya*); otherwise, it would result in an identity with the definition of *anuprāsa*. Likewise, the qualification “having different meanings” (*bhinnārthaka*) must be added to that [definition]; otherwise, in cases such as “*yāmi yāmi*,” the status of *yamaka* would undesirably apply even to those with a single meaning, since *yamaka* is admitted even for words that are devoid of meaning. It should be understood that when meaning is possible, the condition of having different meanings (*bhinnārthatva*) is required.

And here, the repetition follows the previous order; by this, it is indicated that [the pairs] such as "dama" and "moda" have different meanings. By this [definition], the definition of *yamaka* is: when a possible meaning exists, the repetition of a sequence of phonemes consisting of vowels and consonants with different meanings, following the previous order. This was stated by the author of the *Darpaṇa*: "When the meaning is [already] established, the repetition of a collection of vowels and consonants having distinct meanings, in that very same order, is called *yamaka*."

In this regard, both words may sometimes be meaningful, sometimes meaningless, and sometimes one may be meaningful while the other is meaningless; therefore, it is said, "when there is a real meaning. And an example has been cited in that very context: "He beheld before him a forest of fresh palāśa leaves, with lotuses covered in manifest pollen, and tender creepers swaying gently, fragrant with an abundance of blossoms."

Others have also stated: "When syllables of identical phonetic form (*śruti*) but different meanings are repeated among themselves, that is defined as *yamaka*. That *yamaka* verse, however, is not exclusively sweet nor exceedingly possessed of sweetness; for in such a sentence, since there is initially no preoccupation with the investigation of meaning, the apprehension of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) remains unimpeded—this is the sense that there is sweetness in a sentence possessing alliteration (*anuprāsa*).

(One should note that by the word "ekānta" [exclusive], it must be stated that even in *yamaka* there exists sweetness (*mādhurya*) which brings forth aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), yet it is not fully present as it is in *anuprāsa*; otherwise, it would result in its non-status as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). This is because the status of an ornament consists precisely in its assistance to that which constitutes the soul of poetry by generating beauty of word and meaning. Therefore, the meaning is: "later," in the section on ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), it will be "prescribed," that is, described; the word "yamaka" is to be supplied. || 61 ||

Having characterized sweetness (*mādhurya*) as residing in words, he says "kāmam" (to whatever extent) in order to demonstrate that it also resides in meaning. Every poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*)—such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*), verbal punning (*śabdaśleṣa*), the appearance of repetition (*punaruktavadābhāsa*), simile (*upamā*), and so forth—whether residing in words, in meaning, or in both, "kāmaṃ" (to whatever extent), "yatheṣṭaṃ" (as desired), "yathā tathā" (in whatever manner), "niṣiñcati" (sprinkles), that is, nourishes or awakens "rasa" (aesthetic flavor). This is precisely because of the statement: "The presence of rasa exists even in a mere object."

The definition [of sweetness] as residing in the meaning has thus been indicated. To demonstrate specifically that the fault of vulgarity (*grāmyatā*) acts as an obstacle to sweetness residing in the meaning, he says, "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). "Nevertheless," *agrāmyatā* (non-vulgarity) means the state of being non-vulgar—that is, neither the word nor the meaning being such as is employed by common folk (*itarajana*). This quality, for the most part (*bhūyasā*), which means in abundance, bears this burden consisting of the infusion of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

And thus it has been established that sweetness (*mādhurya*) belongs only to that meaning which possesses ornamentation and manifests aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Here, the term "non-vulgar" (*agrāmyatā*) is indicative of [the absence of] indecorousness (*anaślīlatva*) and so forth; consequently, although other defects also act as obstacles to sweetness, the word "vulgar" (*grāmya*) is employed specifically to indicate that this defect is a particularly potent obstacle. In this way, the defects described by others as the opposite of sweetness are also included here.

And it has been stated as follows: "That which arises from the corruption of *rīti* through the loss of sweetness is called 'unrefined' (*anivryūḍha*) by those who know the essence of poetry. For example: "One should never place trust in naked mendicants, horned animals, those with weapons in hand, women, or royal families."

In this regard, because of the inclusion of the genitive endings in *nakhinām* (of clawed beasts) and *nadīnām* (of rivers) by means of the particle *ca*, and because the sequence established at the beginning is not maintained due to the particle *ca* in *śastrapāṇinām* (of those with weapons in hand), and because of the omission of the genitive in *strīṣu* (among women) and *rājakuleṣu* (in royal households), and because of the lack of sweetness (*amadhurārthatvāt*), this is a defect consisting of the reversal of the quality of sweetness (*mādhuryavyatyaya*), which is primarily concerned with word and meaning; therefore, even here, there is no presence of the quality of sweetness.

Because of the inclusion of the word *bhūyasā* ("mostly"), vulgarity (*grāmyatā*) is not a defect when describing the speech of ordinary people; on the contrary, it is indeed a merit. As it has been said: "Vulgarity [is a merit] in the speech of the base"—the word "merit" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

(62) He shows an example of vulgarity pertaining to the meaning (*arthagata*) with the verse beginning "O maiden" (*kanye*). (This is the speech of a clever person: "While you were away, he was despondent; now that he sits near you...")

[This is the first half of the verse: "O maiden! Why do you not desire me—who am longing for you, who am wasting away in separation from you, and who sit right beside you? In this context, the address "O maiden! (*kanye*) is appropriate only for those who stand in the position of a daughter; however, when addressing a heroine (*nāyikā*), expressions such as "O beloved" (*priye*) or "O beautiful one" (*sundari*) alone are correct. Others, however, maintain that because the expression is vulgar (*grāmyatā*), it lacks luster (*kānti*); thus, they classify this as the fault known as "the opposite of luster" (*kāntiviparyaya*), which consists primarily in the lack of aesthetic charm.

As it has been said: "The opposite of *kānta* (lovely) is designated as *grāmya* (vulgar). Therefore, in this instance, the vulgarity belongs to the meaning (*artha*), not to the word *kanyā*; for if a word were vulgar in itself, refined people would not employ it. However, the word *kanyā* is seen even in their usage, as in: "This maiden possesses a luster as soft as gold; there is no fame beyond this," and so forth. By the ancients, however, only words such as *kaṭī* (hip), which are used exclusively by common folk, were declared to be vulgar.

Furthermore, in passages such as "kāmayamānam" (desiring), the desire of lovers—which consists of the longing for sexual union—is more beautiful when it is not explicitly expressed by words but is somehow merely suggested. However, when it is not concealed and is stated clearly by words, it brings about a sense of distaste for sensitive readers (*sahṛdayas*) because it produces shame. Thus, because the object of desire is denoted by clear words even in the phrase "kāmayamānam," there is the fault of vulgarity residing in the meaning (*arthagata-grāmyatā-doṣa*).

And here, although the cause—the form of the hero's desire—is present, because of the absence of the effect—the form of the heroine's desire—the figure of speech is *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation); as stated by the author of the *Darpaṇa*: "When the cause is present but the effect is absent, *viśeṣokti* likewise occurs in two ways. Thus, even though the word and meaning are endowed with figures of speech and possess alliteration (*anuprāsa*), they convey only a lack of relish due to vulgarity (*grāmyatva*); therefore, there is no presence of sweetness (*mādhurya*). He explains this with the words "iti" (thus).

Thus described, this "vulgar" (grāmya) [fault], being possessed of that named defect, pertains to the nature of the meaning—the form of what is to be communicated—and it leads to a lack of aesthetic flavor (vairasya), which is to say, it acts as an obstacle to the arousal of rasa. || 63 ||

He demonstrates non-vulgarity (*agrāmyatā*): "O lovely-eyed one!"—addressing her whose eyes are beautiful or curved—the meaning is: "The fierce outcaste of Love (*kandarpacāṇḍāla*) may roar at will against me; by good fortune (*diṣṭyā*), through luck, he is free from malice toward you, meaning he is compassionate. Thus, the meaning of the previous verse is stated here in a concealed form. The sense—that "I desire you, but you do not desire me"—is non-vulgar, being free from the defect of vulgarity (*grāmyadoṣa*).

The meaning is that the letters *bha*, *ḍha*, *ṭha*, *ḍha*, and *ga* produce a sense of variety (*vaicitrya*) when indicated [in the composition], thereby awakening the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). For this very reason, it is called *rasāvaha*—that which brings about or nourishes the flavor; the sense is that it is endowed with the quality of softness (*mādhuryaguṇa*) by virtue of being an auxiliary to the flavor.

The meaning is as follows: the vocative address "O fair-eyed one" (*vāmākṣī*) suggests the beauty of the heroine and the hero's flattering words directed toward her. By the statement, "Kandarpa is merciless toward me, but toward you he is free from envy," the very same matter previously mentioned is indicated through a stylistic turn (*bhaṅgyā*): "Though I desire you, you do not desire me. Thus, by revealing aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through its appeal to the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahr̥daya*), this lack of vulgarity (*agrāmyatā*) brings about the quality of sweetness (*mādhuryya*). || 64 ||

He also demonstrates that vulgarity resides in words themselves with the phrase "even in words. Vulgarity indeed exists even in words; that is "verbal vulgarity" (*śābdagrāmyatā*). That which is "refined" (*sabhya*) or "correct" (*sādhu*), its opposite is "unrefined" (*asabhya*), meaning speech employed by villagers, plowmen, and the like. Because of the mention of such [speech]—the implication being "by cultured people"—[vulgarity] occurs; this is the sense, with "it becomes" understood as the ellipsis.

The sense is this: since the word beginning with the letter *ya*—that is, a word such as *yanbhanādi* (derived from the root *yabh*, meaning "to copulate")—is incomparable for the festival of erotic passion (*ratyutsava*), its employment by a speaker results in his being ridiculed for vulgarity and causes the listener to feel ashamed; consequently, because the savoring of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*) is completely obscured, there is no manifestation of the quality of sweetness (*mādhurya-guṇa*) here. || 65 ||

Demonstrating that what others have described as "obscenity" (*aślīlatā*) is, in his own system, included within "vulgarity" (*grāmyatā*), he says: "pada... etc. The meaning is: *padasandhānam* is a sentence (*vākya*), which is that in which there is a conjunction (*sandhāna*) or inclusion of words. (In the reading *vākyasaṅghāta*, the meaning is the same. By means of its function (*tadvṛttyā*), or by being contained therein (*tadgatatvena*); or again (*punaḥ*), or rather (*athavā*), by means of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthatvena*), or by being contained in that meaning (*tadarthagatatvena*)—this is the sense. That which produces a faulty or defective cognition (*duṣpratīti*) is so called.

The meaning is that *aślīlatva* (indecency) consists in the capacity of a sentence or its meaning to produce feelings such as shame, disgust, impurity, or inauspiciousness; it is included within *grāmyatā* (vulgarity), the sense being that this too is a subverter of sweetness (*mādhurya*). Among these, he provides an example occurring in a sentence, beginning with "for instance" (*yathā*).

The literal meaning is "your beloved wife. However, in the phrase "of you" (*bhavataḥ*), there arises the word *yābhaḥ*, derived from the root *yabha* (meaning "to copulate") with the suffix *ghañ*. Since this implies "one who possesses such [copulation]" (*yābhavān*), the sentence is marred by the defect of vulgarity (*aślīlatva*) because it suggests shamefulness; therefore, the sense is that there is no presence of sweetness (*mādhurya*) here. || 66 ||

Having explained the impropriety residing in the sentence itself, he points out that which resides in its meaning, namely, the word *kharam*. A certain man, powerful and full of prowess, having struck—meaning, having attacked—the enemies with such extreme sharpness (*kharam*), finds rest; this is the meaning consistent with the context. However, [there is also] another meaning: a certain man, powerful and virile (*vīryavān śukralaḥ*), having struck—that is, having engaged in sexual intercourse—with such intensity (*kharam gāḍham*), has found rest. (This is also an indecorous meaning, distinct from the previous one due to the ambiguity of the word.)

It is perceived, and because it manifests shame, it constitutes vulgarity (*grāmyatva*) in the form of semantic indecorum (*arthāślīlatva*); nor should it be thought that here there is indecorum pertaining to the sentence (*vākyāgata-aślīlatva*), for sentence-level indecorum occurs only where a second meaning is understood through verbal suggestion (*śābdī vyañjanā*); whereas where another meaning is perceived through non-verbal suggestion (*ārdhyā vyañjanā*) due to the particularity of the speaker and other factors, [that is a different matter].

And as it has been stated by the author of the *Darpaṇa*: "When a word with multiple meanings is restricted by [contextual factors] such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like, that which causes the cognition of another meaning in one specific sense is *vyañjanā* (suggestion), and it is based upon *abhidhā* (denotation). In this case, however, since it is impossible to restrict the words contained in the sentence beginning with "kharam" (*donkey*, etc.)—which convey only a single meaning each—to a specific context through factors such as *prakaraṇa* (context), the cognition of the second meaning, which is of an incompatible nature, occurs solely through *vyañjanā* based on the particularity of the speaker and so forth; thus, it resides strictly within the meaning (*arthagatatva*).

Furthermore, in the determination of whether defects (*doṣa*), figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), and so forth reside in the word or the meaning, this is established by their capacity or incapacity to withstand the substitution of the word (*śabdaparivṛtti*). In this case, however, although the word *bala* denotes both the sense of strength and the sense of Śukra (the planet Venus), it is accepted as being one because it is the word for Śukra; thus, even when the synonymous word *vīrya* is substituted, since it conveys an indecent meaning, the defect of vulgarity (*aślīlatva*) remains unimpaired, and therefore it resides solely in the meaning.

However, it should be understood that where a fault persists even when the word is substituted with a synonym, in that case alone does the fault reside in the word itself. Such [poetry], characterized by the aforementioned faults such as vulgarity (*grāmyatā*), is what is meant by the term "poetry"—the word "poetry" being the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). (By the word "etcetera," other faulty compositions are included. Neither in the Gauḍa nor in the Vaidarbha path (*mārga*) do the wise praise or respect it; "the wise" being the ellipsis.

(One might object: "Is it not observed that the Gauḍa and Vaidarbha styles are actually the reverse of one another? Therefore, how can there be similarity here? This objection should not be raised, because by the word *prāyaḥ* ("mostly") in the verse, "A reversal of these is mostly seen in the Gauḍa path," he himself has stated that in some instances there is indeed similarity. || 67 ||

He states an exception (*pratiprasava*) to vulgarity with the word "sister" (*bhaginī*). That word whose beginning is "sister," "divine lady" (*bhagavatī*), and so forth—including the terms "vagina" (*yoni*) and "penis" (*liṅga*)—is everywhere in poetry and in common usage accepted as non-defective by people; that is to say, it is acknowledged by the world because there is an absence of the perception of fault when those respective words are employed, since no sense of distaste arises for ordinary people. (And it has been said: "Vulgarity is that which is uttered as loathsome, indecent, or having a crude, blunt, or coarse meaning.")

"Therein, it is not faulty when [the word] is concealed (*saṃvīta*), hidden (*gupta*), or marked (*lakṣita*). Among these, an example of the concealed is: "Exert yourself to unite that self-restrained one with the daughter of the Himalayas, who is purified for his sake; for it was taught by the Self-born (Brahmā) that among women, she alone is capable of being the ground for the pouring of his seed. In this instance, because the phrase "she alone is capable of being the ground for the pouring of his seed" is concealed, even though it is indecorous (*aślīla*), it possesses the nature of a poetic quality (*guṇa*).

"Conventional usage" (*saṃvītatva*) indeed means being employed by all people from time immemorial; and this has been stated as follows: "In this world, it is not appropriate to seek out faults in that which is conventional (*saṃvīta*); for who would perceive indecorousness in the established form of a *śilaṅga*? [The term] "in secret" (*gupteṣu*) refers to those meanings which are not well-known as indecorous; as in: "Although one's birthplace is difficult to abandon, it was traversed by elephants without obstruction; yet, O fortunate sister, this immeasurable man of pride is not your first connection. [In this verse, the word *śilaṅga* is used conventionally to mean "elephant," while its indecorous meaning remains hidden.]

In this case, although the words *janema*, *bhūmisambādha*, and *bhaginī* possess indecorous secondary meanings, they are considered merits because their indecorous senses are concealed by the cultivation of the power of their primary meanings. As it has been said: "The thing itself is concealed by the cultivation of the power of the word-meaning; thus, [words such as] *bhaginī* and *bhagavatī* are not perceived as indecorous. Regarding those indicated by indication (*lakṣita*) which convey indecorous meanings through figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*); for example: "He who placed the seed of himself in the waters, the cause of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)."

"I offer my salutation to him, the slayer of the serpent Śeṣa. Here, although the words *brahmāṇḍa* (the cosmic egg) and *upasthāna* (salutation) cause the recollection of inappropriate objects, they are considered subordinate (*guṇatva*) because they have been employed elsewhere [in a non-offensive sense]. Likewise, in the assembly of those who delight in amorous play, the quality of vulgarity (*aślīlatva*) is treated by others as a subordinate quality when it suggests sentiments such as the peaceful (*śānta*) or the loathsome (*bībhatsa*). Thus, in the manner described, *mādhurya* (sweetness) has been analyzed and demonstrated.
Now, *saukumārya* (tenderness)—that subordinate quality which follows in order—is being discussed. (68)

Regarding the term *anuṣṭhara*: it refers to that [verse] (*padyam*)—the word "verse" being understood as the remainder—in which the syllables (*akṣarāṇi*) are for the most part (*prāyaḥ*), meaning in great abundance, not harsh (*aniṣṭharāṇi*) or rough (*aparuṣāṇi*). This means it is *sukumāra*, i.e., endowed with the quality of softness (*saukumārya*). By the word "for the most part," it is indicated that occasionally harsh syllables should also be inserted. (For this very reason it has been said: "The lack of rigidity in the composition is cited as softness. Here, the particle *tu* expresses a reason.

For, in a composition that is entirely soft (*sarvakomala*), the employment of exclusively delicate syllables results in the defect of looseness (*śaithilyadoṣa*)—that is, the defect of laxity or lack of firmness—as demonstrated in the example cited by me: "like a garland of *mālatī* flowers, swarming with restless bees. Furthermore, that very quality which makes a composition pleasing to the hearts of the connoisseurs through the firmness of its structure, achieved by the strategic placement of harsh syllables amidst many soft ones, is precisely what is designated by the term "delicacy" (*saukumārya*).

The distinction between these two lies in the fact that *śleṣa* (cohesion) consists in the lack of looseness in the composition formed by syllables of few breath-units (*alpaprāṇa*) and many breath-units (*mahāprāṇa*), whereas this *saukumārya* (delicacy) is a quality of sound (*śabdaguṇa*). However, as a quality of meaning (*arthaguṇa*), it is non-roughness (*apāruṣya*) consisting in the absence of vulgarity in the sense. As stated by Vāmana: "Delicacy is non-roughness."

Even when the necessary conditions are present, that which does not produce a melting of the heart and is devoid of aesthetic flavor is called *pārūṣya* (harshness); however, that which is not so, and whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is capable of immediately becoming one with the subject matter, is *sukumāra* (delicate). This is what is meant by *apārūṣya* (absence of harshness). For example: "Having gone only three or four steps on the outskirts of the city—she who was as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower—Sītā, without saying 'there is still some distance to go,' brought about the first shedding of Rāma's tears."

Thus, regarding this passage, the wise should discern that for Rāma—who, hearing Sītā’s words, “How much further must we go even here on the outskirts of the city?”—tears fell upon seeing her limbs as tender as a *śirīṣa* flower, it is precisely the melting of his heart (*cittadruti*), caused by those tears, that constitutes her delicacy (*saukumārya*). 69.

He provides an example of this, saying "maṇḍalī": peacocks (*kalāpin*) in the season garlanded with clouds—that is, during the rainy season—having formed circles (*maṇḍalīkṛtya*), meaning having spread themselves out in a circular shape, and being characterized by throats possessing sounds similar to sweet songs (*madhuragītibhiḥ*), they dance (*pranṛtyanti*). (The third case is used here for a qualifier.)

(Here, amidst soft syllables such as *ma*, *ka*, and others, there is harshness due to the presence of three conjuncts—*maṇḍa*, *kṛtya*, and *barha*—in the first quarter; two conjuncts—*ṇṭhe* and *rm*—in the second; and the visarga-conjoined syllables *naḥ* and *pranṛtyanti* in the third; furthermore, in the fourth quarter, there is harshness because of the intermittent placement of long vowels. Nevertheless, this composition, being for the most part free from harshness, resorts to delicacy.)

And here, because the conventional behavior of dancers is superimposed upon the peacocks (*kalāpin*), the poetic figure is *samāsokti* (abridged expression). As it is stated in the *Darpakāra*: "Samāsokti occurs when, through similarity of action, characteristic mark, or attribute, there is a superimposition of the conventional behavior of another thing upon the subject at hand. (70)

Addressing those moderns who do not accept that the aforementioned kind of delicacy (*saukumārya*) is a poetic quality (*guṇa*), he says "iti" (thus). "Iti" means of the aforementioned kind; "arthaḥ" means the subject matter expressed by the verse beginning with "maṇḍalīkṛtya," namely, the form of the peacock's dance. It is "not *ūrjita*"—meaning not merely forceful or brilliant, but rather not excessively captivating—and the figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is of the nature of *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state) animated by *samāsokti* (speech of brevity). Such [a composition] does not produce such variety; nevertheless, this verse, by virtue of its delicacy (*sukumāratā*)...
