By means of such an arrangement of syllables endowed with the quality of *gauḍīya* (sweetness), the mind of the virtuous—that is, the connoisseurs (*sāmājika*), and not of the ordinary—ascends, that is, takes refuge [in it], or rather, becomes enchanted. This is the underlying sense: whereas the figure of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) is perceived through careful deliberation, the quality (*guṇa*) is not so; for the distinction produced by the quality is perceived even before the understanding of the sense or the figure of sense, because the quality consists in a specific mode of arrangement.

For this very reason it has been said: "Of what use is that poetry, or of what use is such a woman, by whom the mind is not captivated merely through the arrangement of words? By this it is shown that, in the absence of the variety of poetic excellences (*guṇa*), even if there is the variety of figurative meanings (*arthālaṅkāra*), the poetry does not shine in that way. Therefore, King Bhoja has said: "If speech is devoid of excellences, it is like the body of a woman lacking youth; even if its ornaments are beloved by the people, they inevitably fall into a state of misfortune."

By this, it is stated that the *guṇas* reside in the soul (*ātman*), while the *alaṅkāras* reside in the word and the meaning (*śabda* and *artha*). And it has been said: "The *guṇas* are ten. Vāmana and others have stated that *rīti* is the soul, that the *guṇas* reside in the *rīti* which constitutes the soul, and that the *alaṅkāras* reside in the word and meaning which constitute its body.

The author of the *Dhvanyāloka* also established that *dhvani* constitutes the soul (*ātman*), while the *guṇas* (poetic qualities) reside therein; he likewise accepted that the pair of word and meaning constitutes the body (*śarīra*), and that the *alaṅkāras* (figures of speech) reside therein as well. Thus, we consider it the author’s intention that, by virtue of being *guṇas*, *śleṣa* and the like exist in the soul through the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*); whereas, by virtue of being *alaṅkāras*, *yamaka*, *upamā*, and the like exist in the body through the mode of conjunction (*saṃyoga-vṛtti*).

For even one who is not wise would not assert or recognize that qualities reside in the self as if in a channel, or that figures of speech reside in the pair of word and meaning—which serves as their body—as if by way of inherence; this is what should be understood. (71)

To demonstrate the difference of opinion between the Gauḍas and the Vaidarbhas regarding delicacy (*saukumārya*), he says: "The radiant" (*dīptam*). By others—the Gauḍa poets—"radiance" (*dīpti*) means brilliance; that is, the expansion of the mind through the arousal of energy (*utsāha*). That which is endowed with this is "radiant," meaning it is stimulating by its nature consisting of the heroic (*vīra*), the furious (*raudra*), and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) sentiments. For this reason—that is, because of its vigor (*ojasvitva*)—even that which is difficult to compose is [considered such] due to its abundance, because it consists of harsh phonemes (*paruṣavarṇa*) that manifest vigor.

The sense is that even that which is elevated with difficulty, and even that which is devoid of softness (*saukumārya*), is "bound"—that is, it is strung together or composed. For the Gauḍīyas do not admit softness in that context, because they hold that when the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) consists of a radiant sentiment such as the Heroic (*vīra-rasa*), it is precisely the arrangement of harsh syllables that serves as its suggester (*vyañjaka*), and thus that alone is appropriate. This is the intended meaning.

Just as by Dhṛtarāṣṭra—who was completely (*nyakṣeṇa*) sightless, meaning blind—the host (*pakṣa*), that is, the entire assembly of Kṣatriyas, meaning the whole Kṣatriya clan, was destroyed (*kṣayitaḥ*), ruined; [this occurred] in a mere moment (*kṣaṇāt*), that is, in a very short time, during the Battle of Kurukṣetra (as is understood from the context).

However, some hold that *nyañcaḥ* refers to those who bow down—that is, those who perform base deeds—such as Kārtavīrya; and that *nyakṣaḥ* refers to Paraśurāma because he "scatters" (*syati*) or destroys them. They consider this meaning of the word *nyakṣa* to be "difficult" (*kṛcchra*), for it is inappropriate for the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) in the context of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s destruction of the Kṣatriyas. (In this regard, the Gauḍīya school maintains that when describing the heroic sentiment, the employment of harsh-sounding and rough syllables alone produces aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*); thus, the abandonment of softness (*saukumārya*) is actually a merit.)

The Vaidarbhas, however, cherish delicacy even in such compositions as those possessing the heroic (*vīra*), loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and furious (*raudra*) sentiments; this distinction between the two [styles] should be understood here. For example: "By those beast-like men—who, raising their weapons, were devoid of all restraint, and who have done, approved, or witnessed this great crime—along with Naraka’s enemy (Kṛṣṇa), together with Bhīma and Arjuna, I shall now offer a sacrifice to the quarters with their blood and flesh! Thus [ends the example].

In this case, even though the sentiment is the Furious (raudra), excessively harsh syllables have not been employed; therefore, for the Vaidarbhas, the abandonment of softness (*saukumārya*) is indeed a defect. As stated by King Bhoja in the context of defects: "From the reversal of softness, the harsh arises. || 72 ||

He states the quality called *arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning) along with its illustration, beginning with the words "Arthavyakti. The meaning is that *arthavyakti* is the non-ambiguity (*aneyatva*) of the sense; it is the presentation [of the meaning] from the very words employed, without the need for forced constructions such as supplying ellipses (*adhyāhāra*). As stated by Kramadīśvara: "The full expression of what is to be expressed—that is the definition of *arthavyakti*. Likewise, Bhoja has also said: "They call that *arthavyakti* wherein there is the completeness of the sentence."

Thus, the conclusion is that wherever and however many types of qualifiers and qualificands are intended, all of them are understood without obstruction by the mere collection of words employed; therein lies "clarity of meaning" (*arthavyakti*). For example, in the verse "As if speech and meaning were joined together," the first person singular pronoun "I" (*aham*) is obtained solely through the use of the first person singular verb form "I praise" (*vande*), because of the rule stating "the substitute [is like] the original" (*sthānini*) in the context of "the first person is not used with the madhyama [person]."

What [is the object]? In response to this expectation for an object (*karman*), [the answer is] "Pārvatī and Parameśvara. And of what nature are they? "The parents of the world. For what purpose does he offer salutation? "For the comprehension of word and meaning"—thus, through the completion of the sentence, the meaning becomes manifest. Regarding this, the moderns (*navya*) hold that this [clarity] pertains only to the words (*śabda-gā*); as for clarity pertaining to the meaning (*artha-gā*), since it is already subsumed under the figure of speech *svabhāvokti* (description of inherent nature), it is not mentioned separately. The ancients (*prācya*), however, accept that there is also a manifestation of meaning (*ārthī arthavyakti*).

This has been stated by Daṇḍin: "Clarity of meaning (*arthavyakti*) is the making manifest of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). He explains this clarity of meaning as follows: "Clarity of meaning is the vividness of the essential nature of the thing. Likewise, Bhoja has also said: "Clarity of meaning is said to be the direct statement of the thing's own form."

The meaning of *arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning) is this: it is the direct expression of the *svarūpa*—the form that is a source of wonder accessible solely through the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*)—which, by virtue of the poet’s power, possesses words that generate a cognition akin to direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). An example of this is as follows: "On the backs of the lotus petals, which possess the luster of conch fragments, the water-lily in the pond rejoices, its outer leaves brownish-tawny with yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), while the interior is intensely red with lac-dye, marked by a single line."

Thus, in this context, because the very nature of the night-lotus (*kumuda*) is perceived as if directly present, that explicit expression of its form is what constitutes *arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning) pertaining to the sense. Others, however, call the quality of words conveying meaning instantaneously *śābdī arthavyakti* (verbal clarity of meaning); as it has been said: "For *arthavyakti* is the immediate presentation of the meaning by words. Furthermore: "Where the movement of speech is as if from behind and the object [appears] as if from the front, because it serves as the cause for the manifestation of meaning, that is remembered as the quality of *arthavyakti*."

Thus: by Hari, in the form of a boar (Varāha), that is, by Viṣṇu; with his own hooves—that is the meaning—by means of the blood of the crushed serpents, that is, the *pannagas* who dwell in the subterranean realm (*rasātala*), from the red, that is, the bloody ocean, the earth—the world—was lifted up, brought to the surface. Here, as many words as there are, so many meanings are understood without any forced interpretation. || 73 ||

By stating that "the manifestation of meaning consists in being not subject to misinterpretation" (*aneyatvam arthavyaktiḥ*), [the author] indicates that there is a requirement for knowledge of what is not subject to misinterpretation. When the expectation arises as to "what kind of thing is that," he demonstrates what is meant by "not subject to misinterpretation" with the word "mahī. When such a description—namely, "the earth was lifted from the red ocean by the Great Boar"—is presented and employed, then for this word *uragāsṛjaḥ*, "being subject to misinterpretation" (*neyatvam*)—that is, the necessity of being understood through supplementation (*adhyāhāreṇa*)—occurs; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

For instance, when "red" is stated, there arises an expectation as to "how," and the portion "by the blood of elephants crushed by hooves" must be stated; since this is not possible without ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), the word *na* is used, for otherwise the meaning would not be clear—this is the intended sense.

(Where, due to a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) that is otherwise possible, there would be an inconsistency in the subsequent comprehension of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*), there the meaning must be led [to consistency] through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and so forth; likewise, even when a meaning is understood by accepting a figurative sense applied in the absence of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or a specific purpose (*prayojana*), that meaning is still to be led [to consistency], and there is no manifestation of the meaning [as it stands]. || 74 ||

Here, he demonstrates the similarity between both paths with the word "not. Between both paths—that is, between the two specific styles (*rīti*), Vaidarbhī and Gauḍī—the poets (the ellipsis being supplied) do not highly regard, nor do they honor, such a sentence as previously described, which is characterized by being "neyārtha" (requiring forced interpretation). Furthermore, in this case, what has been stated by others as a fault regarding the manifestation of meaning (*arthavyakti*) actually constitutes a merit. (As it has been said: "A sentence becomes *neyārtha* due to the reversal of the manifestation of meaning.")

For "the rule of words" (śabdanyāya) means the restriction governing verbal cognition, whose nature is that the understanding of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs only among those meanings conveyed by the words themselves and presented through their respective functions (*vṛtti*). "Transgressing that" means achieving its violation; "cognition" refers to the understanding of syntactic connection through arduous mental constructions such as supplying ellipses (*adhyāhāra*), and so forth; "not beautiful" means not correct or proper.

(One should note that this was stated while relying on the theory of qualified denotation (*viśiṣṭa-śakti-vāda*); for the cognition of a meaning supplied through ellipsis or brought forth by implication, as well as the cognition of another meaning resulting from the consideration of the intended sense (*tātparya*), arise only after the verbal comprehension [of the literal sentence] has occurred, and therefore they do not constitute verbal comprehension itself. || 75 ||

He defines the quality of *audārya* (loftiness) as "utkarṣa" (excellence). When a certain sentence is uttered or spoken, if a specific quality (*guṇa*), which is a particular attribute (*dharmaviśeṣa*) that produces excellence in the subject being described and causes a world-transcending aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), is perceived or understood, then that sentence is "udāra"—that is, possessed of the quality of *audārya*. Thus, the definition is: *audārya* is a description characterized by the perception of an attribute that generates excellence.

And *jhrutkarṣa* (superiority) occurs sometimes through delicacy, sometimes through generosity, heroism, and so forth, sometimes through rusticity (*grāmyatva*), and sometimes through non-rusticity (*agrāmyatva*). For this very reason, Vāmana stated in the context of rusticity that "non-rusticity is *udāratā*," providing the definition: "Non-rusticity is *udāratā*. And he himself illustrated it there with the following example: "You are thus possessed of beauty, and he is well-acquainted with loveliness; you two alone here attain the supreme limit of the arts."

"O fortunate one! By good fortune, that pair [of qualities] corresponds; if the remainder should also agree with the opinion held, then victory has been achieved here by the Guṇitā. And so, he says "by that," meaning that by this quality of *udāratva* (loftiness), the path of poetry—the style of composition belonging to both the Gauḍa and Vaidarbha traditions—is rendered well-supported, complete, and excellent. This demonstrates that even when there is a clear distinction between the Gauḍa and Vaidarbha styles, they are shown to be identical in such loftiness.

Regarding the statement, "In the Gauḍa path, a reversal of these [qualities] is generally observed," the inclusion of the word *prāyaḥ* (generally) implies that in some instances there is even a similarity between the Gauḍa and Vaidarbha styles. This [reversal] pertains to meaning (*arthagata*); however, that which pertains to sound (*śabdagata*) is characterized by *vikaṭatva* (grandiosity). The meaning of *vikaṭatva* is that it is the quality of words being as if dancing—such that when it is present, people have the impression that the words are actually dancing. And Vāmana has stated: "Grandiosity is *udāratā* (nobility)."

And it has been illustrated by that very same [author] as follows: "There, the anklets fixed upon their own feet produced a 'jhaṇiti' sound from the dancers, which was both wonderful and sweet. A counter-example is as follows: "There, the anklets clinging to the lotus-feet of the dancers produced a 'jhaṭiti' sound, which was charming and wonderful. By this, the following is also indicated: for "vikaṭatva" (extraordinary quality) is indeed "vakratva" (artistic curvature); indeed, without the curvature of both word and meaning, the attainment of the status of poetry is not possible.

And this has been stated: "That speech which is crooked in both the treatise and the world is merely speech; that which is crooked [in its expression] yet bestows passion (*anurāga*) is known as *kāvya*. However, others maintain that when there is the opposite of this, one accepts the fault of "lack of nobility" (*audārya-viparyaya-doṣa*), being devoid of ornamentation. As they say: "Those who know ornaments recognize that sentence as lacking ornamentation which, due to the failure to sustain the style (*rīti*), is a reversal of nobility. For example: "Long-tailed, four-footed, humped, with a hanging dewlap..."

"The offspring of a cow (gorapatya) eats grass with its mouth like a bull"—this is said to be "unrefined" (*anudāra*) because of its lack of significant meaning (*apuṣṭārthatva*), lacking an excellent qualifier (*anutkṛṣṭaviśeṣaṇa*), and devoid of ornament (*niralaṅkāra*). This is the defect called "the reversal of excellence" (*audāryaviparyaya*), which consists primarily in a deficiency of the qualities (*guṇaviparyaya*) pertaining to both word and sense. 76.

He shows an example of magnanimity with the words "of those who seek" (*arthinām*). O King! The gaze of supplicants—pitiable and wretched—has fallen upon your face again and again; yet, remaining in that same wretched state, it does not look toward the face of another. (By this, it is indicated that the King possesses such power of abundant giving that there is no need for supplicants to approach other donors; this is the heart of the matter, which is exceedingly striking to those of sensitive taste. || 77 ||

Regarding the word *iti*: in this sentence of the aforementioned form, the excellence (*utkarṣa*) of renunciation—that is, of giving—which consists in its capacity to impart a particular variety [of aesthetic flavor], is well (*sādhu*) observed, perceived, or experienced by the audience; such is the meaning. In the reading "khalu" instead of "sādhu," the word "khalu" means "certainly."

In other verses as well, by this very same path or manner previously shown, that which possesses a similar or equal logic or rule—let that be inferred or contemplated; the meaning is that one should compose a verse by resorting to this very same method. 78.

He shows a difference of opinion with the words "ślāghyaiḥ" (by praiseworthy [adjectives]). By "ślāghyaiḥ" (praiseworthy), it is meant those adjectives which, by imparting excellence to the particular [subject], are pleasing to the audience; "yuktam" (joined) means endowed with; "viśeṣaṇaiḥ" (by adjectives)—the use of the plural indicates that this quality [of *audārya*] does not exist when there is only one or two adjectives; "vākyam" (sentence) is "udāram" (lofty), meaning endowed with the quality of loftiness (*audārya*); this is what is desired by certain poets.

(Note: It should be understood that the phrase "by some" (*kaiścit*) is stated to indicate that this position—that it is improper to speak of [the figure] as a *guṇa* because a sentence possessing qualifiers conforming to the intended meaning is free from the fault of "lack of enrichment" (*apuṣṭārthatva*) and is instead the ornament *parikara*—is not the author's own view. He illustrates the point already stated with the word "for example" (*yathā*).

For example, in the case of "Līlāmbujakrīḍāmaro Hemāṅgadādayaḥ," by the qualifier *līlā* (playful) in the term *līlāmbuja* (play-lotus), there is the perception of its excellence in color, form, and fragrance; by the expression *krīḍāsaraḥ* (pleasure-lake), there is the perception of the beauty produced by the lotuses, water-lilies, and so forth used for play; and likewise, by saying *hemāṅgada* (golden armlet), there is the perception of the armlet’s great visibility due to its being made of gold. Thus, it should be understood that [the compound] is enchanting to the hearts of connoisseurs. || 79 ||

He defines the quality of *ojas* (vigor) with the words "Ojas is... A compound (*samāsa*) is the unification of two or more words; its abundance means its frequency or length—that is to say, a compound consisting of many words. This is *ojas*, which constitutes the very life-force of the aforementioned prose (*gadya*), specifically that particular literary composition (*prabandha*) characterized by the *utkalikā* and other forms. And this [quality] is common to both poetic paths (*mārga*). To demonstrate the difference [between them], he says: "Even in verse (*padye'pi*)."

"Of the non-Dakṣiṇātyas" means those other than the Dakṣiṇātyas, namely the Gauḍas. Although the word "api" (even) appears in the verse, it is employed here to include prose as well. "This is the one, the peerless, supreme resort"—the sense is that this is their ultimate goal because they cherish the tightness of their bonds [of style]. Furthermore, this charm resides in the words, since a compound pertains solely to the words themselves.

Vāmana, however, states that the tightness of composition (*bandha*) is *ojaḥ* as it pertains to sound (*śabda*), as in: "The tightness of composition is *ojaḥ*"; and that the maturity of the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is *ojaḥ* as it pertains to meaning (*artha*), as in: "The maturity of the meaning is *ojaḥ*. Having thus defined its characteristics, he established its fivefold nature as follows: "The expression of a sentence in the place of a word-meaning, and the expression of a word-meaning in the place of a sentence-meaning; as well as mature expansion (*prauḍhavyāsa*) and contraction (*samāsa*), and the presence of intention (*sābhiprāyatva*)—these are its [five] varieties."

In that regard, the expression of a sentence (*vākya*) when a single word-meaning (*padārtha*) should be expressed is as follows: "Now, like the sky [beholding] the light arising from the eyes of Atri... Here, while the single word-meaning "moon" ought to be stated, the expression of a sentence is used: "the light arising from the eyes of Atri.

The expression of a word (*pada*) when the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) should be expressed is as follows: while it ought to be said, "This is not divine, but rather human," one says "she blinks. Or, for instance, in some cases, while the meaning of the sentence "an excellent woman, delicate-bodied, [exposed to] the heat of summer and the cold of winter" ought to be expressed, there is the expression of the word "two excellent women" (*varavarinī*).

In some cases, *vyāsa* (expansion) is the expression of a single sentence-meaning through many sentences by introducing certain qualifications; in other cases, *samāsa* (contraction) is the expression of what is conveyed by many sentences through a single sentence. Regarding these, an example of *vyāsa* is as follows: "This manifold experience of the intermingling of pleasure and pain becomes either pleasure or pain, or it does not become [either], yet it certainly exists from that [source]."

"Furthermore, above that, there is some kind of pleasure and pain; furthermore, above that, there is neither pain nor pleasure. Thus [it is said]. As for the compound (samāsa), it is as follows: "Having taken leave of Himālaya and having looked again upon the Wielder of the Trident (Śūlin), and having reported the matter accomplished to him, they, being dismissed by him, departed for their own [abodes]. Thus [it is said].

*Intentionality* (*sābhiprāyatva*) is the capacity to convey a specific meaning without the employment of other words; for example: "This very son of Candragupta, Candraprakāśa, a youth, has now become king—the refuge of those with cultured intellects; by good fortune, his efforts have borne fruit. Here, the phrase "refuge of those with cultured intellects" possesses intentionality because it is intended to suggest Subandhu’s assistance. However, some say that the aforementioned fourfold *prauḍhi* (boldness) is a verbal quality (*śabdaguṇa*), whereas intentionality is a semantic quality (*arthaguṇa*). 80.

Regarding the word *tat*: that is *ojas* (vigorousness), which consists in an abundance of compounds. "Of the heavy" (*gurūṇām*) means of those syllables characterized by great effort, namely those pronounced with long articulatory effort (*dīrghaprayatna*) as parts of the words forming a compound; "of the light" (*laghūnām*) means of those soft syllables pronounced with little effort, namely those of low breath-force (*alpaprāṇa*). "Abundance" (*bāhulyam*) refers to their frequent employment in the sentence; "scarcity" (*alpatvam*) refers to their infrequent employment; "mixture" (*miśraṇam*) refers to their equality [in number]. By these [factors] acting as instruments, it becomes manifold (*uccāvacaprakāram*), consisting of many varieties; and that [manifoldness] occurs sometimes through an abundance of heavy syllables.

It may occur through the scarcity of short compounds, or in some cases through the abundance of short compounds and the scarcity of long ones, or in some instances through the mixture of both types; this is to be observed in prose works such as the *ākhyāyikā* (and by "etcetera," the inclusion of *campū*, *viruda*, and so forth). Furthermore, by the mention of the *ākhyāyikā*, it follows that even in the *kathā* when the *raudra* (fierce) or other such rasas are present, long compounds should not be employed.

Furthermore, it should be noted that even in the verse-texts of the Gauḍīya school, such as the *Sūryaśataka* and others, an abundance of compounds has been mentioned previously. In the third quarter, for the word "tat," some manuscripts read "sat"; for "prakāram," they read "prakāreṇa"; and for "dṛśyam," they read "dṛṣṭam. (81)

He demonstrates the Gauḍa school's preference for an abundance of compounds even in verse, beginning with "asta...": The western direction—implied—is one whose covering (*saṃstara*) consists of all the rays of the sun (*arkāṃśu*) that have fallen (*paryasta*) upon the summit (*astamastaka*) of the sunset mountain (*astācala*). It is like a beautiful (*kamra*) garment, slightly reddened (*ātāmra*) and resting upon full breasts; the sense is that this is because the solar rays of the evening time are naturally so. The word *vāruṇī* refers to the direction presided over by Varuṇa. The word *vastra* [is used here] in the sense of a covering.

She who is thus [described], like a woman of passion (*kāminī*), shines—this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). (In both of these quarters, there is an abundance of compounds. King Bhoja also, having stated the definition "Vigor (*ojas*) is an abundance of compounds," cited a verse rich in compounds as an example, as follows: "Victorious is he by whose skull-cups—[cups] from which the state of being a corpse has ceased due to the flowing nectar squeezed out by the ropes of his arms acting as a noose... )

The resonant Vedic chant of the many matured Brahmās upon the head of Purāri, which instantly forms a bond of praise, [is an example]. Here, because of the abundance of compounds beginning with "the knot of the serpent-rope" (*bhujagarajjugranthi*), there is the verbal quality known as *ojas* (vigor). || 82 ||

Having demonstrated the abundance of compounds favored by the Gauḍas, he introduces another opinion with two verses beginning with "iti. The "Easterners" (paurastyāḥ) are the inhabitants of Gauḍa; in the manner previously described, they compose verses (*padye*) that are forceful (*ojasvinīḥ*), meaning abounding in compounds. But others, namely the learned (*paṇḍitāḥ*), [prefer] that which is "unconfused" (*anākula*)—here there is a reference to the state (*bhāva-nirdeśaḥ*)—meaning the quality of being unconfused (*anākulatvam*). This consists in the absence of long compounds and the like, because these act as obstacles to immediate comprehension; that is to say, it is the absence of such things. Furthermore, it is "pleasing" (*hṛdyam*), meaning it captivates the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya-manohāri*). And "force" (*ojaḥ*) is the essential meaning of the term; this is the conclusion. || 83 ||

Here he provides an illustration, beginning with "yathā" (as follows): *payodhara* means a cloud, and [here] *payodhara* means a breast; that very [cloud/breast] is the slope (*taṭa*), the region. The evening glow (*sandhyātapa*)—the radiance of the sun's rays at twilight—is clinging to its lap (*utsaṅga*). She whose *aṃśuka* (garment) is such [an evening glow] is the western direction (*vāruṇī*), meaning the west. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Whose heart will she not render afflicted by love?"

(Here, although there is an abundance of compounds in the first half-verse, as before, they do not tax the intellect of the listeners but rather produce mere pleasure for their ears. In the second half-verse, in the phrase "kāmāturam," there is a paucity of compounds, and elsewhere there are no compounds at all; nevertheless, because there is no looseness of composition, it delights the audience.)

And thus, even in a composition that conveys a meaning entered by intense flavor (*dīptarasa*), where the intensity of the meaning is not obstructed in the absence of compounds, the lack of compound is accepted as a merit (*guṇa*) itself, and not as a defect (*doṣa*) resulting from the reversal of a merit. As it has been said: "Intensity (*ojas*) consists in an abundance of compounds; it is employed in the case of intense meanings. Its reverse is the absence of compounds; if that [absence] is intense, it does not incur the status of a defect."

Regarding this, an example has been cited: "Whosoever among the Pāṇḍava armies bears a weapon with great pride in his own arms," and so forth. Here, although there is a lack of *samāsa* (compound), its status as a *guṇa* (poetic quality) is established because of the maturity of the composition (*prauḍhabandhatva*). Thus, the coexistence [of qualities] is demonstrated. Therefore, it should be understood that what was previously explained here as *ojaḥ*—the verbal quality consisting of compactness—is actually *prasāda*. || 84 ||

He defines the quality of *kānti* (loveliness): "The word *kāntim*" [is used]. The meaning is: because it does not transgress—that is, does not abandon—the worldly, i.e., that which is established in common experience, and because it describes only that; [it refers to] that which is lovely and charming to all the world, common to everyone. Because there is an absence of defects such as ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and because the comprehension of the syntactical connection (*anvaya-bodha*) is easy due to the ease with which the meaning is understood, it is "pleasing to the hearts" (*hṛdya*) of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*). The word "verse" (*padya*) is to be supplied as the subject; thus, "lovely" means distinguished by the quality of *kānti*.

And thus, the quality of *kānti* (loveliness) is precisely the description of objects that are accompanied by sounds which delight the minds of sensitive readers (*sahṛdayas*). As it has been stated by Kramadīśvara: "That description which is devoid of hyperbole (*atyukti*) is called *kānta*. This *kānti* resides in the meaning (*artha*), because there is no apprehension of it in the absence of a consideration of the meaning.

And that lovely speech—where *vārtā* means pleasant conversation (based on the statement: "In the context of health or pleasant conversation, *vārtā* and *vārtā* are spoken")—is seen in her utterances (*abhidhāneṣu*), that is, in her narrations, as well as in her descriptions (*varṇanāsu*), which are the mere delineation of the form of an object. The sense is that since it is appropriate to describe things exactly as they are in inquiries after health, in pleasant conversations, and in descriptions, a discrepancy with worldly convention would arise if one were to describe them otherwise.

Some, however, interpret the phrase "in the narration of news" (*vārtābhidhāneṣu*) to mean "in the descriptions of historical accounts" (*itihāsavarṇaneṣu*), arguing that it is only logical to describe historical events exactly as they occurred. They maintain that if the description were untrue, the audience would not engage with it at all due to false cognition; consequently, the instruction regarding what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided—such as "one should act like Rāma and not like Rāvaṇa"—would be impossible.

By this [it is shown that] there is no fault even when there is a description that is not as it truly is, provided it is other than a description of news or a factual report; for this very reason, modern [theorists] have stated that poetry is of two kinds, according to whether the suggestive meaning (*vyañjakārtha*) is inherently possible (*svataḥ-sambhavī*) or established through bold assertion (*prauḍhokti-siddha*). (85)

In explaining the word *vārtā* (news), he shows [the meaning] with the word *gṛhān*. Those very houses are what is denoted by the word *gṛha*; the sense is that they are "praiseworthy houses," because the word *gṛha* here functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean "excellent houses"—this is the intended meaning. A mass of austerity (*taporāśiḥ*), one of great asceticism, such as your honor—a noble person—honors (*sambhāvayati*), that is, purifies, those houses with the dust of his feet (*pādapāṃśubhiḥ*), which are sanctifying (*pāvanaiḥ*).

(For this is news in the form of pleasant speech; and since the excellence of the place—characterized as an object of description—is established by common worldly experience through contact with the region of great-souled persons, it should be understood that this is the *kānti* (elegant diction) consisting of the expression of such news. || 86 ||

He illustrates *kānti* (loveliness) in description with the verse beginning "of these two" (*anayor*). O lady of faultless limbs, O beautiful-bodied one! In the space between your vine-like arms—that is, in the center of your two arms, upon your chest—there is no sufficient room for the two swelling, expanding jar-like breasts to remain. The sense is that, because the breasts resemble the frontal globes of elephants, they can only somehow find a place upon the chest—which is relatively small in comparison—by pressing against one another.

In this description, the fact that the breasts remain pressed against the chest is a matter well-known in the world. Therefore, because the description does not overstep the bounds of worldly reality, the quality of *kānti* (loveliness) is present here.

[87] Regarding the two verses mentioned, he connects them with the word "iti" (thus). The sense is that the subject matter established by the two preceding verses is indeed possible; it is not something that must be imagined through poetic exaggeration (*prauḍhokti*) as if it were impossible.

And this [beauty] becomes lovely and delightful to every person—who follows the ways of the world and is devoted to worldly conduct—when it is "adorned with a specific description" (*viśeṣākhyāna*). By this term, "specific description" is meant a qualifier that conveys variety; when [the subject] is embellished by such a qualifier, it becomes charming. By this it is shown that beauty arises only through the description of an object well-known in the world that possesses qualifiers conveying excellence, and not merely through the description of an object established in the world.

If that were the case, then even such statements as "the sun sets" or "the cow lies down" would incur the status of poetry (*kāvyatva*), since they are possible in common worldly usage and thus possess *kānti* (loveliness); for the description of such [ordinary] qualifiers does not produce *vaicitrya* (charm), and *vaicitrya* alone constitutes the nature of *guṇa* and so forth, and it is the possession of *guṇas*, *alaṅkāras*, and the like that constitutes poetry—this should be discerned by the wise. Others, however, say that *arthagā kānti* (loveliness residing in the meaning) exists only where the *rasas* such as *śṛṅgāra* appear with brilliance.

For it has been stated by Vāmana: "Lustre (*kānti*) is the state of having radiant aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). And the example given there is as follows: "When her beloved was dismissed at evening after he had prostrated at her feet with oaths, before he could take two or three steps from the bedchamber with a heavy heart, she ran forward and held him by his hips, where the knot of her lower garment was loosening from her slipping hands—having already made her salutation! Oh, how varied is the course of love! However, that which consists of brilliance (*aujjvalya*) is a quality of sound (*śabda-guṇa*).

As Vāmana stated: "Lustre (*kānti*) is brilliance (*aujjvalya*). And this brilliance consists in possessing a supermundane beauty by avoiding words used in common parlance by plowmen and the like; for example, instead of saying "leaf," one says "sprout" (*kisalaya*); instead of saying "in the ocean," one says "in the king"; and instead of saying "like a lotus," one says "it acts like a lotus" (*kamalāyate*), and so forth. Furthermore: "That brilliance of the composition which exists in poetry is desired as *kānti*," as in the example: "The vicinity of the forest rows was thick with the eyes of the female deer. (88)

He states the disagreement of the Gauḍas regarding the beauty of etymological derivation (*niruktakānti*) with the words "loka... and so forth. Here, the word *iva* has the sense of *api* ("even"). The meaning is: even an object that is "excessive" (*atyartha*), "transcending the world" (*lokātīta*), and "extraordinary" (*alaukika*), when it is "superimposed" (*adhyāropya*)—that is, imagined—and "intended" (*vivakṣita*) for expression, being employed by those who are "clever" (*budha*) and who pride themselves on being sensitive connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*)—(this is a sarcastic remark)—meaning the Gauḍas, they are "highly pleased. The underlying idea is that this is because they are fond of bold assertions (*prauḍhokti*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no comprehension of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) because the intended meaning lacks fitness due to superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and the like; for in the case of the figure of speech *rūpaka* in examples such as "the luxuriance [of her hair]," all theorists of poetics accept the syntactic connection of identity through the knowledge of *āhārya*—as it has been stated: "Even when there is sublation (*bādha*), the state of being employed by the cognizer's desire is what constitutes *āhāryatva*. Therefore, it has been said: "For a word indeed produces a cognition even regarding an object that is absolutely non-existent."

The meaning is that other people—the poets of Vidarbha—are not [the ones who favor it], because they delight in describing things as they truly are; consequently, the implied sense is that the aforementioned *kānti* (elegant diction) is not accepted by the Gauḍas at all. 89.

In the *Vārttika*, he describes the opposite of the definition of "desirability" (*kānti*), saying "O God": "From this day forward, our house—having its entire sin and transgression washed away by the falling of the dust of your feet, the falling of the pollen of your feet—shall become like the abode of a deity (*devadhiṣṇya*), worthy of worship and service. This is the sense.

(Here, although it is a worldly fact that the touch of the dust of the feet of great souls purifies a house, the poet has superimposed upon it the quality of being worthy of worship like a temple of the gods; thus, a reversal of the intended beauty (*kānti-viparyaya*) is to be understood.

| 90 | He describes the reversal of the aforementioned beauty in the description, saying "insignificant" (*alpa*): "The swelling—that is, the growth—of your breasts will be so extensive; without having considered this, without even reflecting upon it, the Creator fashioned the sky as something insignificant."

In this passage, by means of a description based on hyperbole—wherein even the Creator, though acting with full deliberation, failed to perceive [the vastness of space] and thus fashioned even the great sky as small—the extraordinary plumpness and height of the breasts, which resemble *vilva* and *dāḍima* fruits, are established despite being improbable. All of this that is being described is indeed contrary to worldly convention; therefore, it should be understood that the "splendor" (*kānti*) defined previously is not present here.

However, some, following the Vaidarbha style, maintain that in the absence of such *kānti* (elegant diction), there is a defect pertaining to the poetic qualities (*guṇa*) called the "absence of *kānti*"; as it is said: "A sentence is called *grāmya* (vulgar) due to the absence of *kānti*. For example: "O maiden! Why do you not desire me, who am languishing in separation from you and sitting right beside you, longing for you? This is considered a defect consisting in the absence of *kānti* because of its vulgarity (*grāmyatā*), which is primarily a matter of meaning. (91)

"This" refers to this kind of poetry. "Exaggerated" (*atyukti*) means it is spoken with the designation of *atyukti*; the word "by poets" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. (As stated by King Bhoja: "Where a mode of expression is described that transcends worldly reality, that is called *atyukti*, for the delight of the minds of the Gauḍas. This verse has been cherished—that is, accepted for its heart-pleasing quality—by the Gauḍa poets.

Previously, it was stated that the *prasthāna*—the mode consisting of the description of objects established in the world—is the essence of the other path, namely the Vaidarbha way; that is to say, it is captivating. The point is that this very distinction between the Gauḍa and Vaidarbha styles consists in the description of objects, whether well-known or obscure, within the quality of *kānti*. || 92 ||

He defines *samādhi* with examples, beginning with the words "another property" (*anyadharma*), and so forth. [The phrase] "by the speaker" (*vaktrā*) is to be supplied; [this means] by one who conforms to the limits of the world (*lokasīmānurodhinā*), that is, by following the established conventions of the world (*lokasthitim anuvartamānena*), or rather, by following properties well-known in the world (*lokaprasiddhadharmam anusaratā*). (By this, it is indicated that this is not *samādhi* when one imposes a property contrary to worldly convention according to one's own whim.

For example, in the verse "Where mosquitoes grow large, there sleep is very difficult to find," the imposition of the elephant-property of "growing large" (*vṛṃhaṇa*) upon a mosquito is contrary to worldly convention.)

When a quality, action, or other property belonging to one thing—that is, something non-contextual (*aprakṛta*)—is properly attributed (*ādhīyate*), meaning superimposed (*āropita*) through a metaphorical indication (*gauṇī lakṣaṇā*) characterized by complete identification (*sādhyavasānā*), onto another thing that is distinct from it, namely the contextual subject (*prakṛta*), within the sense of a sentence; that [sentence] is endowed with the poetic quality (*guṇa*) called *samādhi*. Thus, when there is a superimposition of identity (*tādātmyāropa*) upon the contextual object by means of the non-contextual property of a similar object, through the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of its own property and the forceful imposition of the other's property, provided this is well-known in the world, it is *samādhi*.

The meaning of the verse is as follows. It has been stated by others as well: "Metaphorical identification (*samādhi*) is the superimposition of the attributes of one thing upon another. By using the term "attribute" (*dharma*), it is indicated that when the substratum (*dharmī*) itself is superimposed, this is not merely a quality, but rather the figure of speech known as *atiśayokti* (hyperbole); for example: "At the foot of the creeper lies the moon, deprived of its deer; from the water-lily falls a stream of water in the form of shimmering stars."

"Even the breeze born from *tilaka* flowers shakes the *bandhūka* blossoms; the merit of some fortunate person ripens even within the heart of fire. In such instances, there is the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of a subject—such as the moon—upon another subject—such as the face. (93)

Regarding the phrase "the night-lotuses" (*kumudāni*): for instance, the night-lotuses (*kumudāni*) close, that is, they undergo contraction, while the day-lotuses (*kamalāni*) open and expand. (This is a description of dawn; during the day, the closing and opening of the night-lotuses and day-lotuses—which are not [normally] associated with eyes—are metaphorically attributed to the closing and opening of the petals of the night-lotuses and day-lotuses, respectively, through the power of an extreme similarity between these two properties and their substrates, which is established in the world). He points this very thing out himself with the word "thus" (*iti*).

Thus, together with the two aforementioned ocular actions—closing and opening—the *adhyāsa* (superimposition) consists in the attribution of identity to the closing and opening of the petals of the night-lotus and the day-lotus. The *śruti* (scriptural expression), which denotes those two—meaning the word expressing those respective actions such as "closing" and so forth—is "obtained," that is, acquired, by virtue of its conveying the sense of contraction and expansion.

Because these two possess such an excellence of similarity that they are almost indistinguishable, they are seen to be expressible by a single word, as in such examples as "the night-lily closes, the eye closes" or "the lotus opens, the eye opens. Here, the contextual attribute—consisting of contraction and expansion—is swallowed up in its own nature; and because it is perceived through its similarity [to the other], it is identified with closing and opening. This is the quality of *samādhi*.

And this [type of *samādhi*] pertains solely to the meaning (*artha*), because in the context of the subject matter at hand, there is the superimposition (*āropa*) of a non-contextual meaning itself. Others, however, state that there is a twofold division of *samādhi*—which is a quality of meaning (*artha-guṇa*) consisting of the perception of meaning—as "having no source" (*ayoni*) and "having another as its source" (*anyacchāyāyoni*). Regarding this, Vāmana says: "The perception of meaning is *samādhi*"; and "Meaning is of two kinds: having no source and having another as its source. In this context, "having no source" means being without a cause, that is to say, having mere attention (*avadhāna*) as its sole cause.

For example: "Begone from my vessel of *sīdhu* wine, lest you be bitten by my prominent teeth," and so forth. Another type is that which has its origin in the shadow (*chāyā*) of another poem, yet is not derived from that very source; for instance: "Do not fear, O Moon; there is no Rāhu in my *sīdhu* wine," and so forth.

Viśvanātha, however, considers it thus: an *ayoni* (unconventional) meaning is one that, even without being established by the tradition of poets, is fashioned from one's own imagination (*svakapolakalpita*) in the form of a relationship such as that between the standard of comparison and the object compared (*upamānopameyabhāva*), as in: "The orange fruit vies with the chin of a drunken Hūṇa who has just been shaven. Here, the similarity of the orange fruit with the chin of a Hūṇa has not been expressed by any ancient poets; it was merely brought forth by one's own intellect.

Another [type of *anyokti*] has its source in shadow (*chāyāyoni*); it was properly employed by ancient poets and is well-known in poetic convention, yet it is composed with a certain lack of striking novelty (*vaicitrya*). For example: "A certain flower-gatherer, repeatedly deceived by the reflections of her own eyes in the water, even when faced with a blue lotus, hesitates to place her hand upon it. In this instance, although the similarity between the eye and the blue lotus is well-established, it is depicted through a particular kind of artistic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*).

The quality of *śabdaguṇa* called *samādhi* consists in the absence of discordance (*vairasyābhāva*) when a loose composition is employed within a tight composition, or a tight composition is employed within a loose composition. As Vāmana said: "The sequence of ascent and descent is *samādhi*. This means that the sequence of ascent and descent is *samādhi*, which is a resolution (*parihāra*). It is a resolution when there is a descent following an ascent, or an ascent following a descent.

In this regard, ascent preceded by descent is as follows: "joyless in the *kaunda* flower, its sweetness exhausted in the honey. Descent preceded by ascent is as follows: "trees, like men fallen from virtue, sink down as if into calamity. In the former case, in the phrase "joyless in the *kaunda*," there is ascent due to the abundance of heavy syllables; in the phrase "in the honey," there is descent due to the prevalence of light syllables. When descent is proceeding, there is the relinquishing of ascent.

The intention is that there are two types of *samādhi*: in the subsequent passage, at the word "men" (*narāḥ*), there is a descent due to looseness; at the word "fallen from virtue" (*śīlabhraṣṭāḥ*), there is an ascent due to the abundance of heavy syllables; and while proceeding with the ascent, there is the abandonment of the descent. However, some interpret this to mean an ascent in sequence and a descent in sequence. 94.

He shows that *samādhi* has transcended secondary characteristics (*gauṇalakṣaṇa*), by means of the term "harshness" (*niṣṭhūratā*). "Harshness" refers to words such as "raised up," "vomited," and so forth; the sense is that it is based on a secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*), namely *lakṣaṇā*, because of its connection with a quality (*guṇa*). That very [function] is its specific support (*viśiṣṭa āśraya*). Its state exists in an object similar to the primary meaning; when it is otherwise—that is, in the absence of that [primary meaning] and in the absence of a support for secondary function—it is employed in an object similar to the primary meaning. This is exceedingly beautiful and most enchanting; the sense is that this alone is the locus of *samādhi*.

The meaning is as follows: "elsewhere" means when that [primary sense] is absent, i.e., when there is no basis for resorting to figurative usage (*gauṇavṛtti*); "in the primary sense alone" refers to its employment in its literal meaning. It "plunges into" or incurs the "rustic level," which is the turbidity of the defect of vulgarity (*grāmyatā*). Thus, a word such as *niṣṭhūta*, when employed in its primary sense, is indeed vulgar; however, when used in a metaphorical sense, it becomes possessed of poetic quality (*guṇavat*) due to the superimposition of identity with that [primary object]. This is the established conclusion. (As it has been said: "That which is uttered as vulgar, disgusting, indecent, or inauspicious does not become a fault when it is veiled, concealed, or indicated [through metaphor]. || 95 ||)

He illustrates the point already stated with the verse beginning "padmāni" (the lotuses). With mouths that have drunk and then regurgitated the sparks of fire—scattered by the rays of the sun—their red pollen-dust; such are the lotuses that seem to vomit again and again. (This is a description of lotuses whose pollen is falling away due to contact with the evening breeze.)

In this context, although the words *niṣṭhūyata* (spitting) and *udgīrṇa* (vomited) are capable of denoting the discharge of bodily phlegm and the like, they are used here figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in the sense of a general discharge. Furthermore, the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here is based on a perception of similarity—just as the discharge of phlegm is similar to the discharge of *vaḍi*, *hiḍḍha*, *ṭhaḍana*, and *kaṇā*—and is thus secondary (*gauṇī*). As Viśvanātha has stated: "All those [metaphorical indications] other than similarity are pure (*śuddhā*); however, those based on similarity are considered secondary (*gauṇyaḥ*)."

And because that similarity is not perceived [as a mere resemblance], the aesthetic appeal (*sahṛdayahṛdyatā*) of its meaning remains unimpeded, and thus the poetic figure *samādhi* is intact. If it is argued that in the phrase "they seem to vomit," since there is no comprehension of the connection (*anvaya*) between the act of vomiting and the lotuses as its agent, and since similarity is impossible, one must necessarily admit *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication), we say no. This is because the word *iva* has the sense of "possibility" (*sambhāvanā*). Even in the case of possibility, the emergence of a sublation (*bādhodaya*) is irrelevant and does not obstruct the comprehension of the connection, just as in the case of a superimposed [meaning]; therefore, the comprehension of the connection is indeed unimpeded.

On the contrary, it should be noted that even the cognition of identity (*tādṛpyapratīti*) arising from indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of *sambhāvanā* (poetic fancy) does not produce aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*). By this, it should be understood that the term "secondary function" (*gauṇavṛtti*) mentioned previously is intended as an illustration of *sambhāvanā*.

Regarding the word "thus" (*iti*): the meaning is that the aforementioned words such as "spitting out" (*niṣṭhūta*) are "pleasing" (*hṛdya*) because they possess a poetic resolution through secondary indication. However, the sentence "the young woman spits out phlegm and the like" is "unpleasant" (*ahṛdya*), being disagreeable to sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) due to its being defiled by the fault of vulgarity (*grāmyatā*).

The word "spits" (*niṣṭhīvati*), employed in its primary sense (*mukhyārtha*) through the function of direct denotation (*abhidhā-vṛtti*), manifests loathing; therein, the word "bride" (*badhū*) further intensifies the vulgarity, because the spitting of phlegm by a bride is extremely disgusting. To demonstrate the excellence of beauty (*cārutva-atiśaya*) in the figure of *samādhi*—defined as the superimposition (*āropa*) of the attributes of one thing upon another, as previously mentioned—the author speaks of the superimposition of many attributes simultaneously, using the word "at once" (*yugapat*).

In this context, "superimposition" (*adhyāsa*) refers to the simultaneous—meaning at one and the same time, and not through a succession of times—superimposition of many properties belonging to one thing onto other things, specifically onto that which is under discussion (*prastuta*) and not elsewhere. It is recognized by scholars as a superior form of *samādhi* because it generates an excellence of beauty; it consists in the suppression of the actual properties [of the object] and the attribution of identity based on similarity.

Thus, the essential meaning is that *samādhi* is the superimposition of the properties of one thing onto another, or likewise, the superimposition of many properties of other things onto the subject at hand. (97)

He illustrates the meaning already stated with the verse beginning "guru" (heavy). "Guru" means heavy due to being filled with water; elsewhere, it means having a large belly due to the presence of a fetus. Or, it may mean belonging to the great or powerful (the cloud); elsewhere, it means well-nourished (a specific type of fetus). Likewise, by the weight of the "garbha"—that which contains the internal mass of water—elsewhere, the weight of the living being residing in the womb—they become weary, sluggish, and thundering; elsewhere, [they are] crying out.

Causing weariness, languor, and other such states, these rows of clouds now rest upon the lap—the central region—of the mountain’s plateau (for "upatyakā" is the land near the foot of a mountain and "adhityakā" is the land rising above it, according to Amara), just as they previously rested upon the lap of their friend.

(Here, because of the swallowing up of the attributes of the row of clouds [into the woman], there is a similarity; and due to the simultaneous superimposition of many attributes of a pregnant woman, an excellence of variety arises that captivates the hearts of connoisseurs—this is how it should be understood—and the poetic figure is *samāsokti*. || 98 || In the aforementioned verse, he demonstrates the attributes of a pregnant woman with the words "on her lap" (*utsaṅge*), etc. Here, in the stated verse, these many attributes of a pregnant woman—namely, lying on the lap of a friend, sighing, heaviness, and exhaustion—are shown as being superimposed; this is the implied sense.

Even if, according to the statement of Amara—“*stanitam* [means] *garjitam*, [the roar] of a cloud”—the word *stanana* is understood as referring only to the thundering of clouds, nevertheless, since the verbal root *stan* has the general sense of making sound, the use of the word *stanantyaḥ* for a pregnant woman in reference to such a sound is appropriate.

Furthermore, by another statement—"In the case of anklets and the like, it is primarily *raṇita*; in the case of birds, it is *kūjita* and so forth; in sexual union, it is *stanita*, *maṇita*, and so on; and in the case of clouds and the like, it is *garjita* and so forth"—the fact that the word *stanita* denotes sexual union is also established. Therefore, the root *stan* does not have only the thundering of clouds as its meaning, but rather it is a general term [applicable to various sounds].

[Objection: Even if it is established that [the word *stanantyaḥ*] has the mere word-meaning [of "sounding"], how is the specific sound of a pregnant woman’s moaning (*kunthanādi*) accounted for by the word *stanantyaḥ*? [Response: This is not so; because [moaning] falls within the category of uncommon characteristics of a pregnant woman such as lying on one's lap (*utsaṅgaśayana*), and because it contributes to aesthetic variety (*vaicitrya*), it is logical that moaning also possesses the nature of being a characteristic of a pregnant woman, since it is precisely this variety that constitutes poetry (*kāvyatva*). Thus, it must be understood that its necessary dependence [on such characteristics] is indeed proper. || 99 ||

He brings forth the quality of *samādhi*; "that" means for that reason, because it possesses an extreme variety in the manner described. *Samādhi* is the quality which is the entire wealth—meaning the very essence—of this poetry. The "entirety of the community of poets"—meaning the poetic tradition, whether of the Gauḍīya or Vaidarbha style—follows that such *samādhi*; the meaning is that they proceed in their poetry in accordance with it.

(And although among these ten qualities some have been disregarded by the moderns because they consist merely in the absence of specific defects and others because they constitute figures of speech—such as [the statement]: "Those three called *mādhurya*, *ojas*, and *prasāda* exist, but not ten"—nevertheless, it should be noted that the author of this work has defined exactly ten as qualities, following the tradition of the ancients. || 100 ||

Having thus described the distinction between the Gauḍa and Vaidarbha styles, he concludes that exposition with the word "iti" (thus). "Iti" means in the manner stated; "of those two," namely the Gauḍa and Vaidarbha, "due to the determination of their essential nature," that is, from the formulation of their definitions, "the two paths"—meaning the two manners of style delineated—are "distinct," that is, mutually different.

Their divisions (*tadbhedāḥ*): by those two paths; "division" means differentiated, that is to say, the Lāṭa, Pāñcāla, and so forth—according to the maxim, "A state expressed by *kṛt*-affixes appears like a substance. Alternatively, their divisions: the divisions of that path of poetry (*kāvyamārgasya*), distinct from the Gauḍa and Vaidarbha styles, which are specific varieties existing among the poets of various respective regions; however, they cannot be fully described because of their extreme vastness—this is the sense.

Their characteristics have been described by others as follows: "In that regard, the Vaidarbha style is held to be composed of uncompounded words, woven with all the qualities such as *śleṣa* (coalescence) and the rest, and possessing the beauty of the sound of the lute (*vipañcī*). The wise know the Pāñcālī style to consist of five or six compounded words, devoid of the qualities of *ojas* (vigour) and *kānti* (splendor), yet sweet and delicate. Those expert in styles recognize the Gauḍīyā style as consisting of highly compounded words and endowed with the qualities of *ojas* and *kānti*. But that which stands between the Pāñcālī and the Vaidarbha is the Antarālā."

The *Avantika* style consists of all [the qualities] together with two or three, or three or four, words. The *Lāṭīyā* style is desired as a mixture of all the aforementioned styles. When the previous style cannot be fully sustained, there is the *Khaṇḍarīti*, which is the *Māgadhī*. Among these, the *Pāñcālī* is as follows: "The sound of jewels became resonant with a jingling noise, belonging to those whose armlets were shattered by the impact against their limbs, who were struck by the playful hands of the elephant-keepers, and whose crowns were knocked askew by the friction of their crests being tossed in the agitation."

In this [Pāñcālī style], there is an absence of vigor (*ojas*) and charm (*kānti*), yet it possesses sweetness (*mādhurya*) and delicacy (*saukumārya*); it is devoid of compounds (*samāsa*) and consists of six additional [syllables] per foot. The *Āvantikā* style is as follows: "These disjointed steps of her, whose body has lost its strength, portend a vacant mind; and these trees by the path proclaim her fever with their sprouts that have withered after being embraced [by her]."

This style, which consists of an aggregate of two, three, or four words and occupies an intermediate position between the Vaidarbhī and Pāñcālī, is called the Āvantikā. Likewise, the Lāṭīyā is as follows: "This [sun] rises, breaking the seal of the lotuses; the morning mountain-bower creeper, like a young mandāra flower; the kinsman of the pair of cakravāka birds distressed by separation; piercing the darkness, copper-red like the cheek of an angry monkey. This style, being a mixture of all the aforementioned styles, is named the Lāṭīyā.

Among these, the Māgadhī style is as follows: "These foothills of the Vindhyas terrify [us] on all sides with vegetable branches and leaf-tips left over from the elephants' feeding, their paths reddened; they are agitated by wild boars startled by the fierce sound of cow-horns blown by the moving Śabara armies. This is the *khaṇḍarīti* (fragmentary style) of the Māgadhī, due to the failure to carry through the style that was begun. Alternatively, the phrase "its varieties" (*tadbhedāḥ*) means the specific sub-varieties included within those two, namely the Gauḍī and Vaidarbhī styles. || 101 ||

He supports the stated point by means of an illustration with the words "ikṣu" and so forth. Regarding sugarcane, milk, jaggery, and the like (the word "etc. including all that is sweet), although there is a great difference—a distinction clearly capable of being perceived—nevertheless, even Sarasvatī herself, the goddess of speech, cannot describe or express that difference, let alone others. This is the sense.

Thus, because the sweetness of poetic paths—such as that of sugarcane and the like—is infinite, it is impossible to enumerate all their varieties; therefore, the intended meaning is that only two types of distinctions, whose differences are clearly perceived, have been specifically defined. 102.

Having thus defined the nature of poetry (*kāvyasvarūpa*), he states its causes, beginning with the word *naisargikī*. *Naisargikī* means innate, established by one's own nature. *Pratibhā* is a flashing intuition or creative genius. *Bahu* means manifold; it refers to grammar, lexicons, the arts, prosody, elephant-lore, horsemanship, and so forth. *Nirmalam* means completely purified through thorough study. *Śrutam* refers to scriptural knowledge as well as knowledge of worldly conduct and the like. Likewise, *amandaḥ* means intense; *abhiyogaḥ* means application or dedication. Through instruction from those proficient in poetry, there arises *abhyāsa*, or practice.

This is the meaning: these three are the *kāraṇam*—the cause—of this "perfection of poetry," that is, of the excellence consisting of the poetic form. By the use of the singular number in the word *kāraṇam*, it is indicated that the totality [of the three] constitutes the cause, and not each one individually.

For instance, in the composition of poetry, we observe that for children and others who lack effort and proficiency, there is no production of poetry even though they possess *pratibhā* (creative intuition). Furthermore, at a subsequent time, when those same individuals have acquired proficiency through practice, we observe the production of poetry in them. Likewise, we see that some who possess both effort and proficiency lack [the capacity for poetry] in the absence of *pratibhā*. Thus, because it is observed in those who have made an effort and not observed in those who have not made an effort, it is logical that all [these factors] together constitute the cause.

The Conclusion: And it has been stated by the author of the *Prakāśa*: "Power (*śakti*), skill (*nipuṇatā*) acquired through the study of the world, the sciences, poetry, and so forth, and practice (*abhyāsa*) under the instruction of those who know poetry—these are the causes for its arising. This has been explained in that very same work: "Thus, these three taken together—and not separately—are the cause (*hetu*) for the arising, the composition, and the manifestation of that poetry; they are not [individually] the causes (*hetavaḥ*)."

However, some say that *pratibhā* (creative intuition) alone is the cause of poetry, while *vyutpatti* (erudition) is the cause of its beauty, and *abhyāsa* (practice) is the cause of its increase; they further maintain that *pratibhā* arises in some cases through the grace of the gods, and that since poetry does not arise even when *pratibhā* exists in children who possess innate poetic talent, time must be accepted as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*). As it has been said: "Poetic talent is born from innate power and grows through the application of practice; yet for the perfection of its beauty, erudition is the most important factor."

These very subjects were shown by Vāmana as the constituent parts of poetry (*kāvyāṅga*). For therein, first, in response to the inquiry "What can be described without knowledge of the conduct (*vṛtta*) of the world consisting of the mobile and the immobile? there is the conduct of the world (*lokavṛtta*); then, refined words (*saṃskṛta-śabda*); following that, their meanings (*tadartha*); immediately after, skill in the arts (*kalākauśala*), which is a limb of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārāṅga*) and the cause for the variety of plot (*itivṛtta*); then, the conduct of love (*kāmavyavahāra*), which is useful for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); then, the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), which is the cause for discerning between profit and loss (*arthānarthaviveka*); and finally, afterwards—

The sequence beginning with "knowledge of the subject matter" (*lakṣyajñatva*) and so forth is for the purpose of instruction; thus, this aphorism was formulated: "The world (*loka*), the sciences (*vidyā*), and miscellaneous [learning] (*prakīrṇa*) are the limbs of poetry. Furthermore, for the sake of clarifying its meaning: "The world is the conduct of the world (*lokavṛtta*); the sciences are those preceded by grammar (*śabdasmṛti*), lexicography (*abhidhānakoṣa*), prosody (*chandaḥ*), the arts (*kalā*), the treatises on love (*kāmaśāstra*), and statecraft (*daṇḍanīti*); miscellaneous learning consists of knowledge of the subject matter (*lakṣyajñatva*), diligent application (*abhiyoga*), observation of the elders (*vṛddhasamāvekṣaṇa*), intuition (*pratibhāna*), and concentration (*avadhāna*); therein, familiarity with poetry is 'knowledge of the subject matter' (*layajñatva*)."

The exertion in composing poetry is *abhiyoga*; service to teachers who instruct in poetry is *vṛddhasevā*; the careful observation of the placement and removal of words is *padādhānoddharaṇāvekṣaṇa*; creative intuition (*pratibhāna*) is the seed of poetry; and one-pointed concentration of the mind is *cittaikāgrāvadhāna*. By these aphorisms, the author of the *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra* has demonstrated that this triad—beginning with *pratibhā*—is the cause for both the production and the flourishing of poems. Since the body of a poem cannot exist without these, their status as constituent parts (*kāvyāṅga*) of poetry is established;
thus, all of this is faultless. || 103 ||

With the intention that even in the absence of all the aforementioned causes, success in the fruit may somehow be achieved by those who are diligent and devoted to the study of the scriptures, he says: "No. Although there exists no *pratibhāna*—which means a natural capacity (*svabhāvikī śaktiḥ*), in the sense of a predisposition from previous lives (*pūrvavāsanā*); and which is marvelous (*adbhuta*), meaning extraordinary (*alaukika*), connected with excellence (*guṇānubandhi*), bringing about variety, and the cause of preeminence through the composition of poetry; nevertheless, by means of *śruta*, that is, by the study of the scriptures...

Whether through the instruction of one who knows poetry, or through effort and lack of dogmatic attachment, speech that is attended to and cultivated certainly—meaning with certainty—bestows some favor; that is to say, it necessarily extends a certain capacity for the composition of poetry. (If there is perfect capacity, however, the aforementioned triad alone is the cause; thus, there is no mutual contradiction. || 104 ||

He concludes with the word "tad" (therefore). "Tat" means for that reason; by those who are "astatandraiḥ"—that is, by those whose lassitude has been cast away, meaning those free from indolence—by people desiring "kīrtim," which is fame born of poetic skill; the word "janaiḥ" (by people) is to be supplied as the subject. "Śramāt" means having undertaken diligent effort; "sarasvatī" indeed—"khalu" indicates certainty—must be "aniśam upāsyā," meaning she must be served constantly. The sense is that the scripture must certainly be thoroughly studied. He asks "how? and answers with "kṛśa."

Even when the capacity for composing poetry (*kavitva*) is meager or slight, people who have exerted effort through the diligent study of the treatises are able to shine (*vihartum īśate*) in assemblies of the learned (*vidagdhagoṣṭhīṣu*), that is, in circles of poets; for even a small amount of this [knowledge] results in the attainment of fruits both in this world and the next, according to the Vedic revelation: "A single word, well-employed and correctly understood, becomes a cow of plenty (*kāmadhuk*) in heaven and in the world. (105) The Third Chapter.

In the second chapter, having stated the general definition of verbal and semantic ornaments with the words, "They declare those properties that produce the beauty of poetry to be ornaments," [the author] did not first examine the verbal ornaments—even though they would have been more appropriate to define first because they are the objects of the initial cognition—since they do not impart an extreme degree of variety; instead, he demonstrated only the semantic ornaments, which do impart an excellence of variety.

Now, having reached the appropriate occasion in the first chapter, intending to define the various sub-types of *yamaka* distinct from alliteration (*anuprāsa*), and intending to state the definition of defects (*doṣa*), [the author] restates the previously mentioned definition of *yamaka* and enumerates its divisions, beginning with the words "avyapeta" (unseparated). "Avyapeta" means unseparated; "vyapeta" means separated. That which has such a nature—namely, the specific repetition (*vyāvṛtti*) of a collection of phonemes (*varṇasaṃhati*), i.e., a grouping of vowels and consonants—is *yamaka*.

(The specific definition of this has already been stated previously, so it is not repeated here. The phrase beginning with "avyapeta" is stated in order to demonstrate the distinction based on whether the constituent words of the *yamaka* are immediate or separated. Thus, the first two varieties are mentioned: the repetition of a group of phonemes previously uttered, either without interval or with an interval. And it is said in the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*: "The repetition of a group of phonemes which possesses the same form but different meanings..."

"That which consists of both non-separate and separate [syllables] is called *yamaka*. To define the positions of that *yamaka*, he says: "And that... This refers to that whose scope (*gocara*)—its domain—is the beginning, the middle, and the end of the quarters (*pāda*), namely the feet of the verse consisting of one, two, three, or four parts.

Furthermore, the method of division is as follows: for the first quarter, it occurs in the initial portion, the middle portion, and the final portion; likewise for the second and subsequent quarters, it occurs in the initial, middle, and final portions.

Consequently, since the *yamaka* resides in exactly three parts of the feet, one should not suspect a restriction regarding the position [of the feet], because it is obtained in any part that may occur with the middle foot; this rule should be understood to apply even to four or more parts, as stated by the author of the *Prakāśa*: "In a three-part [verse] there are thirty, and in a four-part [verse] there are forty."

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); by this, that which occurs within a quarter-verse (*pāda*) should also be understood. And Vāmana has stated: "The position [of *yamaka*] consists of the initial, middle, and final parts of one quarter-verse or of several quarters. Here too, "quarter-verse" is an elliptical indication; therefore, it should be understood that the positions of *yamaka* are the quarter-verse, the segments of a quarter-verse, half a verse, and the entire verse. In the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa* as well: "That [yamaka] is divided into non-intervened (*avyapeta*) and intervened (*vyapeta*), and further distinguished by the division of positions and non-positions, and by the distinctions of the quarters.
Among these, the beginning, middle, and end of the quarters are conceived as the 'positions' (*sthāna*). || 1 ||

Having described the varieties of *yamaka* (rhyme) according to their positions, the author now demonstrates the varieties occurring within the quarters (*pāda*), pointing out each specific type in succession, beginning with "one," and so forth. The meaning is that these are the unmixed varieties of *yamakas* consisting of one, two, three, or four quarters. The phrase "the variations of the quarters' scope regarding the beginning, middle, and end" refers to the general subdivisions mentioned immediately prior; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "they are to be known. This is because a verse composed of four quarters is divided into three parts—beginning, middle, and end—with respect to each individual quarter.

Furthermore, the meaning is that its twelvefold nature is to be understood. (And these are to be known as being exclusively unmixed. For instance, the *ādimātrā-yamaka* (rhyme at the beginning) is fourfold: occurring at the beginning of the first quarter, the beginning of the second quarter, the beginning of the third quarter, and the beginning of the fourth quarter. Likewise, there are those occurring in the middle and end portions of the first and other quarters. Thus, when combined, the unmixed *yamaka* is of twelve kinds; this is the summary.)

And this division is common to both the contiguous (*avyapeta*) and non-contiguous (*vyapeta*) types. However, some explain the half-verse beginning with "one, two," etc., as follows: "Since a verse consists of four quarters, one should understand that there are four divisions for each section; just as the *ādi-bhāga-yamaka* (alliteration at the beginning) is fourfold—occurring in the first quarter alone, the second alone, the third alone, or the fourth alone—so too is the *madhyādi-bhāga-yamaka* (alliteration at the middle and beginning) fourfold in each case."

[The text says: "It is fourfold. Having thus shown the division according to position (*abhiśrabheda*), he now shows the division according to mixture (*miśrayamakabheda*) with the word "firstly" (*ādau*). "Mixture" (*sambheda*) means the mutual blending of similar *yamakas*; those for which such [mixture] is their source are "mixed," which is the meaning. Of those *yamakas*, the divisions—due to being situated at the beginning, middle, end, middle-and-end, middle-and-beginning, beginning-and-end, and everywhere—are extremely numerous and very extensive; the word "are to be known" (*jñeyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The word division (*padaccheda*), however, is of this form: *ādi-madhya-anta*, *madhya-anta*, *madhya-ādi*, *ādi-anta*, and *sarvataḥ*. In every case, the middle term indicates the second and third quarters (*pāda*s), while the remainder [the first term] refers to the first quarter because it stands at the beginning. Consequently, in the expression *ādi-madhya-ante*, since the middle term consists of the two quarters—the second and the third—there are two varieties based on their occurrence in the beginning and the middle, and one variety based on their occurrence at the end; thus, three varieties in total should be understood.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these three [cases] occur by virtue of being situated in the first and second feet (*ādi-madhya-pāda*), the first and third feet (*ādi-madhya-pāda*), and the first and fourth feet (*ādy-anta-pāda*). In the case of *madhyānta* as well, since the middle term (*madhya-pada*) indicates both the second and third feet, only three varieties are to be understood.

For example, there is one [type] with the middle of the second and third quarters (*madhyamadhyayoh*); and two [types] with the middle and end of the second and fourth quarters, and the third and fourth quarters; thus, combined, there are three varieties of the *prākāra* [meter]. Regarding the term *madhyādya*: because the second and third quarters constitute the "middle," there is only one variety occurring in the first, second, and third quarters. Here, in the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as "the first (*ādya*) and the two middles (*madhyau*)," the word *ādya* is placed last according to its inclusion in the *dharmārtha-* group of words.

In the term *ādyanta* ("beginning and end"), since the word *ādi* refers to the first, second, and third quarters (*pādas*), only three varieties are possible: those occurring in the first, second, and fourth quarters; those occurring in the first, third, and fourth quarters; and those occurring in the second, third, and fourth quarters. In the term *sarvataḥ* ("everywhere"), however, there is only one variety, consisting of those occurring in all four quarters—first, second, third, and fourth.

Thus, by combining these, eleven varieties of *vyāmiśrayamaka* (mixed yamaka) are to be understood; other varieties of yamaka, such as those based on non-sequential placement (*asthāna*) or gross and subtle forms (*sthūla-sūkṣma*), are to be seen in the works of Bhoja and others. The word "sarvataḥ" ends in the locative plural case, meaning "in all [four] quarters."
