And these [styles] are easy to perform, easy to accomplish, and easy to understand for poets and connoisseurs—this is the implied sense; as well as difficult to perform, difficult to accomplish, and difficult to understand. Therefore, some of them are shown here, meaning they are illustrated, but not all of them; such is the intention. (In the phrase "te 'tra," the reading "tatra" is mentioned by Bhoja. 2.

Therein, he indicates the unmixed [feeling] situated in the first quarter, which is considered to belong to the initial portion, by means of the word "mānena" (by pride). O friend! toward a beloved person, one who is affectionate—by this kind of *māna* (pride), the sense being that it causes pain even to us because of its extreme intensity—along with *māna*, that is, jealousy-born anger (according to the definition: "Māna is anger; it is of two kinds, arising from affection and from jealousy"), let there be no *praṇaya* (intimacy)—the word "of yours" being understood—toward that beloved person; do not exercise such pride toward your beloved.

This is the meaning: she is a *khaṇḍitā* (one who has been deceived), defined by the verse: "She whose lover comes to her side after being struck by the marks of another woman's enjoyment is called a *khaṇḍitā* by the wise, her heart turbid with jealousy. [The word] "you" (*tvam*) is to be supplied as the subject; having embraced his neck—that is, having hugged that very lover—make him feel ashamed (*salajjam*). The sense is that showing affection toward one who has done you wrong is itself a source of shame for him, and thus it constitutes a "heavy command" (*guru śāsanam*).

This is a statement by a friend to a woman who has been slighted and is full of pride. Here, in the phrase "mānena mānena," there is an *ādimāgayamaka* (yamaka occurring in the initial portion) belonging to the immediately preceding part; and because it is not interspersed with other feet, it is "unmixed. However, where there is a connection with another foot, there is "mixedness," whereas elsewhere there is "purity"; thus, the distinction—just as in the case of the *vyapeta* (separated) and *avyapeta* (unseparated) types—should be inferred by oneself. || 4 ||

He explains that very same point found in the second quarter: by the "thundering of clouds" (*meghanāda*), Kāma—the destroyer of self-restraint—is, together with his wife Rati and through passion, accompanied by the thundering of clouds (*meghagarjita*) which dispels the pride of swans, for it is well known that during the rainy season swans lose their intoxication; thus, the meaning is that the minds of women—which have had their pride removed—are plunged into, stirred, and agitated, because the roar of the clouds acts as an excitant (*uddīpaka*).

The sense is that during the rainy season, the minds of young women become full of passion and desire. (Here, in the second quarter, there is an unmixed, non-interspersed *ādiyamaka* occurring at the beginning of the line: "madano madano"). 5.

He provides an illustration of that very [quality] found in the third quarter with the words "rājanvatyaḥ" (possessing a king). Of the Earth—whose girdles are the four oceans; that is to say, the four oceans themselves are her girdles, meaning specific ornaments for the waist; she who is delimited by the four seas—regarding the taking of tribute (*karagrahe*), which consists of the royal share amounting to one-sixth, or regarding the grasping of the hand (*pāṇigrahe*); you, who are clever (*catura*)—meaning skillful in collecting tribute as far as the oceans—are her true husband (*satpatim*).

Having obtained a protector and a good ruler, the subjects became possessed of a king and endowed with a virtuous monarch (*rājanvatyaḥ sunṛpatiyuktāḥ*)—according to Amara’s lexicon, "one is *rājanvān* in a land with a good king, otherwise one is merely *rājavān*"—and thus they were truly well-governed. (In this verse, the third quarter contains an immediate *ādibhāgayamaka* of the form "caturaṃ caturam"). 6.

He explains that very same point found in the fourth quarter [of the verse] with the words "apaṇyam" (not for sale). By certain enemies who are unfriendly—meaning those who have fled while still alive—that is, by those deprived of the fourfold army consisting of infantry, chariots, elephants, and horses (as Amara says: "The four components of an army are elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry"), having fled to the forest—the sense being that it is impossible for people to remain in their own abodes once they have fled for their lives—and likewise by certain others through face-to-face combat.

The sense is "by those who have died" (here too, it should be construed as "devoid of foot-soldiers and the like"). "The abode of the dwellers of heaven" means the celestial realm; the meaning is that it was "overrun," i.e., occupied, because death in battle leads to the attainment of heaven (as stated by the Blessed One in the *Gītā*: "Either slain you shall attain heaven, or victorious you shall enjoy the earth"). Here, the *amiśra* type of *bhāga-yamaka* occurs in the fourth quarter, with the words "rahitair ahitaiḥ" immediately following one another. || 7 ||

Now, having explained the varieties of *avyapeta-yamaka* (non-repeated) that are not separated by a single syllable (*sabhedayoni*), he provides an illustration at the beginning of the section on "beginning, middle, end," etc., regarding the three types of divisions located in the first, second, and third, and first and fourth quarters; first, he illustrates the *ādimāga-yamaka* (alliteration at the beginning of the first and second quarters) located in the first and second quarters, starting with the word "madhuram."

O lotus-faced one! O lotus-mouthed one! Spring (madhuḥ), through the delusion that these two eyes of yours are two bees—this delusion being appropriate because the eyes reside upon the lotus-face and because it is possible for a pair of bees to dwell upon a lotus—exceedingly impels or bestows a sweet grace (vibhramaṃ śobhām). (This is from the root *ḍanva* in the sense of "impelling," belonging to the curādigaṇa, with the suffix *rīp*. Indeed.

"O you who possess such deliberation (*vitarka*), tell me, speak! Has this such-like bewilderment (*vibhrama*) of your eyes been produced by the Spring itself, which is filled with the wandering of bees?"—this is the intended meaning. (The word *nu* is indeed appropriate here as it conveys a deliberation, for when the spring has arisen, the play of bees occurs in the lotus. Some, however, state that *ambhojavadane* ends in the locative case and connect it with "of the two eyes residing therein."

In the reading "na" for "nu" here, the meaning is: "Does it not mock [it]?"—rather, it certainly does mock it. Here, because the constituent words of the *yamaka*, namely "madhuraṃ madhuram" and "vadane vadane," are situated at the beginning of the first and second quarters (i.e., the initial and middle quarters), they possess the characteristic of being "initial-part" (*ādibhāga*). Furthermore, because of the mixing of two quarters, it is designated as "mixed" (*miśra*); and since there is no interval between the words, it is "unseparated" (*avyapeta*). Thus, this is an "unseparated initial-part *yamaka*" occurring in the mixed [quarters] of the first and second quarters. || 8 ||

(Here, because the words forming the *yamaka*—namely "vāramo vāraṇo" and "nayato nayato"—occur at the beginning of the first and third quarters [and the middle], it should be understood as a mixed, contiguous *ādimāga-yamaka* occurring in the first and third quarters [and the middle]. | 9 |

He provides an illustration of that very [alliteration] occurring in the first and fourth quarters [the beginning and end], with the words "rajitaiḥ" and so on. *Āji* means battle; therein, by means of sharpness—that is, by the intoxication of war—they are *rājitaiḥ*, meaning adorned. By kings such as you—meaning those like your majesty—the *vasudhā*, the earth, that is, the people dwelling there, is *jīyate*; it is first brought under control through victory, which implies it is oppressed by the activities of war. Furthermore, after the victory, by the *vasudhārā*, the showers of wealth...

By means of a stream—that is, by an incessant shower of wealth, meaning through unceasing giving—he is led to satisfaction and contentment. (In this verse, because the constituent words of the *yamaka*—"rājitai rājitai" and "vasudhā vasudhā"—occur at the beginning of the first and fourth quarters respectively, and due to the intermingling of two quarters without any intervening space, it should be known as "mixed, contiguous, initial-part *yamaka*" occurring in the first and fourth quarters.)
By the verse beginning with "sweet" (*madhuram*), the three varieties defined by the terms "beginning," "middle," and "end" have been illustrated in sequence. (10)

In this way, he demonstrates the distinction between the beginning, middle, and end by means of the term *madhyānta*. Having established that there is a middle-middle (*madhyamadhya*), a middle-end (*madhyānta*), and an end-middle (*antamadhyam*), he shows these three varieties in sequence. First, he provides an example of non-interrupted (*avyapeta*) and other types of *bhāgayamaka* occurring in the first, second, and third quarters (*pāda*), beginning with the word *karoti*. The bud (*kalikā*) of the mango tree (*sahakāra*), as well as my own mind (*manmanaḥ*)—[the latter being] in the vernacular of one's own region, [used] at the root of the ear during sexual union (*surata*).

"That which is the conversation between a husband and wife is called *manmana*. This is the definition provided [in the lexicon]. Here, the secret whispering at the root of the ear is to be understood as such; and even this sound of the cuckoos, intoxicated by the arrival of spring, makes my mind (*manmana*) full of longing (*utkalikottara*), meaning agitated by yearning. The sense is that both the mango buds and the cooing of the cuckoos are exceedingly provocative. (This is the speech of one separated from their beloved.)

In this instance, because the words forming the *yamaka*—namely "kaliko kaliko" and "manmano manmano"—occur at the beginning of the second and third quarters respectively, and because those two quarters are situated in the middle [of the verse], it should be understood as an *avyapeta-ādi-bhāga-yamaka* occurring in the middle of the second and third quarters; furthermore, due to the intermingling of these two quarters, it is designated as "mixed" (*miśra*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that in the case of the phrase "kalikotkalikā," although the letter *t* occurs in the middle, because it is void of its own [phonemic] essence, it is not counted within the interval as it fails to complete the number of syllables in the verse; thus, there is no loss of the *avyapeta* (unseparated) nature of the *yamaka*. This is because it is accepted that only a consonant accompanied by a vowel functions as an intervener. || 11 ||

He gives an example of that same [state] occurring in the second and fourth quarters [of the verse], asking "How so? Here, in this place, your "upalambha" means your attainment; the "āśā" (hope) for that is "pratyāśā" (expectation); in its "vihati" (frustration) or destruction, there is a state being experienced that is "aṅganāśinī," meaning it cuts the body to pieces—a particular stage of the condition of love (*smaradaśā*). How is such a state not "alaṃ" (sufficient/capable) to "āroḍhum" (ascend/overpower) the "aṅganā," the weak woman—meaning me? Indeed, it is quite capable; for in separation from you, I am [overwhelmed].

The intended meaning is: "I have become as if dead. (In this verse, because the words forming the *yamaka*—namely *vihata* and *aṅganā*—occur at the beginning of the second and fourth quarters respectively, and since the second quarter is the middle and the fourth quarter is the end, this is a mixed (*miśra*) non-intervened initial-part *yamaka* occurring in the middle and final quarters. Some call this a *yukpādayamaka* [alternating-quarter *yamaka*].)

The definition of *tallakṣaṇa* (yamaka at even places) is as follows: "Where a *yamaka* is seen in both the second and the fourth [feet], that should be recognized by the best of poets as *yukpādayamaka*. Another example is found in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*: "That one, honored by Rāma (*rāmamahita*), skilled in battle, waged war (*kalahaṃ kṛtavān*) in the city of the foremost enemy of the gods; and he, who was honored by the swan-like Rāma (*kalahaṃsarāmamahitaḥ*), forcibly set fire to Rāvaṇa’s house (*jvaladagni rāvaṇagṛhaṃ ca*). (12)

He illustrates that very point found in the third and fourth quarters [of the verse], beginning with "having restrained" (*nigṛhya*). Upon the *nalinas*, which are lotuses, the bees (*ālinaḥ*)—whose faces are turned upward and who are intent on falling—are drawn away by young men (*taruṇaiḥ*), who have forcibly seized their eyes (*netre nigṛhya*) by means of what is described as being "beautiful with young shoots" (*bālapallavaiḥ*); the meaning is that they cause the bees to become eager to look at themselves.

(Here, because the words "taruṇā taruṇā" and "nalino nalino" occur at the beginning of the third and fourth quarters respectively, with the former being in the middle and the latter at the end of the third quarter, and because they are characterized by the mixing of two quarters, this is a case of *avyavahita-miśra-ādi-bhāga-yamaka* occurring in the middle and end of the third and fourth quarters. Thus, only the three aforementioned varieties defined by the middle and end positions have been illustrated; such is the general direction. || 13 ||

By the phrase "having come from the middle" (*madhyādetya*), he states the single mode found in the first, second, and third quarters [of the verse], namely: "clearly" (*viśadā*). Entering—that is, making their entrance—into the *sārasa* water, which is the lake-water characterized by intoxicated (*āmatta*) or frenzied *sārasa* birds; in such water, this *haṃsī* (a female royal swan), being clear—that is, white in color—[is crying] with a wretched sound (*kurutena*); the reason for the sound being wretched is that it is provocative and thus unbearable for those separated from their lovers—this is the sense. [She is crying out] to me.

That is to say, [he treats me] like a prey for Antaka, i.e., Yama; "āmiṣa" is a neuter noun meaning an object of enjoyment (according to the Medinīkośa: "āmiṣaṃ is masculine and neuter; it refers to an object of enjoyment, sexual union, a bribe, and also to meat"). The meaning is that he exerts himself to kill me.

(Here, because the words *viśadā viśadā*, *sārase sārase*, and *kurute kurute* occur respectively in the first, second, and third quarters, and as being between the second and third quarters, there is a mixed *avyavahita-ādibhāga-yamaka* occurring in the first, second, and third (and middle/first) quarters; it should be understood that this is of only one variety. || 14 || Having thus defined the three varieties [of *ādibhāga-yamaka*], he now demonstrates them in sequence. First, he clarifies with an example that which occurs in the first, second, third, and fourth quarters (*ādyanta-pāda-gata*), beginning with the word *viṣamam*.

The Malaya breeze—the delighter of Madana—is not gladdening me, a man separated from his beloved; for it is accompanied by a digit of the moon (indukala), which, having cast off its turbidity (apoḍhamalaya)—the sense being that this occurs at the end of winter—acts as a producer of my own distress. Thus, being a source of joy to me [in other times], it now pursues (anveti) Madana, the god of love, in the form of poison (viṣa)—that is, it becomes unbearable poison—and inflames him. The sense is that because both the lunar digit and the Malaya breeze are excitants of passion, they cause torment to those separated from their lovers.

Here, because the words *viṣama-viṣama*, *madana-madana*, and *malayā-malayā* occur in the first, second, and fourth quarters respectively—being at the beginning of the first and second quarters and at the end of the fourth quarter—this is a mixed *ādi-anta-yamaka* (beginning-and-end rhyme) occurring in the first, second, and fourth quarters, without any intervening space.

If one is dissatisfied with the reading "viṣamaṃ viṣamanveti" because of the presence of an *anusvāra* in one of the two words being compared (*yāmyamāna*), then the first quarter-verse should be read as "viṣamaṃ viṣamaṃ kṣṇauti. The second instance of "viṣamam" is derived from the analysis "that which has poison (*viṣa*) as its comparison (*upamā*)," meaning "resembling poison. Some read [the verb] as "kṣṇauti," meaning "he makes sharp. || 15 ||

He provides an illustration of that very [principle] occurring at the beginning, end, and middle of the verse, namely: "māninī" (the proud woman). O Anaṅga (O Bodiless One)! desiring to lead—that is, wishing to bring—this proud woman (*māninī*) to the state of being your quiver (*niṣaṅgatva*), by means of the incessant discharge of your arrows, which implies she serves as their receptacle; and who is *hāriṇī*, adorned with the ornament of a necklace (*hāra*), and for that very reason *hāriṇī*, captivating; [she is] this woman who is attaining—that is, reaching—*tanutām*, emaciation. Thus is the meaning.

The sense is: "by the thought that [this] has been produced by the rejection [of my advances]"; "may it grant" (tanutām) means "may it bestow," namely, "peace" (śarma), which is happiness, for "me" (mama). The underlying intention is: "favor should be shown in such a way that this proud woman (māninī), casting aside her pride, takes refuge in me."

(Here, because the words *māninī māninī*, *hāriṇī hāriṇī*, and *tanutāṃ tanutāṃ* occur at the beginning of the first, third, and fourth quarters—and since the third quarter also begins [where the second ends] and the fourth quarter ends [where the third ends]—this is a mixed, uninterrupted *ādimāga-yamaka* occurring at the beginning and end of the first, third, and fourth quarters. || 16 ||

He provides an illustration of that very [comparison] occurring in the second, third, and fourth lines (beginning and end), starting with "jayatā": "O beloved of mine! O my dearest! By your face, which conquers—that is, brings under its sway—us, and which adorns—that is, beautifies—the water (*kaṃ*); likewise, the lotus (*kamalaṃ*), which possesses petals (*dalāni*) that have bees (*alimanti*) upon them, has become *akathaṃ*, meaning devoid of talk, that is, beyond dispute; or alternatively, *akatham*..."

This should be construed as an adjective qualifying the lotuses; the meaning is "devoid of speech. The implication is that they are insentient because they lack the capacity for speaking. How so? What has not been conquered? Rather, it means that everything has indeed been conquered. The sense is: "What need is there for further words? Since even sentient beings have been defeated by Your face, how could such insentient lotuses possibly not be conquered?"

(Here, because the words forming the *yamaka*—namely "nakathaṃ nakathaṃ," "kamalaṃkamalaṃ," and "dalimat dalimat"—occur at the beginning of the second, third, and fourth [and first] quarters, and because they are designated as being at the beginning of the second and third quarters, this is an unmixed *ādimāgayamaka* occurring in the second, third, and fourth [and first] quarters. Thus, these three varieties mentioned by the term "beginning and end" have been illustrated by the example. || 17 ||

By the phrase "that very [thing] from all sides," he provides an example of what pertains to the four quarters, namely: "the lovely woman. Like the *pāṭala*—meaning like the flower of the tree called *pāṭala*, which is pale-red (*pāṭala*)—she is one whose garment (*aṃśuka*) is such; likewise, she is a "locus of fragrance" (*saurabhāspada*), meaning a place (*āspada*) of scent (*saurabha*), that is, possessing a beautiful odor; the sense is that she belongs to the lotus class (*padminījātīyā*). A certain lovely woman (*ramaṇī*), having become reddened (*aruṇībhūtā*), that is, turned crimson, is like the solar (*saurī*) light.

"She who possesses such radiance, like Vāruṇī, the goddess of wine, may she be my delightful beloved"—this is the ellipsis. (In this instance, because the rhyming words—"ramaṇī ramaṇī," "pāṭalā pāṭalā," "vāruṇī vāruṇī," and "saurabhā saurabhā"—occur in all four quarters, there is a mixed *ādi-bhāga-yamaka* (rhyme on the initial parts) occurring in the first, second, third, and fourth quarters, without interruption.

Thus, the eleven varieties of *avyapeta-ādi-bhāga-yamaka* (uninterrupted rhyme on initial parts), as defined by the rule beginning with "beginning, middle, and end," have been demonstrated through examples. 18.

"Thus" (*iti*) means in the manner described above. The *avyapeta* (unseparated) *yamaka*, occurring at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), has been illustrated along with its various subdivisions. Now, some of the variations (*vikalpa*) or types of that aforementioned *vyapeta* (separated) and *avyavahita* (intervened) *yamaka*, which follow in sequence, are being described.

(19) Having shown the *avyapeta* *yamaka* occurring in the divisions of a quarter-verse and so forth, since such a [separated] *yamaka* is impossible within a single quarter-verse, he first illustrates the one occurring in the first and second quarters, beginning with the word "madhu."

Spring is sweet; with the rising of the mango buds—that is, with the emergence of the blossoms of the *sahakāra* tree, which are fragrant and charming—it will render the pride (the indignation born of jealousy or the resentment of love) of the fawn-eyed women nothing more than a word, meaning it will leave only the name "pride" remaining, but will not preserve it in actual fact.

(Here, because the two words forming the *yamaka* at the beginning of the first and second quarters—"madhureṇa madhureṇa"—are separated by the two words "dṛśām mānam," this is a case of *miśra-ādibhāga-yamaka* occurring in the first and second quarters that is characterized by separation. | 20 |

He provides an illustration of that very [figure] occurring in the first and third quarters with the word *kara*: "The hand"—that is, the palm—of beautiful women (*rāmāṇām*), which is exceedingly copper-red (*atitāmraḥ*) or deeply flushed, performs the graceful action (*vibhramam*) of striking the lute (*tantrītāḍana*), consisting of the playing of the *vīṇā*; likewise, toward the beloved (*kānte*), meaning toward the lover who has committed an offense, it performs the striking of the ear-lotus (*śravaṇotpalatāḍanam*), that is, the act of hitting with two lotuses, in a manner full of jealousy (*seryam*), accompanied by anger and envy.

(Here, because the words "karoti karoti" occur at the beginning of the first and third quarters, they constitute a *vyavahita* [separated] instance; thus, this conforms to the definition of *vyapeta-yamaka*. Consequently, as before, it should be understood as a *miśra* [mixed] *ādibhāga-yamaka* occurring in the first and third quarters with separation. || 21 ||

He provides an illustration occurring in both the first and fourth quarters with the verse beginning *sakalāpa*: "The entire row of clouds (*meghālī*), meaning a dense mass of clouds, being *nartitā*—that is, moved or shaken—by the winds, *vimuñcati*, meaning it rains; and immediately thereafter (*anu*), that is, right after that, the peahen (*kalāpinī*) dances together with the *ullasana*—meaning the expansion—of her *kalāpa*, that is, her plumage. (This is a description of the rainy season).

Here, because of the two *yamaka* words "sakalāpo sakalāpo," which occur at the beginning of the first and fourth quarters and are thus separated, this is a mixed, separated initial-quarter *ādiyamaka*. (22)

He provides an illustration of that very [stanza] occurring in the second and third quarters, beginning with "svayam" (itself). O lovely woman! "Svayam eva" means without even the entreaties of a lover; "galan" means departing; "mānarūpaḥ kaliḥ" means a quarrel in the form of jealous anger. From such a state, what condition or state (*daśām*) would your mind not touch during these rains? That is to say, it will surely undergo every state of passion (*smaradaśā*), because during the rainy season, the *nīpa* or *kadamba* flower is exceedingly tender.

The meaning is: "How will you console your mind, which is devoid of fortitude, during separation? (In this verse, it should be understood that because of the intervention of the two *yamaka* words "kalikāmi kalikāmi" at the beginning of the second and third quarters, the *ādibhāga-yamaka* occurring in the second and third quarters is a mixed type known as *vyavahita* [interrupted]). 23.

He illustrates that very same [figure] occurring in the second and fourth quarters with the verse beginning "āruhya. Having ascended this *sthalī*—a place fashioned from a particular kind of moonstone (*candrakānta-maṇi*)—belonging to that mountain, the pleasure-hill (*krīḍā-parvata*) in the garden (*ākrīḍa*), this peacock (*mayūra*) named Śikhābala, moving about here and there, being beautiful and charming (*cāru*), and thus delightful within (*antaḥ-ramaṇīya*) due to its dark-blue eye-spots (*candraka*), or rather, [delightful] within the beautiful eye-spot...

Being such that its [final] portion is at the end, it dances. (In this regard, because the two *yamaka* words "candrakānta candrakānta" occupy the beginnings of the second and fourth quarters, there is an interval; thus, it should be understood as a mixed, separated initial-portion *yamaka* occurring in the second and fourth quarters. 24.

This [verse] brings together the third and fourth quarters, beginning with "uddhṛtya" (having lifted up). O King! That very earth (*urvī*), which was formerly lifted up—meaning raised from the single ocean—by the Blessed Viṣṇu in the form of a boar (*varāha*), and which stood upon the head of Vāsuki, the best of serpents; that same earth is now, at this present time, being upheld by your arm, having been rescued from the assembly of kings.

(Here, because the two *yamaka* words "varāhe varāhe" occur at the beginning of the third and fourth quarters respectively, they are separated; thus, this is a mixed *vyavahita-ādibhāga-yamaka* occurring in the third and fourth quarters. | 25 |

He provides an illustration of that very [simile] occurring in the first, second, and third quarters with the verse beginning "kareṇa": O King, in battles, the lordly elephants (*kareṇavaḥ*)—struck by your hand (*kareṇa*), which is the destroyer (*antakareṇa*) of enemies (*dviṣatām*), and therefore streaming with blood (*kṣaradraktāḥ*)—shine like evening clouds (*sandhyāghanāḥ*). (According to Amara: "The word *kareṇu* is feminine when referring to a female elephant and masculine when referring to a male elephant. They are beautiful like the clouds of twilight.

(Here, because the yamaka words "kareṇa kareṇa kareṇa" occur at the beginning of the first, second, and third quarters respectively, they are separated; thus, this is a mixed, distant initial-quarter yamaka occurring in the first, second, and third quarters. | 26 |

He illustrates that very [simile] as it occurs in the first, third, and fourth quarters with the verse beginning "parāga-": "O King! By the soldiers—[the word] *tava* (your) being understood—the enemy host (*camū*), belonging to the opposing side, was destroyed (*dhvastā*); [the verb *dhvaṃs* here must be intended as transitive because its causative sense is inherent even though it is intransitive]. It was like a row of trees (*tarurājī*) on Mount Agastya, which was destroyed (*dhvastā*, meaning uprooted) by the winds (*vātaiḥ*). And [thus], by the dust (*parāgaiḥ*, meaning particles of pollen/dust)..."

The meaning is that the sky (*ambaram*) was pervaded (*tataṃ*) by the dust raised by the feet of the enemy soldiers who remained after the destruction and were fleeing; it seemed as if the sky had itself fled (*parāgatamiva*) to some other region (*kvāpi*), because the surface of the heavens became invisible due to the dust—this is the intended sense.

(In this verse, the repetition of "parāgata parāgata parāgata" constitutes a *yamaka* where the first, third, and fourth quarters are involved; since they occur at the beginning of these quarters and are separated [by the intervening syllables], it is a "mixed" *vyavahita-ādibhāga-yamaka* occurring in the first, third, and fourth quarters. || 27 ||

He illustrates that very [verse] as it occurs in its second, third, and fourth quarters with the words "pātu" and so forth: May the Lord Viṣṇu—who possesses the luster of a fresh cloud (navaghanadyuti), who is dark like a new rain-cloud; who is the destroyer of the race of Dānavas (dānavakuladhvaṃsī), the slayer of the Daitya lineage; who is ever-giving (sadānaḥ) and full of compassion (samadaḥ); and who slew that excellent elephant Varadantī, namely the one called Kuvalayāpīḍa—may he, the renowned Lord Viṣṇu, protect you all at all times.

(Here, because the *yamaka* words "sadānava sadānava sadānava" occur at the beginning of the second, third, and fourth quarters respectively, they are separated; thus, this is a mixed, separated initial-quarter *ādi-bhāga-yamaka* occurring in the second, third, and fourth quarters. 28.

He illustrates that very [pun] as it applies to all the words: "O beloved! *kam* (your) *kaṃ* (head)—for Śāśvata states, 'The word *kaṃ* means water or head'—is such that its hair is equal to (*samāḥ*), meaning similar to, the bee (*ali*) in being thick and black; and it is *muktaṃ*, meaning it causes envy for the lotus (*kamala*), that is, it is a conqueror of the lotus. Therefore, like Kamalā (Lakṣmī), who are you that make me—who am intoxicated among the intoxicated—countless (*alekhya*), that is, beyond reckoning?"

Rather, the intended meaning is that you drive everyone to madness. (In this instance, because the word *kamale*, which forms part of the *yamaka*, occurs at the beginning of every quarter-verse and is separated [from its repetition], it is a case of "mixed *vyavahita-ādibhāga-yamaka*" occurring across all quarters. | 29 |

Having thus illustrated the distinction between the contiguous (*avyapeta*) and non-contiguous (*vyapeta*), he now demonstrates the different varieties of the non-contiguous itself according to its homogeneous and heterogeneous nature. First, he provides an example of one kind for the first and second [cases], and another kind for the third and fourth, beginning with "mudā": "Noble" (*udārāḥ*) means excellent; "jewels" (*maṇayaḥ*) means gems; "ornament" (*bhūṣaṇam*).

[The women] were adorned with magnificent and highly valuable jeweled ornaments and precious gems; their eyes were rolling or reeling due to intoxication—either from drinking wine or from the particular agitation produced by [the pride of] good fortune and the like; and they possessed broad hips (or, according to alternative readings, "possessing love" or "possessing minds"). [The word] *pramadāḥ* (women) is to be supplied as the subject. (Regarding the reading *jaghanāḥ*, the variants *manmathāḥ* or *manasaḥ* for the first and second quarters of the verse are more appropriate.)

Because of the presence of a *yamaka* (rhyme) formed by four syllables, it is appropriate here as well [to interpret it thus]: "capable" means having the power; "to make" means to render; "the lover" (*ramaṇa*) "followed by joy" (*mudānvīta*) means accompanied by joy, or rather, dependent upon joy; or alternatively, "the lover followed by joy" means the lover endowed with happiness.

(Here, because the words forming the *yamaka*—namely "mudārama mudārama" at the beginning of the first and second quarters and "madabhra madabhra" at the beginning of the third and fourth quarters—are presented as being of different types and separated [by intervening syllables], this is a case of heterogeneous, mixed, and separated initial-quarter *yamaka* for both the first-second pair and the third-fourth pair. | 30 |

He provides examples of the first and third types being of one kind and the second and fourth being of another kind, exactly as previously described, with the words "uditaiḥ" (by those uttered). O messenger! by the *uditaiḥ*—meaning arisen—*ārutaiḥ*—meaning warblings—of the cuckoos (*anyapuṣṭa*), that is, by their sounds all around; likewise, by your *uditaiḥ*—meaning spoken—words, that is, even by your words indicating the suffering of your beloved; and likewise, by the *dakṣiṇaiḥ*—meaning southern—*mārutaiḥ*—meaning Malaya breezes—my mind has been struck.

The meaning is "distressed. (In this example, because the recurring words "uditai uditai" at the beginning of the first and third quarters and "mārutai mārutai" at the beginning of the second and fourth quarters are of different types, and because they are situated at the beginning of the quarters, are separated [by other words], and are thus non-identical, there is a non-identical, mixed, and separated *ādimāga-yamaka* [rhyme] between the first and third, as well as the second and fourth quarters. || 31 ||

He provides an illustration where the first and fourth quarters are of one kind, while the second and third are of another, as previously stated, beginning with the word *sura*: "Women—those whose slender waists (the region of the hips) are diminished, whose moon-like faces are beautifully adorned (*surājitāḥ*) by trickling drops of perspiration (*sveda*) arising from the manifestation of *sāttvika* emotions, and who have surpassed (*jitāḥ*, meaning overcome) intoxication (*sura*) through their wine-drinking, and are thus free from shame (*hrī*). [Note: The term *surājitāḥ* is a pun; it means both "beautifully adorned" (*su-rājitāḥ*) and "conquered by wine" (*surayā jitāḥ*).]

Those who are such truths, they occupy (*adhyāsate*)—that is, they preside over—the body (*tanuṃ*) of young men (*yūnām*, i.e., youths). (In this verse, because the constituent parts of the *yamaka*—"surājita surājita" at the beginning of the first and fourth quarters, and "tanumadhyā tanumadhyā" at the beginning of the second and third quarters—are of different types and separated by intervening words, there is a "mixed, separated initial-quarter *yamaka*" between the first and fourth, and between the second and third. || 32 ||

Having separately illustrated *yamaka* that is both non-intervened (*avyapeta*) and intervened (*vyapeta*), he now speaks—saying "iti"—to show other varieties resulting from the mixture of those two together. "In this manner" (*iti uktaprakāreṇa*), "this" (*eṣaḥ*) variety of intervened (*vyapeta*, i.e., separated) *yamakas* has been shown (*darśitaḥ*, i.e., illustrated). By the use of the particle "api," it is implied that the previously mentioned varieties of non-intervened *yamaka* are also included in this collection.

"Unseparated" (*avyapeta*) means not intervened by others, and "separated" (*vyapeta*) means intervened; that which has such a nature—meaning consisting of both—is a variety (*vikalpa*), that is, a sub-division. The phrase "for example" (*tat yathā*) is for the sake of illustration. (33) Therein, he provides an example of the first type in the first and second quarters, and another type, consisting of both unseparated and separated forms, in the third and fourth quarters, beginning with the word *sā*.

That *ālī* (female friend) is my companion; *sālambā* means existing together with *ālamba*, that is, with those which hang down properly—meaning the hanging buds (*kalikā*) or flower-buds (*koraka*). [The tree] is such that it moves (*salati*), shakes, or sways because of them; or rather, it is so called because it shines (*salati*) by means of them. To see—that is, to look upon—the *sāla* tree (either a tree in general or specifically a *sarja* tree; as Medinī says: "The word *sāla* applies to any tree, to a rampart, and to the *sarja* tree"), she is not *alaṃ*, meaning she is not capable.

The sense is that this is because the *kalikā* (bud) acts as an excitant (*uddīpaka*). Likewise, "those upon whom *vakula* trees have settled" (*ālīnavakulān*) means those who have properly resorted to them; the meaning is "those to whom *vakula* trees are attached. (The suffix *-kta* is used here in the sense of location, as in "they settle here"). "Bees" (*alīn*) refers to *bhramaras*; the word "even" (*api*) is to be supplied [after "bees"]. "Not able to see" (*na... alam vīkṣitum*) is to be construed with what precedes.

Likewise, "even those who are *alīkinīḥ*—that is, even those who speak falsely (*mithyāvādinīḥ*), meaning even those consoling her with false words such as 'your beloved will arrive before long'"; the word "friends" (*sakhīḥ*) is to be supplied; and "not able to look [upon them]" is also to be supplied here. (This is the speech of a messenger sent by a heroine to a hero abroad.)

Here, at the beginning of the first and second quarters, there is the repetition of "sālaṃ sālaṃ sālaṃ sālaṃ," and at the beginning of the third and fourth quarters, "nālī nālī nālī nālī"; thus, because these repeated words are without interval, they constitute *avyapeta* (unseparated) Yamaka. Furthermore, because the syllables "vakalikā" and "navakulā" are separated by an interval in the middle, this is *vyapeta* (separated) Yamaka. Consequently, it possesses both characteristics. Moreover, because it occurs at the beginnings of the quarters, it is designated by the number of those initial parts; and because the latter half differs from the former half, it is of a heterogeneous (*vijātīya*) nature.

It should be understood that when [the *yamaka*] occurs in both the first and second quarters and the third and fourth quarters, it is of a dual nature, such as the *vijātīyamiśra* (heterogeneous mixture) type of *bhāgayamaka*. || 34 ||

He provides an example where the first and fourth quarters are of one kind, while the second and third are of another, beginning with the word *kālam*. The word *kā* refers to a woman separated from her lover (*virahiṇī ramaṇī*), as is understood from the context. [The quarters describe a place] where the stars (*tārā*)—meaning large and intensely brilliant—are not visible (*anālakṣya*) because they are obscured by clouds; likewise, it is a place where the thundering of clouds (*rasitāni*) is unpleasant (*aramyāṇi*) to the ear due to its extreme height (*tāratayā*), and where the darkness (*kālāḥ*) is vast and black in color.

Is anyone capable (*alam*) of beholding (*ikṣitum*) such a time—the rainy season—which is dense with thick clouds, which is like Yama himself because it destroys the lives of those separated from their lovers, and which is Time itself? The meaning is: no one at all.

(In this verse, in the beginning of the first and fourth quarters, we have "kālaṃ kālaṃ kālaṃ kālam," and in the beginning of the second and third quarters, "tāratāra tāratāra. Thus, as before, there is a mixed type of *ādimāga-yamaka* consisting of both immediate and non-immediate repetition of the same words.)

Regarding the phrase "kālaṃ kālamānālakṣya," some consider the reading "kālaṃ kālaṃkṛtaṃ ghanaiḥ" to be correct; for since both instances of "kālaṃ kālam" in the first quarter of the verse contain the anusvāra, it is appropriate for that same form to appear in the fourth quarter as well. The meaning there is: "made dark by the clouds," or "made to possess inferior ornaments. (35)

He illustrates that very same [verse] occurring in four quarters with the words "yāmaṃ... and so on. "Yāmatrayasya" means of the three watches, i.e., the three *praharas*; "adhīnaḥ" means dependent; "āyāmaḥ" means length—[referring to] such a [night] extending over three very long watches. (From the statement, "They say the night consists of three *yāmas*, O King, having abandoned the fourfold beginning and end," one should understand that the night is composed of three *yāmas*. "Niśā" means by reason of the night; "maraṇaṃ yāma" means may we attain death; "vayam" is the ellipsis (the subject). (The *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of a benediction or prayer. Of the night...

The sense is that [this is said] because it serves to intensify the longing caused by separation. Now, one might ask: "Why is such an inauspicious thing being prayed for? To this he says, "yām" (her whom...). With the mind (*dhiyā*), we went to (*ayāma*) that beloved; the meaning is that we spent our time in thought of her, or rather, that we made her the ultimate object of our pride regarding our entire life's wealth. She—by means of this night, which is *āyāmayā* (extremely long), as if it were hundreds of millions of kalpas, and thus exceedingly protracted—and by means of *asvattaryā* (the distress of the vital breaths), that is, by the pain (*artiḥ*) of the affliction of the life-forces (*asūn*).

"By means of [the night] acting as a gateway, she has already been crushed—that is, she is almost certainly destroyed; the word 'ūrdhvī' (rising up) is to be understood as the remainder [of the verb]. By that night, through separation from me, the life-breaths of my most delicate beloved will surely depart; therefore, the sense is that my own death alone is better. Or else, "We shall go to death" (using the *loṭ* suffix in the sense of deliberation); the meaning is that we deliberate, "We shall die."

Let our death be; there is no sorrow in that. However, that [sorrow] which comes—that is, which reaches her—who goes toward a state of helplessness (*asvartim*) due to my absence (this is the form of the third person plural *liṅ* of the root *yā* with the prefix *ā*), such a one has been crushed and destroyed by me alone. The sense is: "It is my great sorrow that she, miserable in separation from me, her lover who has gone abroad, is dying."

(This is the mention of a lamp in the night. Here, because the *yamaka* word "yāma yāma" occurs at the beginning of each of the four quarters, it constitutes a mixed *ādibhāgayamaka* (initial-position *yamaka*) that pertains to all quarters, being both immediate and non-immediate. || 36 ||

Having described the varieties of *ādimāga-yamaka* (alliteration at the beginning of metrical quarters), he concludes that section with the word "iti" (*iti*). The meaning is as follows: "iti" refers to the aforementioned types; "of the *vikalpa*," that is, of the variety of *yamakas* situated at the beginning of the quarters; "such" (*īdṛśī*), meaning of this kind; "the *gati*," that is, the rule [of application]; "the others"—namely, those situated in the middle and end of the quarters, whether unseparated (*avyapeta*), separated (*vyapeta*), or mixed (*tanmiśrita*)—these *yamakas* also are to be "varied" (*vikalpyāni*), meaning they are to be divided, in exactly the same manner as previously stated, in forms such as one, two, three, etc., and likewise in forms such as beginning, middle, and end.

To the question, "Why have all the varieties of *yamaka* not been shown by me, the author of this work? he replies: "No. For fear of prolixity—that is, for fear of excessive expansion—I have not endeavored to describe the varieties in their entirety (*kārtsnyena*). However, those varieties which are considered difficult by others—this is the ellipsis—"some of them" (*te kecanātra*) are described and illustrated here. The sense is that only some varieties will be shown by me, but not all; as for the others, they should be understood by oneself in the manner previously mentioned regarding the *ardhabhāga-yamaka*. || 38 ||

In this regard, he illustrates the *madhyayamaka* (middle rhyme), which consists of all syllables and is inseparable in nature, with the verse beginning "sthirāyate. The word *sthirāyate* is a vocative: *sthirā* means lasting for a long time, and *āyatiḥ* refers to the future time; thus, it means "O you whose future is stable! (*"uttaraḥ kāla āyatiḥ"* according to Amarasimha). O you who partake in the bliss of the senses (*akṣavyasukhabhājana*)! You are one whose senses are restrained (*yatendriyaḥ*). Therefore, because of your restraint (*yataḥ*), meaning through self-control or meditative concentration (*samādhi*), you do not fall away (*na hīyate*) from it; for without the restraint of the senses, there can be no stability in meditative concentration.

"Bhāva" means that which comes into being; as it has been said, "The powerful collection of the senses drags away even the wise man. Your "amāyatā"—that is, your lack of guile, meaning your freedom from deceit—is for "iyate," meaning for that which is immeasurable, meaning for that which cannot be delimited; likewise, for "kṣayam," meaning destruction or loss, "ayate" means for that which does not go toward [destruction], meaning for the imperishable; it became for the sake of supreme bliss.

(Here, in all four quarters, the word "yate yate" is repeated within the middle of each quarter; and since it is repeated again within a single quarter, it is "unseparated" (*avyapeta*), while with respect to the other quarters, it is "separated" (*vyapeta*). Thus, this is a "separated-and-unseparated" internal rhyme (*madhyabhāgayamaka*) occurring across all quarters. || 39 ||

He provides an example of *kevalavyapeta-madhyama-dhyayamaka* (internal rhyme occurring only in the middle of each quarter-verse) with the verse beginning "sabhāsu": "O King! [Those who] in the assemblies are praised by the *mahīsurās*—that is, by the Brahmins—who are not struck by *asuras*, meaning they are not ruined by the drinking of wine; who are pure because they are averse to the consumption of intoxicants; who are resplendent (*rājita*) with wealth (*vasu*), that is, with splendor or the acquisition of riches bestowed by Śiva; who are radiant (*bhāsura*) and thus shining; and likewise..."

Among the subjects—the people—who are devoted to passion and intent upon affection, your virtues have attained a state of abundance, meaning they have reached a condition of great esteem; they do not fail to reach, that is, they do not fail to attain, the gods who are [themselves] passionate (surān). This is emphatic: they certainly do attain them. The sense is that only the gods possess such qualities. (Here, the word *surāḥ* appears at the beginning of every quarter; because it is separated by intervening words and situated in the middle of the quarters, it constitutes a mixed *vyapeta* (separated) *madhyamadhyabhāga-yamaka*.

Having illustrated the *madhyayamaka* (middle-verse yamaka) that is displaced from each quarter, he now provides an example of such an *antayamaka* (end-verse yamaka) occurring across all quarters, beginning with the words "tava" etc. O you of wicked conduct!

O rogue! O heedless one! O inattentive one! At this very moment—meaning, now—in that same way, by her who was your beloved and affectionate, meaning, she who is currently being celebrated by you as the object of your love in the assembly of people; by her, that is, while she was intoxicated—that is, deeply attached—to the particular joy derived from the festival of sexual union, [she] wore a radiant ornament—that is, a jewel—shining like the sun; and thus, regarding the wearing of that ornament...

The purpose [of her action] is to provide joy through the festival of love; however, that is not possible for my friend while she is attached to another than you. Therefore, why should she maintain it? The sense is that it is only fitting for your present beloved to maintain it.

"Surely, even for the sake of beauty, your friend should wear ornaments there. To this she replies: "Indeed, as for the purpose... For it is thus: by reason of her *kāntimat-tva*—that is, by virtue of possessing innate beauty—the word "of my friend" being understood, there is no "purpose," meaning there is no necessity, for the wearing of ornaments; the sense is that her natural and extraordinary radiance alone produces her loveliness, so what need is there for the wearing of other ornaments?

This is a statement by a female friend to one who asks how this woman could have lost her passion for a deceitful lover who is attached to another and wears ornaments: “O you of wicked conduct, you are intoxicated! (In some versions, the reading here is *sañcaritāpramatta* instead of *asaccarita pramatta*). Here, because the word *mattayā* occurs at the end of the first quarter and is separated [from its counterpart], it constitutes a *miśra-vyapeta-antabhāga-yamaka* that spans all four quarters. || 41 ||

He illustrates the *anta-bhāga-yamaka* (end-part rhyme), which occurs across four quarters and may be either contiguous (*avyapeta*) or non-contiguous (*vyapeta*), with the verse beginning "bhavādṛśāḥ": "O Lord! O Master! People like you do not know the 'rasa'—the aesthetic flavor—of 'natibhāva' (humility). For, on the one hand, there is 'sannata' (perfect humility) and, on the other, 'inatā' (lordship); these two, namely humility and lordship, are indeed (*khalu*) contradictory (*viruddhe*) and certainly do not reside in a single substratum (*naikādhāre vartate*). This is the sense: those people [like you] [do not know it].

The wretched are the poor; they alone, by means of that well-known poison in the form of misery—the word *rasa* here signifying "misery" (as Medinī states: "The word *rasa* [is used] for smell, water, the erotic sentiment and others, poison, potency, the bitter taste and others, a type of bodily constituent, mercury, and flavor")—bow their heads and, through that, serve you excessively; the genitive case in *tava* functions as an objective genitive, meaning they serve you to the utmost degree.

(Here, in all four quarters, the word "nate nate" occurring at the end is repeated; and since it is not separated by a single quarter within each individual quarter, but rather separated by other quarters, this is a mixed type of *antayamaka* possessing both characteristics. | 42 |

He provides an example of *madhyāntayamaka* (rhyme at the middle and end of each quarter-verse) occurring with intervals between the feet, beginning with "līlā": That heroine, by means of speech that was pure (*śucinā*), meaning stainless; playful (*savilāsa*) due to her graceful smile (*līlāsmitena*); soft (*mṛdunā*), meaning tender; uttered (*uditena*); light (*laghunā*), meaning desired or requested—or alternatively, "light" meaning small or incomplete (as Amara states: "the word *laghu* is used for the three [qualities], for the desired, and for the small"); by a sidelong glance (*vyalokitena*), meaning a look from the corner of the eye; and by a gait (*gatena*) that was heavy (*guruṇā*), meaning slow and languid due to the weight of her hips and other limbs... [the rest of the verse follows].

By her walking, by her yawning—specifically by the act of yawning (as it has been said that yawning reveals passion, for example: "She yawns, stretches her limbs, and having embraced the child, she kisses him")—and likewise by her displaying her hips (meaning by some pretext of showing her hips), she strikes—that is, she pains me; this is the ellipsis. And for that reason, my life is "gone"—that is, departed, as if almost destroyed. (The past passive participle suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract state.)

In this [verse], the word "tena" (by that) recurs repeatedly in the middle and at the end of each quarter-verse; and since it is separated [from its correlate], this is a mixed *vyavahita-madhyānta-yamaka* (intermediate-and-final rhyme with separation). || 43 ||

He provides an example of *madhyāntayamaka*—occurring within each quarter-verse (*pāda*), both non-separate (*avyapeta*) and separate (*vyapeta*)—in the verse beginning with "śrīmān. (The word division here is as follows: *śrīmān*, *amān*, *amaravatrmasamānamānam*, *ātmānam*, *ānatajagatprathamānamānam*, *bhūmānam*, *ānamata*, *yaḥ*, *sthitimān*, *amānanāmānam*, *ānamatam*, *apratimānamānam*). O devotee! *Amaravartman* is the sky; that which has a measure (*māna*) equal to it is so described—that is, like the sky.

The meaning is "all-pervading. Regarding those who are *ānateṣu*—those who are well-known, or those who have become bowed down for the sake of worship—the term *prathamānaḥ* means having attained expansion. *Mānaḥ* means honor or worship; it refers to one whose [name] is such, meaning one who is worshipped by the entire world. *Bhūmānam* means great. *Amānam* means immeasurable, meaning innumerable. One whose name is of such a nature is [described as] *tathā*. Furthermore, *ā* means slightly; *ananti* means they breathe, meaning they live (*śvasanti*). Those who [breathe] are the *ānāḥ*.

The meaning is "devoted to breath-control" (prāṇāyāma), referring to yogins; by them it is "honored" (mataṃ) or "worshipped," or alternatively, "known through yoga" (yogena jñātam). Or, "revered by yogins" (ānamataṃ) means honored by yogins or accessible to yogins. Likewise, "without comparison" (apratimānaḥ) means peerless; that which has such [comparison] is "the beloved of all" (sarvābhimataṃ). Alternatively, "apratimāna" means incomparable, and "māna" means knowledge; thus, it refers to Him whose knowledge is incomparable, meaning He is known solely through the restraint of the mind (manaḥ-saṃyama). Such is the Self (ātmānaṃ), the Supreme Self (paramātmānaṃ), meaning Brahman.

"Salute him, for whom [the salutation] is due; you," is the ellipsis. Now, one might ask: "What is the proof for the acceptance of such a Self (ātman), which has not been accepted by the Cārvākas and others? To this, he says: "He who... He who is the Self (ātmā)—glorious, self-luminous; pervasive and immeasurable, because of His omnipresence (vibhutva), there is no sense of Him being limited anywhere; likewise, He is enduring, remaining eternally in the form of existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda); the meaning is that He is eternal as the cause of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe.

(Here, because the word *mānamāna* recurs repeatedly without interruption both in the middle and at the end of all four quarters, there is the *avyapeta* (unseparated) type; likewise, because the syllables such as *maravatrmasa* are separated [by other sounds], there is also the *avyapeta* type of *madhyāntayamaka*. One should not raise the objection: "How can this be considered *madhyayamaka* since the word *māna* recurs after only a single syllable? For the term "middle" (*madhya*) is defined precisely as the interval between the first and last syllables. || 44 ||

He provides an example of [the *sāra*] occurring at every foot, devoid of beginning or middle: *sārayantīm*. She is so called because she wears golden ornaments (*urusāra*)—for "urusāra" means gold (according to Vyāḍi)—and likewise, she is one by whom a *sārasa*, a particular bird, has been imitated; the sense is that she possesses a warbling like the cry of a *sārasa*. Thus, the meaning is "one whose girdle (*kāñcī*) corresponds to the warbling of a *sārasa*. The placement of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) at the end follows the rule: "The past participle should be stated as following words denoting genus, time, pleasure, and so forth. Therefore, *sārasā* means "accompanied by sound," referring to the girdle.

That woman, who wore a girdle (*mekhalā*) upon her waist, was delighting—that is, pleasing—her husband, who was the very essence of the worlds, reckoned as preeminent among all beings, and who had become the entirety of her life; she delighted him by embracing him (the form *sārayantam* is from the root *sṛ* in the *cur*-class meaning "to embrace," or alternatively, "causing herself to be approached"), with her breast—that is, her chest—and thus, through her reciprocal embrace, providing him with happiness, he became like an elixir (*rasāyanam*) that removes old age and disease.

Even medicine—and by implication, even nectar (*amṛta*)—is *asāra*, meaning worthless or trivial, because it cannot prevent one from being overcome by old age and disease; this is what he understands. The sense is that he realizes even nectar is trivial compared to the bliss of embracing his beloved. (In this verse, within each quarter-verse, the word "sārasāra"—which constitutes the *yamaka*—is repeated again and again with an intervening space between its initial and middle occurrences; thus, it is a "mixed" *vyavahita-ādimadhya-yamaka*). 45.

In the first and third quarters, it demonstrates *avyapeta-vyapeta* (both contiguous and non-contiguous) *ādyanta-yamaka* (initial-final rhyme), and in the second and fourth quarters, it shows a similar *ādimadhya-yamaka* (initial-middle rhyme). The analysis of the word division (*padaviccheda*) should be understood as follows: *nayetiṣa* [is divided as] *nayānayālocanayā*, *anayā*, *anayān*; *ayānayān*, *ayān*, *tān*, *janaya*, *anayāśritān*. O *anayāyate*! [This is a vocative: "O you whose future (*āyatiḥ*), meaning the subsequent time, is *anayā*—that is, not going (*na ayate*), thus free from misfortune (*apāya-rahitā*)."

O Lord of unerring doctrine! By this very [teaching], which is thus observed—by this [means] which is beneficial to the eyes, and for that very reason, by the bringing (*ānayena*) of *aya*, that is, auspicious action (according to Amara: "*ayaḥ* is an auspicious rite")—toward the performance [of duty], [please] discipline those people who are blind, meaning those who do not perceive their own welfare; [the word] "people" is to be supplied as the object. Discipline them so that they may become followers of the path of ethics; that is to say, ordain it in such a way that they may follow the way of policy. Furthermore, the Jina-vehicle...

Those who go toward the Jain path are so described; they are followers of the Buddhist doctrine. For this very reason, they "go toward what is not a path" (*ayāna*), meaning an improper way or a contrary road; thus they are "those who travel on a wrong path" (*apathagāminaḥ*). For this same reason, they are "those who rely on a bad course" (*anayāśritān*), meaning those who take hold of their own inauspicious support. Those people whom you did not approach (*na ayāsauḥ*), that is, with whom you did not form an association—meaning those followers of the Buddhist doctrine—they [the devotees] go toward *Aṃ*, which is Viṣṇu.

"...thus become, those who rely upon the Vaiṣṇava dharma—produce [them], create them. (In this verse, because the sequence "nayānayā" occurs at the beginning and end of the first and second quarters without interruption, and because it recurs at the beginning and middle of the third and fourth quarters without interruption, both *avyapeta-ādyantayamaka* and *ādimadhyayamaka* are demonstrated together in a single instance; such is the direction. || 46 ||

He provides an example of *ādyantayamaka* (rhyme at the beginning and end) that is free from all other types of *pādayamaka*: "raveṇa... [etc.]. *Bhaumaḥ* means the son of the Earth (*bhūmisuta*), namely the demon Naraka; *dhvajavartinaḥ* means situated upon the banner of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s chariot; *vīrasya* means of the heroic; *veḥ* means of the bird, that is, of Garuḍa; *raveṇa* means by the sound or roar; *atulam* means incomparable; *astrāṇāṃ gauravam* refers to the weightiness or abundance of weapons; *bhairave* means terrifying; and *saṃyati* means in battle; *aveji* means he was agitated or terrified.

The meaning is "terrified. For instance, [know] that before this Hari Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who is like the sun (*ravi*), that is, like a fierce mass of splendor—and who is also like a lion, the enemy, namely the demon Naraka, is equal to a sheep (*avi*); know (*aveta*) this, you [should understand], as the ellipsis implies. (This is a description of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s battle with the demon Naraka.
Here, because the word *rave* appears repeatedly at the beginning and end of all four quarters of the verse, separated by intervening words, it is a "mixed" *vyavahitādyantayamaka*. || 47 ||

He provides an example of initial and final *yamaka* occurring across four quarters, both with and without intervening syllables, beginning with the verse "mayā": (here the word division is as follows: *mayāmayālambyakalāmayāmayām*; *ayām*, *amayā*).

*Amaya*, *āmaya*, *amūm*, *karuṇāmaya*, *āmayā itai*. O *amaya*! [The word] *mayaḥ* means that which measures (*minoti*), casts away (*kṣipati*), or abandons (*tyajati*) to a distance; that which is not such is *amayaḥ*. It refers to You who follow me in all circumstances—this is the vocative. (The suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *ḍu miñ* "to cast" in the sense of the agent. Alternatively, O *amaya*! [it means] O You in whom there is no *māyā* (illusion/deceit)—the meaning is "O guileless one! (The elision of the vowel *ā* is not contrary to usage because it appears in the works of great poets). Therefore, O...

O you who consist of compassion! O you who consist of mercy! (The word "friend" is understood as the remainder; by these two vocative phrases, it is suggested that he will certainly grant favor to one's own prayer. *Āmaya* means disease, that is to say, the affliction of desire. One who goes toward (*yāti*) or attains (*prāpnoti*) this is *āmayāḥ*; thus, by *āmayā*, the meaning is "by one subject to desire. [In the form *āmayā*,] there is the elision of the vowel *ā* according to the rule "āto dhātoḥ. *Mayaḥ* means decline, that is to say, the waning of digits (as in the moon). [This is a form of the root *may* in the sense of "going. *Amayaḥ* means increase.

The meaning is that because of her habit of increasing [the digits of] the *kalās* (digits of the moon); "to be resorted to" (*ālambya*) means she is to be relied upon; "from that which consists of *kalās*" refers to the moon, which is composed of *kalās*; "from that, disease" (*āmaya*) means the affliction of desire; "one who has such [a disease]"—the sense being that the moon is an excitant of passion; "delightful" (*amam*) means charming; "since I am not to be reached" (*ayātavya*) means unattainable; "those whose watches have come to an end" (*virāmayāmāḥ*) refers to those for whom the *yāmas* (watches) have ceased; "of such a long duration" (*dīrghayāmayā*) is the meaning; and for this very reason, "there is no measure" (*nāsti mā*) means there is no limit.

The meaning is: by that night (*niśā*) which was "thus" (*tathābhūtayā*), that is, very long; for this very reason, she is called "lacking beauty" (*amayā*), meaning one whose beauty (*mā*) is absent—that is, extremely loathsome—referring to the nights of those separated from their lovers. "Mayaḥ" means going or reaching (according to the rule: "all roots meaning 'to go' mean 'to reach'"); its opposite is *amayaḥ*, meaning non-reaching. By that *amaya*—that is, by not reaching her—the sense is that she experienced *arti*, meaning pain, which became excessive due to not attaining her.

"I have reached this state of being tormented by desire"—this is the meaning (the form of the root *yā* in the sense of "going"). This is a statement by a friend to a certain lover separated from his beloved. (In this verse, there is a mixed type of initial and final *yamaka*, characterized by the repeated proximity of the word *mayā mayā* at the beginning and end of each quarter-verse, as well as the intervention of the syllables *la-mb-y-a-k-l-ā* and so forth in the middle. 48.

He provides an example of the *vyapetādimadhyāntayamaka* (the alliterative repetition occurring at the beginning, middle, and end, with intervals): *matāmitiṣa* (the word division being as follows: *matām*, *dhunānā*, *āramatām*, *akāmatām*; *atāpalabdhā*, *agrimatānulomatā*; *mataḥ*, *ayatī*, *uttamatāvilomatā*; *atāmyataḥ*, *te*, *samatā*, *na*, *vāmatā*). Here, the vocative term *he sādho!* (O good man! is to be supplied.

"Of those who never tire"—meaning those whose minds are always serene—"in your thought," that is, in your heart; "of those who delight in themselves alone"—meaning of yogis who have withdrawn from sense-objects—"esteemed," meaning approved by yogis; "even desirelessness"—the word "even" (api) being understood here—meaning freedom from longing; "shaking," meaning causing it to tremble, that is, surpassing it due to its own excellence; and likewise, "obtained without heat," meaning attained without effort or distress.

The meaning is that it possesses its own inherent nature (*svābhāvikī*); likewise, it is "conformable" (*anulomatā*)—meaning favorability—toward excellence (*agrimatā*), which is to say, it brings about such excellence. Similarly, regarding superiority (*uttamatā*), which is the possession of qualities (*guṇavattā*), it does not go toward "contrariety" (*vilomatā*), that is, opposition; the sense is that it is co-extensive with the possession of qualities. Equanimity (*samatā*), meaning impartiality or seeing all things as equal, exists—this is the ellipsis. However, perversity (*vāmatā*), meaning contrariety, does not exist—this is the ellipsis.

[This is a praise of a certain virtuous person. Here, because the word “matā” (*regarded*) is repeated at the beginning, middle, and end of each quarter-verse with intervening words, this is an example of *vyavahita-ādimadhyānta-yamaka* (separated initial, middle, and final rhyme). Now, he provides an example of *ādimadhyānta-yamaka* consisting of both non-intervened (*avyapeta*) and intervened (*vyapeta*) forms, beginning with the verse starting “kāla...”. The word division is as follows: in the first quarter-verse there is one word: *kālakālaghanakālakālapanakāla*, [and then] *kāla*.

(kālakālasitakālakā, lalanikā, alakālakālakā, alagatu, kālakāla, kālikāla, kāla iti) O Kālakālagalakālakālamukhakālakāla! [This refers to: *kāla* (Time), meaning Śiva—the Destroyer (*saṃhāraka*)—as stated in the scriptural passage, "He is proclaimed as Time because of his reckoning (*kalana*) of all beings"; *kālagala* (the blue-colored throat); *kāla* (Yama); and *kālamukha* (a specific type of monkey). [These are joined in a copulative compound. *Kālakāla* means the one who is the death even of Death. *Sitakālakā* means the white-colored Time. *Lalanikā* means a beautiful woman. *Alakālakālakā* means the black hair on the forehead. *Alagatu* means a serpent. *Kālakāla* and *kālikāla* are synonyms for Time. *Kāla* means Time itself. Thus, [the address] is: O you who are the Time of the Time, the Blue-throated One, Yama, the Monkey-faced One, and so forth!

"O you whose mouth has the blackness of the throat of Kāla (Death)! [This is an address] to one who takes or assumes that blackness (*kālakam*); O you of dark complexion, like the throat of Śiva and so forth! Likewise, O you who are the time (*kāla*) for the sound-making (*kāyan*) of the cloud (*ghana*) which is black (*kāla*) at the time (*kāla*) of the black (*kāla*) water-bearing (*kāla*) cloud (*kāla*)! [The word *kāla* here means] 'water' (*kam*), and it 'takes' (*ālāti*) or 'holds' (*bibharti*) it; thus it is *kāla*, meaning 'possessing water'. For this very reason, it is *kāla*, meaning 'black-colored'. That which is the *ghana*—the cloud—at its *kāla*—the season, meaning during the rainy season—it is *kāyan*—it makes sounds."

The term *kālakālaghanakālakāḥ* means peacocks (the form is derived from the root *kai* "to sound" with the suffix *kvip*). Their *ālapanāni* are their mouths; thus, *kālakālaghanakālakālapanāni*. One who *kalate*—that is, sounds like them—is addressed as such: "O you who, like a peacock, have the habit of calling out with the *ṣaḍja* note! [Alternatively,] in the reading *kālakālapanakālakālaghanakāla*, the meaning is: in the *kāla* (time) of the rainy season (*varṣāsu*), those that *kāyanti* (sound) are *kālakāḥ*, i.e., peacocks. Their *ālapanam* is their cry; one who *kālayati* (measures or directs) that...

It means "he impels" or "he manifests. Such [is He]. Likewise, by the previously mentioned etymology, *kāla* means "filled with water"; *ghana* means "cloud. Thus, *kāla-ghana-vat* means "O Dark One!"—that is, dark like a water-laden cloud. Furthermore, O *kāla-kāla*!—*kāla* refers to Yama, the Restrainer; *kāla* here means the Destroyer. This is an address to Him who is the Destroyer [of Yama], meaning "O Dispeller of the fear of Yama! Alternatively, *kāla* refers to Time (*samaya*) by which [He] impels (*kālayati*) or urges on living beings (*bhūtāni*), as the ellipsis implies.

Regarding the vocative *tatsambuddhau*: according to the Smṛti, "O Maitreya, that form which is the very nature of Time belongs to Viṣṇu," one should understand that Viṣṇu has the nature of Time (*kālasvarūpa*). Furthermore, O *kalikālakāla*! [This means: the *kāla* (Time/death) of *kalikāla*, that is, of the Kali Age; the meaning is "the punisher in the form of Kalki. Thus, in that vocative: O *kāla*! O Kṛṣṇa! [The compound *kālakālasitakālakā* is analyzed as follows: those whose *alaka*s (curls of hair) have *kāla* (blackness) for their *kāla* (time/measure)—that is, who are adorned (*ālasita*) with black color (*kālakena*), and whose *ka* (head) is thus characterized by such *alaka*s.

She whose hair is curly (*cūrṇakuntalā*). Regarding this, some explain: "Water is *ka*; that which takes it [water] is *kāla*, a lake. Those who move about there are *kālakāḥ*, swans. She whose feet possess a languid, playful gait like theirs is *kālakapadī*. Furthermore, she is *alakālakālakā*: she who adorns (*alate*) her curls (*alakān*), meaning her ringlets, with pearls and other ornaments—such is *alakālī* (the form derived from the root *alaṅ* 'to adorn' with the suffix *aṇ*). Likewise, *kalakāla* means sweet, in the sense of being melodious.

And thus, *alakālī* means both *alaka* (curls) and *kālikā* (darkness), forming a *karmadhāraya* compound; *lalanikā* refers to a pitiable young woman, meaning Rādhā; the final sense is: "May she cling to you," that is, may she be united with you. (This is a statement by a friend of Śrī Rādhā addressed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Here, the word *kālakāla* is repeated without interruption at the beginning, middle, and end of all four quarters, constituting *avyavahita-ādimadhyāntayamaka*; likewise, words such as *gala* and *mukha* appear with intervals, constituting *vyavahita-ādimadhyāntayamaka*). || 50 ||

Now he points out the position of the *sandaṣṭa* (interlocking) *yamaka*, beginning with the word "sandaṣṭa. The meaning is: in two feet situated one above the other in proximity—that is, between two verses—the end of the first foot and the beginning of the second foot, as well as the end of the second foot and the beginning of the third foot, and likewise the end of the third foot and the beginning of the fourth foot; these portions of the feet are the "position" or domain of the *sandaṣṭa-yamaka*, which is a *yamaka* shaped like a pair of tongs (*sandaṃśa*).

The explicit meaning is that just as a pair of tongs (sandāśaḥ) functions by grasping both ends, so too does this [type of *yamaka*] function by grasping the end and beginning portions of the two lines. This is the "mandasṛṣṭa-yamaka" (the loosely joined *yamaka*); among the *yamakas* mentioned, it is included even within those such as "raveṇa bhaumaḥ," meaning it has already fallen under their category. However, here it is praised—that is, described—separately and independently, because of its specific distinction; this is the sense.

(This *yamaka* is cited here because it has been mentioned by others; however, it should be understood that in our own system, it is indeed included within the varieties previously described. Some call this the *kāñcīyamaka*; as it is said: "If a similar sound is seen at the end of one word and the beginning of another, that is called *kāñcīyamaka* by the best of sages. An other example from the *Bhaṭṭikāvya* is: "The creeper-like [mass of] bones of the flesh-eaters, being scattered in every direction, attained a state of utter clarity.")
"Thus, the great man has repeatedly performed deeds devoid of greatness, which are as unstable as a flickering flame. (51)

In this regard, he illustrates the *sandaṣṭa-yamaka* (interlaced rhyme) with the verse beginning "upoḍhe" (*Upoḍharāgā*). That weak woman—by whom passion (*rāga*), whether arising from the transformation produced by youth or from the drinking of wine, has become intensified (*upoḍha*) or increased—is thus one who is full of love for me; the meaning is that she is devoted to me. For this very reason, her mind (*ātman*) is fixed upon me. She is one who torments—that is, afflicts—the "tormentor of the bodiless one" (*anaṅgatāpin*); the sense is that [the god of love] is incapable of performing his own function [because she surpasses him]. Of such a woman... [of her].

The meaning is: even though she had gone [to him], O you who are free from passion for me, and even though she was desirous of me; by my transgression (*madenasā*), that is, by reason of my offense, she was joined with—meaning permeated by—the force of resentment (*manyurasena*), that is, having become subject to anger; she did not go (*na āsa*) to such an extent of torment (*tāpāya*), meaning suffering, "not so," but rather she certainly did go; the sense is that she became the cause of extreme anguish for me. (This is a form of the root *as*, meaning "to go," "to take," or "to shine.")

This is the speech of a proud woman who has rejected a certain suitor. Because of the occurrence of these phrases in the form of a *saṃdaṣṭa* (interlocking) structure—namely, "madena sā madenasā" at the end of the first foot and the beginning of the third; "na yojitā na yojitā" at the end of the second foot and the beginning of the third; and "ṅgatāpitā ṅgatāpitā" at the end of the third foot and the beginning of the fourth—it is called *saṃdaṣṭayamaka*. (52)

Having thus demonstrated the *yamakas* consisting of parts of the quarters, he now demonstrates the *yamakas* occurring in entire quarters, beginning first with the *samudra-yamaka*, stating: "The repetition of two halves. Here, "two halves" (*ardhābhyām*) refers to two quarters (it should be understood that the word *ardha* here does not refer solely to the first and second halves of a verse, but rather to any two quarters). "Repetition" (*abhyāsa*) means recurrence; this constitutes what is called the *samudra*.

By the word *samudra*, a *sampuṭaka* is meant; just as that consists of two parts, so too does this consist of two quarters, and thus it is designated in that way. As it has been said by Rudrabhaṭṭa: "That which produces a *yamaka* by repeating the second half is called *samudraka*. Of this *samudra*, three varieties are recognized and well-known.

(And thus: first and third quarters identical with second and fourth is the first type; first and second identical with third and fourth is the second; likewise, first and fourth identical with second and third is the third. Regarding the *yamakas* occurring across all quarters, he describes the *pādābhyāsa-yamaka* [repetition of quarters] with the words "pādābhyāsa."

The repetition of the quarters (*pādābhyāsa*) is the recurrence of each individual quarter; it is "of many natures" (*anekātmā*), meaning it is of eleven kinds due to the repetition of one, two, or three quarters [as follows]: first in the second, third, and fourth [making three]; second in the third and fourth [making two]; and third in the fourth [making one].

Furthermore, there are four types where the first [pada] occurs with the second and third, the second and fourth, the third and fourth, and the second, third, and fourth; likewise, there is one type where the first [pada] occurs with the second, third, and fourth. Thus, taken together, there are eleven varieties. This "half-repetition" (*ardhābhyāsa*) and "quarter-repetition" (*pādābhyāsa*) are manifested—that is, made clear—by the examples (*nidarśana*) which will be stated as illustrations. || 53 ||

In this regard, intending to demonstrate three varieties of *samudra* (alliteration), he first shows a *yamaka* characterized by the equality of the first and third quarters and the second and fourth quarters, based on the correspondence between the first half of the first quarter and the second half of the subsequent quarter. He says: "No.

Even by you—who are *paramāyataḥ* (extremely long) and whose *mānaḥ* (pride/dignity) is such—by one whose *astheyasattvam* (nature or resolve) is not very firm, that man (*sa nā*), meaning the beloved, is not to be rejected (*na vāryaḥ*).

However, you must remain steadfast and diligent, being truthful; you must win him over through affectionate conduct and bring him under your influence. Your disposition or resolve is not very firm, and therefore the result of abandoning your beloved will surely be regret. Thus, the sense is that you should exert effort so that he remains under your control. (This is a statement by a friend to a proud woman.)

In this case, the first and third quarters are identical, as are the second and fourth; thus, it is a variety of *samudra*. Another example is found in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*: "samiddhaśaraṇā dīptā dehe laṅkā mateśvarā | samiddhaśaraṇādīptā dehe'laṅkāmateśvarā ||" (54).

By means of an example, he demonstrates another variety of *samudra* characterized by the identity of the first and second quarters, as well as the third and fourth quarters, starting with the word *narā*.

Having supplied the words "by meeting" (*sametya*) and "by remaining" (*sthitena*), the meaning is "by one possessing honor" (*mānavatā*). By your "going" (*ayanena*), that is, by your journey for battle, the "men"—meaning enemies—were "conquered," that is, defeated. Having reached the "absence" (*āsaṃkṣepam*), meaning the non-existence, of "honoring" (*māna*) and "policy" (*naya*)—that is, of being honored and of sound policy—the enemies were "not made to shine" (*na rājitāḥ*), meaning they did not appear splendid. This is because, having fled from your presence, those enemies who have somehow preserved their lives are utterly devoid of honor and policy.

The meaning is that a miserable state has arisen. This course of action was described for those who were fleeing; however, for those who are reckless and do not act thus, he states their fate with the word "vināśitāḥ" (destroyed). "Vaibhavam" means the state of possessing power (*vibhutvam*); it is so called because it "extends" (*tāyati*) or expands [one's influence]—[the suffix *lyu* is applied here from the root *tāyṛñ* in the sense of "protection and expansion," according to the rule of the *Nandigana*]. By you, they have indeed been destroyed—that is, the enemies have been slain. The word "without" (*vinā*) means "by the bird," that is, by the vulture; they have been "eaten" (*aśitāḥ*), i.e., devoured. (This is a praise of the King.)
In this case, the first and second [lines] are equal, as are the third and fourth; thus, it is a *samudra* variety. || 55 ||

He states another variety of *samudga* (enclosure), characterized by the similarity between the first and fourth quarters on one hand and the second and third quarters on the other: "By the cry of peacocks (*kalāpinām*), that is, by the sound of their *kekā* calls, the rainy season (*ghanakālaḥ*) has been reached; the meaning is that the arrival of the clouds (*ghanāgamaḥ*, i.e., the monsoon) has been made manifest. The flocks (*vṛndāni*), that is, the multitudes, of such peacocks (*kalāpinām*) come together (*upayānti*) with beauty (*cārutayā*), meaning with the splendor produced by the rainy season."

The meaning is that they attain [this].
