Likewise, by the "wind of the Vṛnda" (vṛndanila)—that is, by the wind of the assembly of the rainy season (vārṣika-saṅghāta-vāyu)—the "thick" (ghana) dance (nṛtya-viśeṣa) [is] cast off or dispelled; for as Medinī states: "Ghana may refer to bell-metal, cymbals and other musical instruments, or to a specific type of dance. The arrival (āgama) characterized by that [dispelling] means an arrival accompanied by grace (savilāsa-āgamana); the meaning is "of those whose graceful gait has been abandoned. Having explained the various types of *samudrayamaka*, he now intends to provide examples of the many kinds of *pādābhyāsa-yamaka* (repetition within the feet of a verse); first, he provides an example occurring in the first and second feet, beginning with "na".

The meaning is: by one who is dull-witted (*mandā*) and deluded (*mūḍhā*), that is, one who is devoid of the appropriate conduct for that occasion; while *āvarjite* means not abandoned (*atyakte*), referring to pride (*māna*) born of life or born of jealousy, or anger (*kopa*); *sātmayā* means with effort (*sayatnayā*), that is, one who is exerting herself, meaning one who preserves her pride through effort (as Medinī states: "The word *ātman* refers to a person, essential nature, as well as effort and mind"); or alternatively, *āvarjitaḥ* means accepted after considering [the lover] favorable; thus, she is one by whom pride—characterized by jealousy and resentment—is [thus] possessed, and she is likewise *sātmā*.

By her who possessed a soul characterized by such compassion—that is, by me whose mind, self, and very nature were devoid of pity even upon seeing the beloved’s soiled face; by me, bowing down and falling at his feet due to having committed an offense—even so, the lord of my life, my husband, did not [embrace me] in such a way that my pair of breasts was spread out and offered upon his chest, as would have been expected.

She was embraced, yet she did not cling [to him]. (Regarding the reading *sārthayā* for *sātmayā*: in one case it means "with a group of minds (*manas*) not abandoned," and in the other, "with a purpose of the mind characterized by compassion. He provides an illustration of that very [simile] occurring in the first and third quarters with the verse beginning "sabhā": "O King! In that [city], where the assembly hall of the gods (surāṇām), known as Sudharmā, has ascended—meaning that now, following the destruction of Bala and Asura, the inhabitants of the divine assembly, being free from fear, sing of your virtues—you, while delighting and gladdening the adorned women (abalāḥ), should enjoy the splendors and sovereign powers of the radiant, prosperous cities (purām).
(This is the speech of a bard addressed to a king. Here, the first and third quarters are repeated, which constitutes *pādābhyāsa-yamaka* [repetition of the entire quarter]).

The meaning is "in counting"; for (*hi*) certainly, the ring finger (*anāmikā*) is the fourth finger from the thumb; "stainless" means faultless; "embodied" means possessing a body; "another being" means another living creature; "does not go" means it does not reach [that person]; the meaning is that it does not count anyone other than you. In this world, when the occasion for counting arises as to who are those with conquered senses, having first counted you with the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*), one is unable to count anyone else with the ring finger.

The meaning is that there is no one else like you who has conquered the senses. (This is a statement addressed to some great person. Here, the first and fourth quarters [of the verse] are repeated; thus, it is *pādābhyāsa-yamaka* [rhyme by repetition of a quarter]).

In this regard, the following should be noted: regarding the word *tanumaddhyānāmikā* in the fourth quarter, if one were to analyze it as *tanumat hi anāmikā*, then in the resulting form *tanumaddhyanāmikā*, the letter *dh* would be joined with the letter *d*. Therefore, we consider the following here in the fourth quarter:

He provides an example of *pādābhyāsa* (repetition of the first quarter) occurring in the second and third quarters with the verse beginning "sa yaśaḥ. O Ajopa!—O you who resemble Aja (the Unborn), or one equal to Nārāyaṇa, or one equal to Hara (Amara: "Aja refers to Viṣṇu, Hara, and the goat")—your soldiers, those warriors equipped with armor (*daṃśitāḥ*), possessing sharp (*śitāni*) weapons (*āyudhāni*), and full of vigor (*tarasvinaḥ*), meaning they possess unimpeded speed, [have filled] the directions with battle (*yudhā*).

He provides an illustration of that very [point] occurring in the second and fourth quarters with the verse beginning "bibharti": "O King! the serpent Vāsuki bears the circle of the earth—the entire world—with your arm; that is to say, by means of the assistance of your arm's strength. The meaning is that for those devoted to righteousness (*dharmiṣṭha*), sacrifices and other rites proceeded constantly. (This is a praise of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Here, because of the repetition of the first, second, and third quarters, it is an example of *pādatrayābhyāsa-yamaka*.

(In this regard, it should be understood that repetition once pertains to two quarters, repetition twice pertains to three quarters, and repetition thrice pertains to four quarters.)

"Yuktaḥ" means connected; "saṅgatārtham" means that whose meaning (the subject matter) is coherent, which is to say, it has attained the status of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). This is "remembered" or stated as being called "repetition of verses" (*ślokābhyāsa*). The word "yathā" (as for example) is for the purpose of providing an illustration that will be mentioned hereafter. || 67 ||

He cites that very verse by means of two [lines]: "By the Leader," O King!—that is, by the Guide (*vināyaka*), meaning by the ruler of those difficult to know; likewise, by him who possesses arms (*bāhu*) that are round (*vṛtta*), well-developed (*upacita*), and thick (*pīna*)—meaning, by the one with mighty arms (*mahābhuja*); by the one who is the uprooter (*uddhārin*), that is, the destroyer, of his own friends (*svamitra*)—meaning, of those who are truly beautiful—and of enemies (*amitra*)—meaning, even of those who are handsome and endowed with valor and other virtues; and likewise, by the one who has surpassed the incomparable (*atulāśrita*)—the comparison (*tulā*) or weighing.

"Dependent on a scale" (*tulāśrita*) means that which relies upon a balance; "not dependent on a scale" (*atulāśrita*) means by that [which is] not so, meaning by that which does not share similarity with anything whatsoever—that is, by the incomparable (*nirupama*). By one who is "leaderless" (*vināyakena*), meaning deprived of a leader; likewise, by one whose arms (*bāhū*) are "reached to the funeral pyre" (*citāmupagatau*)—that is, grown long and having reached the pyre, meaning they have ascended the pyre situated in the cremation ground (in the analysis *citām upagatau*, a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā*). Such is the description of him.

Likewise, one who abandons or renounces his own friends and kinsmen, or his own wealth, as well as friends and relatives—such a person is called *svamitroddhā* (one who has cast off his own friends). This means one by whom kinsmen have been abandoned and wealth and relatives have been forsaken. [Grammatically: from the word *svamitra*, with the root *jahāti* preceded by the prefix *ud* and the suffix *kvip*, the third case singular is formed; the vowel *ā* of the root is elided according to the rule *āto dhātoḥ*. By you, being such as previously described, the earth is heavy, like the incomparable scale of Yama, the Ender.

The meaning is that it is a "balance-scale instrument" (*tulā-parimāṇa-saṃtra*), which is to say, a place of deliberation (*vicāra-sthāna*). (Just as one determines deficiency or excess in a measuring instrument, because it effects the determination of merit and demerit even within the assembly of the Lord of Death’s deliberation, it should be understood as being equal to a balance-scale. "Resorted to" (*āśritā*) means having arrived; the sense is that she has gone to the abode of Yama. (These two verses concern the praise of the King. He provides the designation "mahāyamaka" (great yamaka) for a yamaka consisting of three repetitions occurring across all four quarters, because a specific variety arises from its intermediate repetition within each quarter; thus he says, "having one form. That yamaka in which the four quarters (*pāda*) are of a single form—that is, non-different—is to be known by the name "mahāyamaka," as the remainder [of the sentence] implies.

Even there, in the case of a great *yamaka* (rhyme) consisting of four quarters (*pāda*) with a single form, repetition—meaning recurrence—is observed even within the middle of a quarter; that is the sense of "repetition of a quarter-part. Therefore, that is the supreme or best method of *yamaka*, meaning the manner of rhyming, which is the composition of a verse as a *yamaka*. The essential point is this: when there is repetition of all four quarters, and therein also the repetition of a quarter-part, that is a "great *yamaka*."

It should be understood that the greatness of such a *mahāyamaka* lies in its capacity to produce variety through its diverse arrangement. Now, one might object: "If, according to the definition of *abhyāsa-yamaka*, there is an identical repetition of all four quarters just as in the case of four-footed animals, then what variety is there in this *mahāyamaka*? To demonstrate the distinction, it is stated that the very variety arising from the repetition of quarter-segments (*pādakhaṇḍa*) constitutes the defining characteristic of *mahāyamaka*. Consequently, even though both [the *abhyāsa-yamaka* and the *mahāyamaka*] consist of four quarters of a single form, regarding each individual quarter-segment...

The essential point is that *mahāyamaka* consists in the uniformity of all four quarters (*catuṣpāda*) preceded by repetition. As it is stated in the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa*: "That which has four quarters of identical form is called *mahāyamaka*; and among those, the first [type] deserves to be repeated as a verse. (Here the word division is as follows: *samānayāsa*, *mā*, *anayā*; *samānaya*, *asamānayā*; *samānayā*, *samānayā*; *samāna*, *yā*, *samānayā*). O you who have brought together! (*he samānayāsa*)... [text continues] ...O you who are equal! (*samāna*)... [text continues] ...O you who bring together! (*samānaya*)... [text continues] ...O you who are not equal! (*asamānayā*)... [text continues] ...O you who are equal! (*samānayā*)... [text continues] ...O you who bring together! (*samānayā*)... [text continues] ...O you who are equal! (*samāna*)... [text continues] ...O you who go! (*yā*)... [text continues] ...O you who bring together! (*samānayā*). Thus: "O you who have brought together! (*he samānayāsa*).

"Samānaḥ" means uniform or of one form; "yāsa yatnaḥ" refers to the vocative case of that [word], meaning "O you whose effort is equal in all respects. Likewise, "samāna! means O you who see with equanimity; the meaning is "O you whose vision of the Self is the same everywhere. Alternatively, "samaḥ" means undivided, and "ānaḥ" means breath (prāṇa); thus, it means "O you whose heart is undivided," O friend—this is the sense. As for the heroine: "samānayā" means with Lakṣmī, meaning with beauty; "nayaḥ" means policy, meaning knowledge. Or alternatively, "samānayāsamānayā" is a single compound word.

The meaning is: by this heroine, whose *yāsaḥ* (exertion) and *mānaḥ* (pride)—the latter being jealousy and anger—are equal; [pray] "mā māṃ samānaya," that is, unite me with her. The sense is: since union with her is so highly desirable, quickly pacify this pride of hers—which causes such great torment—and join me with her. (This is a prayer by someone overcome by the torments of love to a friend. Here, because of the repetition of the four quarters of the verse and even the repetition of its halves, it is a *mahāyamaka*. ) 71.

Among the many varieties established by the passage beginning with "atyantabahavasteṣām," the subdivisions produced by the mixing of similar types have been shown previously; now, he demonstrates an example of the mixing of dissimilar types, starting with the word "dhara."

"Those who bear the form of the earth-supporter"—the earth-supporter (*dhara*) is the sustainer of the earth (*dharā*, i.e., *pṛthivī*), meaning the King of Serpents (*nāgarāja*); those who bear (*dharanti*) his form or likeness are "those who bear the form of the earth-supporter," meaning they are exceedingly long. "Possessing undiminished prowess" (*ahīnavikramāḥ*) means those whose valor (*vikrama*) or strength (*vīrya*) is not small (*ahīna*); or alternatively, those whose prowess is like that of Ahīna—the Lord of Serpents (*ahīnām prabhuḥ*), meaning Ananta, the sovereign of the *nāgas*. Likewise, they are "those who have suddenly, by force, struck down their enemies."

Those by whom enemies—that is, foes—have been struck down or destroyed; likewise, those who are "rayoddhurāḥ," meaning "rayeṇa" (by speed) "uddhurāḥ" (exalted), that is, possessing excessive velocity; and likewise, those who "mānadhurāvalambinaḥ," meaning they "avalambante" (support) the "dhurām" (burden) of "mānasya" (pride)—that is, protectors of their honor—the arms of kings, "kramāt" (gradually) from the enemy's assault, or "śaktitaḥ" (by power), that is, by their own capability. (Note: *krama* means sequence and also capability).

And even when not traversed during a *kalpa*, [the earth]—"thus says the *Medinī* lexicon"—endures, that is, it is able to bear, protect, or preserve the *mahī*, the earth. (In this verse, in the first quarter there is immediate *ādi-yamaka*; at the junctions of the quarters, there is immediate *antādi-yamaka* and *sandaṃśa-yamaka*; furthermore, in the second quarter, there is separated *madhya-yamaka* in the form "mahī mahī," with two syllables intervening; and in the third quarter, there is "saha saha," with one syllable intervening; and in the fourth...)
The middle [syllable] is "dhurā dhurā," separated by two vowels; thus, one should note that there is here a mixture of many dissimilar elements. || 72 ||

Having thus stated the divisions of *anuloma* (direct order), [the author] now states the divisions of *pratiloma* (inverse order): "repetition" (*āvṛtti*), meaning "in inverse order" (*prātilomyena*), that is, in reverse order. Its scope (*viṣaya*) consists of the quarters (*pāda*), the half-verses (*ardhaśloka*), and the full verses (*śloka*). Thus, it is of three kinds: having the quarters as its scope, the half-verses as its scope, and the full verses as its scope. "Repetition" (*āvṛtti*) means recitation; because it is repeated in reverse order—that is, by way of inversion—it is known as *pratiloma-yamaka* (inverse chime).

And thus, where the second quarter arises through the inverse repetition of the first quarter, and the first quarter is possible through the inverse repetition of the second quarter as well, that is *pratilomayamaka* occurring within the quarters; likewise, if the first half of the verse occurs through the inverse repetition of the second half, then it is *pratilomayamaka* occurring within the half-verses.

Likewise, if by the reverse-order repetition (*pratilomāvṛtti*) of one verse another verse is produced, and by the same reverse-order repetition of that other verse the original verse is restored, then the conclusion is that it is a *pratilomayamaka* (reverse-order yamaka) having verses as its scope. And, according to the method stated above, it is of three kinds. || 73 ||

Demonstrating the threefold nature of *pratiloma-yamaka* (inverse palindrome), he first provides an example occurring at the level of the verse-quarter, beginning with "yā": "O you whose hope (*āśā*)—meaning the thirst directed toward attachment to another—is known (*matā*)! That emaciation (*kṛśatā*), which was produced (*kṛtāyāsā*)—that is, for which distress (*āyāsa*) was generated, as it were by me; the sense is that it gave me excessive suffering—and which has now arrived (*āyātā*) through your misconduct, that very great emaciation was already attained by me [long ago]."

Even now she will be the same; what difference could there be? Therefore, the sense is: "Do as you please," O Raman! O bringer of satisfaction! O Stute!—the word *stute* being derived from *stuta* (praise), meaning "O you who are worthy of praise" (*stavārha*). Alternatively, *stuta* means "praiseworthy," and *ita* means "going" or "conduct"; thus, it refers to one whose conduct is praiseworthy. Or else, *stutāt* means "fallen from praise," i.e., "one unworthy of praise" (*astavārha*), meaning one whose conduct is censurable and thus not to be commended; [this is used] in addressing such a person. Likewise, O... [he continues].

O Akaraṇāmara! [The term] *akaraṇe* means in the performance of what should not be done; *amaraḥ* means like a god (*devasadṛśa*). The sense is that, like a god, you do not perform what should not be done, or rather, that you are devoted to the non-performance of what should not be done. This is the vocative address. (It should be understood that for gods, "what should not be done" includes such acts as being a paramour to Mahalaya.)

All of this vocative address should be understood as being primarily sarcastic, because it is irrelevant to the context. "Ārakatā" means the state of being an *āraka*—one who goes (*ṛcchati*), derived from the root *ṛ* with the suffix *ṇaka*, meaning "the act of going," that is, the state of moving according to one's own will; let it be so. The sense is: "Go wherever you desire; you must not remain here. (This is an angry utterance by an indignant woman toward her lover.)

Here, by the reverse repetition of the first quarter [pāda], the second quarter is formed; likewise, by the reverse repetition of the second quarter, the first quarter is formed; and so too for the third and fourth quarters. Therefore, this is a *pratiloma-yamaka* (reverse-order yamaka) concerning the quarters. 74.

He provides an example of the scope of half a verse, beginning with "nādinaḥ. "Nādinaḥ" means one who possesses *nāda-brahman* (the Brahman in the form of sound); the meaning is: for one who is devoted to the meditation upon *nāda-brahman*. "Me" means for me. "Madanādhī" refers to both *madana* (lust) and *ādhi* (mental anguish)—that is, desire and the mental distress produced by desire. Likewise, "svā kācana kāmitā" refers to any personal longing for sense objects. [The phrase] "na" [means]: due to the experience of *nāda-brahman*, neither desire, nor the mental distress born of it, nor attachment to one's own sense objects exists.

The meaning is that [these things] exist. Likewise, *dama* is the restraint of the external senses. By that which is so described—by *kāma*, by passion, acting as the cause that destroys such restraint of the senses—she has become *svādhīnā*: one whose own self (*svaḥ ātmā*) is *adhīnaḥ*, dependent or subject to it; the meaning is "one who causes her own self to be agitated. And there is also *tāmyikā*, meaning exhaustion or fainting (derived from the root *tam* with the suffix *ṇaka* in the sense of an abstract state, with feminine gender). It is not the case that these do not exist; the word "for me" (*mama*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

The arising of the *nāda* is born from the practice of *prāṇāyāma*; as it was stated by Sureśvarācārya: "When all the channels have been purified by the exhalations, inhalations, and retentions of the vital air, the *nāda*, which is to be realized as one's own self, arises spontaneously from the unstruck lotus. This is the statement of a certain yogin.

Here, the second half-verse is produced by the reverse order of the first half-verse, and the first half-verse is produced by the reverse order of the second half-verse; thus, this is a *pratilomayamaka* (reverse palindrome) occurring within the scope of the half-verses. (75)

He shows the reverse order of the verse, beginning with "the vehicle" (yānam). The word "friend" (sakhe) is to be supplied; "vehicle" (yānam) means a conveyance, such as a horse or any other [animal], meaning "bring it," with "you" (tvam) being the understood subject. He asks "how? and replies with "which" (yām).

I have gone to that courtesan—meaning, she who has brought under her control (adhīnām), i.e., become subject to, a hundred "exalted ones" (udāharaṇām), meaning wealthy men; or alternatively, she who is under the control of a hundred noble men (udāraśatasya adhīnām)—she who is like a whip (kaśā) for the ram (aviḥ) that is Māra (Kāma); that is to say, she who strikes away the afflictions of desire for lovers. Furthermore, those whose life-breaths (anaḥ) are diminished (ūnaḥ)—the sense being "deprived" due to lack of wealth—are called *ūnānāḥ*. [She is the one who restores them. (The word "I" is to be supplied as the subject.)

The meaning is "as if dead"; "ūnāḥ" means deficient or lowly, that is, even those who are destitute of wealth; or alternatively, "those who breathe" (i.e., live), such persons being meant. "Ūnānājanāḥ" refers to those people who are deficient; "ūnānajanāsanā" is one who casts out or rejects them—that is, one who excludes the indigent—meaning the prostitute. "Āyam" means arrival; "anādi" was stated [as the verb]. (The form "anādi" is the aorist [luṅ] in the passive sense of the root √nad, used with two objects; since there are two objects, the word "sā" [she] expresses the secondary object. The word "mayā" (by me) is to be supplied.
The meaning is that she was told, "I shall come into your presence today.

She too, being enamored with me, says: "By her" (amuyā) means by that [autumn] which has arrived; "by autumn" (śaradā), that is, by the autumn season—the sense being that it is an excitant (uddīpana). "He" (saḥ) refers to the lover. "Attained mental anguish" (ādhitā ādhim) means he has reached mental pain (manas-pīḍā), the sense being due to separation from me. Therefore, "she who displays the deceit of illness during the day" (dināmayamāyāmā): "during the day" (dine) means on the day; "the deceit of illness" (āmayamāyām) means the trickery of disease; "displays" (amati) means she goes toward it, or reveals it. Such is she: one who, during the day, in the presence of her friends, [expresses] the suffering of separation under the pretext of illness.

The meaning is "she conceals. Furthermore, she is "not producing a seat," meaning there is no production (*janana*)—that is, the act—of a seat (*āsana*), which implies sitting or stability; because she lacks stability, due to the pain of separation, she does not sit down in one place. She is described as "going," meaning she is looking toward the path of my departure. That courtesan is "one for whom grief has ceased"—the meaning is that she is not one for whom there is a cessation (*virāma*), an end, of grief (*śoka*), the suffering of separation; [she is] "exerting herself" (this is the ellipsis).

The meaning is that she experiences the suffering of separation. (This is a statement by a friend to someone who is attached to a passionate courtesan. Here, because the first verse is completed by reading the second verse in reverse order, and the second verse is likewise completed by reading the first verse in reverse order, this is a *pratilomayamaka* (reverse palindrome) concerning the verses. || 77 ||

Now, intending to describe some of the figures of speech (*citrālaṅkāra*), he first points out the *gomūtrikā* [pattern] with the words "of the letters" (*varṇānām*). (In this regard, it should be noted that although it is necessary to state the definition of each variety of *citrālaṅkāra* when they are to be discussed, the author has not mentioned it because it is well-known; however, for the sake of the students' ease of instruction, we shall say something: a *citra* is like a painting, and similarly, a *citra* [figure of speech] is devoid of *dhvani*, which serves as its life-breath.)

The Kashmiris [hold that] it is "poetry" (*kāvyam*). That is incorrect, because they do not accept the primacy of *dhvani* (suggestion), and because the suggested meaning (*pratīyamānabhāva*) is impossible in some cases. In that case, let it simply be called "painting" (*citra*) when it is endowed with specific figures of speech (*ākṛtiviśeṣa*). But even that is not right, because it is too narrow (*avyāpakatva*). Therefore, the resolution is this: since it produces wonder (*āścaryakāritā*) through the restriction of phonemes and other elements, the word "painting" (*citra*) here has the sense of "wonder. And some say that it is of six kinds.

For it is said: "In this regard, that which consists of a restriction concerning color, position, tone, form, movement, and composition is called 'the sixfold citra' by the wise. Having first demonstrated *gaticitra* (movement-citra) with this [verse], he has now shown *varṇacitra*, *svaracitra*, and *sthānacitra*. However, *ākāra* (form) and *bandha* (composition) have not been shown at all.

In this context, *ākāra* is the sealing with the form of a lotus and so forth, while *bandha* is the *viviḍita* and other such positions; the distinction between these two is difficult to grasp because both consist essentially of forms.

The meaning is as follows: of two firm (solid) verses, written in two rows—one above and one below—in the order of the first half and the second half respectively; of the syllables (*varṇa*), that which is "separated by one" (*ekāntara*), meaning separated by a single syllable; that "identity of form" (*ekarūpatva*), meaning the state of having an identical appearance; the "arrangement of the same kind of syllable" with the intervention of each individual syllable—those who know this, the experts in the *citrālaṅkāra* (puzzle-ornament), find it difficult to perform suddenly, i.e., impossible to execute. That very thing [is what is meant]. (Regarding the word *tat*, where *tat* occurs, it should be read as *tam*).

In this reading, the meaning is "that ornament. They call it *gomūtrikā* because the composition of the verse is fashioned in the shape of a stream of urine from a moving cow; thus it bears the name *gomūtrikā*. As it is said in the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa*: "Where the movement is up and down like the path of a cow’s urine, those who know the marvelous (*citravedinaḥ*) call that the *gomūtrikā*, a difficult [figure of speech]."

The *gomūtrikā* is primarily of three kinds: the *pādagomūtrikā*, the *ślokārdhagomūtrikā*, and the *ślokagomūtrikā*; furthermore, there are other intermediate varieties of it, such as the *viparītā* and others. This definition, however, should be understood as applying to the *ardhagomūtrikā*, because the syllables of the second half-verse correspond to those of the first half-verse by being separated by one intervening syllable.

Furthermore, the *pādagomūtrikā* (foot-cow’s-urine pattern) is to be understood as that wherein there is a uniformity of identical syllables between the first and second quarters, and likewise a different kind of uniformity between the third and fourth quarters. An example is as follows: "May he who destroyed the illusion [of Māra], the slayer of Namuci, protect you from the fear of calamity—he who, casting aside his magic, let loose the rain-clouds, while longing for the strikes upon the breasts of Puloman’s daughter and the pressure of her arms pressed against his chest. The structural arrangement (*bandhaprākāra*) is like the *pādagomūtrikā* formation.

*Kāṃ napu ma na sta tā tā kṣa lo ta yā na ḍi ni va stha chi ra ñca po tā pā da ya ya na ci hā yā pā bha to mu pra rī mā ma sya va 'mbu cāṃ sā*. Furthermore, in the *gomūtrikā* [puzzle] of verses, two verses must be placed in an upward and downward sequence. Then, the alternate letters of the first quarter of the first verse are to be paired with the alternate letters of the first quarter of the second verse; likewise for the second and subsequent quarters.

The single repetition of the letters separated by one intervening letter in each quarter, beginning from the second, is to be understood. "Yathā" (as for example) is for the purpose of illustration. || 78 ||

He provides an example of the *ardhagomūtrikā* meter from the *Śloka*, beginning with "madana": "This Madana, [that is] Kāma, having the corners of the eyes (*apāṅga*) as his weapon—referring to those women with eyes like intoxicated *khañjana* birds—if he should conquer me, that is to say, if he should strike me, then my sin (*madanaḥ*) would be exhausted; this is the ellipsis. And then, to Anaṅga, to Madana, I offer my joined palms (*añjaliṃ dade*), meaning I offer a handful of flowers; this is the ellipsis, provided that I [am conquered] by the amorous women."

The underlying meaning is: "I shall gaze with a sidelong glance; then I shall have achieved my purpose. (In this verse, the odd-numbered syllables in both the first and second halves are identical in form, while the even-numbered syllables are different; thus, due to this uniformity at intervals of one, there is a structural consistency with the definition of the *gomūtrikā* pattern.)

In the case of a verse written in a "bound" (*bandha*) arrangement where the syllables of the two halves have different colors but a single uniform form, one should begin with the first syllable of the second half and recite the second syllable of the first half; then, having recited the third syllable of the second half, recite the fourth syllable of the first half. By following this sequence of recitation, the first half of the verse will be completed. Thereafter, beginning from the first syllable of the first half, the second half should be recited.

In cases where the syllables are identical and possess a uniform form, the second half-verse should be produced starting from the first syllable of the first half-verse; therefore, the second half-verse must be recited starting precisely from the first syllable of the first half-verse. In cases where the syllables are identical and possess a uniform form, the first half-verse should be recited starting from the first syllable of the first half-verse itself, and the second half-verse should be recited starting from the first syllable of the second half-verse.

The recitation of syllables of uneven color (viṣamavarṇa) in the manner previously described for those of even color (samavarṇa), whereby the complete verse is produced, is called the *ardhagomūtrikā* (half-ox-urine) composition. Another method of composition is as follows: the opposites of these are also possible; only a mere indication has been shown here. This is the *ardhagomūtrikā* composition. [The verse is: *dama rā ṇā pā strī ye yama ma no di kṣī ma ṅā ja da deya tat ṇa na yāñ liṃ de*. Regarding the varieties of *ākāra* (shape) and *citra* (picture) compositions, however, there are many subdivisions.

These, such as the sword (*khaḍga*), the drum (*muraja*), the lotus (*padma*), the mace (*muṣala*), the spear (*śakti*), the plough (*hala*), and so forth, are to be understood as described by others. Among these, the sword-arrangement (*khaḍgabandha*) is as follows: "May Umā, the daughter of the mountain, grant me prosperity—she who is constantly praised with intense effort by the enemies of Māra, Indra, Rāma, and the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa) with the speed of a downpour; she who is capable of removing their afflictions; the mother of those who bow to her; the confluence of glories; she whose agitation has been dispelled; the venerable one; and the limit of beautiful women. By these two verses, the sword-arrangement is displayed.

In that regard, there are two branches above and below the fist. Having placed the initial letter *mā* at the four-way junction of the upper branches, one should place the fourteen letters beginning with *rā* and ending with *ha* in horizontal and vertical succession; this constitutes one edge (*dhārā*). Then, one should place the letter *sā* joined to the tip of the sword-blade. Following that, having written the fourteen letters beginning with *rārabdha* in horizontal and vertical order, one should form the other edge. Thus, the letter *mā* enters into the letter *mā*.

Likewise, having imagined that [the mantra] has entered there at the front as well, one should place the seven syllables beginning with "tā" on the right branch; then, on the left branch, one should write the seven syllables beginning with "śrī" horizontally in reverse order. At the crossroads of the letter "mā," one enters the initial "mā"; then, starting from that very same "mā," the three syllables "nyā-tha-sī" are to be written downward in the fist.

Then, having placed that final syllable *mā* in the middle of the crossroads below, one should place the four syllables *rāmāṇāṃ śaṃ* on its right branch; then, on the left branch, one should write the four syllables *me diśyādu* in reverse order. The syllable *mā* enters the syllable *mā* situated at the crossroads below. Then, the two syllables *drijā* are to be written on the hilt (*tsaru*) below the fist; thus is the sword completed.

The *murajabandha* (drum-pattern) is as follows: "sā senā gamanārambhe rasenāsīdanāratā | tāranādajanā mattadhīranāgamanāmayā ||" In this example, by taking the letters in the following order from the four lines written in a square—namely, the first, second, third, and fourth letters respectively from the bottom row of each successive line—one obtains the first quarter-verse (*pāda*). Specifically, one takes the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth letters [from the bottom] of the first line; the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth letters of the second line; the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth letters of the third line; and the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth letters of the fourth line. This constitutes the first *pāda*.

Taking the first from the second, the second and third from the first, the fourth and fifth from the second, the sixth and seventh from the first, and the eighth from the second, the second quarter-verse is formed. Taking the first from the third, the second and third from the fourth, the fourth and fifth from the third, the sixth and seventh from the fourth, and the eighth from the third, the third quarter-verse is formed.

By taking the first, second, third, and fourth feet in ascending order, and the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth feet in descending order, the fourth foot is to be recited; thus is the accomplishment of the *muraja* [drum] pattern. Regarding that, the method for the *muraja* composition is as follows, and likewise the *padma* [lotus] composition is as follows: "O essence of genius, your assembly shines—resplendent with aesthetic flavor, free from the division of enemies, its soul purified, auspicious in debate, and possessing the splendor of the gods!"

Here, an eight-petalled lotus should be drawn extending across the eight directions. In its pericarp, the first syllable "Mā" should be written. Then, two letters each should be written on the petals according to the sequence of exit and entry; however, in the petals of the cardinal directions, there is both exit and entry. Among these, in the eastern petal, there is first an exit and then an entry at the end of the verse; in the southern and northern petals, there is entry only after having exited; but in the western petal, there is exit only after having entered.

In the petals of the southeast (Āgneya) and northwest (Vāyavya), there is only entry; however, in the southwest (Nairṛta) and northeast (Īśāna), there is only exit—this is the arrangement of the eight-petaled lotus (*aṣṭadala-padma-bandha*). Thus it has been said: "One should place one [syllable] in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and two each in the cardinal and intermediate directions. One should effect entry and exit in the cardinal directions within the eight-petaled lotus. In this manner, other patterns such as the *muṣala* and so forth are also to be understood; this is the general direction. 79.

In this regard, the definition of *ardhabhrama* is as follows: "Now they describe *ardhabhrama*, which is auspicious in every respect," beginning with the word *prāhuḥ*. If there is a *śloka-ardhabhramaṇa*—meaning the revolving of the four quarters (*pāda*) of a verse—by means of the "half" (*ardhena*), that is, by way of the "half-path" (*ardhamārgeṇa*), specifically through the path of recitation consisting solely of direct order (*anuloma*) among the two paths of recitation (direct and reverse), then they call such a figure of speech *ardhabhrama*. This "revolving" (*bhramaṇa*) refers to the presentation of the quarters (*pāda*) by means of such a rotation. Thus, they say that when this occurs, it is the poetic figure named *ardhabhrama*.

If there is a rotation in both directions—meaning by both forward and reverse orders of the two paths—then that is considered the diagram named *sarvatobhadra*. (For instance, this [diagram] is generally seen as consisting of eight-syllable meters; therein, first, sixty-four squares arranged in eight rows should be drawn. Then, the syllables of the four quarters should be placed in order within the first four rows, and subsequently in the four lower rows.)

The fourth, third, second, and first quarters (pādas) are to be written in reverse order; in that regard, the distinction is that in the *adṛḍhabhrama*, the writing of the fourth and subsequent quarters occurs by rotation within the four bottom rows, whereas in the *sarvatobhadra*, it occurs both by rotation and by circumambulation.

As for the order of rotation: in the case of a firm delusion, within the vertical column consisting of four quarters, one proceeds from left to right; likewise, within the horizontal row consisting of four quarters, one proceeds from right to left. Thus, by moving downward from the upper-left cell and upward from the lower-right cell, the first quarter is established through a clockwise rotation.

In the *sarvatobhadra* [maṇḍala], however, it should be understood that the establishment of the quarters occurs by revolving in all directions through both direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*pratiloma*) order—from right to left and from left to right, and by the sequence of up and down, as well as down and up.

Thus, the author has demonstrated two varieties of *gaticitra* (verse-puzzle based on word-order) consisting of specific permutations of syllables: *adṛḍhabhrama* and *sarvatobhadra*. Other varieties of this same *gaticitra*, such as *gatapratyāgata* and so forth, should be understood from other works. To provide a mere indication, it is as follows: "vāraṇāgagabhīrā sā sārābhīgagaṇāravā| kāritāribadhā senā nāsedhā varitārikā||" [That army, deep with the sound of elephants, possessing an abundance of brave warriors, causing the destruction of enemies, was unstoppable and chose its foes.]

In this instance, having taken the sequence of syllables from the first and third quarters in direct order (*ānulomyena*), the second and fourth quarters are taken in their reverse form (*pratiloma*). Thus, because of the movement from one syllable to another within the recitation, it is a *gati-citra* (a poetic figure of movement) called *gatapratyāgata* (going and returning). Likewise, another verse is as follows: *vāhanā'jani mānāse sārājāvanamā tataḥ | mattasāragarājebhe bhārīhāvajjnadhvani ||* [The commentary on this verse would explain how its syllables, when read forward and backward, produce a symmetrical pattern.]
Here, by reading it in reverse order, another verse arises, as follows: "nidhvanajjavahārībhā bheje rāgāsāttamaḥ| tatamānavajārāsā senā mānijanāhavā|" and so forth. (80)

Therein, he gives an example of the "unsteady" (adr̥ḍha), beginning with the words *manobhava*. O *manobhava*—O Kāma! O *nata*—O you who are saluted by those filled with longing! This proud woman (*māninī*), who is like an army (*anīka*) belonging to you, is for your rise—that is, for your increase or victory; the word "your" (*tava*) is to be supplied as the remainder. It is not that she is not [for your rise], but rather she is indeed for your rise. Now, one might object: "The army of victors is for punishing the guilty, but you are not guilty; so what is your purpose here? To this he replies: "Out of fear" (*bhayāt*).

Whether we are indeed sinful and guilty, or not, we are nonetheless afflicted by immeasurable suffering—where "immeasurable" (*ameya*) means beyond measure, and "sickness" (*āma*) means disease—if even when we are innocent, we have become intensely tormented by fear. (Another example of this is: "In that which constantly bestows speed and destroys fear and anger, the excellence of its delight is heightened by the loud clamor of excessive haste. 81.

He illustrates the *sarvatobhadra* [meter] with the word *sā*: (*atra ayam padavibhāgaḥ, sā, amāyāmāmāyā, māsā; mārānāyāyānārāmā; yānāvārārāvā, anāyā; māyā, rāmā, mārāyasa amā iti*). The phrase *amāyāmāmāyā* means: of one who is *amāya*—that is, free from deceit (*akapaṭa*)—and *ama*—unmeasured (*aparimita*)—[yet] *āmāyā*, meaning that by which there is the arrival (*āgamanam*) of *āma*, namely disease (*roga*), in other words, the affliction of desire (*kāmapīḍā*). Likewise, *mārānāyāyānārāmā* means: *māra* is simply desire (*kāma*); *ānāya* is a net (*jāla*), because [desire] is the cause of bondage—this is the sense. *Yānāvārārāvā* means: she whose sound (*rāva*) is the vessel (*avāra*) for the vehicle (*yāna*). *Anāyā* means: she who is without effort (*anāya*). *Māyā* means: she who is illusory (*māyinī*). *Rāmā* means: she who is beautiful (*ramaṇīyā*). *Mārāyasa amā* means: she who is the non-measure (*amā*) of the son of Māra (*mārāya*). Thus [the meter is established].

By his coming—that is, by his arrival—the pleasure of which is such that she is "one whose delight lies in his approach," meaning she was constantly engaged in amorous activities; furthermore, she was "one whose voice is a check to travel," for *yāna* means traveling abroad and *āvāra* means one who restrains or prohibits; thus, she was one whose speech (*ārāva*) consisted of a prohibition against traveling abroad, meaning she prevented my departure from home with her sweet words; moreover, she was "one who has no policy," for *naya* (in the form *ānāya*) means policy or conduct (as Amara states: "naya" means policy).

The meaning is that she is devoid of discernment as to whether or not there would be a failure of duty (*kāryahāni*) on my part if I were not to go abroad; likewise, she is called "Māyā" because she goes toward me, Lakṣmī—that is, she is exceedingly beautiful—and she has appeared in my memory; she is a "Rāmā," a lovely woman—the remainder being that she is my beloved; and by "Māsa" (the month), [meaning] with the moon (*candra*)—according to the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* in its list of synonyms for the moon: "Māḥ is the king who bears the deer in his shadow"—and by "Amā" (together)—according to Amara: "Amā means together or near"—[the phrase] is for the sake of "Māra," my destruction.

The meaning is that both the remembrance of her and the rising of the moon now greatly agitate me. (This is the lamentation of a lover separated from his beloved as he recalls her. Another example is as follows: "de vā kā ni ni kā vā de vā hi kā sva sva kā hi vā| kā kā re bha bha re kā kā ni sva bha vya vya bha sva ni||")

Here, the writing is done in four lines; the recitation is performed both in direct and reverse order, by way of ascending and descending sequences, and descending and ascending sequences respectively. Furthermore, since even when one writes half a *mātrā* from each quarter-verse (*pāda*) and recites in reverse order, a complete quarter-verse is produced, this should be understood as the *sarvatobhadra-bandha*, because the verse is accomplished through rotation in every direction. (82) He says "ya" etc., demonstrating each of the four difficult varieties of the many-fold restriction of vowels and so forth, which has been accepted by the ancients as a figure of speech (*citrālaṅkāra*).

Regarding "the restriction of vowels, places of articulation, and consonants": the vowels are *a* and so forth; the places of articulation are the throat and so forth, meaning the consonants such as those produced in the throat; likewise, the "consonants" refer to all the guttural, palatal, and other classes without distinction. The "restriction" (*niyama*) concerning these means the determination that poetry should be composed using only four vowels, or only three, or only two, or even only one, and likewise with such places of articulation or consonants; this is the sense. The phrase "stated by the ancients as an ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Among these difficult and laborious tasks, that which is intended—that is, considered difficult—is precisely the rule regarding the vowels, places of articulation, and consonants; this is what is fit to be shown as being laborious. "Beginning with four" means four, numbering four, vowels, places of articulation, and consonants; "wherein these are the first" (prābhṛtayaḥ) refers to that [rule]—this is an adverbial modifier—and it should be understood that the state of "beginning with four" is relative to one and so forth. Thus, starting from four vowels...

The meaning is "up to a single sound," with the word "rule" (*niyama*) understood as the remainder of the sentence. It is observed that because there are four, three, two, or one forms, four varieties are observed; "another" (*paraḥ*) refers to [varieties] beginning with five, which are "easy" (*sukara*), meaning they can be accomplished without effort. Therefore, examples for those should be sought out according to their respective cases. The sense is that effort is exerted solely for the purpose of demonstrating difficult constructions, whereas the demonstration of easy ones has been omitted for fear of making the book too voluminous.

(Here, this should be noted: among the six varieties of *citrālaṅkāra*, after showing some examples of *gaticitra*, this verse indicates the threefold *citra*—namely *svaracitra*, *sthānacitra*, and *varṇacitra*—as well as their twelvefold nature through four varieties for each. || 83 ||

In this regard, he first provides an illustration using four long vowels, beginning with the word "āmnāyānām. Of the *āmnāyas*, that is, the Vedas, the final [vowel]—the last one—is speech, meaning the *upaniṣad*. "Songs" (*gītayaḥ*) refers to chants; "calamities" (*ītayaḥ*) refers to afflictions such as excessive rain and so forth, the sense being that these cause agitation of the mind. Likewise, "delights" (*prītayaḥ*) refer to the attachment to children, wife, and others; "fears" (*bhītayaḥ*) means terrifying things, the sense being that they produce suffering through the separation from children and so forth. He says this; therefore, it is "enjoyment" (*bhogaḥ*).

The enjoyment of objects such as music and the like is disease, which is the very nature of affliction; likewise, joy is the pleasure derived from sense-objects, and delusion is simply ignorance—this is what he also says, the rest being understood. He does not merely say that song is calamity and affection is fear, but further states that enjoyment is disease, joy is delusion; therefore, the implication is that all of this is to be abandoned.

Then, what should be done? He says: in a secure place (*kṣeme deśe*), that is, on a sacred ground (*puṇyabhūmau*); regarding the object of meditation (*dhyeye*), which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); *dhāḥ* means retention (*dhāraṇā*), that is, the stabilization of the mind; and *icchā* is the desire for its attainment. These two are to be practiced—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. (Regarding the phrase "dhecche" and so forth, in an alternative reading, "cecchet kṣeme deśe," the meaning is: one should meditate upon (*dhyeye*) the object to be meditated upon (*dhyātavya*), in a secure place (*kṣeme*) free from afflictions (*kleśa*), that is, in the sphere (*deśe*) characterized by liberation (*mokṣa*); and one should exercise the will (*icchecca*), that is, one should form the desire.)

Regarding the reading "dhyecche" for "dhecche," the meaning is that *dhyā* signifies meditation (*dhyāna*). Here, the composition of the verse is formed using only the four long vowels: *ā*, *ī*, *o*, and *e*. This is the *vidyunmālā* meter. (84)

He illustrates the short tri-syllable [meter], beginning with "kṣiti-". "Kṣiteḥ" means of the earth; "vijitiḥ" means victory; "sthiteḥ" means of the established order, the sense being that characterized by the system of castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*); "vihitiḥ" means the ordinance or injunction. These two are the vows (*vrata*) or observances (*niyama*). Those who possess *rati*—that is, devotion—toward these two, namely the vow of victory over the earth and the vow of maintaining the established order, are so described. Likewise, those whose *gati*—meaning supreme knowledge (the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *gati* is feminine and denotes path, day, knowledge, journey, and means")—is such, are the Kurus.

The kings born of the Kuru lineage, in battle—that is, in combat—completely (*uru*) obstructed their own (*svaṃ*) enemy host (*arikulaṃ*), and likewise excessively (*guru*) shook it. (In this verse, the metrical structure consists of only three short vowels: *i*, *a*, and *u*; this meter is called *tvaritagati*). || 85 ||

He cites examples of long vowels followed by two consonants: *śrīdīptī* (glory and splendor). *Śrīḥ* is Lakṣmī; *dīptīḥ* is radiance—these two. *Hrīḥ* is modesty; *kārttiḥ* is fame—these two. *Dhīḥ* is intellect; *nītiḥ* is policy—these two. *Goḥ* is speech; *vāgamitā* means one who possesses sweet speech—this is the sense. *Prītiḥ* is affection—these two. These pairs, each consisting of two, *edhete* (thrive) even in the presence of *deveśe*, the lord of the gods—that is, in Indra as well; [the word] *na* (not) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

(Here, the metrical structure of the verse consists of only two long vowels, *ī* and *e*. This is the *vāṇī* meter. An example of two short vowels is as follows: "O you who know the rules for casting down the stability of the earth, O you who possess the attainment of treasures! O Three-eyed One! O you whose skill is bowed to! O Hara! O destroyer of Smara! Remember me! || 86 ||)

He provides an example of a single long vowel: *seti*. This verse was previously written and explained as an example of [the meter] *sarvatobhadra*. (In this case, the composition of the verse is formed by the single vowel *ā*). Another example is as follows: "By various Vedic, Āgamic, Śaiva, Aindra, Yājñika, Āila, Jaina, and Siddha [texts]; by manifold Maitra and Dhairyavaira; and by their own respective Daiva [sciences], [he shines]. Thus [ends the section].

The single-vowel sounds of *ḍha*, *ṭha*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *la*, and *s* are as follows: "They cried out loudly in battles, they praised the Lord of the heavens greatly; they were greedy for pleasures, they nourished their joys, and they were repeatedly bewildered again and again. Thus, it should be understood that four varieties of vowels have been shown. (87)

Now, in order to demonstrate the restriction of locations, [the author] first shows the four locations that lack labial sounds, beginning with "nayanā...": O "nayanānandajanane" (O producer of joy for the eyes), O giver of festival to the eyes! O "aṅgane" (O beautiful woman)! O "aghane" (O cloudless one), and therefore "nakṣatragaṇaśālini" (O adorned with clusters of stars), in the "gagane" (sky), let the "dṛṣṭiḥ" (sight) be given—that is, let the eye be cast—even "sakṛt" (once). (The epithet "nayanānandajanane" is also appropriately construed as an adjective for "gagane").

The intended meaning is that as the hero consoles his indignant beloved, the sight of such a sky—serving as a stimulus for passion—will cause her pride to break effortlessly. Here, because the verse is composed solely with dentals, palatals, gutturals, and retroflexes (*mūrdhanya*), it should be understood as having four places of articulation. An example of a four-place [verse] devoid of dentals and retroflexes is as follows: "Like moths rushing [into a flame], the arrows of that king..."

"Arrows cut down fell there at the boundary of the battle. Thus [is an example]. An example of *niṣkaṇṭhya* (absence of the *kaṇṭhya* or guttural class) is: "O Viriñca, whose intellect is keen as a needle! [I bow to you] who are the support of the earth, the delight of the world, of vast form, and established in the highest state, with pure and non-decaying [qualities] in all directions. Thus [is an example]. An example of *nistālavya* (absence of the *tālavya* or palatal class) is: "With the mass of jewels from his shimmering earrings, variegated like Indra’s bow, and sounding like a cloud, he then shone in the encounter like the rainy season. Thus [is an example].

An example of what is to be excluded (*nirdantya*) is as follows: "May that wielder of the discus (*cakrapāṇi*), who removes the serpent [of worldly existence], who is skilled in the act of slaying [the demon] Caṇḍa, who is united with the fierce Lord (*īśa*), and who is worshipped by the hosts of principal gods, grant me liberation from the fatigue of worldly prosperity. (88)

It shows that [the word] *ali* has three places of articulation, is without labials, and is produced by the upper palate (*ūrdhanya*). O you with firm breasts (*ghamastani*), o you with dense bosoms! Your face—wherein the creepers of curls (*alakalatā*) are like bees (*avalaya*), dark-colored and black; wherein the eyes possess the luster of a lotus (*nalina*), resembling a lotus in their shade; and which possesses a splendor like the radiance of the moon—what person does it not strike? Does it not agitate? Indeed, it does.

The meaning is "all indeed. (In this context, it should be understood that the poetic composition (*padyabandha*) consists solely of letters produced by the throat (*kaṇṭhya*), the teeth (*dantya*), and the palate (*tālavya*); thus, the three places [of articulation] are those excluding the labial (*oṣṭhya*) and the guttural (*mūrdhanya*) sounds. An example of such a three-place composition, devoid of labials and dentals, is as follows: "May Hari—the one whose body is the very essence of Kṛṣṇa, who is worshipped by the wheel of his most excellent and noble movements throughout the world, who is the destroyer of the body of Hiraṇyākṣa, who dwells upon the king of birds, and whose bed is sought for refuge by Śrī—be victorious! || 89 ||

He provides an example of the *dvisthānacitram* (double-positioned figure) using syllables that are dental (*dan*) and labial (*tyakaṇṭhya*), beginning with the verse "anaṅga": O you who are always sinless (*sadānagha*)—that is, O one who is forever free from suffering and devoid of pain in all circumstances; the sense is "O you who are free from anxiety" (*niścinta*). (According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *agha* is neuter and denotes misfortune, suffering, and sin. Likewise, O you whose body is bent by constant bliss (*sadānandanatāṅga*).

O you whose limbs and members are always bent—that is, captivated or occupied—by the delight of singing, instrumental music, and the like; [even] that virtuous woman, whose limbs are ever-soft (or, who is ever-devoted), [is affected], as the word "api" implies. From association with the unattached—that is, from contact with wicked people who are themselves free from attachment—through the transgression of the bodiless one (Kāma), they have become attached, meaning they have become corrupted; [these are] various and manifold.

It becomes such that it is filled with *ātaṅkas*—meaning diseases, torments, or apprehensions (*ātaṅko rogasantāpaśaṅkāsu murajadhvanau*, according to the *Medinī*). The sense is that even though she is a virtuous wife (*satī*), through her separation from her husband, she falls away due to association with wicked people. (Therefore, "consider your wife; enough of this idle merriment"—this is the speech of someone to a friend. Here, the composition of the verse consists solely of dentals and gutturals; thus, it possesses the quality of being situated in two places).

Regarding the phrase "natāṅgāsaṅgasaṅgataḥ," there is also a variant reading: "natāṅgīmaṅgasaṅgatā! In that case, the address is split as follows: "O Sadānanda! meaning "O you who are always endowed with bliss through the attainment of your beloved! Furthermore, there is another address: "O you who are united with the body (aṅga) of some other woman, a 'natāṅgī' (one with bent limbs)! The meaning is a plaintive prayer: "Your constant companion exists in various forms for the purpose of assailing [your] desire; therefore, have compassion for her."

However, this reading is not pleasing, because the vowel *ī* possesses temporal duration (*kālatva*), and thus it would result in the mere loss of its status as a dental-palatal sound (*dantyakaṇṭhatva*). (90)

He illustrates the variety [of alliteration] occurring in a single location (*ekasthāna*) by means of throat-armors (*kaṇṭhāvarma*), beginning with the verse *agā*... (The word division is as follows: *āgāḥ*, *gām*, *gāṅgakākākagāhaka*, *aghakakākahā*; *ahāhāṅga*, *khagāṅkāgakaṅka*, *agakhagakākaka*). O *gāṅgakākākagāhaka*! [This refers to one who plunges into] that which belongs to the Gaṅgā (*gāṅga*), namely the water (*kaṃ*); its *ākāka* is a crooked movement accompanied by sound (*saśabda-vakra-gati*). (From the root *kai* meaning "to sound," preceded by the prefix *ā*, the form *ākāḥ* is derived in the sense of an action using the suffix *kvip*. From the root *aka* meaning "to move crookedly,"...)

The suffix *ṅa* is applied [to *aka*] according to the rule *akaḥ*. *Ākākaḥ* means "together with *ākā*," that is, a wave (*taraṅga*); one who plunges (*gāhate*) into that is so described. In the vocative case of that: "O you who plunge into the waves of the Gaṅgā water!"—this is the meaning. Furthermore, "O Ahāhāṅga!"—*hāhā* is a specific sound indicating wretchedness; one who goes (*aṅgati*) toward that is *hāhāṅgaḥ*; one who is not *hāhāṅgaḥ* is *ahāhāṅgaḥ*, in the vocative of which: "O you who are eternally blissful (*sadānanda*)!"—this is the meaning. Moreover, "O Khagāṅkāgakaṅka!"—those who go (*gacchanti*) to the sky (*kham*), i.e., the atmosphere, are *khagāḥ* (birds).

The sun and others are the "limbs" (*aṅka*), and that which possesses these as its "marks" (*ciḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍanāni*) is *khagāṅka*. That which is both *sa* (he) and *aga* (a mountain) is *khagāṅkāga*, meaning Sumeru; one who goes to (*kaṅkate*) that is so described (from the root *kaki* "to go," with the suffix *aṇ*). In the vocative case of that [term]: "O you who are worthy of traveling as far as Mount Sumeru by the power of your merit! Furthermore, O *agakhagakākaka*: *aga* means that which goes (*gacchati*), i.e., the perishable; *khāni* refers to the sense organs.

"Khaga" means that which goes (to the objects of the senses). Therefore, "aga-khaga" refers to that which is both non-going and going. "Ka" means happiness. He does not "kaka"—that is, he does not act for its sake, nor desires it, nor longs for it; such is the meaning. Thus, "Agakhagakākaka" is his vocative address (the form of the root *kak* being used in the sense of pride, desire, and fickleness); the meaning is one who is unattached to sensory pleasure. (Note: In the case of the full compound reading "Ahāhāṅgakhagāṅkāgakaṅkāgakhagakākaka": "Hā" means abandonment (*hānam*). "Ahā" means not abandoning (*na hāḥ*). One who attains or reaches that is [Ahāhāṅga].)

O you whose body is imperishable (*akṣayaśarīra*), meaning one who possesses such a firm and solid frame; O you whose very mark (*aṅka*) is the sky (*khaga*)—whether Garuḍa or the Sun—and who are like the mountain Meru (*aga*); O you to whom even the *kaṅkas* (a type of bird), the forest-dwelling birds (*agakhaga*), are eager to follow (*kākakāḥ*)—that is, O you whose journey is celebrated even by winged creatures! You.

*aghakākakaha*: "Aghas" refers to despicable sins, which are like "kākas," or crows, because they are the cause of misfortune; he who destroys them is thus called *aghakākakaha*, meaning one who is free from sin. Being such, you have "gone to" (*agāḥ*) the earth (*gām*), that is, you have circumambulated it. Alternatively, you have "gone to" (*agāḥ*) heaven (*gām*)—for Amara states: "The word *go* [is used] for heaven, cattle, speech, thunderbolt, direction, eye, sun, water, and as a visible object; it is feminine when referring to a cow. The sense is that you shall go there.

(An aorist suffix is used in the sense of expectation; this is a praise of a certain traveler. Here, the composition of the verse consists solely of guttural sounds. || 91 || Now, while demonstrating the restriction of phonemes (*varṇa*) among the varieties of the *citra* ornament, since vowels are mentioned separately, the word "phoneme" (*varṇa*) here refers only to the consonant-form phoneme. He provides an example of a four-phoneme [verse] consisting entirely of consonants, beginning with "re re."

(*Re re* is an indeclinable particle indicating a call to lowly persons. O you *māmama*!—*māyām* means "in Lakṣmī," and *mama* (an indeclinable) means "possessiveness"; he who has that [is addressed here], meaning a miser (*kṛpaṇa*). According to some, *māyām amama amamatvam yasya saḥ* means "one who is devoid of Lakṣmī. *Mā mā* means "not, not" (an expression of negation, where the doubling occurs due to excess of agitation). *Ama* means "go"; the sense is "do not go near me"—the word "you" being understood as the subject—because:

A *kāka* is a crow; what [is there] of the *kekā-kākuka*—where *kekā* is the cry of a peacock and its *kākuka* is the modulation of that cry caused by intoxication—he who "calls out" (*kāyati*) or makes sound such a cry (the suffix *ḍa* being added to the root *kai* meaning "to sound")—does he become like that? This is the ellipsis; the sense is "but certainly not. The implication is that just as a crow's desire for the peacock's cry is one of futile longing, so too is your longing for me.

Furthermore, "rorūrurūrorugāgogaḥ": one who cries out repeatedly (*punaḥ punaḥ*) or excessively (*atiśayena*) out of fear is called *rorūḥ* (from the root *ru*, with the suffix *kvip* after the intensive *yaṅ*-lopa). That very one is a *ruru*, a species of deer; thus, he is *rorūruru*. The *ruk*—the pain produced by being pierced by arrows—from his *uraḥ*, his chest, is itself the *āgaḥ*, the offense or sin (*pāpam*). He goes toward or attains that [pain], meaning he has become such a person; because he is a slayer of defenseless living beings, he is exceedingly sinful. You, on account of performing such base deeds...

The sense is: "I am not suitable for you. Furthermore, you are *agāṅgaga*: one who goes to (*gacchati*) or dwells upon (*adhivasati*) the limb (*aṅga*), that is, a portion of Mount Agastya (*agasya parvatasya*); thus you are a mountaineer (*pārvatya*), and because you dwell in a lowly region, the sense is: "I am not suitable for you. Likewise, *agaguḥ*: "not going" or "not associating," meaning "unconnected" (*asambaddha*). *Gauḥ* means speech (*vāk*). [As the lexicon states: "Heaven, desire, cattle, speech, thunderbolt, direction, eye, sun, earth, and water... [The verse continues with further wordplay on these meanings.]

According to Amara’s lexicon (*Amara-kośa*), the word *go* can refer to a woman or a man when viewed from the perspective of its etymological derivation (*lakṣyadṛṣṭyā*). Since you are like that—that is, one who speaks incoherently—it follows that you are not suitable for me; this is the underlying sense. (This is a rejection by her toward a certain hunter who desired the name of a courtesan. Here, the poetic composition is formed by the four consonantal syllables *ra*, *ga*, *ka*, and *ma* alone.)

By the term *varṇa* (syllable), there is the inclusion of those syllables used for filling out the verse; therefore, even with the presence of the letter *ṅa* in the word *aṅga*, there is no violation of the four-fold classification (*cāturvarṇya*), because that [ṅa] lacks the quality of being a verse-filler. If this example, due to its connection with the letter *ṣa*, is considered incorrect by some, then an example of a correct [verse] is as follows: "jajaujojājijijjājī taṃ tato'titatātitut| bhābhā'bhobhābhibhībhābhūrārāririrī raraḥ||" (92) [End of verse 92]

He cites three types of alliteration (*trivyañjana*) among those variegated by color (*varṇacitra*): *devānām ati*. [This means: He is the delighter (*nandana*) of the gods (*devānām*), such as Indra and others, because he causes joy by subduing the Daityas; likewise, he is the repeller (*nodana*), that is, the one who drives away the revilers of the Vedas (*vedanindinaḥ*), meaning the atheistic folk (note: there is an alternative reading here, *vedanindinām*). The Lord in the form of Nṛsiṃha is the god (*devaḥ*); he is called the reviler of the Dānavas (*dānavandinaḥ*) because he delights (*nandayati*) the Dānavas—that is, satisfies them—by his victory over the three worlds.

Hiraṇyakaśipu tormented the sky—the intermediate space—with his gift-giving, with the rending of his chest, and with his roaring, that is, his lion-like roar; here, the poetic composition is formed by the three consonants *da*, *va*, and *na* alone. 93.

The author illustrates the variety of colors consisting of divine letters with the word "sūri. "Sūri" means a learned man. Furthermore, he is one whose strength (*sāra*) is such that it "rushes against" (*āsarati*) or assails both gods (*surān*) and demons (*asurān*); moreover, he is "possessed of beautiful thighs" (*sasūruḥ*), meaning he has lovely thighs (*su-ūrū*). And finally, he is the well-known "Sīrī," who possesses the "taste for liquor" (*surā-rasī*), where "taste" (*rasa*) signifies the enjoyment of drinking wine, or rather, passion (*anurāga*).

Baladeva is so called because he possesses a plough (*sīra*) that is equal to a *lāṅga* (a type of ox). He went to the lakes (*sarasaḥ*)—those lakes in which there were cranes (*sārasāḥ*), specifically those birds born in the water (*sarasi bhavāḥ*) that were accompanied by loud cries (*ārasena*), meaning they were crying out loudly—for the purpose of sporting in the water (*sasāra*). (This is a verse concerning Baladeva’s water-sports; here, the poetic composition (*padyabandha*) is formed using only the two syllables "sa-ra").

Or for example: "The fearless female elephants (abhīrubhaiḥ), heavy with their burdens (bhāribhiḥ), [were] struck by the clouds (abhrābhaiḥ) with many heavy, loud-sounding drums (bherībhiḥ) that were themselves heavy (bhāribhiḥ) and terrifying (bhīraubhiḥ). (94)

He provides an example of a verse containing a single consonant (*ekavyañjana*) with the word *citrālaḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍakārabedam*. [The commentary begins: "Surely" (*nūnam*). By this powerful one—meaning by this one seen before; by "this one" (*enena*), where the form *ena* is the substitute for *idam* or *etad* according to the rule "the second case endings *ṭā*, *auṣ*, and *ṅasi* become *ena*"—the sense is "by the enemy. Alternatively, *ina* means "lord," and *a-ina* means "one who is not a lord"; thus, by that non-lord, meaning by the enemy. By the face itself as the instrument—meaning by the face marked with a frown—of us (*naḥ*), meaning of ourselves.

"ananāni" means villages; "nūnam" means certainly or indeed; "nunnani" means removed or cast aside; "na iti na" means not so, but rather they have indeed been removed. The sense is: "Upon merely seeing his knitting of the eyebrows, we were as good as dead; what need is there to mention a full-scale battle? However, [one might object]: "But, sir! [the answer is: no.

*Inaḥ* means a lord; *nā* means a man; thus the meaning is "our lord. *Anān* means vital breaths. *Ninīḥ*, meaning desiring to protect (*ninīḥ* being derived from the root *ni-* with the desiderative suffix *-sa-* and the primary suffix *-kvip* in the nominative singular), means desiring to lead [them] away. *Anenāḥ* means one who is not sinful, or one who is not evil; the word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The sense is that for one who has conquered the enemy, death in battle is better even than life; therefore, he should fight according to his ability.

This is an expression of the dejection of the troops of a certain king defeated by his enemies. Here, the poetic composition (*padyabandha*) is formed solely by the phonemes in the form of the letter *na*. In this manner, some authorities also accept such compositions even when using all the consonantal phonemes (*sarvavyañjana-varṇa*), due to the extraordinary variety (*vaicitryātiśaya*) they produce; an example of this is as follows: "Who is he who possesses the splendor of a multitude of birds (*khaga-ogha-aṅa-cic-chau-jā*), who is the destroyer of the pride of the wicked (*jhāññā-ṭoṭhī-ḍaḍaṃ-ḍhaṇaḥ*), who likewise [subdues] the oceans (*tathodadhīna*), who is the one who swallows the waters (*paphar-vā-bīr-mayoḥ*), and who endures the blessings (*ilvā-śiṣāṃ sahaḥ*)? Thus it is said.

Likewise, those ten phonemes ending in *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *sa*, *ta*, *ja*, *bha*, *na*, *ga*, and *la* have been determined for the purpose of establishing the characteristics of prosody (*chandas*). That which is composed of them—consisting of both vowels (*akṣara*) and consonants (*vyañjana*)—is also described, as in: "May the smile of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva), whose three eyes are joined upon the lotus-face of Girijā, arise for the welfare of the world and for the protection of the worshippers who remain awake against the fear of the enemy of the gods. Similarly: "The seven notes, beginning with the vowels, are *sa*, *ri*, *ga*, *ma*, *pa*, *dha*, and *ni*."

The conventions established for *ṣaḍja* and the other notes are observed by those learned in the *Gāndharvaveda*. Thus, there is the illustration consisting merely of the indication of characteristics, such as the indication of *ṣaḍja* and so forth: "She who is the receptacle of the destruction of my enemies, the one who accomplishes the abode of the essence of the *Sāman*, the proud one possessing the weight of *ga* and *ri*, she who is free from sin, she who flows away, equal to the equal, yet incomparable. In this manner, other varieties should also be understood. (95)

Having shown a certain portion of the *citrālaṅkāra* (pictorial ornamentation) due to its difficulty and the resulting bulk of the text, he concludes that section and points out the *prahelikā* (enigma), saying "iti" (thus). "Iti" means in the manner previously described; even among the difficult paths, because they consist of four, three, two, or one [syllables], a rule that is hard to accomplish has been shown—that is, illustrated—even though it is a mere fraction (*alpamātra*). By this much, it is implied that there are other difficult *citrālaṅkāras*, such as the *padmabandha* and others mentioned by ancient authorities.

For fear of excessive prolixity, these have not been stated here; it is indicated that they should be understood from other works. Now, furthermore, the rule regarding the movement of the specific types of riddles (*prahelikā*) is being proclaimed and examined. (The definition of that has been stated in general; for example: "A *prahelikā* is to be known as that speech which effects concealment. Therefore, the definition of a *prahelikā* should be understood as a particular arrangement of words consisting of the concealment of one's intended meaning. || 96 ||

By the statement, "Because it acts as an obstacle to rasa, *prāhelikā* is not an ornament," if *prāhelikā*—like *yamaka* and other such figures—is not considered an ornament because it lacks the quality of being an embellishment (*upaskāraka*) of word and meaning due to its non-conformity with rasa, nevertheless, [the author] states its utility by saying, "It plays."

In playful assemblies and recreation halls—those amusements and delights; or alternatively, "play" (*krīḍā*) being the curiosity consisting of mutual verbal dexterity, "assembly" (*goṣṭhī*) being the gathering of the learned, and "amusement" (*vinoda*) being the passing of time through the critical appreciation of poetry—in those [settings], as well as with those who know such things, namely experts in riddles (*prahelikā*), in a crowded place filled with people, regarding that which is counsel (*mantraṇa*), i.e., secret discourse, meaning mutual conversation; likewise, regarding another person distinct from the one to be understood [by the speaker].

In the case of a person, when there is mental agitation due to a specific lack of understanding of the meaning—intended for the purpose of deluding—or regarding the concealment of comprehension, *prahelita*s (puzzling riddles) are useful, that is, they serve a purpose; the sense is that they are beneficial. (Therefore, it should be understood that these possess the status of an *alaṅkāra* [ornament] when used in contexts such as playful assemblies, but elsewhere they are detrimental. || 97 ||

He states its definitions and names in sequence, beginning with "they say": they call that which has arrived [at them] a *prahelikā* (riddle) whose meaning is hidden—that is, difficult to understand—due to the *sandhi* (euphonic junction) between two words, specifically through the effect of *sandhi* produced by the proximity of word-forms ending in vowels (*sup*) or verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). Regarding "deceived" (*vañcitā*): where there is a deception or a delusion caused by a word that is well-known (*rūḍha*) in a sense other than the one intended, that is a *vañcitā* riddle; such is the meaning.

"Transgressed" (*vyatkrāntā*): due to the employment—that is, the arrangement—of words that are excessively remote, meaning situated at a great distance, it causes confusion, which is to say, it produces a deficiency in the comprehension of the meaning; such is the *prahelikā* called "transgressed" (*vyutkrāntā*). "And that" (*sā*): in that *prahelikā*, the collection of words (*padāvalī*) is difficult to understand because of the use of obscure terms, and its meaning is likewise hard to grasp; such a *prahelikā* would be called "stolen" (*pramuṣitā*), because the intellect is thoroughly robbed [of its clarity].

(Regarding the distinction between these two: in *vañcitā*, there is a single word whose meaning is difficult to understand, whereas here [in *paruṣā*], there are multiple words; furthermore, in *vañcitā*, there is the use of a word with various meanings in an unfamiliar sense, whereas here, even words that have only a single meaning [are used]. For this reason as well, there is a difference between these two. || 99 || "Of similar form" (*samānarūpā*) means: it is composed or constructed by words that are figurative (*gauṇa*), indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), superimposed (*āropita*), or metaphorical (*upacarita*). The remainder is that it is called a *prahelikā*. It is "of similar form" because it is based on the similarity between two things: the expressed meaning (*śakyārtha*) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*). "Harsh" (*paruṣā*) means: ||| 100 || It is composed or constructed by words that are harsh (*paruṣa*) due to their phonetic quality (*dhvani*), or by words that are harsh (*paruṣa*) due to their meaning (*artha*). The remainder is that it is called a *prahelikā*. It is "harsh" because it causes pain to the ears through its harsh phonetic quality, or because it causes mental distress through its harsh meaning. ||| 100 || "Inverted" (*vyatyastā*) means: ||| 101 || It is composed or constructed by words that are inverted (*vyatyasta*) in their order of sequence (*krama*). The remainder is that it is called a *prahelikā*. It is "inverted" because the sequence of the words is reversed. ||| 101 || "Confused" (*saṃkīrṇā*) means: ||| 102 || It is composed or constructed by words that are confused (*saṃkīrṇa*) due to being mixed together (*miśra*). The remainder is that it is called a *prahelikā*. It is "confused" because it is characterized by the confusion of the words. ||| 102 || "Hidden" (*gūḍhā*) means: ||| 103 || It is composed or constructed by words that are hidden (*gūḍha*) due to their meaning (*artha*). The remainder is that it is called a *prahelikā*. It is "hidden" because the meaning is concealed by the words. ||| 103 || "Obstructed" (*āvṛtā*) means: ||| 104 || It is composed or constructed by words that are obstructed (*āvṛta*) due to their phonetic quality (*dhvani*). The remainder is that it is called a *prahelikā*. It is "obstructed" because the meaning is obstructed by the phonetic quality of the words. ||| 104 || "Reversed" (*viparyastā*) means: ||| 105 || It is composed or constructed by words that are reversed (*viparyasta*) due to their meaning (*artha*). The remainder is that it is called a *prahelikā*. It is "reversed" because the meaning is inverted by the words. ||| 105 || "Mixed" (*miśrā*) means: ||| 106 || It is composed or constructed by words that are mixed (*miśra*) due to being combined (*saṃyoga*). The remainder is that it is called a *prahelikā*. It is "mixed" because it is characterized by the mixing of the words. ||| 106 || "Unmixed" (*asaṃkīrṇā*) means: ||| 107 || It is composed or constructed by words that are unmixed (*asaṃkīrṇa*) due to being distinct (*vibhinna*). The remainder is that it is called a *prahelikā*. It is "unmixed" because it is characterized by the non-mixing of the words. ||| 107 || "Dependent" (*sāpekṣā*) means: ||| 108 || It is composed or constructed by words that are dependent (*sāpekṣa*) upon another sentence (*vākya*). The remainder is that it is called a *prahelikā*. It is "dependent" because it depends upon

The meaning is that because of the mere existence of a definition—that is, simply because a definition exists—it is not [a riddle] through a discernment of what is possible or impossible; rather, it is such that the etymology, the Vedic citation, or the conventional term has been explained therein. It is called a "rough" (*paruṣā*) enigma, because its basis in impossibility causes a harshness to be perceived by the ears. || 100 ||

"Enumerated" (*saṅkhyātā*): where there is an enumeration—that is, a counting of syllables or a word expressing a number—it is the cause or reason for "delusion," meaning specifically the lack of comprehension of the intended meaning; that is the *prahelikā* named "Enumerated," because it is composed of numbers—this is the sense. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*): where the sentence-meaning appears as something else—that is, where it is perceived in a form different from what is initially understood—that *prahelikā* is named "Constructed" (*prakalpitā*), because of the construction of another meaning—this is the sense. || 101 ||

It is thus: in that riddle (*prahelikā*), within the name—that is, in the sphere of designation—there arises the "conception of multiple meanings" (*nānārthakalpanā*); the sense is that because a word has various capacities, there is a conceptualization or mental construction of many meanings; such a riddle is called *nāmāntaritā*, because its meaning is concealed by another name. [The verse begins with] *nibhṛta*... [etc.]
