And that [figure of speech] in which there is speech (*gīr*)—that is, words—which touches upon a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) of both the subject at hand (*prastuta*) and the subject not at hand (*aprastuta*), wherein another—that is, the other, namely the contextual (*prakṛta*)—meaning is concealed (*nibhṛta*) or hidden, is called *nibhṛtā*. (It should be understood that because the subject is indicated here by the power of the common attribute, this is rooted in *samāsokti*. || 102 ||

"By means of synonymous words": that which is composed or constructed as a riddle (*prahelikā*) by using synonyms—that is, other names—for the words presented, namely those words that convey a Prakrit meaning, is called a "synonymous riddle. (In this context, it should be noted that "synonymy" refers to conveying a single meaning through *lakṣaṇā* [secondary indication], and not to having a single referent through *abhidhā* [primary denotation]; for if it were the latter, the meaning would not be concealed, and thus, lacking the utility of being Prakrit, it would not be a riddle at all. ... "confused."

That which is indicated or defined by a word expressing its meaning directly—that is, even when the meaning has been stated by the expressive word—yet leads to confusion (mūḍhi), meaning a momentary bewilderment, is called *sammūḍhā* (the "perplexed").

Regarding *yogamālā*: that *prahelikā* whose nature (*ātmā*) consists of a garland (*mālā*), meaning a collection, of *yogas*—that is, of etymological (*yaugika*) words—is such that it conveys the individual meanings of words established by convention (*rūḍha*) through a series of etymological words; that is the meaning of *prahelikā*, and it is called *parihārikā* (the "resolving").

[The term *parihārikā*] is designated thus based on the etymology: "it sets aside (*pariharati*) and immediately (*jhaṭiti*) prevents the understanding of the literal meaning. The sense is that because the etymological meaning is rooted in the assumption of various difficulties compared to the meaning obtainable through conventional power (*śakti*), it lacks immediate comprehension. Regarding *ekacchannā*: that [figure of speech] in which the dependent (*āśrita*), the thing to be supported (*ādheya*), is manifest (*vyakta*) or clear, while the support (*āśraya*), the locus (*ādhāra*), is concealed (*gopana*), is called *ekacchannā*. This name is derived from the etymology: "that in which one [element], namely the support (*eka āśrayaḥ*), is concealed (*channaḥ*) or hidden (*nigūḍhaḥ*). || 104 ||

*Seti*: That [riddle] in which there is the concealment (*gopana*) of both—the contained (*ādheya*) and the container (*ādhāra*)—is called *ubhayacchannā* (concealed in both); the essential point is that both the contained and the container are hidden. *Saṅkīrṇā* (mixed): That in which there is a *saṅkara* (commingling), meaning a coexistence, of two, three, or more of the aforementioned varieties of riddles characterized by various definitions, is called *saṅkīrṇā*. || 105 ||

"These" refers to these [verses] beginning with *samāgatā*, which are the sixteen riddles (*prahelikā*) pointed out by the former teachers; the meaning is that they are declared to be non-defective. "Defective" means that other, different fourteen defective riddles—such as those consisting of the elision or addition of syllables (*cyutadattākṣara*) and so forth—were also studied and recited by those very same former teachers; the meaning is that they were proclaimed to be faulty.

Among these, first, six varieties beginning with *cyutākṣara* have been described by others as follows: "The *prahelikā* is a riddle; it is also of six kinds: *cyutākṣara*, *dattākṣara*, *ubhaya*, *muṣṭi*, *vindumatī*, and *atryavatī*. Among these, an example of *cyutākṣara* is: "Oppressed by the weight of her breasts, bending at every step..."

"One does not go even a single step if she is deprived of her necklace"—here, although it should have been said that *vihaṅgikā* (the female bird) does not go if she is deprived of her *kāhāra* (a type of ornament), the word *hāraṇa* (necklace) was used instead of *kāhāra*. Because of this, the syllable *kā* has been dropped; thus, it is *cyutākṣarā* (the "dropped-syllable" figure). The *dattākṣarā* (the "added-syllable" figure) is as follows: "Who is this one, with thick shoulders and arrogant with rut, followed by his beloved, who goes behind the deer—young Śaṃvara? Here, although it should have been said *śavara* (the hunter), the word *śaṃvara* was used. Because of this, the anusvāra (*ṃ*) has been added; thus, it is *dattākṣarā*.

*Cyutadattākṣarā* (the verse with syllables omitted and supplied) is, for example: "Who is this clever, passionate, and charming rogue who, seated upon the hips of a slender-limbed woman, embraces her neck and coos sweetly? In this case, when the syllable *vi* is removed from the word *viṭaḥ* and the syllable *gha* is supplied, the result is "The jar (*ghaṭaḥ*) coos. This is *cyutadattākṣarā*. *Akṣaramuṣṭiḥ* (the "puzzle of syllables") is, for example: *"atiḥ atiḥ anma alaṃ prīdya radya jadya phadya| melā melā melaṃ melaṃ phasa phasa phasa phasa|"*

And this [verse] is called *akṣaramuṣṭikā* because it consists of a handful of syllables (*akṣara*). Here, when written in four lines with four feet each, a verse is established by means of four *murajabandha* (drum-pattern) arrangements, as follows: "Today my joy is fruitful; today my delight is fruitful; today my birth is fruitful; today my fruit is fruitful. An example of *vindumatī* is as follows: "Your instruction at every ocean, at every mountain..."

"His fame is indeed not found anywhere lacking in marvelous means for the sake of the fruit"—by this verse, there is a method of indicating another verse that possesses its constituent vowels, anusvāras, visargas, and conjunct consonants by means of dots (*bindus*) alone; this is *vindumatī*. For example: 0u00ā0u00ā0ā0ā0ṃ0u0e 0ṃ0u0e 00ḥ| 0ā00e0ā00e0i0iḥ00rra0000i0rra 0ḥ| By these dots, this verse is indicated: "udadhāvudadhāvājñā saṃyuge saṃyugaṃ jayaḥ|" (In battle after battle, his command prevailed.)

"In every daring act, your success is proclaimed"—this is an example of the *arthavatī* [prahelikā]: "What radiant thing, possessing the luster of refined gold, with its lips bitten, is kissed passionately even by joyful elders? Here, the answer to this question is the *jaka*-mango fruit (*jakvāmraphala*), yet because it is not understood due to the use of words with double meanings (*dvyarthapada*), this is an *arthaprahelikā*. Furthermore, he describes the sixfold [prahelikā] as follows: "By means of actions, grammatical relations, connections, the feet [of verses], intentions, and objects..."

"Those who know the hidden meaning declare that when the six [elements] are concealed, it is 'Gūḍha' (the Hidden). Thus [ends the section on]. Examples of *kriyāgupta* (concealed verb), *kārakagupta* (concealed case-role), *sambandhagupta* (concealed relation), and so forth have been given. Furthermore, its most extensive subdivisions—such as *antaḥpraśna* (internal question) and *bahiḥpraśna* (external question)—are not demonstrated here for fear of excessive bulk; however, they may be seen in the works of Bhoja and others. || 106 ||

Even if faulty riddles (*prahelikā*) were spoken by previous teachers, we nevertheless have no interest in them; thus he says, "the defects. We, however, considering—that is, knowing—the defects in the form of being obstacles to verbal comprehension, and [finding] only those that are "excellent" (i.e., superior) because they lack an excess of defects, shall describe only the sixteen faultless riddles beginning with *samāgata*, which have attained the status of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).

"We shall provide examples. [Objection: But if you are going to state only excellent riddles (*prahelikā*), how will the students come to know faulty riddles? With this intention, he says "those" (*tāḥ*). Those which are "without characteristics"—meaning not included within the previously stated characteristics—are "faulty," that is, defective; the sense is that I have no effort to provide examples of them. || 107 ||

In this context, he states the consensus: "No. O red-eyed one! (the sense being: "due to anger"); "by me"—that is, by my own self (the instrumental case used in the sense of the genitive)—"the mind," which is "conversant with cow-products," meaning knowledgeable of the taste of milk and such, "is not [so]. The meaning is that the milk and so forth were not taken by me; or alternatively, the connection is with the supplied verb: "my mind, conversant with cow-products, is not [restrained] by me."

"Why are you so angry? Enough of these such [outbursts], these misplaced weepings, these causeless lamentations"—this is the literal meaning, which functions as a concealment (*saṃvṛti*). However, the purpose of this concealment is to make people understand that "by this [act] she has caused the depletion of her milk and so forth"; thus, thinking "she is weeping in pain because she is angry," let them perceive her in this common way.

The hidden meaning, however, is this: my mind is not aware of the "offense"—that is, the transgression consisting of union with another heroine (as Amara states, *āgaḥ*, *aparādhaḥ*, and *mantuḥ* are synonyms)—nor of the "taste," that is, the aesthetic relish. [The sense is: "I do not desire anyone other than you; how then can you have such indignation toward me?"

(Here, by breaking the compound as *me āgorasābhijñam*, the vowel *e* is replaced by *ay* according to the rules of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), resulting in *mayāgorasābhijñam*; thus, the intended meaning is concealed. Consequently, this is a *samāgatā* type of *prahelikā* (riddle), wherein the original sense is hidden by means of *sandhi*. This is a statement by Kṛṣṇa in a public assembly addressed to a certain proud cowherd girl. || 108 ||

He illustrates deception with the verse beginning "kubjām. For you, who were enjoying—that is, making love to—a certain woman who was hunchbacked (*kubjā*) with a bent back, your pleasure (*rati*) and satisfaction increased; yet for you, while enjoying other women who rival the celestial nymphs (*amarastrī*), resembling beautiful goddesses, your pleasure and satisfaction did not increase in that same way. (The words "for you" and "did not increase" are supplied from the context.)

The literal meaning is "a humpbacked woman," while the hidden meaning refers to the city of Kānyakubja or the women residing there, and so forth. (In this case, the word *kubjā* is well-known only in the sense of a woman with a curved back, whereas it is not so known in other senses; thus, this is a riddle called *vañcitā*, which consists of conveying an unfamiliar meaning through a word that is [otherwise] well-known. This is a statement made by someone to a person in love with the city of Kānyakubja or its women. || 109 ||

He provides an example of *vyutkrāntā* [the transposed riddle], beginning with "on the stalk" (*daṇḍe*). The connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: the swan (*haṃsaḥ*), rubbing and grinding its limbs (*aṅgāni*) against the stalk (*daṇḍe*)—that is, the stem (*nāle*)—of a lotus plant (*padminyāḥ*) which is possessed of harsh thorns (*karkaśakaṇṭake paruṣakaṇṭakānvite*), while making a charming sound (*valguravaṃ manojñaṃ nādaṃ*) with its beak (*tuṇḍena mukhena*), kisses the mouth (*mukhaṃ cumbiti*) of the lotus plant. (In this case, because the words constituting the syntactic understanding are arranged with excessive separation, there is a violation of proximity (*āsatti*); thus, it is a *vyutkrāntā* riddle. || 110 ||

He shows her as if she were bewildered, saying "khātaya. O girl! O maiden! (Hemacandra states: "kanyā, kanī, and kumārī [are synonyms]"); *kālyaḥ* means that which is driven or cast forth, thus *kālaḥ* refers to the foot (the form is derived from the root *kal* meaning "to impel," with the suffix *ghañ*). *Sphātayaḥ* means *sphāyanaṃ*, which is *sphāḥ*; the meaning is "increase. *Atiḥ* means "movement" (*gatiḥ*) therein; thus, the meaning is "expanded" (*sphītāḥ*), that is to say, "many" (the form is derived from the root *at* meaning "continuous movement," with the suffix *in*).

*Khātayaḥ* means *kha*, which is space (*ākāśa*); its quality is *kha*, meaning sound. (According to the rule *kha-śabdād-idamarthe ṇaḥ*: those in whom there is *ati*, meaning movement, of *khasya*, i.e., of sound—meaning ornaments such as anklets that produce sound. *Sphārhavalgavaḥ*: *sphārhāḥ* means "deserving of abundance" (*sphītatām arhanti*), thus "plentiful"; *valgavaḥ* means sounds produced from *valganāt*, i.e., from movement or shaking. Therefore, they are called *sphārhavalgavaḥ* because they possess abundant shaking-sounds; the word "shining forth" (*bhavalanti*) is to be supplied [as the verb], referring to them. Of you.

The meaning is that the anklets and other ornaments on the feet jingle excessively at the time of walking; "candati" means it resounds or makes a loud noise. Thus, "in that moon which resounds," refers to your foot adorned with tinkling anklets and the like. The meaning is: when [that foot] is directly perceived before one's eyes, my vital breaths (vāyavaḥ), being "dhāriṇaḥ"—meaning they remain, they become well-stabilized (the form is from the root *dhṛ* in the sense of "remaining").

(Here, because the intended meaning is concealed by many words due to its being unfamiliar, there is a "stealing away" [of the sense]; thus it is *pramuṣitā*. || 111 || It shows a similarity of form: "here" refers to this very place. Here in the garden, I have seen a *vallarī*—a creeper—distinguished by five shoots (*pañcapallavā*), meaning a branch possessing five sprouts. On that creeper, in every shoot (*pallave pallave*), that is, at each individual shoot, a copper-red (*tāmrā*) cluster of blossoms (*kusumamañjarī*) shines; the word "shines" (*śobhate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

(Here, a certain heroine is superimposed as a garden; her arm as a creeper, her fingers as sprouts, and her nails as flower-clusters; and their copper-red color is to be understood as the luster of her reddened fingers. In this case, the cause for the words "garden" and so forth to denote meanings such as "heroine" is precisely the superimposition through secondary indication (*gauṇī-lakṣaṇā*); thus, it is a riddle of identical form. || 112 ||

He shows the harsh [word], namely *surāḥ*. They are well-known; they are called *surāḥ* because they produce *surā*, i.e., intoxicating liquor (*madya*)—[the form arises from the word *surā* with the suffix *ṅa* added after the elision of the suffix *manin*]. Alternatively, *surāḥ* means those who possess *surā*, i.e., drunkards (*śoṇḍitaḥ*)—[the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for the *arśas-ādi* group]. Or again, *su* means "exceedingly," and *rāḥ* is a word meaning "sound" or "noise"; thus, they are those who have such [sounds], meaning they are making loud *cūt* sounds—[this is the form of the root *rai* meaning "to sound" with the suffix *kvip*]. In this interpretation, [the term refers to] drinkers of *surā*.

Thus, the word *kartṛ* (agent) is to be supplied; characterized by their laughter with bared teeth, the rays of which are visible through their open mouths, they are now, as if submerged—immersed—in that lake consisting of wine (*saure*), being intoxicated, they wander at will and according to their own pleasure through the abode of the gods (*surālaya*), that is, the tavern.

(Here, although the word *surā* by rule denotes only a deity, it is employed—either in the sense of a liquor-seller, a drunkard, or one who makes a loud "cīt" sound; thus, because it reveals the speaker's harshness, this is a riddle called *paruṣā*). || 113 ||

It recites the *saṅkhyātā* [meter] and does not study the *nāsikya*. *Nāsikya* means that which exists in the nose; the meaning is the letter *ña*. That which has this *ña* in its middle is called "having *ña* situated in the middle. Furthermore, it is adorned—that is, composed—on both sides by four syllables, i.e., four letters. To be specific, it is of such a form as having two letters, "ka" and "ā," at the beginning, and two letters, "ca" and "ī," at the end, with the letter *ña* in the middle. Such is a certain city, namely Kāñcī.

(Through the metaphorical identification of the name with the named, the two qualifying sentences beginning with "nāsikya" should also be applied to the *pūrvā*, even though they primarily indicate the *kāñcī*. There exists a *pūrvā* in which kings—those whose names are composed of eight syllables (*aṣṭavarṇa*) and who possess the designations *āḍha*, *ḍha*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, and *va*—were situated; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 114 ||

He shows her as she is imagined: "O old woman!"—O venerable elder!—you who are characterized by speech that is faltering and failing, meaning indistinct due to old age; by a head bowed down, precisely because of the weight of old age; and by a gaze that is piteous, timid, and lacking in strength. Even though you are thus distinguished [by these qualities], do you not show compassion toward me, who stand here trembling with a quiver, the implication being that this is due to fear? Do you not feel pity? Thus.

This is the literal meaning. The hidden meaning, however, is: "O Vṛddhe! O Lakṣmī! (According to Amara: *ṛddhiḥ siddhilakṣmyau vṛddherapyāḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍavayā ime*). Why do you not show compassion for me, who am characterized by faltering speech due to the absence of wealth, with my head bowed and eyes dejected, and who am trembling? (In this case, because the first perceived meaning is the primary subject at hand, this riddle (*prahelikā*) is constructed as one where the second meaning is intended. 115.

He shows [the verse] where the meaning is concealed by names, beginning with the word "first" (*ādau*). O you of restless eyes (*adhīrākṣi*), o tremulous-eyed one! A certain *pārthiva*—that which is signified by the word *pārthiva*—is praised and celebrated at the beginning, first, as "King" (*rājā*) and likewise as "Eternal" (*sanātana*). However, this *pārthiva*, in reality, is neither a king, a lord of the earth (*bhūpati*), nor is he eternal; therefore, the natural sense of the question is: "Who is he? The answer, however, is hidden in the form of the *rājātanu* tree.

For instance, a certain *pārthiva*—meaning a particular kind of tree produced from the earth (*pṛthivī*) and water (*vāk*)—is first sung of, that is, referred to, by the initial portion of its name, namely the word "rājā" (king). Furthermore, it is called *nātana*, meaning "not without *tana*," for after the word "rājā," the word "*tana*" also exists; thus, the subsequent meaning is "the *rājātana* tree."

By the word *rājātana*, the *piyāla* tree is meant; as Amara states: "The *piyāla* may be called *rājātana*. Thus, *rājātana*, *rājātana*, and *rājādana* are two names [for the same thing]. Here, while the name should have been stated as *rājātana*, there is instead the fabrication of multiple meanings; this is therefore a *nāmāntaritā* (name-concealed) riddle. In the definition, the word "name" (*nāma*) is intended to refer to the mere object itself; thus: "Embraced by a young woman around the neck and resting upon her hips..."

"Even in the presence of gurus, who coos again and again?"—here, because an irrelevant meaning is imagined regarding the object to be expressed, which is a water-pot, it should be understood as *nāmāntaritā* (concealed by a name). || 116 ||

He illustrates this subtly with the verse beginning "hṛtadravyam. By whom the people have been attracted—that is, brought under their control—through various gestures (*nānābhāṅgibhiḥ*), meaning through manifold playful movements; likewise, those who are difficult to sustain (*durddhurāḥ*), meaning they are held with great difficulty and are thus somehow indispensable; such women, having abandoned a man whose wealth has been taken away—that is, one whose riches are lost—and having left him for a wealthy man, to whom do they go? It follows that only courtesans can possess such characteristics.

To preclude that [misunderstanding], he says: "Not courtesans"; the meaning is that courtesans with such characteristics are not the subject of my question. Therefore, the question "Which ones are they? is intended in its natural sense. However, the answer, which has the sense of something to be concealed, is "the rivers born from the mountains."

For instance: "nānā" means various; "nānābhaṅgi" refers to water possessing various waves (bhaṅga); "samākṛṣṭāḥ" means drawn near or brought close; "lokāḥ" refers to people eager to descend [into the water]; "dudurdharāḥ" means difficult to hold from the mountain (dhara); "duḥ" means gone with difficulty—that is, emerged with great effort—referring to the rivers; "hṛtāni" means carried away or destroyed by the force of the current; "dravyāṇi" refers to mountain-born objects; and "dru-dravyāṇi" refers to things belonging to trees (dru), such as branches, sprouts, and so forth.

Or rather, the meaning is this: they abandon that man—who is like a man, serving as a support—and proceed toward what is effectively a mountain; by implication, they leave behind the wealthy ocean, which is a mine of jewels. (In this case, because the specific attributes are common to both [the man and the mountain], it is logical that when one is negated, the other is understood; thus, "rivers" is the intended object of the question. Furthermore, it should be noted that although the identical attributes are perceived here, it possesses the quality of being "unexpressed" (*nibhṛtatva*) because the denotative word for the comparison is not employed. || 117 ||

He shows a word with the same meaning by saying "jita" (conquered). O sweet-voiced one! O lady of melodious speech! [The phrase] "the name of the most excellent hair"—that is to say, a synonym for it, namely "prabāla" (a sprout); or alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "one whose name is like the name of that which is the most excellent hair."

He by whom those known as "excellent hair" (prābalāḥ) have been conquered and surpassed—that [hair] which is not to be reached by the ground (abhūmisāḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍavayaḥ), meaning that which has no ground (abhūmiḥ), namely the lower lip (*adharaḥ*)—that very thing, having a name identical to it, today makes me intensely eager (*prabhūtotkam*). The meaning is: "Your lower lip, resembling a young sprout (*prabāla*), causes me distress."

(Here, the words *prakṛṣṭakeśa* ("excellent hair") and *abhūmi* ("not ground") indicate, through *lakṣitalakṣaṇā*, the coral and the lower lip respectively; for there is *lakṣaṇā* of the word *prakṛṣṭakeśa* upon the word *prabāla* (coral), and of the word *abhūmi* upon the word *adhara* (lower lip). And from the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) of those two indicated meanings, there arises the presentation of such objects. Thus, because the object of the subject matter is presented by means of synonymous words, this is a *prahelikā* based on synonymous words. || 118 ||

It shows them to be utterly bewildered; "on the bed" means that the two lovers, out of anger (*krudhā*), having turned away on the bed (*śayanīye*), lay down; the meaning is that even while lying down thus turned away, out of passion (*rāgāt*) or affection (*anurāgāt*), they kissed each other's faces according to their own will (*svairaṃ*).

(Here, because it is difficult for two who have turned away from each other in anger to kiss one another's faces at will, there is an initial appearance of confusion; yet in reality, they first lay down having turned away out of affectionate anger, and subsequently, out of passion, lay down again in that same manner, and then turned away once more. Thus, by turning away again after having already turned away and lying on their sides, they become face-to-face, making a kiss of the faces perfectly possible. This verse is called *sammūḍhā* because it initially deceives the listeners.

He shows the exclusion by the word "vijitena" (by the conqueror). Without the bird—that is, by Garuḍa—he was conquered; that is, Indra was defeated at the time of the fetching of the nectar (according to tradition, when Garuḍa went to the world of the gods to fetch the nectar commanded by the Nāgas as the ransom for his mother's slavery, a fierce battle ensued with the Lord of the Gods; there, Garuḍa, having defeated the Lord of the Suras by his own prowess, took the nectar and departed—this is the report). His son is "ātmabhavaḥ."

The son is Arjuna; his enemy is Karṇa; his father is the Sun; by his rays (feet), people are struck—that is, tormented. That which removes cold is fire; its enemies are water; the bearers of those waters are the clouds; by them the sky is pervaded—that is, covered—and this [the poet] welcomes—that is, regards with favor.
(Here, it is called *parihārikā* because the primary meaning is swiftly seized by means of etymological words. | 120 |

He shows [the hand] covered by one [garment], meaning that it does not belong to any non-human being who might otherwise be counted as a man. This hand never at any time touches a weapon or a missile, nor does it touch the circle of breasts of women; nevertheless, this hand appears at first glance to be "not fruitless"—that is, not useless—but rather indeed fruitful. However, since it lacks contact with weapons or the breasts of women, he is neither a hero nor a lover; therefore, how is this...?

Because the phrase "the fruitfulness of the hand" appears as a contradiction, the word *amaṇi* indicates the *gandharva* by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Its "hand" is the *gandharvahasta*, which means the castor-oil plant (*eraṇḍavṛkṣa*). As it is stated in the *Hārāvalī*: "The *amaṇḍapa*, the five-fingered, the increasing, the *gandharvahasta*, and the three-segmented fruit. Since its fruit indeed exists, this [name] is based on the clarity of the fruit that depends [on the tree], rather than on the tree itself which is the substratum; thus, it is a single umbrella [of meaning]. || 121 ||

He shows that [the self] is covered by both; by what? What is the referent of "by what"? By which entity, having come together and joined with it, and having obtained and attained proximity and presence in all activities—if, however, at the time of eating (the word *tu* is used for emphasis), he is seen only at the time of eating, then he is discarded and rejected. This answer is as follows: "Whose is this?"—this is *ka-keśaḥ* (whose hair); [here the suffix *ṇya* is added to *ka* in the sense of "belonging to"]; by what? By which head? Together with what? With which entity? Having come together and joined with it, and having obtained and attained proximity and presence in all activities—if, however, at the time of eating, he is seen only at the time of eating, then he is discarded and rejected. This answer is as follows: "Whose is this?"—this is *ka-keśaḥ* (whose hair); [here the suffix *ṇya* is added to *ka* in the sense of "belonging to"]; by what? By which head? Together with what? With which entity? Having come together and joined with it, and having obtained and attained proximity and presence in all activities—if, however, at the time of eating, he is seen only at the time of eating, then he is discarded and rejected. This answer is as follows: "Whose is this?"—this is *ka-keśaḥ* (whose hair); [here the suffix *ṇya* is added to *ka* in the sense of "belonging to"]; by what? By which head? Together with what? With which entity? Having come together and joined with it, and having obtained and attained proximity and presence in all activities—if, however, at the time of eating, he is seen only at the time of eating, then he is discarded and rejected. This answer is as follows: "Whose is this?"—this is *ka-keśaḥ* (whose hair); [here the suffix *ṇya* is added to *ka* in the sense of "belonging to"]; by what? By which head? Together with what? With which entity? Having come together and joined with it, and having obtained and attained proximity and presence in all activities—if, however, at the time of eating, he is seen only at the time of eating, then he is discarded and rejected. This answer is as follows: "Whose is this?"—this is *ka-keśaḥ* (whose hair); [here the suffix *ṇya* is added to *ka* in the sense of "belonging to"]; by what? By which head? Together with what? With which entity? Having come together and joined with it, and having obtained and attained proximity and presence in all activities—if, however, at the time of eating, he is seen only at the time of eating, then he is discarded and rejected. This answer is as follows: "Whose is this?"—this is *ka-keśaḥ* (whose hair); [here the suffix *ṇya* is added to *ka* in the sense of "belonging to"]; by what? By which head? Together with what? With which entity? Having come together and joined with it, and having obtained and attained proximity and presence in all activities—if, however, at the time of eating, he is seen only at the time of eating, then he is discarded and rejected. This answer is as follows: "Whose is this?"—this is *ka-keśaḥ* (whose hair); [here the suffix *ṇya* is added to *ka* in the sense of "belonging to"]; by what? By which head? Together with what? With which entity? Having come together and joined with it, and having obtained and attained proximity and presence in all activities—if, however, at the time of eating, he is seen only at the time of eating, then he is discarded and rejected. This answer is as follows: "Whose is this?"—this is *ka-keśaḥ* (whose hair); [here the suffix *ṇya* is added to *ka* in the sense of "belonging to"]; by what? By which head? Together with what? With which entity? Having come together and joined with it, and having obtained and attained proximity and presence in all activities—if, however, at the time of eating, he is seen only at the time of eating, then he is discarded and rejected. This answer is as follows: "Whose is this

Having thus gathered for all the ritual duties, he was seen only at the time of the meal and then cast out; here, both the support and the supported—the head and the hair—are concealed, and thus it is "concealed by both" (*ubhayacchannā*). || 122 ||

He shows [the army] to be mixed (*saṅkīrṇā*) by saying "together with" (*sahayā*). "Together with horses" (*sahayā*), "with elephants" (*sagajā*), "with elephants" (*sahastikā*), and "with warriors" (*sabhaṭā*), meaning existing together with warriors who are combatants; this refers to the enemy's host, the opposing army. If it has not been conquered—that is, if it has not been defeated—then for us, this son is "without measure" (*amātrika*). "Measure" (*mātra*) means one's own interest; one who knows that is a "measurer" (*mātrika*), one who understands self-interest. One who is not like that is "without measure" (*amātrika*), meaning one who is averse to considering his own interest. Or, *mātrā*...

*Dravya* means wealth; that is to say, an object (*viṣaya*). (Regarding the word *mātra*: it is used in the sense of limitation, for its own sake, or totality; *mātrā* is used in the sense of a measure, a portion, a syllable-part, a substance, a small amount, or an ear-ornament.)

According to Hemacandra’s lexicon (*kāle vṛtte ca*), one who deserves that [measure] is *mātrika*; one who is not so is *amātrika*, meaning one who is ignorant of the limits of wealth, or rather, devoid of knowledge regarding the objects of the senses. Therefore, even if one knows the *akṣara*—that is, even if one knows Brahman—one may still be a fool (*mūḍha*) or a simpleton (*mūrkha*). The natural sense of this is that, due to the absence of knowledge of one's own true interest or the absence of discernment regarding worldly objects, even a knower of Brahman is to be counted as nothing more than a fool.

The hidden meaning is as follows: this army (*senā*) is accompanied by the letters *ha*, *ya*, *ga*, *ja*, *bha*, and *ṭa*. It is "with the Lord" (*ina-sahitā*), where "Lord" (*ina*) means the presiding authority, that is to say, Brahmā, the creator of the syllables (as it is said: "The syllables were created by the Creator and placed upon leaves in the past"). Thus, the meaning is the alphabet together with its presiding deity. The sense is: what kind of alphabet is it, or what deity presides over them? It is "not conquered" (*na jitā*).

If it has not been practiced—that is, if it is not known—then he is "amātrika. *Mātrā* refers to the duration of time required for the pronunciation of vowels and other phonemes; one who knows that is *mātrika*. One who is not *mātrika* is *amātrika*, meaning devoid of knowledge of the phonemes. Therefore, even one who is an *akṣarajña*—one who knows the Veda as an imperishable text (*akṣara*) and has thus mastered it—is called "deluded" (*mūḍha*), meaning foolish. Alternatively, if [the letters] have not been mastered—that is, have not been learned to write—then he is *amātrika*; *mātrā* here refers to a constituent part of a syllable (*akṣarāvayava*), and he does not know that.

"Amātrika" means one who lacks knowledge of such things as which syllable is suitable for writing in what kind of form; although he knows the syllables and the letters, he is indeed a fool—this is the meaning of the term "saṅkīrṇa" (mixed/confused). || 123 ||

Regarding the phrase "here he effects a mixture": "that" refers to the aforementioned riddle called *saṅkīrṇā* (the mixed). Here, because words such as *haya* and others—which are *nāmāntarita* (hidden by another name)—are conceived to have multiple meanings, it is endowed with the characteristics of the *nāmāntarita* riddle; likewise, because the word *senā* (army), which is associated with the well-known meaning of a military force, deceives through the conception of another meaning, it is associated with the form of the *vañcitā* (deceptive) riddle. Thus, it is "endowed with the characteristics" (*rūpayoginī*) of both, meaning that these two are combined here.

(Therefore, it should be understood that there is a mixture of riddles (*prahelikā*) in the verse cited above. In this very same manner, the "method of commingling"—the way in which other riddles as well are mutually mixed—should be inferred, meaning it must be understood by oneself. || 124 ||

Having thus defined the qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras), which are the attributes that produce the beauty of poetry, [the author] now enumerates ten principal defects (doṣas)—fearing excessive bulk in the treatise—among the many defects that constitute attributes to be rejected in poetry, beginning with "apārtham" (meaningless).

"Meaningless" (apārtha) is that which is devoid of sense; "pointless" (nirarthaka) is that which is useless; "contradictory in meaning" (vyartha) is that which has an opposing sense; "redundant" (ekārtha) is that which has no distinct meaning; "doubtful" (sasaṃśaya) is that which is ambiguous; "disordered" (apakrama) is that which lacks proper sequence; "deficient in words" (śabdahīna) is that which must be supplied by means of inference and so forth; "fallen in cadence" (yatibhraṣṭa) is that which lacks the proper pause; "of broken meter" (bhinnavṛtta) is that which has an uneven meter; "with faulty euphonic combination" (visandhika) is that where the *saṃdhi* has not been applied; and "contrary to place and so forth" (deśādivirodhi). The word "iti" marks the end of the sentence; the meaning is that a sentence of such a nature is defective. These—beginning with meaninglessness—are exactly ten defects.

The meaning is that those factors which detract from poetry must be avoided—rejected—in poetic works by the wise, that is, by the learned; for, by being contrary to verbal comprehension, they manifest the ignorance of the author. And it has been said: "But a word misused proclaims the very stupidity of the speaker. By the use of the particle *eva* (only), there is an exclusion of qualities such as *śrutikaṭu* (harshness to the ear) which produce a slight distaste; the essential point is that because these do not oppose the comprehension of the syntactical connection (*anvaya-bodha*), they do not indicate that the work is absolutely unfit to be discarded.

In this regard, the following should be noted: although it would have been more appropriate to state the specific varieties immediately after stating the general definition, since the qualities (guṇas) enhance the body of poetry, they were presented along with their definitions and examples so that they might be understood; and since defects (doṣas) are the opposite of those [qualities], they were shown by the very force of that context, even without being explicitly stated, once the general definition was understood. Thus, the specific varieties were demonstrated without first showing the general definition.

And thus it has been stated by Vāmana as well: "Defects consist in the reversal of the qualities," and "The comprehension [of the meaning] arises from the sense. To the question, "For what purpose are they elaborated separately? he says: "The elaboration is for the sake of clarity. By this, the definition is established: in poetry, since the qualities possess the nature of being desirable, those factors which cause the obstruction of the intended comprehension therein are defects.

This has been stated in the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*: "There are sixteen defects of words, sentences, and sentence-meanings which must be abandoned in poetry by the best of poets; those very ones we shall first explain. Alternatively, the definition is understood through the etymological derivation itself: a *doṣa* (defect) is that by which poetry (*kāvyam*) becomes corrupted (*duṣyati*) or rendered disfigured (*vikṛtam*). The author of the *Prakāśa* also provided the definition: "A defect is the impairment of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthahatiḥ*)," thereby indicating that it is a derivative noun formed with the suffix *ghañ*.

Consequently, a defect (*doṣa*) is that which causes a diminution (*apakarṣa*) in poetry; and this state of being to be abandoned is its state of being diminished. Since such diminution can occur in words, meanings, sentences, sentence-meanings, and even in the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*), aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and so forth, it is impossible to describe it exhaustively due to its manifold variety; therefore, only ten [types] are shown here. || 125 ||

Is it not the case that the restriction "only ten" is inappropriate, since even *pratijñāhāni* (abandonment of the proposition) and other such points are declared to be defects because they prevent the comprehension of the intended meaning? And it has been stated by the venerable Gautama: "When one admits a property of the counter-example, there is abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) in the example. For this very reason, the status of *pratijñāhāni* and others as points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) was stated in the sūtra beginning with "Abandonment of the proposition, shifting the proposition, contradiction of the proposition," and so forth.

And as it was stated by King Bhoja: "As long as I live, my father is a silent celibate; my mother is barren; and my grandfather is sonless. However, Bhāmaha and others do not accept this as a defect, for they say: "That which is devoid of a proposition, a reason, and an example is considered faulty. To dispel this doubt, he states his own view beginning with the word "proposition."

The proposition (*pratijñā*) is the statement of what is to be proven; the reason (*hetu*) is the means of proving what is to be proven; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the presentation of a well-known illustration. Their loss, contradiction, or absence constitutes a fault (*doṣa*) that establishes the worthlessness of a poem. When there is doubt as to whether [a certain feature] is a fault or not, this deliberation (*vicāra*) concerning that question is the determination (*niścaya*), meaning the ascertainment of one side. It is generally harsh because it belongs to the science of logic (*nyāya-śāstra*); "harsh" may also mean "unpleasant. Therefore, by that deliberation, which has been thoroughly grasped (*ālīḍhena*).

"By that which has been tasted"—meaning, by that which has been known—what is the fruit? The meaning is that there is no fruit whatsoever. (For indeed, the recognition of defects by readers occurs spontaneously, as they are qualities of poetry that produce a sense of distaste; and it is not appropriate to increase the bulk of a book for that purpose. Only a few poetic defects, which must be absolutely avoided, are shown here; however, because of the abandonment of the initial promise [to treat all defects], these are not absolutely avoidable, and even those not explicitly promised [to be treated]..."

It is observed that [the absence of these] has been described by poets as a matter of contextual connection (*prasaṅgasaṅgatyā*). Furthermore, the absence of a logical reason (*hetu*) does not bring about extreme distaste when the probandum (*sādhya*) is already well-known; and since the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is merely a specific form of poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*), its absence does not cause absolute distaste in poetry, because the status of being poetry is accepted by everyone even for those works devoid of ornaments. Therefore, the author of the *Nyāyasūtra-vṛtti* also stated: "There is no harm even if the example is occasional (*sāmayika*) and not universal.
Consequently, it should be understood that the very cause of defectiveness (*dūṣakatāvīja*) consists in producing a diminution of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). || 127 ||

Identifying the various types of defects in sequence, he first defines *apārtha* (meaninglessness), stating "of the aggregate" (*samudāyasya*). The meaning of an aggregate—whether it be an aggregate of words constituting a sentence or an aggregate of sentences constituting a major discourse—is that which is to be communicated as having attained unity through verbal cognition. A sentence that is devoid of such a meaning is considered, or rather stated to be, *apārtha*, meaning it is possessed of the defect named *apārtha*. This occurs due to the absence of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and proximity (*āsatti*) among the meanings of the words or the meanings of the constituent parts of the sentence.

The conclusion is that a sentence whose verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is sublated is "meaningless" (*apārthaka*). This applies elsewhere—that is, to the speech of those who are insane, those seized by madness, those intoxicated and thus mentally deranged by drinking liquor, as well as to children and infants; however, in the case of the speech of the insane and so forth, there is no fault, because their words lack meaningfulness and the like. || 128 ||

He demonstrates the lack of purpose [of the comparison] with the words "the ocean. The ocean is drunk by the gods (*devaiḥ*), meaning the deities or the clouds (wherein the reading "so 'yam" for "devaiḥ" is also observed). I, however, am afflicted by old age, overcome by senility; these clouds (*jīmūtāḥ*) are thundering; and Airāvaṇa, the elephant named Airāvata, is the beloved of Indra.

In this case, because there is no mutual expectancy (*parasparākāṅkṣā*) among the four sentences, they lack the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgitva*); consequently, there is no unity of sentence (*ekavākyatā*), and thus the collective meaning does not exist. As it has been said: "The unity of sentences, which have already completed the comprehension of their own respective meanings, arises again through their combination by virtue of the requirement of principal and subordinate. Therefore, this is indeed a defect pertaining to the meaning of the sentences themselves.

The same has been stated in the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa* as follows: "The defects arising from the meaning of a sentence have been mentioned; I shall now state their definitions. That speech which is devoid of the collective sense of its parts is known as 'meaningless' (*apārtha*). An example of another [type] is as follows: "An old bull, standing at the door with his woolen sandals on, sings auspicious songs. His Brahmin wife, desiring a son, asks: 'O King, what is the price of garlic in Rumā? This should be understood as "meaninglessness" (*apārthatva*) pertaining to multiple sentences.

Thus, even that which has many components is seen [to be a non-word], as for example in *vaḍhiddhaṭhṭhaḍananā siñcati* and so forth; it should be understood that due to the absence of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) and other factors, such expressions lack a collective meaning. || 129 ||

"This" refers to the aforementioned expression of those with unbalanced minds, such as the insane and so forth—namely, the statement "the ocean is being drunk," and so on—which is "unblamed," meaning it is accepted as being non-defective; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "Elsewhere," meaning other than among those with unbalanced minds and so forth—that is, excluding the insane and others—who indeed would employ such [an expression]? The meaning is that no poet at all would employ it.

This was also stated by Bhoja in the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa*: "Now, the non-defectiveness regarding defects of sentence-meaning is being described. That which is devoid of collective meaning is declared to be 'meaningless' (*apārtha*). This is considered faulty except in the speech of those who are intoxicated, insane, or children. For example: 'Where is the deed of the moon-marked one [the moon], and where is she [the beloved] seen even in a dream? Oh, her face is lovely even in anger; alas, it has been heard for the sake of pacifying my faults!'"

"What will those sinless ones of perfected intellect say? Alas, she is but one, yet so unlike [any other]! O mind, attain composure; for who indeed is the fortunate youth that shall drink from her lower lip? (1.30). It should be noted that although this verse is "meaningless" (*apārtha*) due to its lack of a coherent collective sense, it possesses the quality of being the speech of a madman.

He defines the "meaningless" (vyartha) as follows: "In a single sentence. That is, in a single sentence, or in a composition consisting of a great sentence, that which—due to its contradictory meaning, that is, its inverted sense—is "mutually sublated by what precedes and follows," meaning it is inconsistent between the preceding and following parts, i.e., the initial and final sections; such a sentence is "meaningless," being possessed of the defect named "meaninglessness," and is thus enumerated and counted among the defects.

The definition of *vyarthatva* (pointlessness) is the communication of something as being useless due to the lack of coherence between what precedes and what follows because their meanings are mutually contradictory. Bhojarāja, however, states that the word *vi-* in the term *vyartha* signifies "gone away" (*vigata*), based on the etymology: "that whose purpose (*artha*) or utility has departed is *vyartha*. As it is said: "They call that *vyartha* which has its meaning already understood (*gatārtha*), and that which is devoid of purpose (*niṣprayojana*). An example is as follows: "Then the two tigers among the Raghus went to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga..."

"He offered his own body as an oblation; behold Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa! Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, a contradiction in meaning (*arthavirodha*) is perceived through subsequent reflection after the verbal cognition has occurred, whereas in the case of the meaningless (*apārtha*), there is no verbal cognition at all due to the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors; this is the distinction between the two. Here, the wise should discern that the defects described by others—such as *viruddhamatikāritva* (causing a contradictory understanding), *prakāśitaviruddhatva* (manifesting a contradiction), *amataparārthatva* (having a purpose other than what was intended), and *paripanthirasāṅgatva* (obstructing the aesthetic flavor)—are appropriately subsumed within these two categories.

He shows its futility by saying, "Abandon it. Destroy—that is, annihilate—the entire, complete army of enemies; conquer this earth, the sustainer of the universe. For you, who are compassionate toward all beings and full of mercy for all creatures, there is not even a single hater or enemy; such is the sense.

(Here, the total slaughter of enemies by one who is devoid of even the slightest malice, and the conquest of the earth by one who is compassionate toward all beings, are perceived as contradictory upon reflection; consequently, because the meanings of the subsequent sentences contradict those of the preceding ones, they convey a sense of pointlessness—this is the fault of "pointlessness" [vyarthatā]. | 132 |

He states that sometimes even futility possesses a quality, saying "there is": for one who is "possessed by affliction" (*sābhiṣaṅgasya*), meaning overwhelmed by calamities such as separation (according to Amara: "affliction" [*abhiṣaṅga*] refers to a curse or defeat), there exists—meaning there occurs—a certain indescribable state of mind incapable of deliberating upon the desirable, the undesirable, the auspicious, and so forth; in which state, even though speech (*bhāratī*) may have a contradictory meaning, or even be inconsistent, or even futile due to its contradictory meaning, it may become "acceptable," meaning it is honored.
(By the word "desired," it is indicated that its status as a quality arises due to the influence of its particular state. | 133 |

He demonstrates her quality [of being a virtuous woman] with the words "parā" and so forth. How could a longing for another's wife—an attachment toward the wives of others—be appropriate for me, a noble and virtuous man? When shall I drink from her lower lip—the lip of that other woman, meaning one belonging to another—which is trembling due to the agitation caused by shame and fear? (In this passage, there is a contradiction because the first half-verse expresses a state of tranquility, whereas the second half-verse expresses a desire for another's wife; thus, the sentence of the second half-verse is indeed purposeless.)

And that [quality] is consistent as a merit because it overcomes the separation of the speaker. Thus, an example of the word *vi-* having the sense of "gone away" (*vigata*) is as follows: "In whose heart, throat, mouth, and ears does your fame—not the luster of sandalwood, pearl necklaces, camphor, and ivory leaf-ornaments—reside?"

Here too, although the remaining words of comparison are redundant once whiteness is perceived through a single simile, they possess the status of a subordinate element (*guṇatva*) because the presence of fame in the heart and other locations—like sandalwood paste—is perceived through its being remembered, sung, praised, and heard. However, the moderns (*navya*) accept the status of a subordinate element when contradictory elements are stated as being sublated; as it has been said: "The statement of a contradictory element, such as a transitory emotion (*sañcāribhāva*), by way of being sublated, is a subordinate element. Thus, it should be understood that the transformation of a defect into a subordinate element is universally agreed upon. (134)

In order to establish that [the fault] has a single meaning, he says: "without distinction" (*aviśeṣeṇa*). If what was previously stated—that is, what was mentioned before—whether in terms of meaning or in terms of words (meaning: both the meaning and the word), [the word "previously stated" is neuter because it refers to a general concept; "in terms of meaning" and "in terms of words" should be understood as nominative singular forms], if it is stated again—that is, once more—without distinction, that is, without difference, it is considered to have a single meaning, being possessed of the fault known as *ekārtha*.

And thus, this fault resides both in the meaning and in the word that conveys a single meaning; accordingly, it should be understood that there is either the redundancy of the meaning or the redundancy of the synonymous word. By this, the inclusion under the designation "single-meaning" of both the fault of meaning called *punarukta* and the fault of word called *kathitapada*, as stated by others, is accomplished.

Regarding the phrase *śabdataḥ*, the word *śabda* refers here to a word that conveys that [same] meaning; thus, the intention is indicated that repetition of words with different meanings is not a fault, as it does not produce such a sense of distaste. For example, in the verse beginning "The gods (*surāḥ*) by Brahmins, the veins (*sirāḥ*) by the lowly," there is no fault because the meanings are different—namely, *surāḥ* meaning "gods" and *surāḥ* meaning "liquors. The word *yathā* is used for the purpose of providing an illustration. || 135 ||

He shows that they have a single purpose with the word "utkā" (longing). Of that young woman, those clouds—possessing a luster like the hair of a lamb (*elaka*), characterized by thundering, accompanied by lightning, and exceedingly deep (meaning intense)—make the longing girl, distressed by separation, *unmanas* (distraught), because of their nature as excitants; this is the sense.

(Here, the words *utkeman*, *śabda*, *ambhodhara*, *astaḍitvantaḥ*, and *stanitnavaḥ*—though distinct in their own forms—are redundant in meaning because they convey a single sense through a single expressive capacity. Thus, this fault is observed whenever a previously stated meaning is perceived again by any means whatsoever; as shown by Viśvanātha: "One should not perform an action impulsively, for lack of discrimination is the seat of supreme calamities; indeed, riches, longing for excellence, seek out of their own accord the man who acts with deliberation.")

"In this case, since the meaning of the second quarter [of the verse] is identical to that of the second half-verse, there is tautology. Thus, by the phrase "either verbally or semantically," the author of the *Prakāśa* has shown an example of verbal repetition (*kathitapadatā*), as follows: "O fair-faced one! Tell me, whose royal consecration as the crown prince of the sport of Love does this clearly manifest: the palm of her hand resting upon her cheek, her playful sleep enacted, and the throbbing of her eyelids closed in the act of pressing against her temple?"

In these two instances, since the meaning of "sportive manifestation" (*vilāsa-rūpa*) is expressed by the single word *līlā* alone, there is no factor to distinguish between them; thus, the word *līlā* has a single meaning. Regarding the twofold division of "single meaning" (*ekārtha*) stated according to the distinction between word and meaning, this is the intended sense: although the "single meaning" mentioned in the section on defects of sentence-meaning is in fact a defect of sentence-meaning, the postulation of a twofold division based on its residing in either the word or the meaning is entirely irrelevant. And that distinction [applies] where the meaning is conveyed by another synonymous word.

Tautology (*ponaruktya*) is of two kinds: that which pertains to the meaning (*arthagata*), and that which pertains to the word (*śabdagata*). The latter should be understood as occurring where there is a repetition of the same word with the same meaning even when there is no intended emphasis (*tātparya*). However, the moderns (*navya*) state that these two have distinct designations: *kathitapadatva* for that which pertains to the word, and *punaruktatva* for that which pertains to the meaning. (136)

He states an exception to this rule: "compassion" (*anukampā*). If there is an excess of compassion and so forth—an excess of [qualities] such as compassion—the word "of the subject at hand" (*prakṛtasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder. (By the word "and so forth," the inclusion of enjoined restatement and the like is intended; as stated by the author of the *Darpaṇa* under the heading "Qualities": "A word already mentioned may be repeated when it serves as a restatement of what has been enjoined, or in cases of dejection, wonder, anger, dejection, *lāṭānuprāsa*, compassion, and conciliation.")

In the case of *arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya* (where the expressed meaning is transferred to another), when joy (*harṣa*) is not maintained [by the mere statement], if it is intended—that is, desired—to be spoken, then even a tautology (*punarukta*) is not a fault; on the contrary, this very repetition is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), because it bestows beauty upon the poetry—this is the sense. And thus, in the speech of a speaker whose mind is captivated by rasa, a single meaning does not constitute a defect. As it is said in the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa*: "If that which was previously stated is repeated again without distinction..."

That [omission] does not constitute a fault for those whose minds are captivated by the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) which has that single purpose as its object. An example is as follows: "O Creator, why have you resolved to make this world worthless, to rob the three worlds of their jewel, to leave the world without light, to leave kinsmen with death as their only refuge, to render Cupid devoid of pride, to make the creation of human eyes fruitless, and to turn the entire universe into a dilapidated wilderness?"

In this context, although the statements "saṃsāra is essence-less," "the three worlds have their jewels stolen," "the world is devoid of light," and "the universe is a withered forest" do not express specific particulars, they possess the status of a poetic excellence (*guṇa*) because they are uttered by the speaker who is impelled by the aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*). Likewise, it should be understood that even in the speech of the insane and others, repetition is indeed an excellence. || 137 ||

He cites an example regarding non-trembling (*anikampā*): "She is slain. That woman of noble gait, that most excellent lady, is slain by the unseasonable enemy—that is, by the causeless foe, Kāma, the god of love. She, whose every limb is beautiful, is slain; she, who speaks with sweet and charming words, is slain. (In this instance, although the verb "is slain" (*hanyate*) is repeated again and again, it does not constitute a fault because it produces a sense of aesthetic variety by manifesting the pitiable nature of the heroine under discussion.
Other examples of this should likewise be sought elsewhere. || 138 ||

He defines *sasaṃśaya* (the doubtful) as being for the sake of a definitive conclusion (*nirṇayārtham*). That is to say, if words employed—that is, arranged—for the sake of a definitive conclusion, meaning for the purpose of determining one or the other course of action regarding engagement or withdrawal for the listener, should produce or give rise to doubt—a cognition consisting of two conflicting objects—then that very fault is called *sasaṃśaya*; the meaning is that it is tainted by the defect known as doubt. Thus it is traditionally recorded. (Bhoja, however, states the definition: "The doubtful is that which has a dubious meaning.")

And although this definition is concise, it means that a sentence employed for the purpose of determining either engagement or withdrawal regarding what is to be understood must not have a doubtful meaning—that is, it must not produce doubt; for it will be stated by the author himself that if a doubtful sentence is employed for the sake of doubt itself, then this [doubt] constitutes a merit [of the statement]. (139)

He illustrates *saṃśaya* (doubt) with the verse beginning "manoratha": "O you whose eyes are restless with passion for the sight of your beloved of the heart!"—that is, O you whose eyes (*īkṣaṇe*) are tremulous (*lolā*) with that passion (*rasa*) or attachment (*anurāga*) for the sight (*āloka*) of the beloved of your desires (*manorathapriya*). O friend, whose eyes are thus occupied in looking at a paramour! This mother of yours—the word "of yours" being understood—is far away (*ārādvṛtti*), meaning she is situated at a distance; therefore, [this is] such [a situation] suitable for a passionate woman like you.

The meaning is: she is not able to observe the *vyavahāra* (conduct) because she is obstructed; therefore, look without hesitation. Alternatively, *ārādvṛttiḥ* means "dwelling nearby"; thus, the sense is that she is not capable of—that is, not patient with—witnessing such conduct of yours, which is unbecoming of a woman of noble family and constitutes a breach of character. Therefore, the implication is: do not let your eyes wander. (Amara states: "The word *ārāt* is used for both 'far' and 'near'.")

In this context, for the sake of determining what ought to be done by her friend, the heroine’s state of indecision regarding either proceeding or desisting is expressed through a sentence employing the word *ārāt* (near/far), which signifies both proximity and distance. This is because there is no certainty as to whether she will proceed or desist: on one hand, thinking "my mother is far away; therefore, she will not be able to see such an act of mine, so I shall proceed without hesitation," and on the other, thinking "my mother is nearby; therefore, she will not be able to see such a censurable act, so I shall desist from it. Thus, due to the absence of a definitive conclusion between these two courses of action, the figure is *ullekha*.

The defect of doubt (*saṃśaya-doṣa*) consists in the resulting uncertainty. Because this is caused by the employment of words with dual meanings, it is a verbal defect (*śabda-gata*). However, this defect can also pertain to the meaning (*artha-gata*); that is recognized after the comprehension of the meaning through the failure to ascertain the intention of the speaker and so forth. An example is as follows: "Setting aside envy and reflecting upon what ought to be done, may the noble ones state with courtesy: Are the hips of the mountains to be resorted to, or rather those of playful women smiling with passion? In this case, the ambiguity arises from the word *nitamba*, which denotes both "hip" and "slopes. Thus, the defect is verbal because it is rooted in the use of a polysemous term. However, once the sentence meaning is understood, the specific intention remains uncertain, and thus the defect is also considered to pertain to the meaning. It is to be known through the lack of certainty regarding the speaker's intent.

In this case, because there is an absence of any [definitive] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, and because there is no certainty as to whether the speaker is primarily characterized by tranquility (*śama*) or primarily by erotic passion (*śṛṅgāra*), there is doubt. (This is the speech of a female friend addressed to a heroine who is looking longingly at her lover and is terrified by the fear that her mother might discover her conduct. || 140 ||

He states that this [ambiguity] is sometimes a merit, saying "of such a kind. Or rather, although such a sentence is characterized by doubt, if it is employed—that is, used—in order to produce doubt, for the purpose of conveying doubt, then that very doubt would be a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*). In such a case, there is no fault; thus, where doubt itself is intended to be expressed, it is indeed a merit, whereas where it is not intended, it is a fault—this is the sense.
That is its illustration; the word "yathā" (as for example) is for the purpose of indicating what is to be stated hereafter. (In the phrase "vā tu," the reading "jātu" is observed. || 141 ||

"I see her"—meaning one who is blameless and beautiful in every limb; "her," meaning your beloved; "overcome by the affliction born of Anaṅga"—meaning by the disease caused by Kāma, that is, by the torment of love; "therefore, as if already seized by cruel and merciless Time"—meaning by Death, as if already swallowed; "I see. "By your hope"—by your expectation—what [is there] for us? What is the fruit? Not finding you, she is now dying from the torment of love; therefore, for you...

The meaning is that there is no purpose in hope. Alternatively, "not overcome by the affliction born of the bodiless one" (*anaṅgajātaṅkalāṅghitā*) means not overcome by the physical pain arising from the god of love; her, who is being scorched (*grāstām*)—that is, beheld—by the harsh (*kaṭhore*), intense heat of the summer season, what is the use of our hope for you? She has no physical ailment whatsoever; rather, she is utterly tormented by the heat generated by the summer season, her sleep having been stolen away by anxieties and the like caused by not attaining you. This is the meaning of what was stated previously.

Thus, the doubt as to whether the subject matter to be established by this verse is for the sake of another [the hero] is indeed unintended by the messenger; for this is a statement made by the messenger to the hero who has gone abroad. (142)

And here he establishes its status as a *guṇa* (poetic excellence), [saying] "kāmārteti. In order to agitate the young man and make him eager to go to the heroine's presence, the female messenger (*dūtī*), by means of playful artifice (*narmaṇā bhaṅgyā*), speaks words of the aforementioned nature—words that are "uncertain" (*aniścayakaram*), meaning crowded with doubt, such as "is she afflicted by love (*kāmārtā*) or tormented by heat (*gharmataptā*), or perhaps afflicted by the summer heat (*grīṣmārtā*)? Having reflected that the young man, being unable to determine whether she is "afflicted by love or tormented by the summer heat," will become agitated and go to her side, the messenger speaks in such a manner.
The sense is that he spoke words full of ambiguity; this constitutes its quality. || 143 ||

He defines *apakrama* (disorder of sequence): "In accordance with the *uddeśa*. This means that if the *uddeśa*—the initial presentation—is not made in accordance with the *arthas*, which are the subjects to be discussed, being "in accordance" (*anuguṇa*) meaning suitable or fit for the sequence (*anvaya*), and if the subsequent presentation (*upanyāsa*) is not arranged according to that order, then the wise declare that to be the fault named *apakrama*, so called because of the transgression of sequence.

They say: (And thus, the meaning is that for things related as cause and effect, presentation in their proper sequence is indeed a merit, whereas violating it is a fault. Furthermore, this fault is included among the faults of word and meaning known by others as *akrama* (lack of order) and *duṣkrama* (bad order); however, those two are not absolutely avoidable. As Viśvanātha has said: "Both have now fallen into a state of pitiable wretchedness through their prayer for union with the wielder of the Pināka bow..."

"She is a digit of the moon, full of splendor; you are the moon, the joy to the eyes of this world. Here, the particle *ca* ("and") would have been more appropriate immediately after "you" (*tvam*). Likewise: "O King, give me a horse, or an elephant languid with rut. Here, it is more fitting to request the elephant first.

In such cases as these, although the sequence is violated by placing the *ca*, which ought to be used immediately after the sentence being referred to by "both" (*dvayam*), it does not incur a major fault, because the syntactic connection remains unimpaired through the conjunction of even a remote element.

In cases such as "dehi me" (give to me), it is appropriate for the primary object to be requested first; the sequence is that if the giver is unable to grant that, one should request something less than that. Here, however, because that sequence is transgressed, there is a violation of the proper order (*apakramatva*). Nevertheless, since the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) remains unimpeded, it is not absolutely avoidable. One should understand that in both instances, the syntactic connection is not absolutely avoidable because there is no obstruction to its connection. However, the distinction is that here, because the rule that sequential words must connect only with sequential words has been violated, it acts as an obstruction to the comprehension of the sentence meaning, and thus it is absolutely avoidable. || 144 ||

He shows the departure [of the world] by the word "sthitau" (in the maintenance). The maintenance of the worlds is their protection; creation is *nirmāṇa*, and dissolution is *saṃhāra* or destruction. These are the causes or reasons for these [three], meaning they are the agents. These aforementioned ones—Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā—who have arisen from Nārāyaṇa and the lotus-born [Brahmā], may they protect you, that is, may they guard you.

(Here, when the sequence of the previously mentioned [topics]—maintenance, creation, and dissolution—is to be established in their proper order, it would have been appropriate to say "Nārāyaṇa, Ambhojayoni, and Śambhu"; however, since the opposite was stated, this constitutes a lack of sequential order because it obstructs the verbal comprehension. || 145 ||

He states that this [violation of sequence] is not a fault in certain cases in the verse beginning with "yatna" (effort). "Sambandhasya" means of the connection (*anvaya*); "vijñānam" means specifically the comprehension; that which has such [comprehension] as its cause—such an effort, meaning the exertion for the sake of understanding a specific connection even by transgressing the [expected] order, is what is meant. Even if such an effort is made by the poet (the word "by the poet" being the ellipsis), then the wise (*sūrayaḥ*), the learned ones, do not at all say that the violation of sequence is a defect (*dūṣaṇa*) or a source of blemish (*doṣāvaha*). || 146 ||

He illustrates that departing [from home] is not a fault with the words "abandonment of kin" (*bandhityāga*). Abandonment of kin means forsaking one's own people; abandonment of the body means the absence of the physical form; abandonment of place means residing in a foreign land. Among these three objects, the first and last—namely, the abandonment of kin and the abandonment of place—are characterized by long-lasting afflictions (*kleśa*). However, the middle one, the abandonment of the body, is like a momentary fever, meaning it causes distress for only a brief instant. Thus, the abandonment of the body is better and more excellent, and not so the abandonment of kin.

The sense is: "or abandoning the country. (In this context, among the items mentioned in sequence—such as abandoning kinsmen and so forth—the term *bandhutyāga* (abandoning kinsmen), which is included by the word *ādi* ("and so forth"), is the correlate [of the preceding phrase]. Since it is impossible for the other mentioned item, *tanutyāga* (abandoning the body), to be the correlate, one must bypass that and take the final member of the series, *deśatyāga* (abandoning the country), as the correlate. Thus, although there is a transgression of the sequence, it is entirely appropriate because it serves as the cause for understanding the connection; it is not a fault. On the contrary, since the speaker intends *deśatyāga* to be more significant than *tanutyāga*, and indeed more significant than both *tanutyāga* and *bandhutyāga*, it should be understood as a merit rather than a defect. || 147 ||

He defines "devoid of words" (*śabdahīna*) as follows: "unobservable" (*anālakṣyā*), meaning invisible, that is to say, unknowable; the sense is that such [a thing] is not established by scripture (*aśāstrīyatvāt*). "Of the observable" (*lakṣyasya*) means of another example belonging to the same class; likewise, "of the definition" (*lakṣaṇasya*) means of the instruction, that is to say, of the restrictive rule consisting of the *sūtras*, lexicons, lists of roots (*dhātupāṭha*), and so forth. "The path" (*paddhatiḥ*) means the rule; thus, the meaning is "one for whom there is no reckoned instruction" (*agaṇitānuśāsana*). Likewise, "of the unrefined" (*aśiṣṭānām*) means of the ignorant; "desired" (*iṣṭaḥ*) means manifested through a lack of understanding.

The term *śabdahīna* (deficient in words) refers to the employment of words—whether in the singular, dual, or plural—which, because they denote an action through a *kṛt* suffix, are technically termed "employed words" (*prayujyamāna-pada*). It is "deficient in words" (*śabdena hīnam*) in the sense of being deficient according to the grammatical treatise of instruction; that is to say, it possesses the defect known by that name. The essential conclusion is this: the employment of such words for which there is no other similar example—due to their not being used by the wise and the absence of a rule prescribing their formation—and the employment of words not used by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), constitute the defect called *śabdahīna*.

(Therefore, the definition is as follows: a word for which there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) and no other usage among its own class, even if such a rule exists, or a word not employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) in its respective gender and so forth or in its respective meaning, is called the defect known as *śabdahīna*). Furthermore, he states that even if it contradicts the grammatical rules, it is not a defect when used by the learned, saying "by the learned" (*śiṣṭa*).

"But that which is favored by the learned"—that is, which is accepted and employed as being correct by many virtuous people—is not faulty; it does not constitute a defect. Since words are eternal (*nitya*), the instruction provided by Pāṇini and others was made solely for the purpose of their etymological analysis. Thus, when the learned speak, even in the absence of the formal rules (*sūtra*), the fault lies with those who provide the instruction [if they were to find a flaw], and not with the word itself; this is the intended meaning.

Goyīcandra also stated: "The division of stems and suffixes is postulated by the grammatical treatise for the sake of understanding eternal words. By this, it is demonstrated that the authority of the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*) pertains only to words already in use by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Consequently, even in the absence of a specific grammatical rule, the usage of a word employed by many does not fall within the scope of this fault; likewise, even when a rule exists, if such a word-usage has not been practiced by anyone, its employment is indeed a fault—this is how it should be understood.

Regarding the use of words that contradict the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*), others have stated that such usage is incorrect (*asādhutva*); thus Vāmana says: "That which contradicts the traditional rules of grammar (*śabdasmṛti*) is incorrect. It should be understood that by this [definition], the faults of being unidiomatic (*aprayukta*) and lacking expressive power (*asamartha*), as mentioned by others, are also subsumed; this is the general direction. 148.

He provides an example of a sentence lacking a verb (*śabdahīna*): "avate iti. O Great King! Your arm—your own limb—is an ocean; [the earth] whose girdle is the ocean, meaning the earth together with the sea (as Medinī states: "The word *śakkarī* refers to a specific meter, as well as a river and a girdle"), you protect—that is, you rule—this earth. Because there is no desire to know (*ajijñāsā*), meaning due to the absence of doubt, there is no further inquiry here; this is indeed the truth. Such is the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of these aforementioned words (*girāṃ*).

The aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) appropriate to sweetness is absent because the words employed are grammatically incorrect; the sense is that, due to their opposition to the comprehension of syntactic connection (*anvaya*), there is no emergence of the aesthetic emotion (*rasa*) of love (*rati*) directed toward the king, which is sustained by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). (In this regard, the use of the *ātmanepada* for the root *ava*, which is *parasmaipadī*; the use of the dative case in place of the genitive in *bhavate*; the absence of the suffix *ṭac* in the compound *mahārāja* [which should be *mahārājñaḥ*]; and the absence of the suffix *kap* in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *arṇavaśakkarī*—all these are contrary to the grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*) and were put forward by those who are not learned.)

Furthermore, since the word *śakkarī* has not been used by anyone in the sense of a girdle (*mekhalā*), this term—being unestablished in usage (*aprayukta*)—confuses the listener's intellect and becomes an obstacle to the comprehension of the syntactical connection. (149)

He shows [the verse] as being free from defects and devoid of missing syllables, beginning with "dakṣiṇādreḥ" and so forth. "Dakṣiṇādriḥ" refers to the Malaya mountain; "upasaran" means approaching, that is, going toward the Malaya mountain. "Mārutaḥ" means the wind. "Cūtapādapān" refers to mango trees. "Lalitam" means beautifully or gracefully, which implies with gentleness. "Ādhūtāḥ" means shaken. "Prabālāṅkurāḥ" refers to sprouts of fresh foliage, meaning newly emerged shoots. "Śobhinaḥ" means possessed of beauty by means of those [sprouts].

The sentence beginning with "kurute" and so forth, which is of the form previously described, belongs to the *śāstra*, meaning the instruction (*anuśāsana*). For those whose minds are "indifferent" (*alasa*)—that is, averse—to the perception of its "great-souled" (*mahātman*), i.e., profound (*nigūḍha*) meaning; for such learned ones who, due to indolence, have turned their backs on the study of grammatical treatises and the like, [this sentence] appears as if it were an "apabhāṣaṇa," that is, like a corrupt word (*apaśabda*); however, the meaning is that it does not actually exist in the form of a corrupt word.

The point is this: by the force of the grammatical rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("the second case is used for the object"), the accusative case ought indeed to occur for the word *dakṣiṇādreḥ* (the Southern Mountain), which is the object of the action of approaching (*upasaraṇa*). However, even if that [accusative] is not employed, there is no fault here; for the application of the genitive case everywhere when intending to express a mere relation (*sambandha*) is faultless and is approved by the learned. And it has been stated by Dīkṣita: "Even for objects and so forth, when there is a desire to express a mere relation, the genitive alone is used."

Furthermore, there is no fault in usages spoken by the learned (*śiṣṭas*) even in the absence of an explicit grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*); for example, in such instances as "balantī lajjālolaṃ" (trembling with shame) and "cetaḥ paraṃ balati śailavanasthalīṣu" (the mind wanders further into the mountain forests), the root *bal*—though prescribed as ātmanepada—is used in the parasmaipada, which, while contrary to the rules, is not defective. For this very reason, Vāmana established the non-constancy (*anityatva*) of the ātmanepada ending based on its being anudātta, using an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) to justify such usage.

For example, regarding the statement, "The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for [the root] *bal* is non-obligatory because of an indicative mark," he says "and not" (*na ca*), meaning that even in the absence of the accusative case, no distaste arises in the listeners. "Elegance" (*saubhāgya*) and "grace" (*lālitya*) mean excellence of usage due to being approved by the learned; it does not abandon or relinquish this.
