Thus, the sense is that in such instances, if there were aversion in the listener, that would indeed be a fault. (This is a description of a mango tree on Mount Malaya shaken by the wind.)

It should be understood that if the phrase "approaching from the southern mountain" (dakṣiṇādrerupasarpan) is taken to mean "approaching, i.e., coming from the southern mountain, namely the Malaya range," there is no objection whatsoever. || 150 ||

He defines *yati* and its violation with the words "in verses" (*ślokeṣu*). The sense is: "in verses," that is, in poetry (*padyeṣu*), and not in prose (*gadyeṣu*). They know—that is, the wise understand—the *yati* as the fixed pause (*virati*) of a word (*pada*), which consists of either a nominal or verbal form, and whose position has been determined by those learned in the science of prosody (*chandaḥ-śāstra*). The essential point is that *yati* is the place of rest (*viśrāma-sthāna*) at the end of a word, such as *ji*, *ḍha*, *ṭha*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ve*, or *ṣṭa*.

That [verse] is devoid of that [proper pause], and thus it is *vicyuta* (fallen away); for this very reason, it is an *udvejana* (cause of agitation) to the ears—that is, it produces a sense of unease—meaning it is *yatibhraṣṭa*, i.e., possessed of the defect known as *yatibhraṣṭa*; the word "pada" (word/verse-quarter) is to be supplied. The sense is that where a verse becomes harsh to the ear precisely at the pause (*virāma*), there lies the defect. For this very reason it was stated by Vāmana: "A pause occurring at an unpleasant point is *yatibhraṣṭa*. (152)

Regarding the verse beginning with "strīṇām": this refers to the king, a scion of the Solar dynasty (ādityavaṃśya), who, together with refined persons (śiṣṭaiḥ), beholds here in this assembly the flawless and charming essence—the meaning being sweetness—of the rules for women's singing, which consists of the triad of dance, song, and instrumental music. Such verses as these are considered defective because they fail the requirements of metrical pause (yatibhraṣṭatva) and are thus unworthy of respect.

For indeed, in this *mandākrāntā* meter consisting of seventeen syllables, the pauses (*yati*) must be placed at the fourth, then the sixth, and then the seventh syllable from the beginning; as it has been stated: "In *mandākrāntā*, [the feet consist of] four, six, seven, and six [mātrās], with the *ma*, *bha*, *na*, *ta*, *ga*, and a pair of *ga*s. However, in this case, because the fourth and subsequent syllables fall within the interior of a word, there is a violation of the pause (*yatibhraṣṭatā*).

Likewise, in the fourth syllable of "saṅgī" (in *strīṇāṃ saṅgī*) and in the tenth syllable of "mayamā," there is a failure of the pause (*yatibhraṣṭatva*) due to the lack of a break (*viratyabhāva*) resulting in a sense of distaste (*vairasya*). Furthermore, it should be understood that Vāmana stated this to be an example of the division of the name-portion (*nāmabhāga*), as in his remark: "And that [failure] resides in the stem-portion (*pratipadikāṃśagata*)," namely in *saṅgī*. Vāmana, however, states that this [pause] is twofold, by way of being a division of either a verbal root (*dhātu*) or a name (*nāma*); as he says: "That [pause], when occurring generally in the division of a root or a name, is not produced by the euphonic combination of vowels (*svarasandhi*)."

Regarding the division of a portion of a verbal root (*dhātubhāgabheda*) in the *mandākrāntā* meter, as in the example: "etāsāṃ rājati sumanasāṃ dāma kaṇṭhāvalambi" ("The garland of these flowers shines, hanging from the neck"). Here, because there is an absence of a pause at the point where the syllable following the root *rāj-* (in "etāsāṃ rā") would have occurred, a lack of aesthetic flavor (*vairasya*) arises; thus, this constitutes a division of a portion of a verbal root. In this definition, by employing the terms "verbal root" and "noun" instead of the more concise term "word-portion" (*padabhāga*), it is indicated that a violation of the caesura (*yatibhraṃśa*) does not occur when a pause falls between a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix (*pratyaya*), provided it is distinct from the divisions of roots and nouns.

Therefore, in such instances as "This fresh affliction of beautiful women nourishes their splendor," the pause at the words "nourishes their splendor" (*śobhāṃ puṣya*) does not bring about a lack of aesthetic flavor (*vairasya*), because the verbal root portion ends in *puṣ*. However, in the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa*, this is cited with the first quarter-verse being "śobhām" and so forth; the second quarter-verse being "the somewhat languid and simple glances of amorous women" (*kiñcidbhāvālasamasaralaprekṣitaṃ kāminīnām*); and the latter half-verse being "this [affliction] regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done" (*kāryākāryāṇyayam*) and so forth. Thus it has been illustrated.

And he states that this [usage] is not a fault in certain cases, beginning with "kāryya...": the sense is that this king, by means of *āgama* alone—that is, by the science of polity (*nītiśāstra*) itself, and not through acting according to his own whims—perceives what is to be done and what is not to be done (*kāryākāryāṇi*), which are "unimpaired" (*avikalāni*), meaning unobstructed; and thus he "bears," meaning he protects, the "Earth" (*urvim*), who has become submissive (*vaśyām*), having come under his control. Such a construction exists and functions without being defective; [the point regarding the form] "kāryyā" in the phrase "kāryākāryāṇi" is as follows: [The commentary continues: In the word "kāryākāryāṇi," the form "kāryyā" [is derived from the root *kṛ*]. According to Pāṇini’s rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (3.3.113), the suffix *yat* is applied after the root *kṛ*. By the rule *aco ñṇiti* (7.2.115), the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *vṛddhi*, resulting in *ār*. Then, by the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* (7.3.33), the augment *yuk* is added, yielding *kāryya*. However, because the suffix *yat* is included among the *kṛt* suffixes, the *yuk* augment is prohibited by the rule *na kṛd-yog-e* (7.3.34). Consequently, the form becomes *kārya*. Furthermore, since the suffix *yat* is a *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending, the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148) applies, whereby the final *a* of *kārya* is elided, resulting in the form *kāryyāḥ*. Thus, the compound *kāryyā-akāryyāṇi* is formed. This usage is seen in the *Mahābhārata*: "He who, having perceived what is to be done and what is not to be done, acts accordingly, is called a wise man. It is also seen in the *Raghuvamśa*: "Having perceived what is to be done and what is not to be done, he acted accordingly. Therefore, such a usage is established as being without defect. The same applies to the form *vaśyām* [derived from the root *vaś*]. The suffix *yat* is applied after the root *vaś*; the *ṛ* is replaced by *vṛddhi* to become *āś*, and then the *ā* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*. Thus, the form *vaśyā* is established. This is seen in the *Mahābhārata*: "O King, you have conquered the earth, which is submissive, together with its mountains and forests. It is also seen in the *Raghuvamśa*: "The Earth, having become submissive, bore the weight of the king's feet. Therefore, such a usage is established as being without defect. The same applies to the form *vahati* [derived from the root *vah*]. The suffix *tip* is applied after the root *vah*. The *a* of the root is replaced by *guṇa* (*o*), and by the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ* (6.1.78), the *o* is replaced by *av*, resulting in *vahati*. This is seen in the *Mahābhārata*: "The king, having conquered the earth, bears it, along with its mountains and forests. It is also seen in the *Raghuvamśa*: "The Earth, having become submissive, bore the weight of the king's feet. Therefore, such a usage is established as being without defect. The same applies to the form *paśyan* [derived from the root *dṛś*]. The suffix *śatṛ* is applied after the root *dṛś*. The *ṛ* is replaced by *guṇa* (*ar*), and the *a* of the root is elided by

The meaning is that [the rule] does not apply because that [suffix] occurs as part of the nominal stem (prātipadika) and thus falls within the division of the nominal portion. This has also been stated in the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa*: "When a change of vowels (*svarasandhi*) is effected, the wise generally accept that [the suffix] belongs to the verbal root (*dhātu*); and in the case of a change of nominal stems (*nāmabheda*) and in other remaining instances, there is no fault. Furthermore, in cases such as "ṇya," when a vowel-sandhi is relied upon, one should understand that the loss of the pause (*yati*) in the middle of a word, as in "yryā" and so forth, is not a defect.

As for what was said: "In some cases, a pause (*yati*) prescribed by former masters resides within a word; it attains beauty at the end of a word but is abandoned in the middle of a word. Furthermore, when that very pause is joined with a vowel-sandhi (*svaravihitasandhi*), it regains that beauty—as in: *kṛṣṇaḥ puṣṇātyatulamahimā māṃ karuṇayā*. However, in the case of women’s music and the like, because this characteristic is absent, it is indeed a defect. || 153 ||

In both cases, he demonstrates that while the aforementioned violation of the pause (yati), consisting of a rest within a word, is defective in one instance, it is non-defective in the other, by means of the phrase "when [the word] is elided."

At the end of a word—that is, at the final phoneme of a form ending in a *sup* or *tiṅ* suffix—when [the suffix] is elided, as in examples such as *madhu* and *paṭha* where the case-ending (*vibhakti*) has been dropped; here, the singular "at the end of a word" (*padānte*) is not intended to be restrictive, because even when both [suffixes] are elided in a form like *rājā*, the remaining portion (*rāja-*) is accepted as being a word (*pada*). Thus, the status of being a word for the remaining or residual part of the word, which consists of the stem (*prakṛti*), is established by the learned authorities (*śiṣṭa*) as being certain and beyond doubt.

The meaning is "accepted. Likewise, *sandhi* is the conjunction of two vowels; the modification (*vikāra*) produced by that consists in the arising of another phoneme such as a long vowel or a *yara* (semivowel) and so forth. That is to say, it refers to a consonant possessed of such a modification. The phrase "at the end of which" implies "even in the middle of a word. [Conversely,] "only at the end of a word"—this is what is described and stated by poets.

Consequently, in instances such as "kāryākāryāṇyayam," where the end of a word consists of a letter modified by the insertion of *y* due to vowel sandhi (*svarasandhi*), or in cases like "yryā" occurring within a word, a pause (*yati*) does not constitute a fault. Likewise, even if there is a lapse of the pause in the fourth quarter (*pāda*) because it falls upon a simple vowel situated in the middle of the quarter, it is not considered a defect because it is produced by vowel sandhi and because the body of the noun or verb remains undivided. This has already been stated previously.
Conversely, when the opposite occurs, it is indeed a fault, as in the example beginning with "strīṇām. || 154 ||

He shows that even in the case of vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), there may sometimes be a fault; thus he says, "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). Even though, by means of vowel-sandhi, the middle of a word is treated as the end of a word, poets do not employ—that is, they do not use—this verse, which is harsh to the ears and unpleasant to the sense of hearing. [The verse describes] the army (*dhvajinī*) of that king, with its banners (*ketubhiḥ*, i.e., flags), by which the clouds (*jaladāḥ*, i.e., rain-clouds) were raised up or tossed aloft; the meaning is that this was due to their extreme height. Such is this verse.

And in the present case, in the phrase *ketūdasta*, although the syllable *ke* has its final vowel lengthened by the rule of vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*)—resulting in *ketūda*—it nonetheless falls at a point where there should be a pause (*yati*), thereby producing a sense of distaste for the listener; thus, even when a vowel-sandhi occurs, a harshness of sound (*śrutikaṭu*) constitutes a breach of the pause (*yatibhraṃśa*). This is the intended meaning. || 155 ||

He explains "defective meter" (*bhinnavṛtta*), [referring to] "of syllables" (*varṇānām*). The word "where" (*yatra*) is to be supplied, as it is seen later on with the word "there" (*tatra*); where—in a verse—there is a deficiency or excess of syllables (meaning: of one syllable, of two syllables, or of many syllables), or likewise an improper arrangement—that is, an irregular placement—of long or short syllables, in that verse, "that" is defective meter: *bhinnam* means broken; *vṛttam* means meter; the meaning is "a breach of meter. [This refers to] the meter.

The essential point is that whatever verse is composed by deviating from the characteristics of the treatise (śāstra) is considered to possess the fault of *vṛttabhanga* (metrical rupture). As Vāmana stated: "A verse that has fallen away from its own specific characteristics is *bhinnavṛtta*. This fault, known as *vṛttabhanga*, is highly censured because it makes known the poet's status as an object of ridicule due to his ignorance of prosody (*chandas*). This is the underlying sense.

This defect has been designated as *hatavṛtta* (defective meter) by Prakāśakāra and others. That *hatavṛtta* should be understood as being of three types: that which is unmelodious (*aśravyatva*) even when following the formal definition, that which lacks the required final light syllable (*laghu*) despite having reached the proper number of syllables, and that which is incompatible with the aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*). An example of this is as follows: "Amṛtam amṛtam, what doubt can there be? Even honey is not otherwise; the fruit of the mango tree is exceedingly sweet and possesses a clear juice."
"Furthermore, let even an impartial person who knows the various flavors say whether there is anything else here that is as sweet as the lip of my beloved. (156)

He illustrates deficiency and excess with the verse beginning "indupādāḥ. "Indu-pādāḥ" means the cool (śiśirāḥ), that is, cold, rays (pādāḥ) of the moon (indoḥ). As Amara states: "The word *pāda* denotes a ray, a quarter, a foot, a mountain, and a fourth part. Here, there is a deficiency of syllables (*ūnavarṇatā*) because in the first quarter, where eight syllables should be stated, there are only seven; thus, one syllable is deficient. In the phrase "sahakārasya kisalayāny ārdraṇi" (the moist sprouts of the mango tree), there is likewise an excess of syllables (*adhikākṣara*) in the third quarter, which should have eight syllables.

Regarding the statement that there are nine syllables [in a quarter], the meaning is that one letter is in excess. (157) He illustrates the irregularity of heavy and light syllables with the verse beginning "kāmena. Here, sharp arrows have been discharged by Kāma at the deer-eyed women; thus, one should understand that there is an irregularity of heaviness because the first letter of the first quarter, "kā," is made long even though it is otherwise restricted to being light.

And thus, in this preceding verse, the *upendravajrā* meter is employed, according to its definition: "The *upendravajrā* consists of *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, *ta*, *ta*, *ga*, and *ga*. Consequently, having first placed a *jagaṇa*, the syllable *kā* was inserted as a heavy (*guru*) syllable; and since it is stated that a *jagaṇa* is "that which has a heavy syllable at the beginning," it consists of three syllables where the first and last are light (*laghu*) and the middle syllable is heavy.

And thus, because the first syllable is long, the first quarter is characterized by the *indravajrā* meter, while the second quarter consists of the characteristics of the *upendravajrā*; therefore, due to this mixture of *indravajrā* and *upendravajrā*, this is the *upajāti* meter.

In this regard, although it would be appropriate for the first syllable to be long when adopting the *indravajrā* feet at the outset—and thus the fault of irregular heaviness (*ayathāgurutva*) would not occur—nevertheless, because there is a rule that the syllables of the first foot in *upajāti* meters must be light, the fault of irregular heaviness does indeed occur. As it has been said: "Although there may be a mixture [of rules] in establishing the various types of *upajāti*, one should nevertheless make the first syllable of the preceding foot light."

"Obstructed by heavy syllables, as if knotted at the beginning, it first causes some slight distress to the ear. Thus, it should be understood that even the usage of great poets such as "astyuttarasyām" is shown as an example of this defect. Similarly, in the phrase "the sharp arrows of Smara fall upon the beautiful-eyed women," there is a lack of lightness (*ayathālaghutvam*).

And likewise, in the second half [of the verse], the *indravajrā* meter is employed, according to its definition: "The *indravajrā* consists of *ta*, *ta*, *ja*, followed by two *ga*s. Therefore, having first placed the *tagaṇa*, the short syllable "sma" has been inserted; and it should be understood that the *tagaṇa*, being defined as "having the last [syllable] light" (*antalaghu*), consists of three syllables where the first and second are long and the final one is short.

In this case, if one accepts that this is the *upajāti* meter—consisting of *indravajrā* at the beginning and *upendravajrā* thereafter—then this is not an occasion for criticism. However, in reality, the fault of metrical disruption (*vṛttabhaṅga*) was demonstrated by assuming that this is an example of either *upendravajrā* or *indravajrā*. This is merely a brief indication; an example of the pure [meter] is as follows: "In whom the five classes of beings and space are established—the wise Brahmin, having known Him alone, should cultivate wisdom."

In this case, a violation of the meter (*vṛttabhaṅga*) occurs because a long syllable (*guru*) is substituted for a short syllable in the fifth position. For example: "O friend! Do you see [her] resting upon the palace, wearing a garland of dense flowers? In the even feet of the *vaitālīya* meter, according to the rule "those [shorts] should be in even positions, but not in immediate succession," the succession of six short syllables in an even foot is prohibited; however, here in the phrase "aviralasuma," all six are employed as short syllables.

However, some maintain that this demonstration of two defects is intended on the grounds that the second through fourth feet are identical in being either light-initial or heavy-initial; otherwise, in an example of improper heaviness, improper lightness would also be possible, and in an example of improper lightness, improper heaviness would likewise be possible, since both heavy and light syllables exist at the beginning of the first two feet. Thus, in the opinion of those who do not accept *upajāti* as a distinct meter due to the commingling of *upendravajrā* and *indravajrā*:

They say that these are two faults; likewise, by proposing the readings "svabhuvā" for "kāmena" and "madana" for "smarasya," they reconcile [the objection] by claiming that in the former case the third syllable is heavy and in the latter case the second syllable is light, which constitutes improper usage.

Furthermore, regarding that which has been stated by moderns—that a short syllable at the end of a line does not attain the status of a heavy syllable—one must understand that this too is an incorrect notion of lightness. For example, in such instances as "vikasitasahakārabhārahāraparimala eṣa samāgato vasantaḥ," the syllable *ri* in the word *bhāraṅāri* lacks heaviness because it is a short syllable occurring at the end of the first quarter-verse (*pāda*). This constitutes a violation of the meter (*vṛttabhaṅga*), since the heaviness of a short syllable at the end of a *pāda* is stated to apply specifically to the second and fourth quarters. This point should also be reflected upon by the wise.

He points out that [the text] is not taught as being without euphonic combination (*visandhika*). He explains *saṃhitā* as the form resulting from the merging of two phonemes; he does not intend it, nor does he wish to speak it—meaning that even though there exists a rule prescribing such [euphonic combination], he does not perform it. (By this, the views of others, such as "euphonic combination depends on the speaker's will" and "that very [combination] is optionally applied elsewhere," are refuted.)

Thus, having intended this, [the meaning is as follows]: regarding "padesu" (in words), which refers to the phonemes that join words together, "asandhānam" means non-joining; the sense is that there is an absence of *sandhi* (euphonic combination) according to the relevant rule. "Visandhi" means that wherein the *sandhi*—the mutual blending by means of a *sandhi*-rule—is absent; the meaning is that it possesses the defect known as *visandhi*. The word "vākyam" (sentence) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence] (it should be understood that this word is an adjective qualifying "vākya," for otherwise its neuter gender would be untenable). "Nirdiṣṭam" means stated or declared.

He clarifies the statement that the absence of *saṃdhi* caused by the speaker’s intention is indeed a defect, by saying "not so" (*na*). A *pragṛhya* is a specific grammatical rule prohibiting *saṃdhi*; "that which begins with that" (*tadādi*) means starting from that very point (the word "ādi" includes cases such as imitation of sounds). Where that is the cause—that is, where *saṃdhi* is prohibited by a rule on *saṃdhi*—there the defect of *visandhi* does not occur. An example where the cause is a *pragṛhya* is: *amī īśāḥ*, and so forth.

An example of that which has non-establishment as its cause (*asiddhihetuka*) is: "tat udita udāhāridyutiḥ," and so forth. Here, although the elision (*lopa*) is prescribed by the rule "lopaḥ śākalyasya," the rule "pūrvatrāsiddham" renders that elision non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the *guṇa* substitution that would otherwise be obtained by the rule "ādguṇaḥ. Therefore, this disjunction (*viśleṣa*) has non-establishment as its cause.

The absence of euphonic combination (*sandhi*) caused by *pragṛhya* vowels and other such factors is not a defect when occurring only once; however, when it occurs repeatedly, it is indeed a defect because it causes distress to the listener due to the looseness of the verbal bond. Regarding this, Viśvanātha says: "O lady of pure limbs, these two eyes of yours are like blossomed blue lotuses"—in such cases, the absence of euphonic combination is a defect only when used repeatedly. But even if it occurs only once, the absence of euphonic combination [is permissible] if it is done in violation of the grammatical rule out of fear of breaking the meter.

For example: "The moon shines at the face of the eastern quarter like a drop of sandalwood paste. By this, however, the defectiveness attributed to *sandhi* (euphonic combination) in cases of obscenity (*jugupsāvyañjaka-aślīlatva*) and harshness (*kaṣṭatva*) is not intended by him [the author], because such instances do not oppose the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). This has been demonstrated as follows: in the phrase "calaṇḍaāmaraceṣṭim," there is obscenity (*aślīlatva*) in the word *laṇḍaā* within the *sandhi*, which suggests disgust. In the phrase "urvasāvatra tarvāli marvante cārvavasthitiḥ," there is harshness (*kaṣṭatva*) in the *sandhi*.

He illustrates the fault of *visandhi* (lack of euphonic combination) with the verse beginning "by the gentle breeze. In the sky (*nabhasi*), by the gentle breeze (*mandānilena*) blowing (*calatā*), the sweat-water (*gharmāmbhaḥ*) produced (*udbhedī*) upon the cheek-region (*gaṇḍamaṇḍale*) of the woman (*aṅganāyāḥ*) and even upon our own bodies (*asmadvapuṣi*) was wiped away (*luptam*). (Note: Here, although there exists a grammatical rule (*sūtra*) prescribing the lengthening of the vowel 'a' when combined with the preceding letter 'e'—as in *calatā + aṅganā*—the sandhi has not been applied merely out of fear of breaking the meter (*vṛttabhaṅga*); this constitutes the fault of *visandhi*.

He demonstrates the absence of *sandhi* (euphonic combination) caused by *pragṛhya* vowels and other factors: "In this [place], during the winter season (*himartau*), that is, in these present nights—the meaning being 'during the nights of winter'—the pride and jealousy of women toward their beloveds, that is, pride (*mānaḥ*) which is a lover’s anger, and jealousy (*īrṣyā*) which is a specific kind of anger born from the attachment to another woman, both wither away; they perish. In this instance, such a separation [of words] and absence of *sandhi* was intended by the wise authors of the Sūtras."

The learned have explained this. Furthermore, it should be understood that in the case of *māneṣrye iha*, the rule "īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam" prohibits the sandhi of the vowel *e* produced by a dual ending; likewise, in the case of *himaṛtau*, the rule "ṛtyakaḥ" prohibits the optional sandhi of the vowel *a* when followed by the vowel *ṛ*. || 161 ||

Now, intending to define the contradictions of place (*deśa*) and the other factors, he first indicates their definitions, beginning with "place" (*deśa*). A mountain (*adri*), a peak (*parvata*), a forest (*vana*), a realm (*rāṣṭra*), a kingdom (*rājya*), and so forth—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), oceans and the like are included—is "place. Night, day, and the seasons are "time" (*kāla*)—by the plural number, months, years, and so forth are included. "Based on desire and wealth" (*kāmārthasaṃśrayāḥ*): desire (*kāma*) is longing, and wealth (*artha*) is [the object]; the meaning is that these two are the "bases" (*saṃśrayau*), meaning they serve as the causes or supports for those [actions] which possess them.

Thus they are described: the arts (*kalās*) that accomplish desires and accomplish wealth, such as dance, song, and so forth (the word "and so forth" includes instrumental music and the like), which are the sixty-four types of specialized crafts mentioned in the *Tantras*.

And these have been shown by our grandfather in the work titled *Vācaspatya* under the term *kalā*, as follows: "Regarding the various branches of knowledge such as song and so forth, that [knowledge] is of sixty-four kinds as declared in the Śaiva Tantras: namely, singing, instrumental music, dancing, dramatic performance, painting, the art of cutting leaves into patterns, the preparation of offerings of rice and flowers, the arrangement of flower carpets, the ten types of garments and body ointments, the work of inlaying floors with jewels, the arrangement of beds, water-music, water-sports, various artistic applications, and the different methods of weaving garlands."

Arranging hair with crests and ornaments, applications of cosmetics, fashioning ear-leaf designs, the preparation of perfumes, the arrangement of jewelry, the art of *indrajāla* (magic), the application of *kaucumāra* (dyeing techniques), manual dexterity, the preparation of various kinds of vegetables, cakes, and foods, the compounding of syrups, juices, colorants, and fermented liquors, the craft of embroidery, playing the lute and the *ḍamaruka* drum, the use of strings for games, riddles, conundrums, and difficult verbal puzzles, the reading of books, the performance of dramas, stories, and epics, the completion of poetic stanzas, the manufacture of various types of arrows and quivers, and the making of felt.

The science of architecture; the examination of silver and gems; discourse on women; knowledge of the colors of gems; knowledge of mines; the science of arboriculture and medicine for horses; the rules for fighting rams, cocks, and quails; training parrots and mainas to speak; the art of massage; skill in grooming the hair; the art of writing in secret scripts and speaking in code; the various forms of Mleccha (barbarian) languages; knowledge of regional dialects; the science of prognostication through flower-arrangements; the alphabet of mechanical devices; the alphabet of memory-retention techniques; recitation; mental composition; the creation of poetry; and the application of deceptive stratagems.

"Knowledge of dictionaries, prosody, the concealment of garments, specific types of gambling, games of attraction, children's toys, knowledge of the Vaināyikī sciences, knowledge of the Vaijayikī sciences, and knowledge of the Vaitalikī sciences—these are written by Śrīdharasvāmin in the commentary on the *Bhāgavata-śloka*.

(162) Regarding the phrase "of moving and unmoving things": "moving and unmoving" refers to those that are mobile and stationary; "beings" (*bhūtānām*) refers to living creatures and the elements such as earth and so forth; "activity" (*pravṛttiḥ*) means news or occurrence; and "designated by the word 'world'" (*lokasaṃjñitā*) means that which is expressed by the term "world" (*loka*).

The suffix *itac* is applied in the sense of "born from this" (*asya-jāta-arthe*), resulting in the name *loka*. *Hetuvidyā* consists of *hetu*, which means cause or reason; the knowledge (*vidyā*) characterized by that is cognition. *Hetuvidyā* refers to a treatise rooted in logic (*yukti-mūlaka-śāstra*), meaning a system of philosophy (*darśana-śāstra*). It should be understood that these include the systems of *tarka* and so forth, as well as the Buddhist scriptures (*boddha-śāstra*). That which consists of or is composed of those is *nyāya*. The essential point is that the term *nyāya* denotes precisely a philosophical system rooted in logic. Likewise, there is *smṛti*, which means tradition or sacred law.

The word of the sages (*ṛṣivākya*)—meaning the *saṃhitās* of Manu and others—which is produced by the recollection of the meaning of the Vedas; together with that, the *śruti* (revelation) is the *veda*, which is to say, it is what is denoted by the term "āgama. || 163 ||

He states the definition of contradiction regarding place and so forth [with the words] "In those": in those aforementioned places and so forth, if something that is not as it is commonly established—that is, something unestablished—should occur due to the poet's negligence or lack of care, meaning it is set forth or described in such a manner, then this kind of statement is "contradictory to place and so forth," meaning it possesses the defect known by that name; thus it is said, and it is designated by such terms as "contradictory to place," "contradictory to time," and so on.

It should be understood that the contradiction with place, time, and the world has been designated by the term "contradiction with what is renowned" (*khyātaviruddhatā*), while the contradiction with arts, logic, and scriptures has been designated by the term "contradiction with knowledge" (*vidyāviruddhatā*) by the moderns. As for the phrase "together with Smṛti and Śruti," it is understood that by the word "Śruti," the inclusion of treatises characterized by [the arts of] desire, agriculture, elephants, horses, swords, and so forth, is intended; this is the general direction. || 164 ||

He illustrates the contradiction with respect to place (*deśavirodha*) with the verse beginning "karpūra-". The Malaya breeze—the wind blowing from the Malaya mountain—is fragrant through its contact with *karpara* trees; likewise, the elephants born in the forests of the Kaliṅga region—meaning those produced in the woods of the Kaliṅga country—are like deer, that is, as insignificant as deer.

(Here, on the Malaya mountain, camphor trees do not grow, for it is well known that they grow only in regions such as China; thus, there is a contradiction regarding the location in the form of a mountain. Likewise, in the Kaliṅga forest, small elephants resembling deer are impossible; because this describes what is not established [in reality], a contradiction regarding the location in the form of a forest is to be understood. || 165 ||

Having shown the examples of two regions characterized by mountains and forests, he now illustrates the contradiction with a region characterized by a kingdom, beginning with the words "The Colas. The Colas are specific districts within the Karṇāṭaka country; they are "dark" (śyāmāḥ), meaning black-complexioned, due to the "black agallochum" (kālagurubhiḥ), that is, dark-colored aloe-wood; and they are those whose lands are situated on the banks of the Kāverī river.

(Here, on the banks of the Kāverī, black aloe-wood does not grow; thus there is a contradiction with the nature of the country. Regarding the phrase "words contradicting the country," such is the form described; "prāsthānam" means a preeminent place, that is to say, an illustrative instance. (In this regard, a different reading is seen in other manuscripts: "The Colas are dark as black aloe-wood, the Keralas are reddish like saffron, and the lands along the banks of the Kāverī are covered with Nameru forests.")
Another example is as follows: "In Sauvīra there is a famous city named Mathurā, whose surrounding lands abound in walnuts and coconuts. (166)

He demonstrates the contradiction with time—defined as consisting of nights, days, and the six seasons—as follows, using the word *padminī*: "The lotus plant (*padminī*) is blooming at night (*naktaṃ*). (Since the blooming of a lotus plant is well-known to occur only during the day, the mention of "night" here constitutes a contradiction with the nature of time as night. "The night-lily (*kumudvatī*) does not bloom by day; it blossoms [at night]."

(Since the blossoming of the night-lily is well known to occur only at night—as expressed by the saying "aḍhiddhaṭhṭhaḍana"—there is here a contradiction with the time of day, which is daytime. Madhu is spring; "utphulla" means flowers in bloom; "nicula" refers to *sijjala* trees where such [flowers] are found. (Since the growth of *nicula* trees is well known to occur only in the rainy season, by describing them here, there is a contradiction with the time of the spring season. Nadāgha is summer; "durdinam" refers to a day that produces distress due to clouds, that is, cloud-cover.

Since "bad weather" is conventionally known to occur only during the rainy season (*varṣā*), the mention of "the heat of summer" (*nidāgha*) here constitutes a contradiction with the specific time of the summer season. Although bad weather can occasionally occur even in summer—as exemplified by descriptions of "untimely rain" in works such as the *Mṛcchakaṭika*—nevertheless, because this passage is intended to illustrate a contradiction, the fault lies precisely in the description of a phenomenon well-known to one particular season within another season. This is indicated by the phrase "the heat of summer with cloudy, rainy weather."
Some, however, accept the variant reading "nidāgho himajāṅyākṛt" and provide a resolution [to the difficulty]; there is also another variant reading: "nidāghī meghaniḥsvanaḥ. (167)

"Śravyāḥ": the rains (*varṣāḥ*) are "pleasing to hear" (*śravyāḥ*), meaning sweet, because they produce pleasure for the ear; those [rains] in which there are the cries of swans (*haṃsa*). (Since the sweet calling of swans is well-known only in autumn, the mention of "rains" here constitutes a contradiction regarding the season. "Matta-varhiṇaḥ": those autumns (*śaradaḥ*) in which the peacocks (*barhiṇa*) are intoxicated or joyful. (Since the intoxication of peacocks is well-known only during the rainy season, describing them as such in autumn constitutes a contradiction regarding the season of autumn.)

The winter (*hemanta*) is "spotless" (*nirmala*) because of the absence of a covering of snow and is "blazing," being thus characterized by the sun; [here, since the sun is obscured by snow during the winter season, its spotlessness is contrary to common experience, and thus there is a contradiction with the time represented by the winter season]; likewise, the cool season (*śiśira*) is one in which sandalwood—meaning an application of sandalwood paste—is "praiseworthy," that is, worthy of respect.

(Here, because sandalwood is cool, its praise during the cold season is not well-known; thus, there is a contradiction with the time, namely the winter season. In this way, the contradictions regarding all six seasons have been demonstrated. Another example is as follows: "The forest, smiling with kadamba flowers, shone forth in spring. || 168 ||

Since the triad beginning with *turya* (the fourth) provides the greatest pleasure among the arts (*kalās*), its primacy is established; first, he demonstrates the contradiction between that [triad] and [the other rasas], starting with the word "heroic" (*vīra*). Regarding the heroic and the erotic—these two rasas—their respective stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) are anger and wonder; the word "contradictory" is to be supplied. For instance, enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is said to be the stable emotion in the heroic, while love (*rati*) is the stable emotion in the erotic. Anger is specified as the stable emotion of the furious (*raudra*) rasa, and wonder (*vismaya*) as that of the marvelous (*adbhuta*) rasa. Such being the case:

The designation of anger and wonder—which are actually transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*)—as permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) in the cases of the heroic (*vīra*) and erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiments is contradictory; the point is that this is indeed a flaw. Regarding the permanent emotion, the author of the *Darpaṇa* has stated: "That emotion which, whether unopposed or opposed, is incapable of being suppressed by others, and which is the bulbous root of the sprout of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), is recognized as the 'permanent' (*sthāyī*). And it is further said: "An emotion, when it reaches the state of *rasa*, attains the status of permanence."

Anger (*krodha*) and wonder (*vismaya*) have been defined by that same [author] as follows: "Anger is held to be the perception of sharpness toward adverse objects; likewise, that expansion of the mind toward various objects which transcend the limits of the world is called wonder. Since the analysis of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) was performed by Bharata and others in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* itself, and because the author of the *Prakāśa* states, "Eight flavors are recorded for drama," this [classification] does not contradict the art of dramatic representation.

Since the art of song (gītarūpakalā) is likewise a constituent part of drama (nāṭya), he states its contradiction [with the following]: "Complete," etc. "Complete" means employed in their entirety; "seven" means numbering exactly seven; "notes" (svarāḥ) refers to those beginning with Niṣāda. Thus it is said: "Niṣāda, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, Dhaivata, and Pañcama—these are the seven notes produced from the strings and the throat."

(According to Amara: *ityāmaraḥ*). This very [song] proceeds—that is, it flows—possessing a distinct path (*bhinnamārgaḥ*), meaning its path, which is the course of performance, is differentiated by being infused with those specific notes (*svara*) prohibited at particular times. For in the science of music (*saṅgītaśāstra*), since the employment of all seven notes at a single time is censured, their simultaneous use is not prescribed; this is the underlying sense. (The essential point here is that the total employment of the seven notes contradicts the rule regarding the use of unmixed notes, and thus constitutes the fault of *kalāvirodha*—contradiction of the art.)

Bharata has stated that the employment of specific notes at specific times is prohibited, as follows: "At dawn, the *ṛṣabha* and the *pañcama* are censurable when used for amorous expression; indeed, they produce a great conflict, and the *pañcama* may even cause death. This specific rule regarding the *pañcama* was declared by the ancient masters: if it is sung at daybreak, it brings about the opposite of what is seen [i.e., misfortune]. (170)

He concludes the contradiction regarding time with the word "ittham" (thus). "Ittham" means in this manner; "of the sixty-four arts," their "contradiction"; "sādhu" means properly or correctly; "nīyatām" means let it be brought to knowledge—this is the meaning. The essential point is that just as the contradiction between the two arts of dance and song has been demonstrated, so too should the contradiction among other arts be observed in their respective examples.

Now, since sixty-four types of *kalās* have been mentioned, one might ask: "Without knowledge of them, how can their contradiction be understood? To this he says: "Of that" (*tasyāḥ*). In the section on *kalās*, in the treatise bearing that name, "of that *kalā*"—meaning its form, that is, its essential nature or name—"will manifest," meaning it will become clear. The sense is: "I shall compose a treatise named 'The Section on Kalās' (*Kalāpariccheda*) immediately after this; therein alone the specific details of these [sixty-four] are to be seen. (171)

He demonstrates its contradiction with common experience by the word "ādhūta" (shaken). This elephant has "ādhūtāḥ" (shaken) "keśarāḥ" (manes/tufts) which are its locks of hair; such is he described. A "turaṅgamaḥ" is a horse. One whose "śṛṅge" (horns/peaks) are "tīkṣṇe" (sharp) and "sūkṣmāgre" (fine-tipped) is like that. An "eraṇḍaḥ" is the tree so named. One whose "sāraḥ" (essence/core) is "guruḥ" (heavy/great) and "sthirāṃśaḥ" (firm part) is of such a nature. A "khadiradrumaḥ" (khadira tree) is one "niḥsāraḥ" (lacking essence) in whom there is no core.

(An elephant having hair, a horse having sharp horns, a castor-oil plant possessing core-wood, and likewise a khadira tree being devoid of substance—these are contrary to worldly experience. It should be understood that here, in the first half-verse, there is the occurrence of two things that are animate (*carabhūta*), while in the second half-verse, there is the occurrence of two things that are inanimate (*acarabhūta*). || 172 ||

Having concluded the discussion on contradiction with common worldly experience (*lokavirodha*), he says "iti" in order to elaborate upon contradiction with logic (*nyāyavirodha*). "Iti" means of the aforementioned form; this contradiction is "laukika," that is, well-known in the world, and is "garhita," meaning censured by all learned men. Thus, the point is that compared to contradictions regarding place and so forth, the adducing of a contradiction with common worldly experience makes the speaker utterly ridiculous. Now, "virodhaḥ nidarśyate" means contradiction is illustrated in the "hetuvidyās," that is, in the sciences known as Nyāya, which are treatises rooted in reasoning.

He demonstrates the contradiction with the Nyāya system found in the Buddhist view, beginning with the word "satyam" (it is true). Sugata means the Buddha. He said that the *saṃskāras*—meaning the specific types of mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) arising from prior experiences which serve as the causes of memory—are indeed real (*satyam eva*), in the sense of being truly existent and enduring for a long time. For instance, understand this very point: "That previously experienced, *cakora*-eyed woman still dwells even now in my heart—that is, she remains as an object of memory. This refers to memory.

The meaning is that [the impression] is the cause of the recollection, and because it is imperishable, it exists at all times. (However, according to the view of those Buddhists who maintain that every entity is momentary—since in their system every existent lasts for only a single moment, the impression must also be momentary; therefore, the assertion of its imperishability contradicts the Buddhist doctrine, which constitutes a conflict with the science of logic. || 174 ||

He demonstrates the contradiction with the logic of the Sāṅkhya system by means of the words "by the Kāpilas. By the Kāpilas—those who follow the doctrine of Kapila and are experts in the science of Sāṅkhya—it is described (i.e., proclaimed) that the arising (*udbhūti*) of non-existent things—that is, the emergence of impermanent and wicked things—is indeed logical and appropriate. Therefore, we [observe] that the arisings (*udbhavāḥ*), which are the manifestations of things distinct from the existent—that is, of wicked things alone—are seen; for generally, only wicked people are born, and not [the virtuous].

The intended meaning is: "Indeed, [they are] virtuous. (The point is this: those who follow Kapila maintain that only the existent (*sat*) is born, and not the non-existent (*asat*); therefore, the production of the non-existent is not established in their doctrine. Even though this is the case, because the word *asat* is used here in a double sense (*śliṣṭa*), there exists a relationship of cause and effect between the two meanings of the sentence, and thus its logical consistency is described. This is indeed contrary to the Sāṅkhya doctrine; as it has been said: "Because what is non-existent cannot be produced, because of the necessity of employing a material cause, because everything is not possible from everything, because an efficient cause produces only that for which it is capable, and because of the nature of the cause—the effect is existent (*satkāryam*). || 175 ||

He concludes the contradiction with logic (*nyāyavirodha*) by saying, "the course" (*gati*). This aforementioned manner of the Buddhists and the followers of Kapila, as demonstrated, is the "course"—meaning their understanding—or, in other words, their illustrative example; this is seen—that is, known—everywhere, even among the Vaiśeṣikas and others. (Regarding the word "dṛśyate," there is an alternative reading, "darśitā. To provide an illustration of the contradiction with scripture (*āgamavirodha*), he says, "Now" (*atha*). Now, at this point, the "course"—meaning the method or approach—of the contradiction with scripture, that is, the contradiction with the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, is being taught. || 176 ||

He demonstrates the contradiction with the Śruti in the words, "anāhitā" (those who have not established the sacred fires). These Brahmins—who possess unblemished conduct as their ornament, who are endowed with all excellent behaviors, and who have begotten sons—even if they are *anāhitāgnayaḥ*, meaning those who have not performed the formal installation of the sacred fires (*akṛtāgnyādhāna*), [are entitled to perform] the *vaiśvānarī* sacrifice, which pertains to Viśvānara. (Viśvānara, however, is the Virāṭ Puruṣa consisting of the aggregate of beings; and thus, "one should know Viśvānara as composed of fire, sun, wind, ether, water, and earth"—sixfold.)

"...endowed with [the power of] sustenance" (bharūpetam)—from this Vedic revelation—[they] perform, that is, carry out, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice. (And since this Vedic text establishes that only those who have performed the installation of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) and so forth are entitled to the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, describing it for those who have not installed the fires contradicts the Śruti. || 177 ||

He demonstrates the contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) in the form of a contradiction with traditional law (*smṛti*) by saying, "asau" [this person]. This person, even though uninitiated—that is, one who has not undergone the rite of initiation (*upanaya*)—studied the Vedas from the presence of his teacher. For indeed, by its very nature—that is, by its innate character—a pure and stainless crystal, that specific kind of gem so named, does not require purification through refinement (*saṃskāra*). (In this context, the study of the Vedas by one who is uninitiated is contrary to the *smṛti*.)

And it has been said by Manu: "One should not utter the Veda (*brahma*) except for the purposes of *svadhā* and ritual injunctions; for as long as one is not born into the Veda, one is equal to a *śūdra*. Others, however, having stated the definition of contradiction with scripture (*āgamavirodha*) thus—"Whatever contradiction there may be with the treatises on Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and so forth, the wise call that the defect known as contradiction with scripture"—accept a threefold division. Among these, they cite this very verse as an example of contradiction with the Dharmaśāstra.

Contradiction with the *Arthaśāstra* (treatises on statecraft) is as follows: "The conquest of the earth by kings has its fruit in the full enjoyment of desires; when enemies are conquered through pride (*ahaṅkāra*), what is the use of the glory of policy (*naya*)? Here, there is a contradiction with the *Arthaśāstra* because the authors of such treatises do not admit that the enjoyment of desires is the fruit of conquering the earth, and because pride is not considered a cause for the defeat of enemies. Contradiction with the *Kāmaśāstra* (treatises on erotics) is as follows: "On your upper lip, O lady with lips like the bimba fruit... [and so forth].
In this regard, because tooth-marks on the upper lip are not sanctioned by the authors of the *kāmaśāstra*, there is a contradiction with the *kāmaśāstra*. || 178 ||

He states that the aforementioned defect called "contradiction" (virodha) is sometimes a merit: "Contradiction," etc. This, in the form already described—meaning even in its entirety, including all objects from place (deśa) up to scripture (āgama)—is, through the skill of the poet—that is, by means of his proficiency in description—meaning by establishing a strikingness (vaicitrya) even in the description of what is contradictory—sometimes transcends, or leaves behind, the reckoning as a defect—that is, its inclusion among defects—and enters the path of merits; meaning it becomes something to be counted as a merit. (179)

In this regard, he demonstrates that contradiction with place (*deśavirodha*) is actually a poetic excellence (*guṇatva*), using the words "of him" (*tasya*). Of that king, by his power—that is, by his majesty—his gardens became the abode, meaning the dwelling place, of the celestial trees—the trees of the gods, meaning the *kalpa* trees—which possessed sprouts that were like fine silken garments (*aṃśuka*), meaning fresh and moist. Thus they came to be.

(Here, although the growth of celestial trees in human gardens is described as contrary to the nature of the place, it attains the status of a poetic excellence (*guṇa*) because it manifests aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*). This is because it illustrates the extraordinary majesty of the king who is being described, as well as the poet's skill in conveying the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) of *udātta* [the sublime] through the description of his exceptional sovereignty. This is the resultant meaning. | 180 |

He illustrates how contradiction with time can sometimes be a merit, as in the verse beginning "rājñām": "The harsh wind, a harbinger of destruction for kings—that is, rival monarchs—blowing violently, shook the *saptacchada* flowers while scattering the pollen of *kadamba* blossoms. (According to Amara, "piśuna" means a wicked person or a spy. Thus, the fierce wind blew along with the dust of the *kadamba* flowers.

Here, by the mention of "kings" (*rājñām*), there is an implication of the war expedition of the king who is the subject of description. Such a war expedition and the blooming of the *saptacchada* tree both occur only in autumn; however, *kadamba* flowers do not arise then, as they appear only during the rainy season. Consequently, because the emergence of the *saptacchada* is presented as being simultaneous with the dust of those [kadamba] flowers, there is a contradiction regarding time (*kāla-virodha*).

By the statement from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, "The appearance of fruit and flowers out of season is a cause for the destruction of the country," the possibility of the emergence of fruit and flowers even at an improper time is recognized; likewise, like a harsh wind, its nature as an indicator of inauspiciousness is understood. Therefore, because it indicates the certain destruction of rival kings, it serves as a merit (*guṇa*) by manifesting the excellence of the conqueror (*vijigīṣu*). Furthermore, it should be noted that the poet’s skill here consists precisely in the communication of such a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). || 181 ||

He illustrates that the violation of rhythm (*kala*) can sometimes be a merit: "By the swinging... [The verse continues: "By the impelling—that is, the rapid movement—of the swing (*dolā*), a specific type of vehicle, those people became terrified; from their mouths emerged a song (*geyam*) that was characterized by a discordance, a reversal, of the *laya*—the equality between the action and the time of singing, instrumental music, and foot-steps. The word "even" (*api*) is to be supplied, meaning that although the song was inconsistent with the *laya* due to being startled by fear, it nevertheless aroused passion (*rāga*) in the lovers.

He strengthened his passion. (The rule of art is that the purity of tempo (*laya-śuddhi*) alone strengthens passion; here, however, there is the opposite of that, which constitutes a contradiction of art. Yet, because it serves to manifest the intense passion of lovers toward their wives, this is actually a poetic excellence. || 182 ||

He illustrates that even opposition to worldly convention can be a poetic merit, beginning with the words "aindavāt" (from the lunar). This Kāma, being dependent on desire and overwhelmed—distraught—by the suffering caused by separation from his beloved woman, considers the fire (havyavāhana), which is normally hot, to be cool (śiśira) in comparison to the ray (arciḥ) of the moon (aindava); that is, in relation to the lunar ray (the ablative case here is used in the sense of comparison, as when a verbal suffix is dropped).

(Here, the coolness of the fire-god is contrary to worldly experience; yet, because it suggests that even the moonbeams are extremely inflaming for those separated from their lovers, it is indeed a poetic excellence. | 183 |

He illustrates how contradiction with logic (*nyāyavirodha*) can be a poetic excellence (*guṇa*): "O Prameya" and so forth. This is a hymn to the Blessed One. You are *prameya*, meaning the object of knowledge produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), yet you are also *aprameya*, meaning unknowable. You are *saphala*, meaning possessing fruit—that is, possessing the universal form (*viśvarūpa*)—yet you are also *niṣphala*, meaning devoid of fruit, being untainted by effects. You are *eka*, meaning without a second, yet you are also *aneka*, meaning manifold in form. Therefore, salutations (*namaḥ*) to you, whose very nature is the universe (*viśvamūrtaye*).

Such is the logical connection (*anvaya*). The Nyāya principle—that attributes such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, being mutually contradictory, cannot reside in a single substratum—here, although appearing as a contradiction, ascends to the status of a virtue by manifesting the inconceivability of the Supreme Self. || 184 ||

He illustrates the merit of contradicting traditional authority (*āgama*) with the verse beginning "Of five" (*pañcānām*). Draupadī, the daughter of Pañcāla, was the wife of the five sons of Pāṇḍu—Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva—and moreover, she was the foremost, the most excellent, among virtuous women. For indeed, the divine ordinance—that is, the decree pertaining to the gods—is of such a nature; the meaning is that it does not depend upon traditional authority, because they and she were declared by the scriptures to be portions of the gods.

[This is] the state of affairs. (The fact that one woman has multiple husbands while remaining chaste is contrary to the scriptures; however, since this arises here from divine destiny rather than being subject to the [human] treatises, it possesses the very quality of bringing about variety. Some, however, consider this to be an example of what is contrary to dharma. 185.

After defining the figures of speech beginning with *anuprāsa* (alliteration) and *yamaka* (chime), which were previously promised, he concludes this work with the word "śabda" (word). Here, in this treatise titled *Kāvyādarśa*, there are the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) residing in both word and meaning—such as *svabhāvākhyāna* (description of nature) and others—which reside in both because they produce beauty through both word and meaning; such is the intended meaning. Furthermore, they are easily [understood].

The difficult and diverse paths—the paths and rules of various ornaments, meaning those such as *yāmaka* which consist solely of sound; likewise, the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *śleṣa* and the faults (*doṣas*) such as *apārthatva* (the "pointless")—have been shown in brief, that is, presented concisely; the sense is that their divisions have not been displayed in their entirety due to their great multiplicity. || 186 ||

Even though this has been shown in brief, he concludes the work by demonstrating how the attainment of the fruit occurs, with the words "vyutpanna... and so forth. One whose intellect (*buddhi*) is "cultivated" (*vyutpanna*), meaning refined or purified, is thus described; the sense is that such a person is of pure mind. The word "fortunate" (*dhanya*) means one who has performed meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*); the word "person" (*jana*) is to be supplied as the subject. By "this," meaning by what is stated in this treatise, which is "shown through the rules" (*vidhidarśita*); "rules" (*vidhi*) refers to definitions (*lakṣaṇa*), and it is "shown" or indicated by them—namely, by the characteristics of defects (*doṣa*) and excellences (*guṇa*), which consist respectively of the qualities of deficiency and superiority as previously defined.

By way of the path—that is, by means of the method (it should be understood that the term *guṇa* here indicates the *alaṅkāras* as well, since they too produce the beauty of poetry and thereby contribute to its excellence)—having performed the "following," meaning having followed [the path]; that is to say, having exerted effort in the composition of poetry or in the understanding thereof; being with beloved women who are "submissive," meaning dependent on love; and by that which is shown by fate, manifested by divine power in the form of lightning flashes and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: having analyzed that by traveling along this path characterized by faults there is great harm, whereas by this [other] path there is the virtue consisting in the absence of those faults; thus, having set out upon the path clearly defined in this way, he—like a youth who has undertaken a secret tryst (*abhisaraṇa*)—rejoices, experiencing delight, and gains fame. (Just as some youth, by the favor of fate, goes on a secret tryst with a woman along a well-known good path, becomes the object of her affection, and becomes joyful and famous.)

Likewise, one whose intellect is skilled in the thorough study of regions, times, and other such subjects, having applied himself to composing or understanding poetry by means of a complete comprehension of the meaning of sentences—which are constructed according to the characteristics of merits, ornaments, and defects as briefly presented by me—attains success, joy, and fame; this is the intended meaning. The meter is Vasantatilakā. (187) Thus ends the *Kāvyādarśavivṛti* composed by the venerable Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācārya.
